title: Saying which past you mean, and putting the when-words where English keeps them

point_json.grammar_name: Past time markers: yesterday, last …, … ago, in 2016, when I was …

teach.can_do: I can say exactly which past stretch of time I am talking about, and put the words in the right place.
teach.why_it_matters: These words are the evidence a listener uses to place your story. Put one in the wrong slot and the sentence sounds translated rather than wrong.
teach.meaning: A when-word does not make a sentence past. The verb has already done that. What the when-word does is choose which finished stretch of time the sentence lands in: the day before today, a named year, a summer that has ended, or the age you were. It narrows a claim the verb has already made, and it is the reason two speakers can tell the same story about two different decades.

form.pattern: yesterday · last night · last summer · two years ago · in 2016 · when I was twelve
notes: ago always follows the amount and counts backwards from today: three weeks ago
last takes no the in front of it: last summer, not the last summer
in with a year or a month, on with a day, at with a clock time
The natural slot is the end of the sentence; the front is available for emphasis, with a comma
form.negative: I did not train at all last winter.
form.question: When did you last play a full match?

spec.caption: Each word picks a different closed stretch. None of them is doing the work of putting the sentence in the past.

worked_example.sentence: The club moved to the new ground three years ago.
worked_example.why_this_form: Ago counts backwards from today, so the reader can place the move without being told the year, and the amount has to come in front of it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: In three years counts forwards instead, and would put the move in a future the rest of the sentence cannot be reporting.

notice_set.sentence: The pool closed for repairs last winter.
notice_set.question: How long ago was the closing, roughly?
notice_set.why: Last plus a season points at the most recent one that has finished, so it is always inside the past year.

notice_set.sentence: We joined the running club four years ago.
notice_set.question: Does the counting start from today or from some other point?
notice_set.why: Ago measures backwards from the moment of speaking, which is why the number changes as the years pass.

notice_set.sentence: In 2016 the council rebuilt the changing rooms.
notice_set.question: Does the reader need to know today's date to place this?
notice_set.why: A named year is fixed. It says the same thing in any decade, which is why reports prefer it.

notice_set.sentence: When I was eleven I trained twice a week.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker say how old they are now?
notice_set.why: An age marks a stretch of the speaker's own life without saying anything about where they stand today.

notice_set.sentence: The match finished late and the team travelled back the same night.
notice_set.question: Is there any word here naming a date?
notice_set.why: No date is named and none is needed. The verbs alone are enough to place the whole thing behind us.

teach.rule_line: The verb carries the past; the when-words only say which past you mean.
teach.false_rule: That a past sentence needs a when-word to be correct. Most have none, and one in every sentence makes a paragraph read like a diary entry.

errors.wrong: I played yesterday two matches at the sports centre.
errors.right: I played two matches at the sports centre yesterday.
errors.why_it_happens: In many languages the when-word sits comfortably next to the verb. English keeps the verb and the thing it acts on welded together and sends the when-word to the end.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: yesterday goes to the end.
errors.l1_note: Very common where the writer's first language has freer word order.

errors.wrong: Ago two weeks the pitch was flooded and the game was called off.
errors.right: Two weeks ago the pitch was flooded and the game was called off.
errors.why_it_happens: Ago is learned as a word meaning in the past, so it gets used like one, standing at the front. It is not that kind of word: it is a measurement that follows its amount.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: ago goes after the amount.

errors.wrong: We trained the last summer with the harbour club.
errors.right: We trained last summer with the harbour club.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows a particular summer is meant and reaches for the word that usually points at a particular thing. Last is already doing that job on its own.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: the.

errors.wrong: Three years ago the club moves to the ground behind the station.
errors.right: Three years ago the club moved to the ground behind the station.
errors.why_it_happens: Once a date is on the page the writer feels the past has been announced, so the verb seems free to relax. The verb is where English keeps the past, and the date cannot cover for it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one letter: the s becomes a d.

pays_in.note: How long have you been doing that gets answered with one of these.
pays_in.model: I started swimming again about two years ago, mostly at the pool near the station.

pays_in.note: A chart answer places every movement in a named year.
pays_in.model: In 2016 participation rose sharply, and it fell again the following winter.

pays_in.note: Dates and amounts are exactly what the short-answer questions ask for.
pays_in.model: The centre opened three years ago and the second hall was added last spring.

used_in.quote: The card asks when you started, and the answer stands or falls on one of these words landing in the right slot.
Every comparison in this answer has to name the year it belongs to, or the reader cannot follow the movement.

payload.sentence: We joined the running club four years ago.
payload.question: Which year does the speaker mean?

feedback.why_key: Ago measures backwards from the moment somebody is speaking, so the number moves as the years pass.
feedback.feed_forward: Count backwards from today whenever you meet ago.

payload.sentence: The pool closed for repairs last winter.
payload.question: Roughly how far back is this?

feedback.why_key: Last plus a season always points at the most recent one that has already ended.
feedback.feed_forward: Read last as the nearest finished one.

payload.context: From a message about a weekend tournament.
payload.sentence: She finished yesterday the second half of the entry form.
reasons: the when-word has been pushed between the verb and what it acts on
two matches is too many for one day
the sports centre needs naming
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: English keeps a verb and the thing it acts on side by side. The when-word waits at the end for its turn.
feedback.feed_forward: Send the when-word to the end of the sentence.

payload.context: Two members of a club talking about a move that happened in 2021, four years back.
payload.stem: The club moved to the ground behind the station four years ___ .

expected: ago

feedback.why_key: The amount comes first and the measuring word follows it. That order never changes.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the number, then the word that measures back from today.

payload.context: From a short report on a school swimming scheme.
payload.stem: ___ 2016 the council rebuilt the changing rooms and the numbers rose again.

expected: in

feedback.why_key: A year is a wide container, and English uses the wide word for it. A day would take on and a clock time would take at.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the size of the time to the size of the word.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a result that is already in the record books.

expected: the team won the regional cup two seasons ago

feedback.why_key: The verb keeps hold of what it acts on, and the whole measurement travels to the end as one block.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the action first, then add the measurement.

payload.audio_text: The centre opened three years ago and closed again last spring.

expected: the centre opened three years ago and closed again last spring

feedback.why_key: Two different measurements in one sentence, and a listening question will ask for exactly these words.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the number down the moment you hear it.

payload.sentence: Ago three days the club posted the result on its website.

expected: three days ago

feedback.why_key: The measuring word cannot lead. It is glued to the back of the amount it measures.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the amount in front of ago, always.

payload.sentence: We swam in the harbour the last summer and the water was warmer than usual.

expected: last summer

feedback.why_key: Last is already pointing at one particular summer, so the extra pointing word has nothing left to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the word in front of last.

items.decision_cue: the pool closes for six weeks

payload.context: From a paragraph about a local club's history.
payload.sentence: Two winters ago the pool closes for six weeks of repairs.
reasons: the date is doing the work the verb should be doing
three years is too short a period to mention
the ground should be named
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A date cannot stand in for the verb. English needs the past on the verb even when the year is printed beside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the verb first; treat the date as extra.

items.decision_cue: The club won the cup in 2016.

payload.context: Two sentences from different pages of a club history.
sentences: The club won the cup in 2016.
The club won the cup nine years ago.
meanings: A fixed point that will read the same in any future decade.
A distance measured from the day the sentence is being read.

feedback.why_key: One of these will still be true in twenty years and one will quietly become wrong. That is why reports prefer named years.
feedback.feed_forward: Use a named year when the text will outlive the day.

payload.prompt_text: An activity you took up and then stopped. Write one sentence saying when you started and one saying when you stopped, using two different kinds of when-word.

feedback.why_key: Two different measurements force you to place both ends of the stretch, which is what a listener needs.
feedback.feed_forward: Vary the kind of when-word; do not repeat ago twice.

payload.prompt_text: Write the two-sentence overview for the activity chart, naming the years the movement happened in. Four minutes. Every verb past, every year in its proper slot.

feedback.why_key: A chart answer that never names a year leaves the reader unable to place a single movement being described.
feedback.feed_forward: Anchor each movement to its year before you compare them.

title: Saying what I expect to happen, and deciding something out loud as I speak

point_json.grammar_name: will for prediction, instant decision, offer, promise and refusal

teach.can_do: I can say what I expect to happen, and I can decide something out loud while I am speaking.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the first way of pointing forward that English gives you, it costs one unchanging word, and an essay wants it for every prediction you make.
teach.meaning: Will puts something in the part of time that has not arrived yet, and it does so out of your own head rather than out of anything standing in front of you. Reach for it when you believe something is ahead, when you make up your mind at the moment of speaking, when you offer to do something, and when you promise. Nothing has been arranged and nothing has been set up. The future here is your judgement, and it is being made now.

form.pattern: will + the plain verb, with nothing added to it
notes: the plain verb means no -s, no -ed and no to in front of it
in speech and in a friendly message it shrinks to 'll after a pronoun; an essay writes will in full
it never changes for he, she or it, which makes it the easiest thing in this unit to build
form.negative: will not, or won't in speech: The depot won't reopen before April.
form.question: Will + person + the plain verb: Will you send me the figures?

marks.label: you judge, or you decide, here

spec.caption: Will jumps straight from your head now to the thing itself. There is no preparation on the way.

worked_example.sentence: Fares on the Ashfield line will rise again in the spring.
worked_example.why_this_form: This is a judgement inside the speaker's head. No fare has been printed and no announcement has been made; the speaker simply expects it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Fares are rising would say the increase is already fixed and dated by the company, which is a far stronger claim than this speaker can make.

notice_set.sentence: I'll carry those boxes up for you.
notice_set.question: Had the speaker planned this before the conversation started?
notice_set.why: The offer is invented at the moment of speaking, which is exactly the job this word is doing here.

notice_set.sentence: The new footbridge at Sandmouth will open in the autumn.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker giving you something they expect, or something they have arranged themselves?
notice_set.why: The speaker is reporting what they believe is ahead. Nothing here says the plan is theirs.

notice_set.sentence: Kwame won't answer his phone while he is driving.
notice_set.question: Is this about a refusal, or about something happening at this moment?
notice_set.why: Won't very often carries a refusal: he will not do it, and that is his own choice.

notice_set.sentence: Levels in the Verdon will drop once the sluice gates open.
notice_set.question: Have the levels dropped yet?
notice_set.why: The whole sentence sits in a part of time nobody has reached, so nothing in it has happened.

notice_set.sentence: I'll ask Rehana to send the file across.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker already know that Rehana is going to send it?
notice_set.why: The speaker is committing to their own next move. What Rehana then does is left wide open.

teach.rule_line: If the future is coming out of your own head right now, use will.
teach.false_rule: That will is simply how English says the future. English points forward in four ways, and will is only the one that comes out of your own head.

errors.wrong: The council will to publish the figures in June.
errors.right: The council will publish the figures in June.
errors.why_it_happens: Learners meet to in front of most verbs that follow another verb, so the hand supplies it out of habit. Nothing sounds broken on a re-read, so it survives all the way to the page.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: She will goes to the site meeting instead of me.
errors.right: She will go to the site meeting instead of me.
errors.why_it_happens: The ending that belongs on a verb after she has been drilled so hard that it fires anyway, even though will has already taken over the job of saying who and when.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on goes.

errors.wrong: Driverless buses will replace every driver in the country within ten years.
errors.right: Driverless buses will probably replace many drivers within ten years.
errors.why_it_happens: Will feels like a neutral way of pointing forward, so a guess gets attached to it as confidently as a certainty, and the reader hears a promise the writer has no way of keeping.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: probably.

errors.wrong: Careful with that tray, you will drop it.
errors.right: Careful with that tray, you're going to drop it.
errors.why_it_happens: Will is the first future most learners are handed, so it becomes the one that arrives first, even when the reason for saying it is wobbling in front of both people.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will drop becomes are going to drop.

pays_in.note: Every prediction paragraph is built on it, usually with a softening word beside it.
pays_in.model: Rising insurance costs will probably push some households away from the coast altogether.

pays_in.note: Offers, promises and decisions made mid-sentence all live here.
pays_in.model: I'll probably stay in this job another year, then have a look around.

pays_in.note: Announcements about what happens next are made of it.
pays_in.model: The replacement coach will leave from the far end of the car park.

used_in.quote: The examiner asks what the candidate thinks is ahead, and the answer starts with this word almost every time.
Arguing that a shorter week would spread is a prediction, and a prediction needs this and a softener.

payload.sentence: I'll take the early shift on Thursday if nobody else wants it.
payload.question: Was this settled before the conversation began?

feedback.why_key: The speaker is making up their mind while they talk. Nothing was agreed with anybody beforehand.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the speaker decided this while speaking.

payload.sentence: Rainfall across the Verdon catchment will fall by roughly a tenth this century.
payload.question: Where does this sit?

feedback.why_key: The sentence is a judgement about a stretch of time nobody has reached yet, so none of it has happened.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the event on a line before you read anything else.

payload.context: Rehana is answering a colleague who has just asked for a hand in the loading bay.
payload.sentence: I will to move the pallets before lunch.
reasons: there is one word too many after will
the speaker has not decided anything yet
the pallets have already been moved
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Will already carries the job of pointing forward, so the verb behind it stays plain and bare.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip the verb behind will down to its plain shape.

payload.context: From a short note on the Brackenfield regeneration scheme.
payload.stem: If the funding holds, the market square ___ (reopen) before the winter.

expected: will reopen

feedback.why_key: The writer is predicting from what they know about the funding. Nothing has been arranged with anyone.
feedback.feed_forward: Put will in front and leave the verb completely plain.

payload.context: Two colleagues splitting up the jobs nobody has claimed.
payload.stem: Leave the invoices, I ___ (sort) them out this afternoon.

expected: will sort
'll sort
ll sort

feedback.why_key: The speaker takes the job on at the moment of speaking, which is what this word is for.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the short form when you are speaking to somebody.

payload.given: Borrowing costs stand at four per cent. Most analysts expect a small cut in June.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence saying what is expected, and soften it so it is not read as a promise.

expected: will probably fall in june
will probably drop in june
will probably be cut in june
will likely fall in june

feedback.why_key: A prediction with nothing softening it reads as a guarantee, and no writer can guarantee what a committee does.
feedback.feed_forward: Add a softening word between will and the verb.

payload.context: A tutor answering a student on the way out of a seminar.

expected: i will send you the reading list tonight

feedback.why_key: Will sits straight after the person and the verb behind it stays bare, with the rest of the sentence following normally.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep will next to the person and the verb right behind it.

payload.audio_text: They'll put a shuttle bus on until the bridge reopens.

expected: they'll put a shuttle bus on until the bridge reopens
theyll put a shuttle bus on until the bridge reopens
they will put a shuttle bus on until the bridge reopens

feedback.why_key: In speech the whole word shrinks onto the person in front of it, and one unstressed sound is all that is left of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small sound stuck to the person, not for a whole word.

items.decision_cue: will do every job in the country

payload.context: From a first draft of an essay about automation.
payload.sentence: Within twenty years, machines will do every job in the country.
reasons: a guess is being stated as a certainty
the sentence points at the wrong stretch of time
the verb behind will is built wrongly
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Every job is an absolute claim and nobody can stand behind it. The reader stops trusting the paragraph, not just the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Soften any prediction you could not defend if challenged.

payload.sentence: The board will to announce the outcome of the review on Friday morning.

expected: will announce

feedback.why_key: Nothing else in the sentence is wrong. One extra word is doing all the damage, and it is the smallest one there.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the to that has crept in behind will.

payload.context: Two remarks about the same block of flats, made on different days.
sentences: That lift will break down again, I know that building.
That lift is going to break down, listen to the noise it is making.
meanings: The speaker is judging from experience they carry around in their head.
The speaker is pointing at something both people can notice this minute.

feedback.why_key: Both speakers expect the same breakdown. Only one of them can put a finger on the reason while they say it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the reason is in the room or in the speaker.

payload.prompt_text: A colleague has just asked you to cover a task you had not planned on doing. Answer them, take it on, and say when you can get to it.

feedback.why_key: You are agreeing to something at the moment of speaking, and that is the situation this word was made for.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide inside the sentence rather than reporting an old plan.

payload.prompt_text: Open your last essay on city centres and add one closing sentence predicting what happens if nothing is changed. Soften it so a reader could not call it a promise. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: A closing prediction is what turns an argument into a position, and the softener is what keeps the position defensible.
feedback.feed_forward: Predict once, soften once, then stop.

title: Saying what I have already decided to do, and what the signs in front of me point to

point_json.grammar_name: be going to for intention and for evidence-based prediction

teach.can_do: I can say what I have already made up my mind to do, and what the signs around me are pointing to.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the future of ordinary speech, and it carries something will cannot: that the decision is already made, or that the reason is standing in front of you.
teach.meaning: Going to reaches back before the moment of speaking and picks something up. Sometimes it picks up a decision you took earlier and have been carrying since: nothing is booked, nobody else is involved, but your mind is made up. Sometimes it picks up a piece of the world in front of you, right now, that points at what is coming. Either way the future here has a cause the listener could look at, and that is what separates it from a plain opinion about later.

form.pattern: am / is / are + going to + the plain verb
notes: am with I, is with he, she, it and any single thing, are with you, we and they
in speech it runs together as gonna, but nobody writes that in an essay or a letter
the negative and the question are made on am, is or are, not on going
form.negative: am not / isn't / aren't going to: The depot isn't going to take deliveries on Sunday.
form.question: Am, is or are + person + going to: Are you going to apply for it?

marks.label: the decision was taken, or the sign appeared
and it has been sitting there since

spec.caption: The cause is already behind you. Only the result is still ahead.

worked_example.sentence: The tide is coming in fast, so we're going to lose the causeway.
worked_example.why_this_form: The reason is in front of both people. Anyone standing there can see the water, and the sentence simply reads what the water is saying.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: We will lose the causeway would make it a private opinion about the afternoon, as if the speaker had not looked at the water at all.

notice_set.sentence: I'm going to apply for the surveying course in Norland.
notice_set.question: Has the speaker made up their mind before this conversation?
notice_set.why: The decision is already sitting behind the speaker; they are only reporting it now.

notice_set.sentence: Nothing has moved at the barrier for ten minutes, so we're going to be late.
notice_set.question: Can the two people see the reason for saying this?
notice_set.why: The reason is the barrier, and both of them are sitting at it.

notice_set.sentence: Marta is going to hand her notice in at the end of the month.
notice_set.question: Has she agreed a date with anyone yet?
notice_set.why: An intention says her mind is made up. Whether anybody else has been told is simply left out.

notice_set.sentence: Those clouds are going to soak the whole survey team.
notice_set.question: Where is the speaker's reason for saying this?
options: In something they read last week
notice_set.why: The speaker is reading the sky. Take the clouds away and the sentence has nothing left holding it up.

notice_set.sentence: We aren't going to renew the lease on the Marlow unit.
notice_set.question: Is this a plan or a guess?
notice_set.why: It is a decision the speaker's side has already taken, stated as their own.

teach.rule_line: If the cause is already behind you, or in front of you, use going to.
teach.false_rule: That going to is just a longer, more casual will. It carries something will cannot: that the reason for the sentence already exists.

errors.wrong: I think prices are going to fall next year, but nobody really knows.
errors.right: I think prices will fall next year, but nobody really knows.
errors.why_it_happens: Going to gets learned as the everyday future, so it spreads into pure guesswork. The second half of the sentence admits there is no evidence, which is exactly what going to claims there is.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are going to fall becomes will fall.

errors.wrong: The committee going to review the parking charges in March.
errors.right: The committee is going to review the parking charges in March.
errors.why_it_happens: Going to feels like one solid block of meaning, so the small word in front of it drops off without anybody noticing. It carries no meaning of its own, which is precisely why the ear does not miss it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: is.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for speakers of languages that build a sentence without a linking verb.

errors.wrong: Governments are going to have to spend far more on flood defences.
errors.right: Governments will have to spend far more on flood defences.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence is fine English and would pass unremarked in conversation. Written down in a formal argument it sounds like a person talking rather than a case being made.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are going to have becomes will have.

errors.wrong: Hold on, I'm going to give you a hand with that.
errors.right: Hold on, I'll give you a hand with that.
errors.why_it_happens: The offer is invented in the same breath as the sentence, but going to has become the learner's default, so it turns a spontaneous offer into something the speaker seems to have planned in advance.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: am going to give becomes will give.

pays_in.note: A long turn about a plan is carried almost entirely by it.
pays_in.model: I'm going to move closer to the coast once the lease on the flat runs out.

pays_in.note: Explaining what current signs point to, rather than what you merely believe.
pays_in.model: With rents climbing like that, a lot of younger people are going to leave the city.

pays_in.note: Speakers use it to signal that a decision has already been taken.
pays_in.model: We're going to run the second session in the smaller room instead.

used_in.quote: A card asking about a plan for the next few years is answered in this shape from the first sentence to the last.
Arrangements and intentions are stated aloud in the booking conversation, and the detail sits in the second half of them.

payload.sentence: Devi is going to retrain as a water engineer.
payload.question: Has she made up her mind already?

feedback.why_key: The decision sits behind the sentence. She is not choosing while she speaks; she is telling you what she chose.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask when the decision was taken, not when it happens.

payload.sentence: The river has risen four inches since dawn and the low fields are going to flood.
payload.question: Is the writer guessing, or reading something in front of them?
options: Reading something in front of them

feedback.why_key: The first half of the sentence hands you the reason. Remove it and the second half has nothing standing under it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the reason the writer has already given you.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a company's plans.
payload.sentence: The firm going to open a second workshop in Ashfield.
reasons: a small word is missing in front of going
the plan has not been decided yet
the workshop has already opened
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Going to needs a small word carrying the person and the time in front of it. Without one the sentence never gets started.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that am, is or are is sitting in front of going.

payload.context: Somebody explaining a decision they took last month.
payload.stem: We ___ (sell) the flat and rent something nearer the hospital.

expected: are going to sell
're going to sell
re going to sell

feedback.why_key: The decision was taken before the conversation, so the sentence reaches back and reports it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match am, is or are to the person before you go on.

payload.context: A field note written while the readings are still coming in.
payload.stem: The salinity trace has climbed all morning, so the sensors ___ (need) recalibrating.

expected: are going to need

feedback.why_key: The trace on the screen is the reason, and it has been visible for hours before the sentence was written.
feedback.feed_forward: Point at the evidence, then choose the shape that admits it.

payload.given: Osman decided last winter. He wants to walk the whole ridge path in one go.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence reporting the decision he is carrying around with him.

expected: is going to walk the whole ridge path in one go
is going to walk the ridge path in one go

feedback.why_key: The choice was made last winter and has not changed since, which is the situation this shape reports.
feedback.feed_forward: Report the old decision, do not make a new one.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a plan that has already been announced.

expected: the market is going to close for refurbishment

feedback.why_key: The small word goes in third, before going, and the plain verb waits behind to.
feedback.feed_forward: Build it in order: person, small word, going to, plain verb.

payload.audio_text: We're going to take the coast road instead.

expected: we're going to take the coast road instead
were going to take the coast road instead
we are going to take the coast road instead

feedback.why_key: In real speech the small word collapses onto the person and going to blurs into a single sound. The whole meaning is carried by what you can barely hear.
feedback.feed_forward: Slow the replay and count the sounds before the main verb.

items.decision_cue: are going to have to raise

payload.context: From the closing paragraph of a formal argument about public spending.
payload.sentence: Councils are going to have to raise charges whatever happens to central funding.
reasons: the shape belongs to speech rather than to a formal argument
the councils have not decided anything
the verb behind to is built wrongly
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is broken. It simply sounds like somebody talking, and a formal argument wants the flatter word instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Switch to will when the writing is formal.

payload.sentence: The council going to widen the pavements on both sides of the square.

expected: the council is going to widen
the council will widen

feedback.why_key: The plan is real and already taken. The sentence just never says who is doing it or when, because the little word that says so is missing.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the missing is before going.

items.decision_cue: she has been on her feet since six

payload.context: Two things said about the same nurse at the end of a shift.
sentences: She is going to sleep for twelve hours, she has been on her feet since six.
She will sleep badly again, she always does before an inspection.
meanings: The speaker is working from something they have watched happen all day.
The speaker is working from a pattern they carry in their head.

feedback.why_key: One speaker points at today. The other points at every other time it has happened, which is a different kind of reason altogether.
feedback.feed_forward: Separate what you have seen today from what you generally believe.

payload.prompt_text: Think of one thing you decided months ago to do about your work or studies, which nobody has booked or arranged for you. Say it in one sentence.

feedback.why_key: A decision you have been carrying for months is not made in the sentence, so the sentence has to reach back and pick it up.
feedback.feed_forward: Report a decision you already hold, not a new one.

payload.prompt_text: Speak for one minute on a plan you have for the next few years. Use this shape at least three times, and once let a reason you can actually point to carry the sentence.

feedback.why_key: A long turn about a plan collapses into a list without it, because nothing in the answer says the decisions are already yours.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the plan, then give the reason you can point at.

title: Putting two complete ideas into one sentence with and, but, or and so

point_json.grammar_name: Coordination with and, but, or and so

teach.can_do: I can put two complete ideas into one sentence and show how the second one relates to the first.
teach.why_it_matters: Without these four words every sentence stops after one idea, and your reader is left to work out the joins on your behalf.
teach.meaning: A complete idea is a group of words you could put a full stop after and walk away: the fare went up. English lets you put two of them inside one sentence, but not by parking them next to each other. A joining word goes between them, and each one makes a different claim about the join. And adds. But turns. Or offers a choice. So gives the result. The two ideas stay equal in weight; neither is squeezed inside the other.

form.pattern: complete idea + , + and / but / or / so + complete idea
notes: The comma goes in front of the joining word, never after it.
When both ideas are very short the comma can be dropped: the gates opened and the queue moved.
One joining word per join. Two of them is always one too many.
form.negative: Each idea goes negative on its own: the ferry did not run, and the bus was not diverted.
form.question: Questions join in the same way: did the fare rise, or did the service simply get worse?

left.role: idea one, complete on its own
left.text: the fare went up in April

right.role: idea two, complete on its own
right.text: passenger numbers fell within a month

spec.caption: Two things that could each be a sentence, held together by one word: and, but, or, so.

worked_example.sentence: The council added two evening buses, but the last one still leaves before the late shift ends.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second idea works against the first, so the join has to be but. And would tell the reader that the two facts point the same way.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: With so, the sentence would claim the early departure is the result of adding the buses, which is not what happened.

notice_set.sentence: The station car park was full, so we left the car at home.
notice_set.question: Why did they leave the car at home?
options: Because the car park was full
notice_set.why: So marks whatever follows it as the result of what came before it.

notice_set.sentence: We arrived early, but the car park was already full.
notice_set.question: Did arriving early help?
notice_set.why: But warns you that the second idea works against the first, so early was not early enough.

notice_set.sentence: You can buy a ticket at the machine, or you can pay the driver.
notice_set.question: How many ways of paying are there?
notice_set.why: Or lays two possibilities side by side and lets the reader take either.

notice_set.sentence: The lift was out of order and the stairs were closed for cleaning.
notice_set.question: Do the two facts pull in the same direction?
notice_set.why: And simply adds. It makes no claim beyond both things being true.

notice_set.sentence: The service was cut in 2019, so the village lost its only link to the hospital.
notice_set.question: Which idea is the result?
notice_set.why: So always puts the result second. Everything after it happened because of what came first.

teach.rule_line: Two complete ideas in one sentence need a joining word between them.
teach.false_rule: That a comma on its own is enough to hold two complete ideas together. A comma cannot do that job; it needs one of these four words beside it.

errors.wrong: The bus service was cut, many villages now have no way of reaching the hospital.
errors.right: The bus service was cut, so many villages now have no way of reaching the hospital.
errors.why_it_happens: The two facts belong together and the comma feels like the mark for that. Nobody has told the learner that a comma can separate things but cannot join them.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: so.

errors.wrong: The fare went up in April passenger numbers fell within a month.
errors.right: The fare went up in April, and passenger numbers fell within a month.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence was written in one breath and the seam between the two ideas was never heard. It happens most in the second half of a timed answer, when nobody is reading back.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: and.

errors.wrong: The fare went up, however the service did not improve.
errors.right: The fare went up, but the service did not improve.
errors.why_it_happens: However means what but means, so it is put where but would go. The two words mean the same thing and belong to different grammatical classes, and only one of them can sit next to a comma.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: however becomes but.

errors.wrong: Commuters wanted cheaper fares and to have more frequent trains.
errors.right: Commuters wanted cheaper fares and more frequent trains.
errors.why_it_happens: The second item is thought of as a separate wish and comes out with its own verb attached. And demands two things of the same shape, and nothing warns the learner when the shapes drift apart.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: to have.

pays_in.note: Every body paragraph needs at least one join a reader can trust.
pays_in.model: The scheme cut journey times, but it did nothing for the villages beyond the ring road.

pays_in.note: Any answer longer than one sentence hangs on these four words.
pays_in.model: I cycle in most days, so I only really use the train in winter.

pays_in.note: But and so tell you whether the next clause agrees with the last one or overturns it.
pays_in.model: The trial ran for three years, but the findings were never acted on.

used_in.quote: The answer is a chain of small consequences, and every link in it is one of these four words.
A two-clause answer sounds like a person talking; two one-clause answers sound like a form being filled in.

payload.sentence: The last train was cancelled, so we stayed the night in Marlow.
payload.question: Why did they stay the night?

feedback.why_key: So points forwards to the result, so everything after it happened because of the cancelled train.
feedback.feed_forward: Read so as and because of that.

payload.sentence: The reservoir refilled over the winter, but the hosepipe ban stayed in place.
payload.question: Was the ban lifted when the reservoir refilled?

feedback.why_key: But warns you that the second idea works against the first, so the refilling did not bring the ban to an end.
feedback.feed_forward: Read but as a warning that the direction is about to change.

items.decision_cue: the retail park, the old square

payload.context: From a first draft about town centres.
payload.sentence: The market moved to the retail park, the old square emptied within a year.
reasons: two complete ideas are held together by nothing but a comma
the second idea is not complete
the comma is in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Both halves could take a full stop and stand alone. A comma on its own cannot hold them; a joining word has to be there too.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the comma and ask whether each side could be a sentence.

payload.context: From a report on a new park-and-ride site.
payload.stem: The car park opened in March, ___ the buses did not start running until June.

expected: but

feedback.why_key: The second fact undercuts the first: the site was there and useless. But is the only one of the four words that says that.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the second idea helps the first or blocks it.

payload.context: Two neighbours talking on the stairs.
payload.stem: The lift has been broken since Friday, ___ I have been carrying the shopping up six floors.

expected: so

feedback.why_key: The carrying is what the broken lift caused, and so is the word that marks a result.
feedback.feed_forward: If the second idea is the consequence, reach for so.

payload.context: Build one sentence about the Marlow depot.

expected: the depot closed in 2019 so forty drivers lost their jobs

feedback.why_key: The cause comes first and the result follows so. Swap them over and the sentence claims the drivers closed the depot.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the cause in front of so and the consequence after it.

payload.given: The library now opens on Sundays. Very few students use it.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that keeps both facts and shows that the second works against the first.

expected: now opens on sundays but very few students use it
now opens on sundays, but very few students use it

feedback.why_key: One sentence now carries the good news and the disappointment, and but is what tells the reader which is which.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the joining word by asking which way the second idea pulls.

payload.audio_text: We'd finished the shift, so we didn't wait for the late bus.

expected: we'd finished the shift so we didn't wait for the late bus
we had finished the shift so we did not wait for the late bus
wed finished the shift so we didnt wait for the late bus
we'd finished the shift so we did not wait for the late bus

feedback.why_key: In ordinary speech so is one quick unstressed syllable, and a listener who misses it writes two sentences where the speaker said one.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small joining word at the seam between two ideas.

payload.context: From a paragraph on hospital waiting times.
payload.stem: Patients want shorter waits ___ clearer information about their appointments.

expected: and

feedback.why_key: Two things of the same kind are being listed, and and is the word that adds without claiming anything else.
feedback.feed_forward: Use and when the second idea neither turns nor follows from the first.

payload.sentence: The charge came in last April, the queues moved to the ring road within a fortnight.

expected: april and the queues moved
april so the queues moved
april, and the queues moved
april, so the queues moved
april. the queues moved

feedback.why_key: Both halves are complete sentences, so the comma needs a joining word beside it or a full stop in its place.
feedback.feed_forward: When both sides are complete, add a joining word or split the sentence.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph on local newspapers.
payload.sentence: The paper cut its print run, and however it kept the Sunday edition.
reasons: two joining words are doing one job
the two ideas do not belong in one sentence
the comma is missing
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: And has already made the join and however has already marked the turn. Whichever one you keep, the other has nothing left to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep one joining word per join and delete the spare.

payload.prompt_text: A town has put recycling bins on every street and the amount of waste sent for burning has not changed. Write one sentence that holds both facts together and shows how they sit with each other.

feedback.why_key: Both facts are true at once and the second disappoints the first, which is exactly the job one of these four words does.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick the joining word before you start writing the second half.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on free city transport. Find two short sentences standing next to each other and join them into one, choosing the word that shows how they relate. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: A page of short sentences reads as a list. One join, made on purpose, turns two facts into an argument.
feedback.feed_forward: Join two sentences only when you can name the relation between them.

title: Saying when and where with in, on and at

point_json.grammar_name: in / on / at for time and place

teach.can_do: I can put in, on and at in front of a time or a place without guessing.
teach.why_it_matters: They appear in nearly every sentence you will ever write about your life, and getting one wrong is visible to a reader immediately.
teach.meaning: These three are about size, not about vocabulary. In puts something inside something with edges: a country, a town, a month, a year. On puts it on a surface or along a line: a road, a floor, a named day. At pins it to a single point: a doorway, a building on a journey, a moment on the clock. Time copies space exactly, which is why one set of three does both jobs.

form.pattern: in + the big one · on + the surface or the named day · at + the exact point
notes: in: countries, towns, months, years, seasons, and parts of the day (in the morning)
on: roads, floors, days and dates (on Tuesday, on 3 March)
at: buildings on a route, addresses with a number, clock times, at night, at the weekend
no preposition at all before this, last, next and every: the survey closed last Friday
form.negative: The preposition does not change when the sentence goes negative: the depot is not on Verdon Road.
form.question: Is the office on Verdon Road or at number forty?

spec.label: how big is the thing after the preposition?

steps.gloss: something with edges you can be inside: in Sandmouth, in April
a surface or a line you sit along: on Verdon Road, on Tuesday
one point with no width: at the depot, at ten past six

worked_example.sentence: The night bus leaves from the stop on Verdon Road at ten past eleven.
worked_example.why_this_form: A road is a line you sit along, so it takes on. A clock time is one point in the day with no width, so it takes at.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: In Verdon Road would put the stop somewhere inside the road surface, and on ten past eleven would treat a bare moment as something with a top to stand on.

notice_set.sentence: Rana lives on Brackenfield Road.
notice_set.question: Do we know her house number?
notice_set.why: On puts her somewhere along the road and never picks a point on it, so the number stays unsaid.

notice_set.sentence: Rana lives at 14 Brackenfield Road.
notice_set.question: Do we know her house number?
notice_set.why: At pins her to one point, and here the number is that point.

notice_set.sentence: The depot closes at six.
notice_set.question: Could you arrive at half past six and still get in?
notice_set.why: Six is one moment, and the doors are shut from that moment onwards.

notice_set.sentence: The roadworks will finish in August.
notice_set.question: Do we know which day they finish?
notice_set.why: In wraps the whole month round the event without choosing any day inside it.

notice_set.sentence: The market runs on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: Is the market open on Sunday?
notice_set.why: On names the day the market runs. Nothing here says anything at all about the other days.

teach.rule_line: Ask how big it is: inside takes in, along takes on, one point takes at.
teach.false_rule: That the three have to be memorised place by place. Size decides them, and time copies space.

errors.wrong: The training starts in Monday.
errors.right: The training starts on Monday.
errors.why_it_happens: In has been stored as the default time preposition because it works for months and years, and a day of the week is filed away as just another time word.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: in becomes on.

errors.wrong: We arrived in the station just before nine.
errors.right: We arrived at the station just before nine.
errors.why_it_happens: A station is a large building, so being inside it feels like the true description. English is describing the journey instead, and on a journey a station is one point.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: in becomes at.

errors.wrong: The exhibition opens at next week.
errors.right: The exhibition opens next week.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows a time phrase usually needs a preposition in front and supplies one by reflex. Next, last, this and every already do that job themselves.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: at.

pays_in.note: Every answer about your day, your area or your journey needs all three.
pays_in.model: I get to the depot at about eight, and on Fridays I'm there a bit earlier.

pays_in.note: A letter carries dates, times and addresses in almost every line.
pays_in.model: I moved into the flat on Brackenfield Road in March.

pays_in.note: Form-filling answers turn on hearing at, on and in correctly.
pays_in.model: The coach leaves from stand four at quarter past two.

used_in.quote: The complaint has to name the stop, the road and the time waited, which is all three prepositions inside one sentence.

payload.sentence: I'll wait for you at the ticket barrier.
payload.question: Do we know exactly where to stand?

feedback.why_key: At marks one point with no width, so the barrier is the whole of the meeting place and there is nothing left to arrange.
feedback.feed_forward: Read at as a pin in a map rather than as a general area.

payload.sentence: The new health centre is in Ashfield.
payload.question: Do we know which road it is on?

feedback.why_key: In wraps a whole district round the building and picks nothing inside it, so the road is still missing.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice how much of the map each preposition hands you.

payload.context: A colleague is explaining her hours to a new starter.
payload.sentence: I start at seven on Mondays and Thursdays.
reasons: a clock time needs in rather than at
a named day needs in rather than on
the days have been put in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Seven is a point on the clock and Monday is a named day, so at and on are each sitting where they belong.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each preposition against the size of the word straight after it.

payload.context: A note on the college noticeboard about term-time opening.
payload.stem: The library closes ___ eight during term time.

expected: at

feedback.why_key: Eight is a single moment on the clock, and a moment with no width takes at.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for at whenever the time is a point rather than a stretch.

payload.context: The opening line of a letter to a landlord.
payload.stem: I have lived ___ 12 Brackenfield Road since March.

expected: at

feedback.why_key: The number turns the road into one exact point, and one exact point takes at rather than on.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a house number before you choose between on and at.

payload.context: Tell a friend when and where the coach goes from.

expected: the coach leaves from the depot at six on sunday

feedback.why_key: Place comes before time in English, and inside the time part the clock point comes before the named day.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the place first, then the smaller time unit, then the bigger one.

payload.given: The interview is 12 May. It is ten in the morning.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that gives both, each with the right preposition.

expected: at ten in the morning on 12 may
on 12 may at ten in the morning
at ten in the morning on 12th may
on 12th may at ten in the morning

feedback.why_key: A date is a named day, so it takes on; ten is a clock point, so it takes at; the morning is a stretch with edges, so it takes in.
feedback.feed_forward: Set each time word beside its own size before you write it.

payload.audio_text: We're meeting at the depot on Friday, not in town.

expected: we're meeting at the depot on friday not in town
we are meeting at the depot on friday not in town
were meeting at the depot on friday not in town

feedback.why_key: All three are unstressed and squashed in speech, so the only way to catch them is to know which size of word is coming next.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the word after the preposition and let its size confirm what you heard.

payload.sentence: The results will be published in Tuesday morning.

expected: on tuesday morning

feedback.why_key: In the morning takes in, but once a named day is attached the day wins and the whole phrase moves to on.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the named day decide the preposition whenever one is present.

payload.context: A line from a confirmation email sent by a guesthouse.
payload.sentence: Breakfast is served in the terrace from seven.
reasons: a flat open surface takes on rather than in
the time needs at rather than from
the meal has been put in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A terrace has a floor and no walls, so you stand on it. In would put the guests inside the stonework.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the place has edges you can be inside before choosing in.

payload.context: Two lines taken from different letters about the same firm.
sentences: The office is on Verdon Road.
The office is at 40 Verdon Road.
meanings: Somewhere along that road, and the writer is not saying where.
One exact building, and its number is the address.

feedback.why_key: The road is the same in both. On spreads the office along it and at drops it onto a single doorstep.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose at only when you can point at one door.

payload.prompt_text: Describe how you get to work or college. Write one sentence that names the time you leave and the road or the stop you use.

feedback.why_key: One ordinary sentence about your own journey needs a place preposition and a time preposition side by side, which is where the mixing usually starts.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the place part first, then the time part.

payload.prompt_text: Take the letter of complaint about the bus service. Write the paragraph that says where you waited and for how long, then check every preposition against the size of the word after it. Six minutes.

feedback.why_key: A complaint is dense with stops, roads, dates and clock times, so it forces every one of the three into the same short paragraph.
feedback.feed_forward: Underline each preposition and name the size of the word after it.

title: Making the verb match how many you are talking about

point_json.grammar_name: Subject-verb agreement: the basics

teach.can_do: I can make the verb agree with the subject in an ordinary short sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the most-counted small error in marked writing, it costs nothing to fix, and it is fully under your control once you know where to look.
teach.meaning: English asks the verb to say how many the subject is, but only in a few places. In the present simple the verb takes an -s when the subject is exactly one thing, and nothing when it is more than one. The verb be goes further and changes shape three ways. Everywhere else the verb keeps quiet, which is why the marked forms are easy to forget and easy to spot.

form.pattern: one thing → verb + s · more than one thing → bare verb
notes: be is the one that changes most: I am, she is, they are, it was, they were
have splits too: one has, more than one have
after does, doesn't and did, the -s comes off the main verb: she doesn't work Fridays
a modal never takes -s: the scheme can fail, never cans
the past simple marks nothing at all except in was and were
form.negative: The -s moves onto the auxiliary in a negative: the depot does not open on Sundays.
form.question: Does the depot open on Sundays? — again the -s sits on the auxiliary, not on the main verb.

left.text: The driver starts at six.

right.text: The drivers start at six.

spec.caption: The -s is on the noun or on the verb, never on both at once.

worked_example.sentence: The depot opens at six and the offices open at nine.
worked_example.why_this_form: One depot pulls the -s onto opens. Two or more offices leave open bare, because the noun is already carrying the plural.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The depot open would leave the reader waiting for a plural subject that never arrives, and the offices opens would suggest a single office wearing a plural name.

notice_set.sentence: The bus leaves from stand four.
notice_set.question: How many buses are being talked about?
notice_set.why: Leaves carries the -s, and on a verb the -s means exactly one.

notice_set.sentence: The buses leave from stand four.
notice_set.question: How many buses are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The -s has moved onto the noun, so the verb goes bare and the sentence is about a group.

notice_set.sentence: The staff were told on Friday.
notice_set.question: Is this about the past?
notice_set.why: Were is the past of be, and be is the one verb that keeps marking number in the past.

notice_set.sentence: My manager doesn't work weekends.
notice_set.question: How many managers are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The -s has moved onto does, which is where it always goes once an auxiliary turns up.

notice_set.sentence: The two depots handle the same volume of freight.
notice_set.question: How many depots are being talked about?
notice_set.why: Handle is bare, and a bare present-simple verb points at a subject of more than one.

teach.rule_line: One thing takes the -s on the verb; more than one leaves the verb bare.
teach.false_rule: That -s always means more than one. On a noun it does; on a verb it means exactly one.

errors.wrong: My brother work at the freight depot.
errors.right: My brother works at the freight depot.
errors.why_it_happens: The -s carries no meaning a listener needs, so it is the first thing dropped when attention goes to the content of the sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: an s on work.
errors.l1_note: Many languages mark the person on the verb far more heavily, or not at all.

errors.wrong: The two schemes costs the council very little.
errors.right: The two schemes cost the council very little.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has learned that -s and singular go together and applies the marking to the whole sentence rather than to one word in it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on costs.

errors.wrong: She doesn't works on Saturdays.
errors.right: She doesn't work on Saturdays.
errors.why_it_happens: The -s is stored as belonging to she rather than to whichever verb comes first, so it is written twice once an auxiliary appears.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on works.

errors.wrong: The report are ready for the meeting.
errors.right: The report is ready for the meeting.
errors.why_it_happens: Be is irregular enough that its forms are learned as separate words, and the link back to the number of the subject is broken.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: are becomes is.

pays_in.note: Part 1 is almost entirely present simple about your own life.
pays_in.model: My sister works nights, so she sleeps while the rest of us are out.

pays_in.note: Generalisations in an essay are present simple from start to finish.
pays_in.model: Employers expect flexibility, and a four-day week gives them very little of it.

pays_in.note: The -s is often the only clue to whether one thing or several is meant.
pays_in.model: The office opens at nine but the depots open an hour earlier.

used_in.quote: Every answer on this card is a present-simple statement about one person or one workplace.

payload.sentence: The lift runs from six in the morning.
payload.question: How many lifts are there?

feedback.why_key: Runs carries the -s, and on a verb that ending points at exactly one thing.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the ending on the verb as a count, not as decoration.

payload.sentence: The evening courses run from September to May.
payload.question: How many courses are there?

feedback.why_key: The -s has moved onto courses, so run stays bare, and a bare present-simple verb means a group.
feedback.feed_forward: Check which word is wearing the -s before you count.

payload.context: Answering a question about what your family does.
payload.sentence: My brother drives a delivery van and I work in an office.
reasons: the first verb should be bare
the second verb is missing its ending
the two halves need different tenses
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One brother pulls the -s onto drives, and I never takes it, so both verbs are already matched.
feedback.feed_forward: Match each verb to its own subject, not to the sentence as a whole.

payload.context: From a paragraph about how a small firm is run.
payload.stem: The manager ___ (check) the orders before they leave the yard.

expected: checks

feedback.why_key: There is one manager, so the counting job falls to the verb and the -s goes on.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the subject, count it, then write the verb.

payload.context: From a description of a bar chart on freight.
payload.stem: The three routes ___ (carry) almost the same tonnage each year.

expected: carry

feedback.why_key: Routes is already carrying the plural, so the verb has nothing left to say and stays bare.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the verb bare once the noun has taken the -s.

payload.context: Explaining your working week to somebody you have just met.
payload.stem: My shift ___ (not start) until two on Wednesdays.

expected: doesn't start
does not start
dosent start
doesnt start

feedback.why_key: Once an auxiliary turns up it takes the counting job, so does wears the -s and start goes bare.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the -s on the first verb only.

payload.context: Build one sentence about what a college provides.

expected: the college offers two evening courses every term

feedback.why_key: The college is the one thing doing the offering, so offers takes the -s even though courses just after it is plural.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the doer, not to the nearest noun.

payload.given: The new machine sorts the parcels overnight.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that the firm has two machines.

expected: sort the parcels overnight

feedback.why_key: Once the noun goes plural the verb has nothing left to count, so the -s comes straight off.
feedback.feed_forward: When you pluralise the subject, strip the verb back.

payload.audio_text: My colleague works nights and her flatmates work days.

expected: my colleague works nights and her flatmates work days

feedback.why_key: The two verbs are the same word and the only audible difference is a hiss on the end of the first one.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the hiss on the verb and count the subject from it.

payload.sentence: Phones in classrooms distracts everybody, including the teacher.

expected: distract

feedback.why_key: Phones is the doer and it is plural, so the verb goes bare. Classrooms sitting next to it is not the subject.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the words between the subject and the verb, then read it again.

payload.context: From an early draft of an essay about the four-day week.
payload.sentence: Many employers don't works out the real cost before they agree to it.
reasons: the ending has been written on both verbs at once
the subject should be singular
the tense is wrong for a general statement
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Don't already carries the counting job. Works is trying to do it a second time, and one sentence only needs it once.
feedback.feed_forward: After don't, doesn't or didn't, always write the bare verb.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about what you do and what the people around you do: one about a single person and one about a group.

feedback.why_key: Putting the two counts side by side is what makes the ending visible, because nothing else in the sentence changes.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the subject, count it out loud, then write the verb.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about your work or study. Answer four of the questions out loud, then play the recording back and mark every present-simple verb whose subject is one person.

feedback.why_key: The ending is the first thing that disappears under speaking pressure, and hearing your own gaps is what makes it stick.
feedback.feed_forward: Play it back and count the endings you dropped.

title: Asking with what, who and where, and knowing when to leave do out

point_json.grammar_name: Wh- questions: subject questions and object questions

teach.can_do: I can ask about any part of a sentence, and I know which questions need do and which refuse it.
teach.why_it_matters: Almost nobody is taught that some questions take no do at all, so almost everybody puts one in and produces a question no listener would build.
teach.meaning: A question word stands in the hole where the missing information should be. Where that hole sits changes everything. If the hole is where the person or thing doing the verb would go, the question word simply fills it and the sentence keeps its ordinary shape: nothing has moved, so no helper is needed. If the hole is anywhere else, the question word jumps to the front, and the jump is what calls a helper in behind it.

form.pattern: question word + verb ...? when the hole is at the front; question word + helper + subject + plain verb ...? when it is not
notes: who, what and which can stand where the doer stands, and then no helper appears at all
when the hole is somewhere else, the question word goes to the front and do, does, is or can follows it
the ending stays on the verb in the first kind: who runs the desk, not who run the desk
why, when, where and how always leave the hole away from the doer, so they always take a helper
form.negative: Who doesn't sign the sheet? keeps the ordinary shape and still refuses a fronted helper.
form.question: Answer your own question with a name and see where the name lands.

left.role: the hole is where the doer goes
left.text: Who runs the evening desk?

right.role: the hole is somewhere further along
right.text: Who does the editor call first?

spec.caption: Same question word, two different holes. The hole decides whether a helper is needed at all.

worked_example.sentence: Who runs the evening desk at the paper?
worked_example.why_this_form: The missing piece is the person doing the running, so the question word drops straight into that slot and nothing has to move or be fetched.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Who does the paper run? would ask which person the paper is running, which is a different and rather alarming question.

notice_set.sentence: Who edits the Sandmouth weekly?
notice_set.question: What is the speaker missing?
notice_set.why: The question word sits where the person doing the editing would go, so a name is what fills the gap.

notice_set.sentence: Who does the Sandmouth weekly employ?
notice_set.question: What is the speaker missing?
options: The name of the paper's owner
The names of the people it takes on
notice_set.why: The paper is doing the employing here, so the missing piece is the people on the far side of the verb.

notice_set.sentence: What goes on the front page?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking about a thing or about a person?
notice_set.why: What fills the slot where the thing doing the going would sit, and nothing has been fetched in behind it.

notice_set.sentence: Where does Bea file the photographs?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker missing a place or a person?
notice_set.why: Bea is doing the filing, so the hole is somewhere else entirely, and the question word had to travel to reach the front.

notice_set.sentence: Which reporter takes the late calls?
notice_set.question: How many reporters is the speaker asking about?
notice_set.why: The ending on takes ties the verb to a single reporter, which is exactly the person the question wants named.

discovery.prompt: Both columns ask about a newspaper office. What is different about where the missing piece sits?
pairs: Who edits the Sandmouth weekly?
Who does the Sandmouth weekly employ?
What goes on the front page?
What does Bea put on the front page?
Which reporter takes the late calls?
Which reporter does the editor trust?

candidate_rules.text: On the left the question word is standing where the doer stands, so nothing had to move.
On the left the questions are shorter.
Questions beginning with who and what never take do.

teach.rule_line: Answer with a name. If the name lands in front of the verb, leave do out.
teach.false_rule: That every question needs do, or that who never takes it. Who takes it half the time, and the half is decided by where the hole is.

contrast.question: Is the piece I am missing the one doing the verb?

fork.answer: Yes, the missing piece is the one doing it: ask straight, keep the ending, fetch nothing
fork.selects: a question with no helper at all

fork.answer: No, the missing piece is what the verb lands on, or where, when, why or how
fork.selects: a question word at the front with a helper behind it

a.text: Who teaches Halima?
a.means: You are asking which person stands at the front of Halima's class.

b.text: Who does Halima teach?
b.means: You are asking which people sit in front of Halima while she teaches.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Putting do into the first one turns Halima from the pupil into the teacher, and the listener will answer the question you built rather than the one you meant. Both versions are ordinary English, so nothing sounds wrong enough to be queried.

edge_case.text: In careful writing you may still meet whom in the second kind. Nobody says it out loud any more, and who is standard in speech and in almost all writing. Recognise it, then use who.

contrast.stronger_test: Say the answer out loud as one name. A name arriving before the verb means fetch nothing; a name arriving later means a helper is owed.

worked_pairs.a: Who runs the evening desk at the library?
worked_pairs.b: Who does the library send to the evening desk?
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first, the missing person is the runner. In the second, the library does the sending and the missing person lands on the far side of the verb.

worked_pairs.a: What goes into the green bin?
worked_pairs.b: What does the council collect on a Tuesday?
worked_pairs.gloss: Nothing stands between what and its verb in the first, because there was no gap to cross. In the second the council is already in the slot, so the question word had to travel.

worked_pairs.a: Which crew checks the harbour lights?
worked_pairs.b: Which crew does the harbour master call first?
worked_pairs.gloss: The ending on checks is the giveaway: it only appears when the question word is sitting in the doer's slot.

errors.wrong: Who does write the weekly column?
errors.right: Who writes the weekly column?
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored do as the thing that makes a question, so it goes in whenever a question is being built, regardless of whether anything actually needed moving.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: does.

errors.wrong: Who check the fire doors on a Friday?
errors.right: Who checks the fire doors on a Friday?
errors.why_it_happens: Who feels like an unknown, and an unknown feels like it could be several people, so the ending is left off just in case. English treats it as one until told otherwise.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: s on check.

errors.wrong: What the council collects on a Tuesday?
errors.right: What does the council collect on a Tuesday?
errors.why_it_happens: The learner sees the question word already at the front and takes the job as done. Nothing signals that the front position was reached by travelling, and travelling is what calls the helper in.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: does.

errors.wrong: Which crew does checks the harbour lights?
errors.right: Which crew checks the harbour lights?
errors.why_it_happens: Both routes have been taken at once: the helper is fetched and the ending is kept. It shows a learner halfway between two rules with nothing to tell them the rules are alternatives.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: does.

pays_in.note: A candidate who cannot ask a clean question cannot keep a conversation running.

pays_in.note: A letter of enquiry is a stack of these, and a broken one reads as careless.

Who does Halima teach?

feedback.feed_forward: Read where the helper sits before you answer.
