feedback.why_key: The two questions call for opposite moves, and setting them one under the other is the quickest way to feel where the difference sits.
feedback.feed_forward: Answer each question yourself and see where the name lands.

payload.prompt_text: Using the Part 3 card on conversation, talk for three quarters of a minute and put two of your own questions inside the answer, one asking about a doer and one about anything else. Record it, then hunt for a stray helper.

feedback.why_key: Under speaking pressure the helper goes in everywhere, because one habit is cheaper to run than a decision. Hearing it back is what turns it into a decision again.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen back and mark every helper that was not needed.

title: Answering yes or no without repeating the whole sentence back

point_json.grammar_name: Short answers and agreement echoes

teach.can_do: I can answer a question in three words and say that the same is true of me.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between sounding like a person in a conversation and sounding like somebody reading a sentence back to the examiner.
teach.meaning: Once a question has been asked, everything in it is already on the table, so English throws almost all of it away and keeps two things: the person and the helper. That pair is enough to say yes or no, because the helper carries the time and the person carries the who. The same pair, turned round, says that something is true of you as well, which is how agreement is done without repeating a word of what was said.

form.pattern: Yes, + subject + helper. / No, + subject + helper + not.
notes: the helper must be the one the question used: are you ...? takes I am, do you ...? takes I do
the main verb never comes back: Yes, I do, never Yes, I do work
in the short yes there is no squashing: Yes, I am, not Yes, I'm
So + helper + subject says the same is true of me; Neither + helper + subject does it after a no
form.negative: No, + subject + helper + not, usually squashed: No, I don't. No, she isn't.
form.question: The question hands you the helper. Take it and hand it straight back.

left.role: everything the question put on the table
left.text: Do you swim at the harbour pool?

right.text: Yes, I do.

spec.caption: The answer is not a shortened sentence. It is the two parts that were carrying the work all along.

worked_example.sentence: Yes, I do, and so does my brother.
worked_example.why_this_form: The question supplied do, so the answer hands the same helper back, and turning it round in front of my brother says the same thing is true of him.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Yes, I swim, and my brother swims too is not wrong, but it hands back words that were never in question, and it takes twice as long to say.

notice_set.sentence: Are you on the early train? No, I'm not.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker on the early train?
notice_set.why: Two small words carry the whole refusal, and no part of the question had to be said again.

notice_set.sentence: Does Bea play on Saturdays? Yes, she does.
notice_set.question: Does Bea play on Saturdays?
notice_set.why: The answer keeps the person and the helper, and everything else was already understood by both speakers.

notice_set.sentence: I train on Tuesdays. So does Omar.
notice_set.question: Does Omar train on Tuesdays?
notice_set.why: So plus a helper plus a name says that whatever was just claimed is true of that person too.

notice_set.sentence: I can't swim a length. Neither can Lorna.
notice_set.question: Can Lorna swim a length?
notice_set.why: Neither carries the refusal across, so nothing negative has to be said twice.

notice_set.sentence: Have the others arrived? No, they haven't.
notice_set.question: Are the others there?
notice_set.why: The question offered have, and the answer must send that same helper back rather than any other.

teach.rule_line: Keep the person and the helper the question used. Throw the rest away.
teach.false_rule: That a short answer is rude or lazy. Repeating the whole sentence is what sounds odd; the short answer is the ordinary form.

errors.wrong: Are you coming to the match? Yes, I do.
errors.right: Are you coming to the match? Yes, I am.
errors.why_it_happens: Do has been learned as the all-purpose answer word rather than as one helper among several, so it comes back whatever the question offered.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: do becomes am.

errors.wrong: Do you train at the harbour pool? Yes, I train at the harbour pool.
errors.right: Do you train at the harbour pool? Yes, I do.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught to answer in full sentences and carries that instruction into speech, where handing back words nobody queried sounds stiff and slow.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete four words: train at the harbour pool.

errors.wrong: I swim on Sundays. So do Omar.
errors.right: I swim on Sundays. So does Omar.
errors.why_it_happens: The helper has been copied straight from the first sentence, where it belonged to I. Turning the pair round changes who it belongs to, and the ending has to follow.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: es on do.

errors.wrong: Are you ready? Yes, I'm.
errors.right: Are you ready? Yes, I am.
errors.why_it_happens: Squashing is normal everywhere else, so it is applied here too. A helper at the end of an answer has nothing after it to lean on, and English will not squash a word into silence.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: I'm becomes I am.

pays_in.note: Part 1 is a stream of yes-or-no openings, and the short answer buys you time to add a reason.
pays_in.model: Yes, I do, though mostly at weekends rather than after work.

pays_in.note: Agreeing or disagreeing with the examiner's framing starts with one of these.
pays_in.model: Neither do most of the people I know, if I am honest about it.

pays_in.note: A two-word answer is easy to miss, and it is often where the yes or no actually lives.
pays_in.model: No, she hasn't, but the second group have.

used_in.quote: Every question on this card can be opened with three words, and candidates who cannot build them stall on the first one.

payload.sentence: Is Dev running on Sunday? No, he isn't.
payload.question: Will Dev be running on Sunday?

feedback.why_key: Two words settle it. The helper the question offered comes back with not attached, and that is the whole refusal.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the helper and for not, nothing else.

payload.sentence: I never take the lift. Neither does Tamsin.
payload.question: Does Tamsin take the lift?

feedback.why_key: Neither carries the refusal from the first speaker across to Tamsin, so nothing negative had to be said a second time.
feedback.feed_forward: Read neither as carrying the no across.

payload.context: A teammate asks: Are you playing on Saturday?
payload.sentence: Yes, I do.
reasons: the answer sends back a different helper from the one the question used
the speaker is not playing on Saturday
the answer is too short for the question
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The question handed over are, so are is what has to come back. Do belongs to a question that was never asked.
feedback.feed_forward: Take the helper from the question and return it.

payload.context: At the pool desk.
payload.stem: Does the club meet on Thursdays? Yes, it ___.

expected: does

feedback.why_key: Does went out with the question, so does comes back with the answer, and the club is one thing so the ending stays on it.
feedback.feed_forward: Return the same helper, marked for the new person.

payload.context: Two people comparing what they eat before a long shift.
payload.stem: I never cook in the morning. ___ ___ I.

expected: neither, do
neither do

feedback.why_key: The first speaker refused, so the second carries that refusal across with neither, and the helper comes before the person rather than after.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the helper in front of the person after neither.

payload.context: Somebody has just said they train twice a week. Say the same is true of your side.

expected: so does everyone on my team

feedback.why_key: Everyone is treated as one, so the helper takes the ending, and it sits in front of the person rather than behind.
feedback.feed_forward: Order it so, helper, person, in that sequence.

payload.given: Do you cycle to work? Yes, I cycle to work.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the answer the way somebody would actually say it.

expected: i do
i do.

feedback.why_key: Everything after the helper was already on the table when the question was asked, so handing it back adds length and nothing else.
feedback.feed_forward: Cut everything after the helper.

payload.audio_text: Yes, I do, and so does everyone on my shift.

expected: yes i do and so does everyone on my shift

feedback.why_key: The same helper appears twice with different endings, and the second one is the only thing saying the claim now covers the shift as well.
feedback.feed_forward: Write both helpers before you write anything else.

payload.sentence: I walk in most mornings. So do my sister, when the weather holds.

expected: so does my sister

feedback.why_key: The helper was copied out of the first sentence, where it belonged to the speaker. Turning it round hands it to one sister, and the ending has to follow her.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the helper to the new person, not the old one.

items.decision_cue: the opening line of an essay

payload.context: From the opening line of an essay about whether cities should charge drivers.
payload.sentence: Should cities charge drivers to come in? Yes, they should.
reasons: this is a spoken move, and an essay states the position instead
the answer sends back the wrong helper
the person in the answer is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The pair is built correctly. It belongs in a conversation, where somebody asked; on the page it reads as a person talking to themselves.
feedback.feed_forward: State the position in writing; save the short answer for speech.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody has asked whether you do any sport. Answer in three words, then add one sentence saying that the same is true of somebody else you know.

feedback.why_key: The second half is where the helper has to be re-marked for a new person, and that is the move that fails first under speed.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the short answer first, then add the other person.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 1 card about sport and exercise. Answer four questions from it aloud, opening every one with a short answer before you add anything. Record it and check that each helper matches its question.

feedback.why_key: Four questions in a row will offer at least two different helpers, and reaching for the wrong one is what happens when the answer is planned before the question ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Wait for the helper, then open your answer with it.

title: The verbs that refuse to be caught in the middle of happening

point_json.grammar_name: Stative verbs, and the ones that go both ways

teach.can_do: I can tell which verbs describe a state and leave them in their plain shape.
teach.why_it_matters: I am knowing and I am wanting are among the first errors a listener notices, and they set hard: learners produce them years after they can explain them.
teach.meaning: Some verbs do not name an event at all. They name how things stand: what you know, what you own, what something costs, what you think of it, what it looks like. A state has no middle to be caught in and no edges to stretch between, so the shape that stands you inside an unfinished stretch has nothing to work with. A handful of verbs describe both a state and an activity, and those switch meaning rather than switching shape.

form.pattern: state verbs stay in the plain shape: I know, she wants, it costs, they own
notes: knowing, understanding, believing, wanting, needing, preferring, owning, belonging: states, plain shape only
seeming, looking like, sounding like, costing, weighing, containing: states as well
think, have, see, taste, smell and expect describe a state in the plain shape and an activity in the other one
the plain shape here is not a habit. It is simply how things are.
form.negative: I don't know the answer, never I am not knowing the answer.
form.question: Do you want the last one? never Are you wanting the last one?

left.role: a state, with no middle to stand in
left.text: Ines knows the recipe by heart.

right.role: an activity, with a start and an end
right.text: Ines is learning the timings.

spec.caption: Only the box on the right has a stretch in it. The box on the left is simply how things stand.

worked_example.sentence: Omar wants the corner table for the whole evening.
worked_example.why_this_form: Wanting is not something he starts and stops doing. It is how things stand with him, so there is no stretch for the other shape to stand inside.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Omar is wanting the table would try to catch him halfway through a wanting, and a listener cannot picture the halfway point of a want.

notice_set.sentence: This soup tastes of almost nothing.
notice_set.question: Is anybody doing anything to the soup?
notice_set.why: The sentence reports how the soup is, not an action performed on it, so nothing is under way at all.

notice_set.sentence: The chef is tasting the soup.
notice_set.question: Is anybody doing anything to the soup?
notice_set.why: The same verb has become an activity with a start and an end, and the shape has followed the meaning.

notice_set.sentence: Halima owns the bakery on the harbour road.
notice_set.question: Could she stop owning it in the next ten minutes?
notice_set.why: Owning is not a thing you do, so it cannot be paused, and a verb that cannot be paused has no middle to be caught in.

notice_set.sentence: The new oven costs more than the old one did.
notice_set.question: Is the oven doing anything?
notice_set.why: Costing is a fact about the oven rather than an activity of the oven, which is why the plain shape is the only one available.

notice_set.sentence: Dev is thinking about changing supplier.
notice_set.question: Has he made up his mind?
notice_set.why: Thinking here is an activity with a start and no end yet, which is a different verb from the one that reports an opinion.

discovery.prompt: Each pair uses the same verb. What has changed between the left and the right?
pairs: This soup tastes of almost nothing.
The chef is tasting the soup.
Dev thinks the supplier is too slow.
Dev is thinking about changing supplier.
Halima has a bakery on the harbour road.
Halima is having a difficult month.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the verb reports how things stand; on the right it names something being done.
On the right the sentences are about the present and on the left they are about all time.
Verbs like taste, think and have never take the -ing shape.

teach.rule_line: If you could not stop it in ten minutes, you were not doing it. Use the plain shape.
teach.false_rule: That a list of forbidden verbs settles it. Half of them take both shapes, and what changes is the meaning, not the correctness.

contrast.question: Is this something being done, or a way things stand?

fork.answer: A way things stand: what you know, own, want, or what something costs or seems
Something being done, with a start behind it and an end ahead
A verb that does both, such as think, have, see or taste
fork.selects: either shape, and the meaning changes with it

a.text: Ines has lunch at the depot.
a.means: That is where her lunch happens as a matter of course.

b.text: Ines is having lunch at the depot.
b.means: She is at the table with the food in front of her.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Stretching a state verb does not produce a different meaning. It produces no meaning at all, because there is no halfway point of knowing something for a listener to picture, and they stall trying to find one.

edge_case.text: You will meet I'm loving this and I'm liking the new one in advertising and in casual speech. They are deliberate rule-breaks and they work because the rule is felt. They belong in a conversation and nowhere near an essay.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether you could stop doing it in the next ten minutes. If you cannot stop it, you were never doing it, and the plain shape is the only one on offer.

worked_pairs.a: Tamsin has the keys to the cold store.
worked_pairs.b: Tamsin is having trouble with the cold store.
worked_pairs.gloss: Holding keys is how things stand. Having trouble is something that started and will end, so the same verb takes two shapes.

worked_pairs.a: Omar sees the difficulty with the delivery slot.
worked_pairs.b: Omar is seeing the supplier about the delivery slot.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is understanding, which has no middle. The second is a meeting, which has a start, an end and a doorway.

worked_pairs.a: The stall smells of smoked fish.
worked_pairs.b: The inspector is smelling the fish before he signs it off.
worked_pairs.gloss: A stall is not doing anything. An inspector is, and you could interrupt him halfway through it.

errors.wrong: I am knowing the answer to that one.
errors.right: I know the answer to that one.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner wants to mark that this is true right at this moment and reaches for the shape that means right at this moment. Nothing warns them that knowing has no moment to be marked.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two letters and one word: am and the -ing.
errors.l1_note: Several languages allow the stretched shape with verbs of knowing and wanting.

errors.wrong: She is wanting a table for six on Friday.
errors.right: She wants a table for six on Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The stretched shape has been learned as the polite or the current one, so it is used for anything happening around now, including things that are not happening at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is wanting becomes wants.

errors.wrong: The new oven is costing four hundred pounds.
errors.right: The new oven costs four hundred pounds.
errors.why_it_happens: A price feels like something happening in front of the learner, especially while they are looking at a label. Costing is a fact about the oven and the oven is doing nothing.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is costing becomes costs.

errors.wrong: Dev thinks about changing supplier, so he has asked for three quotes.
errors.right: Dev is thinking about changing supplier, so he has asked for three quotes.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has over-learned the ban and applies it to think in both its meanings. Here think is an activity going on in his head, and the ban does not reach it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: thinks becomes is thinking.

pays_in.note: Opinions, preferences and what you own are all states, and Part 1 asks about all three.
pays_in.model: I prefer the market to the supermarket, mostly because I know the people there.

pays_in.note: An essay is full of what people believe, want and need, and every one of them is plain.

title: Choosing between how things generally are and what is going on at the moment

point_json.grammar_name: Present simple vs present continuous

teach.can_do: I can choose between the two present shapes on purpose, and say what the other one would have claimed.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the first choice in the course where both answers are correct English. What decides it is the situation, and getting it wrong says something you did not mean.
teach.meaning: The two shapes are not near and far from now. They are two different claims about the same stretch of time. The plain verb hands over the standing arrangement: how things are set up, what holds whether or not anyone is looking. The stretched shape puts your listener inside an unfinished period with an edge behind and an edge ahead. Same event, two claims: one about the arrangement, one about the stretch you are standing in.

form.pattern: subject + plain verb, against subject + am / is / are + verb + -ing
notes: the plain verb also covers timetables, rules, instructions and anything that repeats
the stretched shape also covers temporary arrangements and changes still under way
state verbs take only the plain shape, whatever the situation is
a whole paragraph should not drift between the two without a reason a reader can see
form.negative: He doesn't work here against He isn't working here this month: the same choice, made twice.
form.question: Do you work here? asks about the arrangement. Are you working here? asks about the stretch.

left.text: Rosa works at the Norland ferry office.

right.text: Rosa is working at the Norland ferry office.

spec.caption: Both are true of the same woman on the same afternoon. Only one of them says she will still be there in a year.

worked_example.sentence: More of the outer estates are losing their evening bus.
worked_example.why_this_form: The withdrawal has begun and has not settled, so the sentence puts the reader inside it rather than reporting a finished state of affairs.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Lose their evening bus would report the arrangement as settled, and a reader would take the cuts as over rather than as still coming.

notice_set.sentence: Halima runs the bakery on the harbour road.
notice_set.question: Would you expect her to be there next year?
notice_set.why: The plain verb reports the standing arrangement, and an arrangement is assumed to hold until something changes it.

notice_set.sentence: Halima is running the bakery on the harbour road.
notice_set.question: Would you expect her to be there next year?
notice_set.why: The stretch has an edge somewhere ahead, so the sentence quietly declines to say how far ahead it is.

notice_set.sentence: The last train leaves at eleven.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker describing something happening in front of them?
notice_set.why: A timetable is a rule about every night, and a rule has no single evening to stand inside.

notice_set.sentence: More people are working from home than a decade ago.
notice_set.question: Has the change finished?
notice_set.why: A change still moving takes the stretched shape, however many years the stretch turns out to cover.

notice_set.sentence: Omar drives the school minibus, but he is covering the depot run this fortnight.
notice_set.question: Which of the two is his usual job?
notice_set.why: One shape reports the arrangement and the other marks a stretch with an end in sight, and the sentence uses both on purpose.

discovery.prompt: Each pair describes the same person on the same afternoon. What is different about what the two sentences claim?
pairs: Halima runs the bakery on the harbour road.
Halima is running the bakery on the harbour road.
Omar drives the school minibus.
Omar is driving the school minibus this fortnight.
Fewer households keep a car in the centre.
Fewer households are keeping a car in the centre.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the sentence reports a standing arrangement; on the right it marks a stretch with an end somewhere ahead.
On the right the events are closer to the present moment.
The right-hand version is used whenever the sentence is about the present.

teach.rule_line: Ask: is this how it is set up, or something I am standing in the middle of?
teach.false_rule: That the plain verb is for habits and the stretched one is for now. A change under way runs for a decade and still takes the stretch.

contrast.question: Am I reporting the arrangement or standing inside an unfinished stretch?

fork.answer: The arrangement: how it is set up, what repeats, what a timetable or a rule says
An unfinished stretch: something under way, something temporary, something still changing
A state, such as knowing, owning, wanting or costing
fork.selects: the plain verb, whatever the situation

a.text: Rosa works at the Norland ferry office.
a.means: That is her job, and nothing in the sentence puts an end on it.

b.text: Rosa is working at the Norland ferry office.
b.means: That is where she is for the time being, and it will finish.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Stretching the verb over a permanent job does not sound broken. It sounds like a temporary posting, and your listener will ask when it ends. The wrong choice here produces a clear sentence saying something you never meant.

edge_case.text: The stretched shape with always is a complaint rather than a mistake: he is always leaving the gate open. It is standard, it is deliberate, and it belongs in speech rather than in an essay.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether the sentence would still be true in three years. If yes, the plain verb. If the honest answer is that it depends, you are inside a stretch.

worked_pairs.a: The council collects the glass on a Thursday.
worked_pairs.b: The council is collecting the glass by hand while the lorry is off the road.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: while the lorry is off the road
worked_pairs.gloss: A day of the week names a slot that repeats. A broken lorry names a stretch that will end when it is mended.

worked_pairs.a: Dev teaches two evening classes at the college.
worked_pairs.b: Dev is teaching two evening classes until the new tutor starts.
worked_pairs.gloss: The second sentence names the far edge out loud, and once an edge is named the arrangement can no longer be reported as settled.

worked_pairs.a: Fewer households keep a car in the centre than in the outer districts.
worked_pairs.b: Fewer households are keeping a car in the centre than five years ago.
worked_pairs.gloss: Comparing two places compares two settled arrangements. Comparing two dates traces a change, and a change that is still moving takes the stretch.

errors.wrong: I am living in Sandmouth. My family has been here for three generations.
errors.right: I live in Sandmouth. My family has been here for three generations.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught that the stretched shape is the one for now, and where they live is true now. Three generations says the arrangement is about as settled as an arrangement gets.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: am living becomes live.

errors.wrong: The number of small shops falls every year and the high street empties as we speak.
errors.right: The number of small shops falls every year and the high street is emptying as we speak.
errors.why_it_happens: Each half was chosen on its own and the second half quietly reports a change under way as though it were a settled fact. Nobody reads the two claims side by side.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: empties becomes is emptying.

errors.wrong: Rosa works at the ferry office. She is starting at six and she finishes at two.
errors.right: Rosa works at the ferry office. She starts at six and she finishes at two.
errors.why_it_happens: The middle verb was picked while the writer was picturing the morning, and the two either side were picked while they were reporting a rota. It always shows up in the second half of a timed task.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is starting becomes starts.

errors.wrong: More people are preferring to shop near where they live.
errors.right: More people prefer to shop near where they live.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer is describing a change and reaches for the change shape without checking the verb. Preferring is a state, and a state refuses the stretch even in a sentence about change.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are preferring becomes prefer.

pays_in.note: A stem that swaps a change under way for a settled fact is false on the shape alone.

payload.context: Salim is answering a question about where he comes from, and his family has been in the town for three generations.

reasons: the stretched shape puts an end on something that is settled
he does not live in Sandmouth
the small word in front of the verb is wrong

payload.context: From a report on how a small firm handles orders.
payload.stem: The office ___ (open) at eight every morning, but the team ___ (work) from home this month while the roof is repaired.

expected: opens, is working
opens is working
opens, are working

feedback.why_key: One half reports the standing arrangement and the other names an edge, the repaired roof, which is exactly what turns an arrangement into a stretch.

payload.context: Answering a question about your working week.
payload.stem: I ___ (start) at seven most days, though I ___ (cover) the late shift until Friday.

expected: start, am covering
start am covering

feedback.why_key: Most days is the arrangement and until Friday is the far edge of a stretch, so one sentence needs both shapes and neither is a slip.

payload.given: Ten years ago most houses here had a coal fire. Very few do.
payload.instruction: Turn it into one sentence reporting a change that has not stopped.

expected: are burning coal
are using coal
are keeping a coal fire

payload.context: Write one line for a timetable notice.

expected: the first ferry sails at six every morning

feedback.why_key: A timetable is a rule about every morning, so there is no single sailing to stand inside and the plain verb is the only fit.

payload.audio_text: He works in Marlow, but he's covering Sandmouth this month.

expected: he works in marlow but he's covering sandmouth this month
he works in marlow but he is covering sandmouth this month
he works in marlow but hes covering sandmouth this month

feedback.why_key: The second shape collapses onto the person ahead of it, and that collapsed beat is all that marks the second half as temporary.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the squashed beat after the person.

title: Putting a past moment inside something that was already going on

point_json.grammar_name: Past continuous

teach.can_do: I can describe what was already going on when something else happened.
teach.why_it_matters: Without it every story is a flat list of events. This form is what lets a listener see the scene the events landed in.
teach.meaning: Was or were plus an -ing word takes an activity and stretches it across a piece of past time, so that other things can happen inside it. It does not tell you the activity finished — only that it was running while you were looking. That is why it is the form English reaches for when it wants to hand you a picture instead of a fact: somebody standing on a platform, rain falling, a queue not moving.

form.pattern: was / were + the -ing word  (was waiting · were queuing)
notes: One thing takes was; more than one, and you, take were
The -ing word is the same one you already use for what is happening now
A few verbs describe a state rather than an activity and stay out of this form: know, want, own, mean, believe
In speech was and were shrink to almost nothing and the -ing word carries the sound
form.negative: was not / wasn't + -ing  ·  were not / weren't + -ing
form.question: Were you + -ing ...?

marks.label: the moment that lands inside it

spec.caption: The bar is what this form draws. The cross is somebody else's sentence.

worked_example.sentence: The 7.40 was standing at the platform with its doors open.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence hands you a picture rather than an event. The train had not just arrived and had not yet left; it was simply there when you looked.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Stood would report it as one finished thing the train did, and would not put you on the platform looking at it at all.

notice_set.sentence: The barriers were closing as I reached the crossing.
notice_set.question: Were the barriers fully down when the speaker arrived?
notice_set.why: The form catches the movement halfway through, so the barriers are still on their way down.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody was checking tickets on the late train.
notice_set.question: What would you have seen if you had walked through the carriage?
notice_set.why: The form describes the state of the carriage across a stretch, not one moment of it.

notice_set.sentence: We were waiting on the wrong side of the station.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker say whether the train came?
notice_set.why: The waiting is a scene. Whether anything arrived is a separate sentence that has not been said.

notice_set.sentence: The lifts weren't working at Ashfield that week.
notice_set.question: Could a passenger use a lift on the Wednesday of that week?
notice_set.why: Stretching the fault across the week puts every day of it inside the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: I knew the driver from the depot.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker describing something they did, or something that was simply true?
notice_set.why: Knowing is not an activity you can be caught in the middle of, which is why English leaves this verb alone.

teach.rule_line: Was or were plus -ing paints what was already going on, not what happened.
teach.false_rule: That the -ing form means the action took a long time. It can last two seconds. It means you are watching it run, not counting it as done.

errors.wrong: I was knowing the driver from the depot.
errors.right: I knew the driver from the depot.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is setting a scene, and this is the scene-setting form, so it gets applied to everything in the scene — including the things that are simply true rather than going on.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was knowing becomes knew.

errors.wrong: The bus was arriving at nine and we got on.
errors.right: The bus arrived at nine and we got on.
errors.why_it_happens: A named clock time feels like a scene, so the scene-setting form arrives with it. Arriving at a stated time is a single landing, not a stretch anything can happen inside.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was arriving becomes arrived.

errors.wrong: We were wanting a later train, so we changed the booking.
errors.right: We wanted a later train, so we changed the booking.
errors.why_it_happens: Wanting feels like something going on inside you, and in a sense it is. English still files it with the states and keeps it out of this form.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: were wanting becomes wanted.

pays_in.note: The long turn needs a scene before it can have events in it.
pays_in.model: It was pouring when we got to the ferry terminal and half the crossings were already cancelled.

pays_in.note: A background clause explains why the example that follows it happened at all.
pays_in.model: Fares were rising steadily, and the council chose that moment to cut two of the evening services.

pays_in.note: The two small words in front of the -ing word almost vanish at speed.
pays_in.model: They were working on the line, so the last two trains were replaced by a bus.

used_in.quote: A journey you remember well needs a scene before it needs events, and the scene is built out of this form.
The speakers describe what was going on at the time of booking, and one answer turns on hearing the two small words.

payload.sentence: The barriers were closing as I reached the crossing.
payload.question: Were the barriers fully down at that moment?

feedback.why_key: The form catches the movement halfway through, so the barriers are still on their way down.
feedback.feed_forward: Read this form as a picture taken mid-action.

payload.sentence: Crews were repairing the sea wall along the Sandmouth front.
payload.question: Where does this sit?
options: a stretch of past time with room inside it

feedback.why_key: The repair is drawn as a stretch, which is exactly why another event can be dropped into the middle of it.

title: Choosing between the event and the scene it happened inside

point_json.grammar_name: Past simple vs past continuous

teach.can_do: I can decide whether to report an event or paint the scene it happened inside.
teach.why_it_matters: Both forms are correct English and you can already build both. What costs marks is choosing the wrong one, and it happens in every story anybody tells.
teach.meaning: These two forms do not describe different events. They describe the same event from two distances. The plain past treats it as a whole thing that landed and finished, so the story can move on to the next item. Was or were plus -ing holds the same thing open and unfinished, so that something else can happen inside it. Choose the first for what happened; choose the second for what was already going on when it happened.

form.pattern: the event: plain past  ·  the scene: was / were + -ing
notes: A chain of finished events is all plain past, one after another
The scene usually comes first and the event lands inside it
Two scenes can run side by side; two events cannot happen at once unless you say so
The state verbs stay out of the -ing form no matter which job they are doing
form.negative: did not check  ·  was not checking
form.question: Did you check ...?  ·  Were you checking ...?

left.text: The guide was checking the tickets.

right.text: The guide checked the tickets.

spec.caption: The event drops into the scene. Reverse them and the story stops making sense.

worked_example.sentence: The rain was coming straight off the sea when the coach finally pulled in.
worked_example.why_this_form: The rain was there before the coach and stayed after it. Holding it open is what lets the arrival land inside it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Came would make the rain a second event, so the reader would understand that it began at the moment the coach appeared.

notice_set.sentence: We were queuing outside the museum when the doors opened.
notice_set.question: Had the queuing begun before the doors opened?

notice_set.sentence: We queued outside the museum and the doors opened.
notice_set.question: Which order does this sentence put things in?
notice_set.why: Two closed events in a row are read in the order they are written. Nothing sits inside anything else.

notice_set.sentence: The guide was talking to the driver and nobody heard the announcement.
notice_set.question: Was the talking finished before the announcement?
notice_set.why: The talking is held open across the announcement, which is exactly why it swallowed it.

notice_set.sentence: It rained on the second day of the trip.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence hand you a picture of the rain, or a fact about it?
notice_set.why: The closed form counts the rain as one whole item in the record of the trip.

notice_set.sentence: We booked the tickets, packed on the Friday and left before six.
notice_set.question: How many separate steps are being reported?
notice_set.why: A chain of finished steps is all in the closed form, and that is what makes it read as a chain.

discovery.prompt: The sentences on the left and on the right describe the same trip. What is different about how the speaker is standing?
pairs: We were queuing outside the museum when the doors opened.
We queued outside the museum and the doors opened.
The guide was talking to the driver.
The guide talked to the driver.
It was raining on the second day of the trip.
It rained on the second day of the trip.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the speaker is inside the moment, watching something that has not finished.
On the left the actions lasted longer than the ones on the right.
On the left the sentence has a word like while or suddenly somewhere in it.

teach.rule_line: Ask: is this the event, or the scene the event happened inside?
teach.false_rule: That the -ing form is for long actions and the plain past for short ones. Length has nothing to do with it. A two-second action can be held open and a ten-year one can be closed.

contrast.question: Is this the event, or the scene the event happened inside?

fork.answer: The event: it lands, it is finished, and the story moves on to the next thing
The scene: it was already running, and something else happens inside it
fork.selects: was or were plus the -ing word

a.text: When the coach arrived, the guide checked the tickets.
a.means: The coach came first and the checking started afterwards. Two steps, in that order.

b.text: When the coach arrived, the guide was checking the tickets.
b.means: The checking was already under way, and the coach turned up in the middle of it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose was collecting. That says the collecting was still running when the coach pulled out, so somebody was left behind on the pavement. If the collecting finished first, the closed form is the honest one.

edge_case.text: A run of completed events is all plain past, every one of them. Learners who fall in love with the -ing form narrate whole holidays in it, and the result is a page of scenery in which nothing ever happens.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover the rest of the sentence and ask what a photograph of that instant would show. If the photograph would catch something half-done, hold it open. If it would show a thing already over, close it.

worked_pairs.a: We were queuing for the boat when the storm warning went up.
worked_pairs.b: We queued for the boat and walked back to the hotel.

worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: and walked back to the hotel
worked_pairs.gloss: The first drops a moment into the queue. The second counts the queue as one finished item and moves straight on to the next.

worked_pairs.a: The guide was pointing at the ruins, so nobody noticed the path.
worked_pairs.b: The guide pointed at the ruins and everybody looked up.
worked_pairs.gloss: Held open, the pointing covers the whole moment and hides the path. Closed, it is one gesture that gets one response.

worked_pairs.a: It was raining hard in Sandmouth that morning.
worked_pairs.b: It rained hard in Sandmouth that morning.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is a scene waiting for something to happen in it. The second is a closed fact about the weather and the morning is over.

errors.wrong: The coach was arriving at the terminal and we climbed on board.
errors.right: The coach arrived at the terminal and we climbed on board.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer wants the sentence to feel vivid, and the held-open form feels more vivid. Two events in a chain do not need atmosphere; they need order.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was arriving becomes arrived.

errors.wrong: We were leaving the hotel, we were catching the ferry and we were reaching the island before noon.
errors.right: We left the hotel, caught the ferry and reached the island before noon.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught the -ing form as the storytelling form and applies it to the whole story. Every event turns into scenery, and a reader is left waiting for something to happen.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: were leaving becomes left, and the rest follow.

errors.wrong: I read the guidebook when the lights went out in the carriage.
errors.right: I was reading the guidebook when the lights went out in the carriage.
errors.why_it_happens: The reading feels like the important action, so it takes the strong closed form. That turns it into a response to the darkness rather than the thing the darkness interrupted.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: read becomes was reading.

title: Saying that something was true for a stretch of the past and is not true now

point_json.grammar_name: used to, and how it differs from would and from the plain past

teach.can_do: I can say that something was the case for a stretch of the past and has since stopped.
teach.why_it_matters: There are three ways to talk about a past habit and they are not the same. Choosing between them is what makes an answer about your childhood sound like English rather than translation.
teach.meaning: Used to makes two claims in three words. First, this was the case over a stretch of past time, not on one occasion. Second, it has stopped. The second claim is the one nobody teaches and the one that does the work: the moment you say used to, your listener understands that things are different now. If that is not what you mean, this is not the phrase you want.

form.pattern: used to + the plain verb  (used to live · used to walk · there used to be)
notes: The d is silent in speech, so it sounds like use to — but it is written used to
After did the d comes off: didn't use to, did you use to
Would plus the plain verb can do repeated actions once the past scene is already set, and it reads as fond or reflective
Would cannot carry a state: there would be a ferry is not an option, and this rule decides most cases
form.negative: did not use to / didn't use to + the plain verb
form.question: Did you use to + the plain verb ...?

left.text: There used to be a bakery on the corner.

right.text: There is no bakery.

spec.caption: The second box comes free with the phrase, whether or not anybody says it out loud.

worked_example.sentence: We used to live above the shop on Bridge Street.
worked_example.why_this_form: It was the case for a stretch of years rather than on one day, and the speaker is telling you plainly that it stopped.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: We lived above the shop reports the same years without promising anything about today; the speaker could still be there for all the sentence says.

notice_set.sentence: There used to be a bakery on the corner of Bridge Street.
notice_set.question: Can you buy bread there today?
notice_set.why: The phrase brings the second claim with it: this has stopped. That is why nobody has to add it.

notice_set.sentence: We lived above the shop for six years.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker tell you whether they still live there?
notice_set.why: The plain past simply reports the six years. Whether they moved is a separate sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Every summer we would walk the ridge path before breakfast.
notice_set.question: Is this about one walk or about a habit?
notice_set.why: The summer sets the scene first, and only then can this word take on repeated actions inside it.

notice_set.sentence: I used to know the whole street by name.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker still know everybody's name?
notice_set.why: This works with a state as easily as with an action, which is exactly where the other option cannot follow.

notice_set.sentence: The rent went up three times that year.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker telling you the rises have stopped?
notice_set.why: A stated number of occasions is a report, not a habit, and the plain past is the only honest choice for it.

teach.rule_line: Used to means it was the case then, and it is not the case now.
teach.false_rule: That used to and would are two ways of saying the same thing. Would cannot carry a state at all, and that single rule decides most of the cases you will meet.

errors.wrong: There use to be a bakery on the corner of Bridge Street.
errors.right: There used to be a bakery on the corner of Bridge Street.
errors.why_it_happens: The d is silent in front of to, so the ear never hears it. The learner writes exactly what they say, which is the right instinct and the wrong spelling.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: use becomes used.

errors.wrong: We used to living above the shop on Bridge Street.
errors.right: We used to live above the shop on Bridge Street.
errors.why_it_happens: To is followed by an -ing word in several phrases the learner already owns, such as look forward to. The pull of that pattern is strong and nothing here resists it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: living becomes live.

errors.wrong: Did you used to rent out the top floor?
errors.right: Did you use to rent out the top floor?
errors.why_it_happens: The phrase is stored as one lump with its d attached, so it comes out whole even after the helper word has already taken the past away.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: used becomes use.

errors.wrong: The flats would be cheaper before the new line opened.
errors.right: The flats were cheaper before the new line opened.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told this word does past habits and applies it to a past situation. It only handles repeated actions, and being cheap is not an action anybody repeats.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would be becomes were.
