payload.sentence: There would be a bakery on the corner and everybody would walk down for bread.
reasons: the first half is a state, and that word cannot carry a state
the second half is a repeated action and does not belong
the bakery should be named
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The walking is a repeated action and survives. The bakery simply being there is not an action anybody repeats, so it has to change.
feedback.feed_forward: Test each half: is it a state or a repeated action?

payload.sentence: Did you used to rent out the top floor before the survey was done?

expected: did you use to

feedback.why_key: The helper word has already taken the past, so the phrase behind it gives up its letter exactly as any other verb gives up its ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip the d whenever did is in front.

payload.prompt_text: Something about your home area that has changed. Write two sentences: one about a state that has ended, and one about an action you repeated when the scene was already set.

feedback.why_key: The state forces one choice and the repeated action allows two, which is the whole shape of this decision in two sentences.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask state or action before you choose the words.

payload.prompt_text: You have two minutes on the card A place you used to go to as a child. Use the phrase at least twice for states that have ended, and let the plain past carry anything you did on one particular visit. One minute to plan.

feedback.why_key: The card is built out of this choice, and mixing the three ways of saying a past habit is what makes an answer sound settled rather than rehearsed.
feedback.feed_forward: Separate the standing state from the one particular day.

title: Telling a past story in an order a listener can follow

point_json.grammar_name: Narrative sequence: the past chain and its joining words

teach.can_do: I can tell a past story so that a listener always knows which part came first.
teach.why_it_matters: The two-minute long turn is a narrative task. A story told out of order costs marks nobody will ever explain to you, because the listener simply stops following.
teach.meaning: A story is a chain: finished event, finished event, finished event, told in the order they happened. The plain past carries the chain, one link at a time. The held-open form drops in wherever you want the listener to see the scene rather than the next step, and the joining words tell them where they are standing. Change nothing about the verbs and the order still works, because English trusts the order of the sentences.

form.pattern: plain past + plain past + plain past, with the joining words between
notes: First, After that and In the end open a sentence and take a comma
While plus was or were plus -ing gives the scene the next event lands in
Keep the events in the order they happened unless you say plainly that you are jumping back
Two or three joining words in a whole story is plenty; one on every sentence reads like a recipe
form.negative: did not tell the rest of it until later
form.question: What happened after that?

spec.caption: Three crosses in a row are the chain. The bar underneath them is the scene they happened in.

worked_example.sentence: We reached the square at seven, found a place near the railings and waited for the procession.
worked_example.why_this_form: Three finished steps in the order they happened, joined without fuss. The listener never has to work out what followed what.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Were reaching, were finding and were waiting would turn all three steps into scenery, and the listener would still be waiting for the story to begin.

notice_set.sentence: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd went quiet.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Nothing tells you the order except the order, and in a chain of finished steps that is enough.

notice_set.sentence: The square was filling up while we looked for a place at the front.
notice_set.question: Was the square empty when they arrived?
notice_set.why: The filling is held open around the looking, so it was already under way before they got there.

notice_set.sentence: We got there late. The procession had passed an hour earlier.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Here the order of the sentences and the order of events come apart, and the second sentence has to say so.

notice_set.sentence: After that, nobody moved for twenty minutes.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you what came before it?
notice_set.why: A joining word points backwards without repeating anything, which is exactly why a story needs a few of them.

notice_set.sentence: In the end we walked home along the harbour.
notice_set.question: Is this near the start or near the finish of the story?
notice_set.why: Some joining words carry a position in the story as part of their meaning, and a listener uses them to know when to relax.

teach.rule_line: Keep the chain in the plain past and let the joining words carry the order.
teach.false_rule: That a story sounds livelier told in the held-open form. A story told entirely in it has scenery on every side and no events anywhere.

errors.wrong: The procession finished and after that everybody was going home.
errors.right: The procession finished and after that everybody went home.
errors.why_it_happens: The last step of a story often gets stretched for effect, as if a slow ending were a better one. It stops the chain from closing and leaves the listener waiting.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: was going becomes went.

errors.wrong: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd goes quiet.
errors.right: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd went quiet.
errors.why_it_happens: The last link in a chain is chosen when the writer is already thinking about the next sentence, and it defaults to the shape they use most often.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: goes becomes went.

errors.wrong: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody is finding a seat.
errors.right: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody found a seat.
errors.why_it_happens: The joining word feels as if it has already done the work of placing the sentence in time, so the verb is left to look after itself and does not.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is finding becomes found.

pays_in.note: The whole long turn is this, from the first sentence to the last.
pays_in.model: We got there at six, waited near the railings and left before the crowd did.

pays_in.note: An example is a small story, and it fails if the order fails.
pays_in.model: The council trialled the scheme for a year, published the figures and quietly dropped it.

pays_in.note: Ordering questions turn on the joining words rather than on the events.
pays_in.model: After that the group moved to the second hall, and the talk started twenty minutes late.

used_in.quote: A time you took part in a traditional occasion is a chain of finished steps with one scene behind it, which is this point exactly.
The order of the steps in the enrolment is what several answers depend on, and the joining words are the only signposts given.

payload.sentence: The drummers started, the lights went down and the crowd went quiet.
payload.question: Which of these happened first?

feedback.why_key: Nothing states the order except the order itself, and in a chain of finished steps that is all a listener needs.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a chain straight through and trust the order.

payload.sentence: The square was filling up while we looked for a place at the front.
payload.question: Was the square empty when they arrived?

feedback.why_key: The filling is held open around the searching, so it had started before they got anywhere near the front.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the scene before you place the steps.

payload.context: Somebody telling the story of an evening at a street festival.
payload.sentence: The band came on, the doors closed and the crowd goes quiet.
reasons: the last link in the chain has slipped into the present
the doors should not have closed
the crowd went quiet too early
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two links are closed and the third is not, so the story stops being a story halfway through the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the last verb of every chain you write.

payload.context: From an account of an evening at the arts centre in Verdon.
payload.stem: We reached the hall at seven and ___ (find) a seat near the back.

expected: found

feedback.why_key: Two finished steps in a row, so the second one closes exactly as the first did.
feedback.feed_forward: Match every link in the chain to the one before it.

payload.context: From the same account, three sentences later.
payload.stem: The hall ___ (fill) up while the first group tuned their instruments.

expected: was filling

feedback.why_key: This one is the scene rather than a step, and the tuning is what happens inside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold the scene open and close the steps.

payload.context: Build the next sentence of a story that already has two steps in it.

expected: after that the procession turned into the harbour road

feedback.why_key: The joining word opens the sentence and points backwards without repeating a word of what came before.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the joining word, then give the next step.

payload.given: The rain started. We were standing at the front of the crowd.
payload.instruction: Join these into one sentence in which the standing is the scene and the rain is the event.

expected: were standing at the front of the crowd when the rain started
were standing at the front of the crowd when it started to rain

feedback.why_key: The scene has to be open for the event to land in it, and putting the scene first is what tells a listener which is which.
feedback.feed_forward: Scene first, then the event that lands in it.

payload.audio_text: After that we walked home and nobody said much.

expected: after that we walked home and nobody said much

feedback.why_key: The ending on the first verb is a single consonant at speed, and it is the only thing keeping the sentence in the story.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the ending you heard, not the one you expected.

payload.context: From the middle of a story about a village hall meeting.
payload.sentence: We arrived at the hall, and after that everybody is finding a seat.
reasons: the joining word cannot place the sentence in time on its own
the meeting was not in a hall
arriving and sitting down are the same step
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The joining word points backwards but it does not carry the past. Only the verb can do that.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the verb yourself; the joining word will not.

payload.sentence: The procession finished and after that everybody was going home.

expected: went home

feedback.why_key: The last step of a story has to close, or the listener is left standing in the square waiting for the rest.
feedback.feed_forward: Close the final step of every story.

items.decision_cue: We got to the square and the procession passed.

payload.context: Two versions of the same evening, written by two people who were there.
sentences: We got to the square and the procession passed.
We got to the square. The procession had passed an hour earlier.
meanings: They arrived first and saw the procession go by afterwards.
They missed it: the procession was over before they arrived.

feedback.why_key: In the first, the order of the sentences is the order of events. In the second, the writer has to say plainly that it is not.
feedback.feed_forward: Say so explicitly whenever you jump backwards.

parts: The hall filled up slowly.
The first speaker arrived twenty minutes late.
Nobody complained about the delay.
model_combinations: The hall was filling up slowly when the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late, and nobody complained.
The hall filled up slowly, the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late and nobody complained about the delay.
While the hall was still filling up, the first speaker arrived twenty minutes late, and not one person complained.

feedback.why_key: One of the three facts is the scene and the other two are steps, and choosing which is which is the whole task.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide which fact is the scene, then chain the rest.

payload.prompt_text: An occasion you took part in. Write three short sentences telling what happened, in order, with one joining word and no more.

feedback.why_key: Three closed steps and one signpost is the whole shape of a spoken story, and adding more signposts makes it worse rather than clearer.
feedback.feed_forward: Use one joining word; let the order do the rest.

payload.prompt_text: You have two minutes on the card A time you took part in a traditional occasion. One scene at the start, then a chain of closed steps, then a closed ending. Two joining words at most. One minute to plan.

feedback.why_key: This is the task the whole unit has been building towards: a scene, a chain and an ending that actually ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Plan three steps before you start speaking.

title: Saying what is already in the diary with a time and usually another person

point_json.grammar_name: Present continuous for fixed future arrangements

teach.can_do: I can say what is already arranged for later, with a time attached and usually somebody else expecting me.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the shape English uses for a diary, and learners who do not have it say everything about next week with will, which sounds like nothing has been settled.
teach.meaning: The -ing shape normally says that something is going on around now. Pointed at later, it says something slightly different but very close: the arrangement is going on around now, even though the event itself is not. A time has been picked, a place is usually known, and somebody else is involved and expecting you. That is why it feels solid. You are not saying what you believe or what you have decided alone; you are reading out something that already exists between you and another person.

form.pattern: am / is / are + the -ing verb, with a later time said or understood
notes: the shape is exactly the one you use for things going on around now; the time word is what points it forward
without a later time in the sentence or in the conversation, a listener will hear it as right now
verbs about states rather than doings resist the -ing shape here as much as anywhere else
form.negative: am not / isn't / aren't + the -ing verb: We aren't running the Tuesday session this month.
form.question: Am, is or are + person + the -ing verb: Are you seeing the supervisor on Friday?

left.text: the arrangement, with a time and another person in it

right.text: the event itself

spec.caption: The thing that is going on around now is the arrangement, not the event.

worked_example.sentence: I'm seeing the site manager at four to go through the survey.
worked_example.why_this_form: A time has been agreed and somebody else has it written down too. The speaker is reading out something that already exists between them.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: I'll see the site manager at four would sound as if the speaker had just thought of it and the manager knew nothing about it.

notice_set.sentence: Halvard is starting at the Norland office on the ninth.
notice_set.question: Do other people already know about this?
notice_set.why: A date this exact does not exist unless somebody else has agreed to it.

notice_set.sentence: We're taking the last train back on Sunday evening.
notice_set.question: Has a time already been settled?
notice_set.why: The train has a departure time and the speakers have picked it, so the arrangement exists before the sentence does.

notice_set.sentence: Lenka is moving into the flat above the bakery.
notice_set.question: Is this happening at this exact moment, or later?
notice_set.why: The shape is the same for both. What decides it is the time word, or the conversation it sits in.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic isn't taking walk-in patients next Thursday.
notice_set.question: Is this something the clinic has decided in advance?
notice_set.why: A named day tells you the arrangement was made before anyone said this sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Bo and I are meeting the landlord about the damp.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker alone in this?
notice_set.why: Two other people are inside the arrangement, which is the usual situation for this shape.

teach.rule_line: If a time is agreed and somebody else expects you, use the -ing shape.
teach.false_rule: That the -ing shape can only mean right now. Point it at a day next week and it says the day is already fixed.

errors.wrong: I meeting my supervisor at half four on Wednesday.
errors.right: I'm meeting my supervisor at half four on Wednesday.
errors.why_it_happens: The -ing verb carries all the meaning, so the small word in front carries none and quietly falls out, especially in speech where it is barely audible in the first place.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: am.

errors.wrong: We are having the laboratory results by Friday afternoon.
errors.right: We will have the laboratory results by Friday afternoon.
errors.why_it_happens: Having here means simply possessing, not doing anything, and a verb that describes a state rather than an activity will not go into the -ing shape however firmly the day has been agreed.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are having becomes will have.

errors.wrong: Rents in the city are rising sharply next year.
errors.right: Rents in the city will probably rise sharply next year.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the shape points forward and stops there. Nobody arranges the rent market, so the sentence claims a diary entry that could not exist.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are rising becomes will probably rise.

errors.wrong: Sorry, I can't come, I will help my sister move house on Saturday.
errors.right: Sorry, I can't come, I'm helping my sister move house on Saturday.
errors.why_it_happens: Will is the future the learner reaches for first, so a promise already made to somebody else comes out sounding as if it were being invented on the spot as an excuse.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will help becomes am helping.

pays_in.note: Any question about your week is answered in this shape.
pays_in.model: I'm doing an evening class on Tuesdays until the end of March.

pays_in.note: A letter changing or confirming an arrangement runs on it.
pays_in.model: I'm arriving on the Thursday evening rather than the Friday morning.

pays_in.note: Booking and enrolment conversations state the settled dates this way.
pays_in.model: You're joining the intermediate group, and that one meets on Mondays.

used_in.quote: Telling a friend that the plan has changed means stating what was arranged and what is arranged now, both in this shape.
The enrolment conversation settles a day and a time, and the settled version is announced in exactly this way.

payload.sentence: Nuria is presenting the flood figures at the Tuesday briefing.
payload.question: Does anybody besides Nuria already know about this?

feedback.why_key: A briefing with a day on it has been organised, and organising it took more than one person.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who else would have to know for this to be true.

payload.sentence: The department is closing the library annexe over the summer.
payload.question: Where does this sit?

feedback.why_key: The decision and the dates are in place today. Only the closing itself is still waiting to happen.
feedback.feed_forward: Separate when it was settled from when it happens.

payload.context: Somebody explaining why they cannot make Thursday.
payload.sentence: I seeing the physiotherapist on Thursday morning.
reasons: a small word is missing before the -ing verb
the appointment has not been arranged
Thursday is already over
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The -ing verb cannot stand on its own. Something in front of it has to say who and when.
feedback.feed_forward: Say am, is or are out loud before the -ing verb.

payload.context: Turning down an invitation for the weekend.
payload.stem: I can't, my brother ___ (get) married on the Saturday.

expected: is getting
's getting
s getting

feedback.why_key: A wedding is the most arranged thing there is, so the sentence reads out a date that already exists.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose is, am or are to fit the person in front.

payload.context: From a short message confirming a visit.
payload.stem: Two of us ___ (travel) up on the Wednesday and staying overnight.

expected: are travelling
're travelling
re travelling

feedback.why_key: The message is confirming something already agreed, which is why the writer can name the day without hedging it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the small word to a plural person: are.

payload.given: The ferry booking is confirmed for the eleventh. Two of us are named on it.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence telling a friend what has been arranged for the eleventh.

expected: are crossing on the eleventh
are travelling on the eleventh
are sailing on the eleventh
are taking the ferry on the eleventh

feedback.why_key: A confirmed booking with names on it is the clearest case there is of something already settled between people.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn the booking into a sentence about the two of you.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a match that has already been fixed.

expected: we are playing the harbour side on sunday

feedback.why_key: The small word comes second and the -ing verb third, with the agreed day pinned on the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the day at the end and the small word second.

payload.audio_text: She's ringing them back first thing tomorrow.

expected: she's ringing them back first thing tomorrow
shes ringing them back first thing tomorrow
she is ringing them back first thing tomorrow

feedback.why_key: The small word has shrunk to a single hissing sound on the end of she, and that sound is the whole difference between an arrangement and nothing at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the end of the person word before the -ing verb.

items.decision_cue: Unemployment is falling steadily over the coming decade

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about the labour market.
payload.sentence: Unemployment is falling steadily over the coming decade as automation spreads.
reasons: nobody arranges unemployment, so it cannot be in anyone's diary
the sentence is about something happening at this moment
the -ing verb is spelt wrongly
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: This shape claims that somebody has settled the matter with somebody else. A whole economy has no such diary, so the claim collapses.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who could possibly have arranged this.

items.decision_cue: we are having the full readings

payload.sentence: By the end of the month we are having the full readings from all four gauges.
payload.error_span: we are having the full readings

expected: we will have the full readings
we'll have the full readings
well have the full readings

feedback.why_key: Having here means simply possessing them. Nothing is being done, so there is no activity for the -ing shape to describe.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap to will have when the verb means owning, not doing.

payload.context: Two things said about the same house in the same week.
sentences: We're moving out on the fourteenth, the surveyor has the keys already.
We're going to move out at some point, we just haven't fixed anything.
meanings: A date exists and other people are working to it.
The mind is made up but nothing has been settled with anybody.

feedback.why_key: Both speakers are leaving. Only one of them has something another person could look up and act on.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether a date exists outside the speaker's head.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody has invited you out on a day you are already busy. Turn them down in one sentence, saying what has already been fixed and who with.

feedback.why_key: Naming the person you are already committed to is what makes the refusal sound true rather than invented.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the day and the other person in the same breath.

payload.prompt_text: Write the middle paragraph of a message telling a friend your holiday plan has changed. Give the old arrangement and the new one, both as settled dates. Five minutes.

feedback.why_key: The reader needs to know what to rewrite in their own diary, and only settled dates give them that.
feedback.feed_forward: State the old date, then the new one, both as fixed.

title: Saying what a timetable does, when the clock belongs to somebody else

point_json.grammar_name: Present simple for timetables and scheduled events

teach.can_do: I can talk about a future set by a timetable, using the same shape I use for things that are generally true.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the smallest of these futures and the one learners skip, so they say the bus will leave at eleven and sound as if they decided it themselves.
teach.meaning: This is the future that belongs to an organisation rather than to a person. A railway, a college, a cinema, a court, a tide table: something outside everybody in the conversation has fixed the clock, published it, and will run to it whether or not anyone in the room turns up. Because it is treated as simply how things are, English uses the same shape it uses for permanent facts. Nobody is predicting and nobody is deciding. The time already exists in print.

form.pattern: the ordinary present shape, with the later time said or understood
notes: he, she, it and any single thing still add -s, exactly as they always do
the negative and the question still use do and does, exactly as they always do
it works only where a timetable really exists: transport, courses, performances, opening hours, tides
form.negative: doesn't / don't + the plain verb: The office doesn't open until ten on Saturdays.
form.question: What time does + person or thing + the plain verb: What time does the last ferry leave?

left.text: a railway, a college, a cinema, the tide

right.text: the ordinary present shape, pointed at a later day

spec.caption: If the time was printed by somebody who has never met you, this is the shape.

worked_example.sentence: The last ferry back from Sandmouth leaves at ten past nine.
worked_example.why_this_form: The time is printed by the ferry company. It is true tonight, it was true last week, and the speaker has no part in setting it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The last ferry will leave at ten past nine would sound like the speaker's own estimate rather than something anybody can look up.

notice_set.sentence: The autumn term starts on the fifth of October.
notice_set.question: Who decided this date?
notice_set.why: A term date is published by an institution, and everybody else simply works around it.

notice_set.sentence: The gates open at half past six and the film starts at seven.
notice_set.question: Could you check these times somewhere?
notice_set.why: These times are printed. That is exactly why English states them as flatly as it does.

notice_set.sentence: High tide at the estuary is just after four tomorrow.
notice_set.question: Is anybody arranging this?
notice_set.why: The tide is fixed by something far outside the conversation, which is the same situation as a timetable.

notice_set.sentence: My flight gets in at twenty past eleven at night.
notice_set.question: Did the speaker choose that arrival time themselves?
notice_set.why: The airline sets the arrival time. The speaker only chose which printed time to buy.

notice_set.sentence: The exhibition closes at the end of March.
notice_set.question: Is this a guess about March?
notice_set.why: A closing date is announced by the gallery, so nobody in the conversation is estimating anything.

teach.rule_line: If the time was printed by an organisation, use the plain present shape.
teach.false_rule: That the present shape can only describe things happening now or things always true. Pointed at a printed timetable, it points forward.

errors.wrong: The last bus leave at eleven from the stop by the market.
errors.right: The last bus leaves at eleven from the stop by the market.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence is about tomorrow night, so the learner stops thinking of it as an ordinary present sentence, and the ending that ordinary present sentences require goes missing with it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: the s on leaves.

errors.wrong: The ferry to the outer islands leave at first light.
errors.right: The ferry to the outer islands leaves at first light.
errors.why_it_happens: Islands is the last thing the writer heard in their own head, and it is plural, so the verb agrees with the nearest word rather than with the one the sentence is actually about.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: the s on leaves.

errors.wrong: The coach is leaving at twenty to seven every morning from the depot.
errors.right: The coach leaves at twenty to seven every morning from the depot.
errors.why_it_happens: Every morning marks a routine set by the company, but the learner has recently learned that the -ing shape points forward and applies it to anything that has not happened yet.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is leaving becomes leaves.

errors.wrong: I meet the course tutor at four on Friday about my project.
errors.right: I'm meeting the course tutor at four on Friday about my project.
errors.why_it_happens: The meeting has a printed-looking time, so the learner treats it as a timetable. It is a private arrangement between two people, and no timetable anywhere in the college mentions it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: meet becomes am meeting.

pays_in.note: Times, platforms and opening hours arrive in this shape and are what the questions ask for.
pays_in.model: The shuttle runs every twenty minutes until the last train gets in.

pays_in.note: Describing a routine week set by somebody else's timetable.
pays_in.model: My first class starts at nine, so I leave the house before eight.

pays_in.note: A letter arranging a visit has to quote the printed times accurately.
pays_in.model: The Thursday service arrives at four, which gives us an hour before the office closes.

used_in.quote: The booking conversation hangs on printed arrival and departure times, and every one of them is said in this shape.
A typical week is mostly other people's timetables, so the answer is mostly this shape.

payload.sentence: The replacement service runs until the end of April.
payload.question: Who decided how long it runs for?

feedback.why_key: The end date belongs to whoever organised the service. The speaker is only reading it out.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who owns the clock in the sentence.

payload.sentence: The gallery reopens on the ninth after the roof work.
payload.question: Where does this sit?

feedback.why_key: The shape looks like an ordinary present sentence, but the date pins it to a day nobody has reached yet.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the date first, then the verb.

payload.context: From a notice on a college door.
payload.sentence: The library close at nine during the examination period.
reasons: the ending on the verb is missing
the notice is about the past
a small word is missing before the verb
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Pointing forward changes nothing about the ordinary rules. One thing still takes the ending it always takes.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the ordinary endings when the shape points forward.

payload.context: From a printed timetable card.
payload.stem: The first train of the day ___ (depart) from platform two at ten to six.

expected: departs

feedback.why_key: One train, so the verb takes its ordinary ending. The printed time is what makes the shape possible at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the things, then put the ending on.

payload.context: Somebody checking the arrangements for a match.
payload.stem: The match against the harbour clubs ___ (kick) off at three on Saturday.

expected: kicks

feedback.why_key: One match, however many clubs get mentioned on the way. The verb agrees with the match, not with the nearest word.
feedback.feed_forward: Track the verb back to what the sentence is really about.

payload.given: The college has published the dates. Enrolment is on the second of September.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence stating the published date as a plain fact about the day.

expected: opens on the second of september
starts on the second of september
begins on the second of september
takes place on the second of september

title: Choosing which way to point forward, by asking where the future actually lives

point_json.grammar_name: will vs going to vs the -ing shape vs the plain present

teach.can_do: I can pick the right way of pointing forward by asking where the future I am describing actually comes from.
teach.why_it_matters: English has no single future. It has four, and the one you pick tells your listener how settled the situation already is, whether you meant that or not.
teach.meaning: Every sentence about later carries a second message underneath it: how much of this is already real. Say it out of your own head and you are giving an opinion or making up your mind on the spot. Say it with going to and you are pointing back at a decision you already took, or at something in front of you both. Say it with the -ing shape and you are reading out an arrangement another person is expecting you to keep. Say it plainly and you are quoting a printed timetable. Same afternoon, four different claims about how settled it is.

form.pattern: will + plain verb · am/is/are going to + plain verb · am/is/are + -ing verb · the ordinary present shape
notes: all four are ordinary, correct English; nothing here is more advanced than anything else
the choice is about where the future came from, not about how far away it is
an essay prefers will with a softening word for a prediction, and treats going to as speech
form.negative: each of the four goes negative in its own ordinary way; the choice itself does not change.
form.question: Ask yourself the question in the rule line before you open your mouth, not afterwards.

spec.label: how settled is this, and who settled it?

steps.gloss: nobody has settled anything; this is my head, right now
I settled it earlier, or something in front of us points at it
another person settled it with me, and there is a time
an organisation settled it and printed it

worked_example.sentence: I'm collecting the samples at seven, so I'll set an alarm.
worked_example.why_this_form: The collection is arranged with the lab and has a time on it. The alarm is a decision the speaker takes in the middle of the sentence, which is why the two halves are not alike.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: I'll collect the samples at seven would make the whole thing the speaker's own idea, and nobody at the lab would be expecting them.

notice_set.sentence: We're taking the early boat across on Friday.
notice_set.question: Has this been settled with anybody else?
notice_set.why: A named day and a named boat mean the speakers are working to something already agreed.

notice_set.sentence: Those cracks are going to spread if nobody repoints the wall.
notice_set.question: Can the speaker point at a reason while they say it?
notice_set.why: The cracks are the reason, and they are on the wall in front of whoever is listening.

notice_set.sentence: I think the scheme will run out of money before the second phase.
notice_set.question: Is anyone in charge planning it that way?
notice_set.why: I think puts the whole thing inside the speaker's head, where no plan and no printed date can live.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic opens at eight on the first of the month.
notice_set.question: Could somebody else check this?
notice_set.why: Opening hours are published by whoever runs the building, so anybody can look them up.

notice_set.sentence: Fine, I'll take the Wednesday slot instead.
notice_set.question: When did the speaker make up their mind?
notice_set.why: Fine is the sound of somebody giving way, which places the decision inside this exchange.

notice_set.sentence: The tide turns at twenty past five tomorrow afternoon.
notice_set.question: Did anybody decide this?
notice_set.why: Nothing in the conversation controls the water. The time is simply printed in a table.

discovery.prompt: All six sentences are about later. Sort them into groups and say what makes each group hang together.
pairs: We're taking the early boat across on Friday.
Fine, I'll take the Wednesday slot instead.
Those cracks are going to spread if nobody repoints the wall.
The clinic opens at eight on the first of the month.
I think the scheme will run out of money before the second phase.
The tide turns at twenty past five tomorrow afternoon.

candidate_rules.text: The shapes differ by how much of the situation was already settled, and by who settled it.
The shapes differ by how far away in time the event is.
The shape is decided by the time word in the sentence: on Friday, at eight, next month.

teach.rule_line: Ask who has already settled this: nobody, only me, another person, or an organisation.
teach.false_rule: That will is the neutral one and the others are decorations you can skip. Skipping them means every sentence you say sounds equally unsettled.

contrast.question: Where does this future live: my head, my plans, our diary, or their timetable?

fork.answer: In my head, right now — I believe it, or I am making up my mind as I speak
In something that already exists — a decision I took earlier, or a sign in front of us
In somebody else's clock — a person expecting me, or a printed timetable if it is an organisation
fork.selects: the -ing shape, or the plain present when nobody in the conversation set the time

a.text: I'll speak to the site manager about the leak.
a.means: The speaker has thought of it this second and is offering to do it.

b.text: I'm speaking to the site manager about the leak.
b.means: It is already arranged, and the manager has it written down too.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose will. That tells your listener the idea has just occurred to you and nobody else knows about it. If the meeting was fixed last week, they will now ask you to arrange it, and you will have to explain twice.

edge_case.text: Shall survives in offers and suggestions, mostly as a question: Shall I carry that? Elsewhere in modern British English will has taken over. Recognise it when you hear it, and do not go looking for places to use it.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask who you would have to tell if you changed your mind. Nobody, because you have only just thought of it, gives you will. Only yourself gives you going to. One named person gives you the -ing shape. Nobody at all, because an organisation owns the time and cannot be argued with, gives you the plain present.

worked_pairs.a: I'll ring the letting agent, I've just thought of it.
worked_pairs.b: I'm ringing the letting agent at nine tomorrow.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first call does not exist yet anywhere except in the speaker's head. The second is a fixed point in the morning.

worked_pairs.a: We're going to convert the loft, we settled it in the spring.
worked_pairs.b: We're converting the loft in October, the builder is booked.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: we settled it in the spring
worked_pairs.gloss: Both families have made up their minds. Only one of them has another person holding a date.

worked_pairs.a: The results come out on the twelfth.
worked_pairs.b: The results are going to be poor, attendance has been down all year.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: attendance has been down all year
worked_pairs.gloss: One sentence quotes an institution. The other reads the evidence the speaker has been watching pile up.

errors.wrong: Slow down, we will come off the road on this bend.
errors.right: Slow down, we're going to come off the road on this bend.
errors.why_it_happens: Will arrives first because it was learned first. The speaker can see the bend and feel the speed, and the sentence throws all of that away and offers a private opinion instead.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will come becomes are going to come.

errors.wrong: I can't make the Friday session, I will collect my daughter from the airport.
errors.right: I can't make the Friday session, I'm collecting my daughter from the airport.
errors.why_it_happens: The arrangement was made days ago with somebody who is counting on it, but the learner reaches for the shape that means deciding on the spot, and the excuse sounds invented.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will collect becomes am collecting.

errors.wrong: If nothing changes, coastal populations are going to shrink by the middle of the century.
errors.right: If nothing changes, coastal populations will probably shrink by the middle of the century.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer has evidence in mind and reaches for the shape that admits evidence. In a formal argument that shape reads as somebody speaking aloud rather than as a case being set out.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are going to shrink becomes will probably shrink.

errors.wrong: Small towns will disappear completely once the last bank branch shuts.
errors.right: Small towns will struggle badly once the last bank branch shuts.
errors.why_it_happens: Having finally chosen the right shape, the writer forgets that the shape alone does not license the size of the claim, and an absolute word turns a reasonable point into one nobody can defend.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: disappear becomes struggle.

pays_in.note: Any question about your week or your year mixes all four in a single answer.
pays_in.model: I'm doing a short course in June, and after that I'll probably look for something nearer home.

pays_in.note: A long turn about a plan needs the settled parts to sound settled.
pays_in.model: I'm starting in September, so I'm going to spend the summer getting the reading out of the way.

pays_in.note: A prediction paragraph wants the flat one plus a softener, never the spoken one.
pays_in.model: Rural surgeries will probably close first, since they carry the highest cost per patient.

pays_in.note: The shape tells you whether a speaker is guessing or reading something out.
pays_in.model: The workshop starts at ten, but we're meeting for coffee beforehand.

used_in.quote: The whole card is about how settled a plan is, so every answer on it is this choice made out loud.
Short answers about planning slide between an arrangement and a guess, and the shape is the only thing marking the difference.

payload.sentence: We're driving up on the Saturday and coming back Monday night.
payload.question: Has this been settled with anybody?

feedback.why_key: Two named days and a shared we tell you a plan already exists between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the people the sentence commits.

payload.sentence: The damp has reached the second floor, so the whole staircase is going to need replacing.
payload.question: Where is the writer's reason?
options: In something they were told years ago

feedback.why_key: The first half of the sentence is the evidence, and the second half simply reads it out loud.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the evidence before you judge the shape.

payload.question: Who set these dates?

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is anybody's opinion or anybody's plan. The dates were published and the writer is quoting them.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who published the number in the sentence.

payload.context: A student is asked when the essay is coming in; the date was agreed with the tutor last week.
payload.sentence: I will hand it in on the fourteenth.
reasons: the date was settled with somebody else, so it is not being decided now
the essay has already been handed in
a small word is missing before hand

payload.context: Two people at a bus stop, watching the sky darken.
payload.stem: Get under the shelter, it ___ (pour) in a minute.

expected: is going to pour
's going to pour
s going to pour

feedback.why_key: The sky is the reason and both of them can see it, so the sentence has evidence rather than an opinion behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the shape that admits the evidence you can see.

payload.context: From a printed noticeboard beside the college office.
payload.stem: The registration desk ___ (open) at nine on the first day of term.

expected: opens

feedback.why_key: A printed notice is the institution speaking, and an institution states its hours as flatly as it states anything else.
feedback.feed_forward: Flatten the verb when an organisation owns the hour.

payload.given: Marta rang the surgery last week and took a slot. It is the twelfth at half past two.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence telling a colleague what she has fixed for the twelfth.

expected: is seeing the doctor at half past two
's seeing the doctor at half past two
s seeing the doctor at half past two
is seeing the doctor on the twelfth at half past two

feedback.why_key: The surgery took her name and holds the slot, which makes it an arrangement between two sides rather than a plan of hers.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the -ing shape when somebody else holds the slot.

payload.audio_text: I'm meeting them at the depot, but I'll ring first.

expected: i'm meeting them at the depot, but i'll ring first
im meeting them at the depot, but ill ring first
i am meeting them at the depot, but i will ring first

payload.context: A colleague has just mentioned that the depot van is free tomorrow and nobody has claimed it.

payload.context: Two neighbours discussing a family who have made their minds up but have not fixed anything with anyone.

options.why_this_means: That the family have decided, and that no date exists outside their own kitchen.
That a date is set and other people are already working to it.

items.decision_cue: whose completion date is set and whose van is booked

payload.context: Two neighbours discussing a family whose completion date is set and whose van is booked.

reasons: nobody has arranged this, so it cannot be stated as settled
the sentence is about something already finished

title: Telling which nouns English counts and which it measures

point_json.grammar_name: Countable and uncountable nouns

pays_in.note: The abstract nouns an essay runs on are almost all measured ones.
pays_in.model: There is little evidence that longer hours produce better work.

pays_in.note: Chart language needs the measured and counted words kept apart.
pays_in.model: Less energy was used in 2020, although the number of households rose.

pays_in.note: Discussion answers are full of these words and the errors are audible.
pays_in.model: There's so much conflicting advice about it that people give up.

pays_in.note: A summary-completion answer is wrong if it pluralises a word the passage measures.
pays_in.model: The study found no evidence of long-term damage to the reed beds.

teach.can_do: I can tell whether a noun is one English counts or one it measures, and choose everything around it accordingly.
teach.why_it_matters: Almost every article and quantity mistake starts here. Get this judgement right and half the noun problems downstream never happen.
teach.meaning: English splits nouns in two. Some it counts one by one: a report, two reports, several reports. Others it treats as a quantity you measure rather than count: research, advice, equipment, evidence, traffic. Those never take an s and never take a in front of them. The split is not about the world, it is about the way English happens to package things, which is why furniture is measured and chairs are counted in the same room.

form.pattern: counted: a report, two reports  ·  measured: research, some research, a great deal of research
notes: a measured noun takes a singular verb: the evidence is clear, the equipment was delivered
to count a measured noun, count its container: a piece of advice, an item of equipment, two pieces of research
the common measured nouns learners pluralise: information, advice, research, equipment, knowledge, evidence, progress, feedback, traffic, furniture, luggage
a few nouns sit on both sides with two meanings: experience, time, paper, work
form.negative: there is not much evidence for it yet
form.question: How much evidence is there?

left.text: a report, two reports, several reports

right.text: evidence, some evidence, plenty of evidence

spec.caption: The line runs through the words, not through the world. Chairs are counted and furniture is measured, and they are the same room.

worked_example.sentence: Her supervisor sent over two pieces of feedback before the deadline.
worked_example.why_this_form: Feedback is measured, so a number cannot sit next to it. English counts the pieces instead, and the number goes there.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two feedbacks is not a smaller slip than a wrong word. It is a shape English has no room for at all, and a reader stops dead at it.

notice_set.sentence: The tutor gave me three pieces of advice about the essay.
notice_set.question: How many separate things did the tutor say?
notice_set.why: The number has moved onto the pieces, because it could not sit next to the word it belongs to.

notice_set.sentence: We need more equipment before the field trip.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you how many items are needed?
notice_set.why: More measures a quantity. If you want a number, you have to name the units it comes in.

notice_set.sentence: The department has ordered four new microscopes.
notice_set.question: Can you count what was ordered?
notice_set.why: They arrive one at a time and English counts them one at a time, which is what the s at the end is doing.

notice_set.sentence: There is not much research on the Verdon estuary.
notice_set.question: Is this about a small number of studies or a small amount of work?
options: They are the same thing here
notice_set.why: Research is a body of work, so English measures it. Studies is the word to use when you want a number.

notice_set.sentence: She has a lot of experience of teaching large groups.
notice_set.question: Is this about events she remembers or about skill built up over years?
notice_set.why: One word, two meanings, and English marks the difference: the skill is measured and the events are counted.

notice_set.sentence: She had two odd experiences on her first day.
notice_set.question: Is she talking about things that happened, or about what she is good at?
notice_set.why: The s does the work. With it, the word means separate happenings you could list.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether English counts this word or measures it, then choose.
teach.false_rule: That anything you can see and touch must be countable. Furniture, luggage and equipment are all things you can carry, and English measures every one of them.

errors.wrong: The report gives useful informations about rural schools.
errors.right: The report gives useful information about rural schools.
errors.why_it_happens: In most other languages this word behaves like an ordinary countable noun, so the plural is produced automatically before any rule about English can fire.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on informations.
errors.l1_note: Nearly universal; the word is countable in French, Spanish, Arabic and many others.

errors.wrong: I would like to give you an advice about the interview.
errors.right: I would like to give you a piece of advice about the interview.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows that a lone singular noun usually needs a small word in front of it and supplies one. The rule is right; this is simply not the kind of noun it applies to.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: an becomes a piece of.

errors.wrong: The evidence from both surveys are difficult to read.
errors.right: The evidence from both surveys is difficult to read.
errors.why_it_happens: Surveys sits right next to the verb and pulls it into the plural. The word the sentence is actually about is four words earlier and is measured, not counted.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: are becomes is.

errors.wrong: There is fewer traffic on the coast road since the charge came in.
errors.right: There is less traffic on the coast road since the charge came in.
errors.why_it_happens: Fewer sounds more careful than less, so it gets used as the polite version of it. They are not two levels of politeness; they belong to the two different halves of the noun system.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: fewer becomes less.

used_in.quote: Information, evidence, coverage and access all appear in the first paragraph, and every one of them is measured.

payload.sentence: My tutor gave me three pieces of advice before the interview.
payload.question: How many separate suggestions were there?

feedback.why_key: The number has been moved onto the word that can carry it, and it still tells you exactly how many there were.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the number on the container word.

expected: there's a lot of information out there and not much of it is checked
there is a lot of information out there and not much of it is checked

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence about how much of what people read online is checked before it is published. Use at least two nouns that English measures rather than counts.

feedback.why_key: Two of these words in one sentence is where the quantity words in front of them start being chosen rather than guessed.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the noun, then choose the word in front of it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the first body paragraph of your social media news answer. Circle every noun you have measured rather than counted and check the verb that follows each one. Five minutes.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure this is the judgement that slips first, so a real paragraph is the only honest test of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check every verb that follows a measured noun.

title: Saying how much or how many without giving a number

point_json.grammar_name: some, any, much, many, a lot of

pays_in.note: Questions about your day, your town and your food need these constantly.
pays_in.model: There aren't many decent cafes round here, to be honest.

pays_in.note: General statements about society run on them.
pays_in.model: A lot of people cook less than their parents did.

pays_in.note: A short-answer item can hang on whether you heard much or many.
pays_in.model: There isn't much space in the storeroom at the moment.

teach.can_do: I can say how much or how many there is without counting anything.
teach.why_it_matters: These are among the most frequent words in spoken English, and the wrong one is heard immediately even when everything else in the sentence is right.
teach.meaning: Most of the time you do not know a number and do not need one. English has a small set of words for saying roughly how much there is, and each of them belongs on one side of the counted and measured split. Two of them, some and any, split a different way: some goes with a plain statement, and any goes with a negative or a question. Once you have those two pairs, you can say how much of anything there is.

form.pattern: some / any + counted or measured  ·  many + counted  ·  much + measured  ·  a lot of + either
notes: some in a plain statement: there are some seats left, there is some bread left
any in a negative or a question: there aren't any seats, is there any bread?
some also appears in an offer or a request, where the answer is expected to be yes: would you like some tea?
much and many sit most comfortably in negatives and questions; plain statements normally take a lot of
form.negative: there isn't much time and there aren't many people
form.question: Is there much time? Are there many people?

left.text: many, a few, several, a lot of

right.text: much, a little, a great deal of, a lot of

spec.caption: A lot of appears in both boxes, which is why it is the safest thing to say when you are not sure.

worked_example.sentence: There isn't much time before the market closes, and there aren't many stalls left open.
worked_example.why_this_form: Time is measured and stalls are counted, so the two halves of the sentence take the two different words even though they are making the same complaint.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Swapping them does not change the meaning at all, which is precisely why it is worth learning: the mistake is audible and it costs you nothing to avoid.

notice_set.sentence: There isn't much bread left.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker talking about loaves or about an amount?
notice_set.why: Bread is measured here, so the word in front of it is the measuring one.

notice_set.sentence: There aren't many rolls left.
notice_set.question: Could you count what is left?
notice_set.why: Rolls come one at a time, so the counting word goes in front of them.

notice_set.sentence: Is there any milk in the fridge?
notice_set.question: Does the speaker already know the answer?
notice_set.why: This word turns up when the speaker does not know, which is why it lives in questions and negatives.

notice_set.sentence: There's some milk in the fridge.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking or telling?
notice_set.why: A plain statement takes the other word of the pair, and the two almost never swap.

notice_set.sentence: Would you like some more soup?
notice_set.question: What is the speaker expecting you to say?
notice_set.why: An offer expects a yes, so it takes the statement word even though it has a question mark on the end.

teach.rule_line: Some for telling and offering, any for asking and denying.
teach.false_rule: That any is just the question version of some. It marks an open, unknown quantity, which is why an offer, whose answer is half agreed already, takes some.

errors.wrong: There were much people waiting outside the hall.
errors.right: There were a lot of people waiting outside the hall.
errors.why_it_happens: Much is learned first and used as the general word for a large amount, without the counted and measured split being attached to it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes a lot of.

errors.wrong: We do not have many time before the coach leaves.
errors.right: We do not have much time before the coach leaves.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is reaching for the more formal-sounding word rather than checking what kind of noun follows it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: many becomes much.

errors.wrong: I did not take any photo of the harbour.
errors.right: I did not take any photos of the harbour.
errors.why_it_happens: Any looks like a singular word because it has no s of its own, so the noun after it is left singular too.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: the s on photo.

used_in.quote: Almost every answer about what you eat and where you buy it needs one of these words.

payload.sentence: There isn't much bread left.
payload.question: Is the speaker thinking about loaves or about an amount?

feedback.why_key: The word in front tells you which way the speaker is thinking about it, before the noun even arrives.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the quantity word as a clue to the noun.

payload.context: A shopkeeper explaining why the shelves are empty.
payload.sentence: There were much people in this morning.
reasons: the quantity word does not go with this noun
the time is wrong
the shop cannot be empty
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: People come one at a time, so the word in front has to be one of the counting ones.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the noun can be counted, then choose.

payload.context: Two people looking in a nearly empty fridge.
payload.stem: Is there ___ (some / any) milk left?

expected: any

feedback.why_key: Nobody knows the answer yet, and that is the situation this word belongs to.
feedback.feed_forward: Use any when you genuinely do not know.

payload.context: A host at the table with a full pan in front of them.
payload.stem: Would you like ___ (some / any) more soup?

expected: some

feedback.why_key: It has a question mark and it is not really a question. The host expects a yes, and that is what decides the word.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether an answer is already half expected.

payload.given: There is a lot of work to do before Friday.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it as a negative statement with the same meaning reversed.

expected: much work to do before friday
there isn't much work to do before friday
there isnt much work to do before friday
there is not much work to do before friday

feedback.why_key: A lot of is what a plain statement takes, and much is what a negative takes, so both words change when the sentence flips.
feedback.feed_forward: Switch to much or many as soon as you go negative.

payload.audio_text: There aren't many places to eat near the office.

expected: there aren't many places to eat near the office
there arent many places to eat near the office
there are not many places to eat near the office

feedback.why_key: Two short words run together at the start and they carry both halves of the meaning: the negative and the counting.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the two small words before you write the rest.

payload.context: Someone describing a market they visited on holiday.

expected: i didn't take any photos of the fish stalls
i didnt take any photos of the fish stalls

feedback.why_key: Any leaves the number open, and an open number in English is a plural unless you mean not even one.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the s on the noun after any.

payload.sentence: There are many evidence for this and not many time to look at all of it.

expected: much evidence
a great deal of evidence
a lot of evidence

feedback.why_key: Both halves are wrong in the same way, and finding the first one usually shows you the second.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix one, then look for the same mistake again.

payload.prompt_text: Write two short sentences about what is in your kitchen at the moment: one about something you can count and one about something you can only measure.

feedback.why_key: Putting the two kinds of noun side by side is the fastest way to feel the difference the words are marking.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the counted one first, then the measured one.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked about food and cooking at home. Speak for forty seconds and use at least three of these words, with the noun each one needs.

feedback.why_key: At speaking speed there is no time to check, so this is where the pairing either has become automatic or has not.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the noun in your head before the word in front of it.

title: Using the when my reader can already tell which one I mean

point_json.grammar_name: the: second mention, unique things, and defining phrases

pays_in.note: A paragraph that introduces an example and then refers back to it needs both halves of this.
pays_in.model: A charge was introduced in Marlow in 2018. The charge has since been raised twice.

pays_in.note: A letter about a problem is one long chain of first and second mentions.
pays_in.model: There is a crack in the ceiling of the back bedroom, and the crack has widened since March.

pays_in.note: Telling a story means bringing things in and then pointing back at them.
pays_in.model: We found a small café near the station, and the café turned out to be run by his cousin.

pays_in.note: Following what a passage refers back to is largely a matter of following these words.
pays_in.model: The proposal described above was withdrawn before the deadline.

teach.can_do: I can use the when my reader can pick out which one I mean, and a when they cannot.
teach.why_it_matters: This is one decision, taken dozens of times in every answer you write. Getting it right costs nothing once the question is the right one.
teach.meaning: The is not about how important a thing is or how much you like it. It is a signal to your reader that they can already pick out which one you mean. There are only a few ways they can: you mentioned it a moment ago, there is only one of it in the situation you are both in, or the words straight after it narrow it down to one. If none of those is true, your reader cannot pick it out, and you need a instead.

form.pattern: the + any noun, counted or measured, singular or plural
notes: second mention: a lift was fitted last year, and the lift broke in June
only one in the situation: the roof, the kitchen, the manager, the sun
narrowed by what follows: the lift in the north block, the report you sent me
the never changes shape, whatever noun comes after it
form.negative: the lift has not worked since June
form.question: Which lift do you mean?

left.role: reader cannot pick it out yet
left.text: a lift, a report, a manager

right.text: the lift, the report you sent, the manager

spec.caption: Things usually travel left to right in a paragraph: you bring something in with a, and from then on it takes the.

worked_example.sentence: A notice went up in the lobby in March, and the notice is still there in October.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first mention brings the notice into the paragraph and the second points back at it, so the reader knows without asking which piece of paper is meant.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opening with the notice would assume the reader already has one in mind, and a reader who does not will stop and look back for it.

notice_set.sentence: A lift was fitted last year. The lift has been out of service since June.
notice_set.question: How many lifts are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The second sentence points back at the one the first sentence brought in.

notice_set.sentence: A lift was fitted last year. A lift has been out of service since June.
notice_set.question: How many lifts are being talked about now?
notice_set.why: The second sentence brings in a new one, so a reader assumes the building has more than one.

notice_set.sentence: Could you shut the door, please?
notice_set.question: Does the speaker need to say which door?
options: No, there is only one in the room
They should have said a door
notice_set.why: In the room the two of you are standing in there is only one, so nothing more needs saying.

notice_set.sentence: The report you sent me last week has gone to the committee.
notice_set.question: What tells you which report is meant?
notice_set.why: The words that follow narrow it down to one, which is the third way a reader can pick something out.

notice_set.sentence: We have moved into a flat above a bakery.
notice_set.question: Has the speaker mentioned this flat before?
options: No, this is the first time
notice_set.why: Both things are being brought in for the first time, which is what a is for.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether your reader can already tell which one is meant.
teach.false_rule: That the goes in front of anything important, or anything you have ever mentioned. It is about what your reader can identify right now, from what they already have.

contrast.question: Can my reader already pick out which one I mean?

fork.answer: Yes: I mentioned it, or there is only one here, or the words after it narrow it down
No: it is one of several and I am bringing it in for the first time

a.text: A lift was fitted last year.
a.means: There may be several lifts, and this is the first time you are hearing about this one.

b.text: The lift was fitted last year.
b.means: We both know which lift. Either there is only one, or we have already been talking about it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Opening a paragraph with the lift when your reader has never heard of it does not look like an article mistake. It reads as though you have skipped a sentence, and the reader goes back to look for the one they think they missed.

edge_case.text: Some things take the because there is only one in the world rather than one in the room: the sun, the government, the environment. Treat them as the same rule with a very large room.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask yourself whether a reader could answer the question which one? from what they have already read. If they can, write the. If they would have to ask you, write a.

worked_pairs.a: We have moved into a flat above a bakery.
worked_pairs.b: The flat above the bakery has been empty for a year.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first sentence introduces both. The second assumes you already have both, which only works if somebody has introduced them first.

worked_pairs.a: Could you shut a door, please?
worked_pairs.b: Could you shut the door, please?
worked_pairs.gloss: The first version makes the listener choose one, which is why it sounds strange in a room that has only one.

worked_pairs.a: I have sent a report to the committee.
worked_pairs.b: I have sent the report you asked for to the committee.
worked_pairs.gloss: The words after the noun do the identifying, so nothing has to have been mentioned before.

errors.wrong: We have moved into flat above a bakery.
errors.right: We have moved into a flat above a bakery.
errors.why_it_happens: In many languages a bare singular noun is a complete phrase, so nothing feels missing. English requires a small word in front of a singular counted noun every single time.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: a.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of languages with no article system.

errors.wrong: A lift was fitted last year. A lift has been out of service since June.
errors.right: A lift was fitted last year. The lift has been out of service since June.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer is thinking about the lift and not about the reader's picture of it. Both sentences are about one lift in the writer's head, and the reader is handed two.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: the second a becomes the.

errors.wrong: Report you sent me last week has gone to the committee.
errors.right: The report you sent me last week has gone to the committee.
errors.why_it_happens: The words after the noun already make it obvious which report is meant, so the small word at the front feels like it has nothing left to do.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: The.

used_in.quote: Any example paragraph on this prompt introduces a city and then refers back to it four or five times.

payload.sentence: A tutor was appointed in September. The tutor has been on leave since March.
payload.question: How many tutors are being talked about?

feedback.why_key: The second small word points back at the person the first sentence brought in, so nobody new arrives.
feedback.feed_forward: Track what the small word is pointing at.

payload.sentence: A tutor was appointed in September. A tutor has been on leave since March.
payload.question: How many tutors does the department seem to have?

feedback.why_key: Bringing somebody in twice tells the reader there are two of them, whatever the writer had in mind.
feedback.feed_forward: Reread your second mention and ask who it introduces.

items.decision_cue: a document that arrived last week

payload.context: From an email about a document that arrived last week.
payload.sentence: Report you sent me has gone to the committee.
reasons: a small word is missing at the front
the time is wrong
the committee cannot receive it
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The words after the noun already say which report it is, and English still wants the small word in front.
feedback.feed_forward: Put a word in front of every singular counted noun.

payload.context: From a letter about a repair. The crack has already been described.
payload.stem: ___ (a / the) crack has widened noticeably since March.

expected: the

feedback.why_key: It has already been introduced, so the reader can pick it out without being told again what it is.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the once a thing has been introduced.

payload.context: Someone telling a friend where they had lunch.
payload.stem: We found ___ (a / the) small café near the station.

expected: a

feedback.why_key: The listener has never heard of this café, so it has to be brought in before it can be pointed at.
feedback.feed_forward: Bring a thing in with a before you point at it.

payload.given: A charge was introduced in Marlow in 2018. A charge has since been raised twice.
payload.instruction: Rewrite the second sentence so that it is clearly about the same charge.

expected: the charge has since been raised twice

feedback.why_key: One word changed, and the paragraph now has one charge in it instead of two.
feedback.feed_forward: Point back with the whenever you mean the same thing.

payload.audio_text: There's a crack in the ceiling of the back bedroom.

expected: there's a crack in the ceiling of the back bedroom
there is a crack in the ceiling of the back bedroom
theres a crack in the ceiling of the back bedroom

feedback.why_key: Three of these words in nine, all unstressed, all nearly inaudible, and all of them doing work.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the small words first, then fill in the rest.

items.decision_cue: A lift was fitted in the north block last year.

payload.context: The line before this one reads: A lift was fitted in the north block last year.
payload.stem: ___ lift has been out of order since June.

options.why_this_means: That a second lift is being brought into the paragraph.
That this is the lift the reader has just been told about.

expected: the

feedback.why_key: The reader is already holding one lift, so a second small word that introduces a new one hands them two.
feedback.feed_forward: Check what your reader is already holding.

items.decision_cue: The north block has four lifts and a service hoist.

payload.context: The line before this one reads: The north block has four lifts and a service hoist.
payload.stem: ___ lift has been out of order since June.

options.why_this_means: That a second lift is being brought into the paragraph.
That this is the lift the reader has just been told about.

expected: a

feedback.why_key: With four of them in the reader's head, pointing at one without saying which is a question rather than a statement.
feedback.feed_forward: Count how many the reader could be thinking of.

payload.context: Two people in a small kitchen with one window, which is open.
payload.stem: Could you shut ___ window, please?

options.why_this_means: That there are several and the listener may pick whichever they like.
That there is one obvious candidate and both of them know which.

expected: the

feedback.why_key: A room with one window has no choice in it, so asking the listener to choose is the odd thing to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at the room before you look at the noun.

payload.context: A stationery cupboard where a dozen identical folders are stacked on a shelf.
payload.stem: Could you pass me ___ folder, please?

options.why_this_means: That there are several and the listener may pick whichever they like.
That there is one obvious candidate and both of them know which.

expected: a

feedback.why_key: Twelve identical folders means there is nothing to point at, and asking for a particular one would leave the listener stuck.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the listener could pick the right one.

payload.context: Two openings from separate emails, both written to one committee.
sentences: I have sent a report to the committee.
I have sent the report you asked for to the committee.
meanings: The committee has not heard about this document before.
The committee already knows which document is meant.

feedback.why_key: Nothing has been mentioned before in the second one either. The words after the noun do the identifying instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at what comes after the noun as well as before it.

items.decision_cue: one railway station and several bus stations

payload.context: A guidebook entry about a town that has one railway station and several bus stations.
payload.stem: The hotel stands opposite ___ station.

options.why_this_means: That the reader is being told there is some station there, without being told which kind.
That the reader is expected to think of the railway station, since there is just one of those.

follow_up.question: Which one would a reader take as meaning the railway station?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct and they point at different buildings, which is why a guidebook cannot afford to choose carelessly.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask which one your reader will actually walk to.

items.decision_cue: introduced a congestion charge in its first

payload.context: From the second paragraph of an essay that introduced a congestion charge in its first.
payload.sentence: A charge has since been raised twice and is now among the highest in the country.
reasons: it introduces a second charge the reader has not met
the time is wrong
charges cannot be raised
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The paragraph is about one charge and the small word at the front has quietly told the reader there are two.
feedback.feed_forward: Reread the paragraph before, then fix the word.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about a place in your town: the first bringing it into the paragraph for the first time, the second saying something more about the same place.

feedback.why_key: Bringing something in and then pointing back at it is the smallest complete unit of a paragraph, and it needs both words.
feedback.feed_forward: Introduce with a, point back with the.

payload.prompt_text: Write the example paragraph of your car-free centres answer. Name one city, then refer back to it and to two things in it. Check every small word in front of a noun. Five minutes.

feedback.why_key: A whole example paragraph is a chain of first and second mentions, and one broken link is enough for a reader to lose the thread.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your paragraph once for these words alone.

title: Leaving the out when I mean the whole category

point_json.grammar_name: The zero article: generic reference

pays_in.note: Every essay opens with a general claim, and every general claim needs this.
pays_in.model: Online courses have made higher education reachable for people who work full time.

pays_in.note: Discussion answers are general claims almost from beginning to end.
pays_in.model: Young people read differently now, not less.

pays_in.note: Telling a general claim from a specific one is often what a true, false or not given item is testing.
pays_in.model: Tidal schemes have never produced electricity at a competitive price.

teach.can_do: I can make a statement about a whole category without putting a word in front of it.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the single most common noun mistake in essay writing, and it happens in the first sentence of the first paragraph, where it does the most damage.
teach.meaning: When you are talking about a whole category rather than about particular members of it, English puts nothing in front of the noun at all. No small word, no signal, nothing. That is why an essay about all computers everywhere starts with computers and not with the computers. Most languages mark a general statement in some way, and English marks it by leaving the space empty, which is exactly what makes it hard to remember.

form.pattern: nothing + plural counted noun  ·  nothing + measured noun
notes: the whole category, plural: computers have changed how offices work
the whole category, measured: pollution is a serious problem in older cities
an abstract idea in general: education, poverty, technology, freedom, research
