feedback.why_key: The endings are unstressed and easy to lose. Lose them and you hear one flat described rather than two flats weighed up.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen to the very end of the describing word.

payload.sentence: Evening classes are the most easiest option to fit round a shift pattern.

expected: the easiest
the simplest
the most straightforward

feedback.why_key: Easiest has already put the classes at the top of the group. Most is a second run at the same job.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete most when the word already ends in -est.

items.decision_cue: the most steeply of the six districts

payload.context: Two lines taken from separate notes on one set of figures.
sentences: Fares in Marlow rose more steeply than fares in Ashfield.
Fares in Marlow rose the most steeply of the six districts.
meanings: Two places are being weighed against each other, and one of them moved further.
Marlow sits at the top of a list of six, with nothing above it.

feedback.why_key: One sentence weighs a pair; the other ranks a group of six. The ending is the only thing telling you which.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask how many things are in the group before you choose the ending.

payload.prompt_text: A graph shows freight moved by road, rail and water over ten years. Road is highest all the way through and water is lowest. Write one sentence that ranks all three.

feedback.why_key: Ranking three things inside one sentence is the move that turns a list of numbers into a description of a graph.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the top, then place the other two against it.

payload.prompt_text: Open your freight graph answer. Rewrite the overview so that it ranks the three modes in a single sentence instead of listing them one after another. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: An overview that ranks is doing the task. An overview that lists is only reading the graph out loud.
feedback.feed_forward: Rank first, then give the numbers that prove the ranking.

title: Saying two things are level, or that one falls short of the other

point_json.grammar_name: as ... as, not as ... as, the same as, similar to, different from

teach.can_do: I can say that two things are level, or that one of them does not reach the other.
teach.why_it_matters: A description that only ever names winners cannot say two figures met, and figures meet constantly. These frames also keep a preposition each, and learners lose all three.
teach.meaning: A comparison does not always have a winner. Sometimes the whole point is that two things sit at the same height, and sometimes it is that one of them stops short of the other. English builds both with a frame rather than with an ending, and the describing word sits inside the frame without changing shape at all. That last part is what makes these easy to build, and it is also why they go wrong: the ending arrives out of habit and has nothing to do.

form.pattern: as + WORD + as  ·  not as + WORD + as  ·  the same as  ·  similar to  ·  different from
notes: the word inside the frame never changes shape: as high as, not as high as — never as higher as
the same needs the in front and one as after it: the fee is the same as last year's
similar always takes to; different always takes from
with things you count the frame stretches to as many ... as; with things you measure it is as much ... as
not so ... as turns up in speech, but not as ... as is safe everywhere and costs nothing
the frame can carry a whole noun phrase: as high a figure as, as long a wait as
form.negative: not as high as, or the gentler not quite as high as
form.question: Is the new pass as cheap as the old one?

worked_example.sentence: Rail carried as much freight in 2016 as it had ten years earlier.
worked_example.why_this_form: The two figures met, so there is no winner to name. The frame holds them side by side and leaves the describing word alone.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Carried more freight than would put 2016 in front, which the figures do not support, and it would hide the fact that a decade produced no movement at all.

notice_set.sentence: The new footbridge is not as wide as the old one.
notice_set.question: Which bridge takes more people side by side?
notice_set.why: Not as wide as stops the new bridge short of the old one, so the old one is the roomier of the two.

notice_set.sentence: Fees in Ashfield are the same as fees in Marlow.
notice_set.question: Would you pay more in Marlow?
notice_set.why: The same as sets the two towns at one figure, so neither of them is the dearer place.

notice_set.sentence: The pool is as busy on Sunday as it is on Saturday.
notice_set.question: Is Sunday the quiet day?
notice_set.why: The frame holds the two days at one level, so neither of them can be the quiet one.

notice_set.sentence: Water use in the south is similar to water use in the east.
notice_set.question: Are the two figures close together?
notice_set.why: Similar claims a short distance between the two. It does not claim there is none.

notice_set.sentence: Journey times on the coast route are nowhere near as reliable as they were.
notice_set.question: Has the route got worse?
notice_set.why: Nowhere near stretches the shortfall as far as it will go, and today's route is on the low end of it.

teach.rule_line: Two ases hold two things level. Put not in front and the first one falls short.
teach.false_rule: That this frame is only for things that are exactly equal. It measures the distance between two things, and one of the distances it measures is none.

errors.wrong: The tunnel is as quicker as the bypass in the evening.
errors.right: The tunnel is as quick as the bypass in the evening.
errors.why_it_happens: Every comparison the learner has built so far needed an ending, so the ending comes along automatically. Inside this frame there is nothing for it to do, because the frame is already doing the comparing.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two letters: quicker becomes quick.

errors.wrong: Rents in Marlow are different than rents in Brackenfield.
errors.right: Rents in Marlow are different from rents in Brackenfield.
errors.why_it_happens: Than is the word that follows every other comparison, so it turns up here as well. Different is not that kind of word and never has been: it takes from.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: than becomes from.

errors.wrong: This year's total is as same as last year's.
errors.right: This year's total is the same as last year's.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has one frame for comparing and pushes same into it. Same is an ordinary describing word that needs the in front of it, and only one as behind.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: the first as becomes the.

errors.wrong: The reserve gets as much visitors as the castle does.
errors.right: The reserve gets as many visitors as the castle does.
errors.why_it_happens: Much and many both mean a large amount and nothing in the meaning separates them, so whichever is nearer the front of the learner's mind goes in. Only many will sit in front of something you count one at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes many.

pays_in.note: Half the sentences in a chart description report a level, not a winner.
pays_in.model: In 2014 the reserve drew as many visitors as the castle.

pays_in.note: Comparing where you live now with where you lived before.
pays_in.model: The new place isn't as noisy as the flat I had before.

pays_in.note: A statement that swaps from for than, or drops the second as, is testing exactly this.
pays_in.model: Rainfall in the uplands was similar to rainfall on the coast.

used_in.quote: Two towns with the same recycling figure cannot be described with a ranking, and the bar chart hands the learner several such pairs.
Part 3 answers about sport compare two activities or two generations, and most of those comparisons end level.

payload.sentence: The five-a-side pitch isn't as busy as it used to be.
payload.question: Do fewer people use it now?

feedback.why_key: The frame holds today's pitch below its own past, so use has come down since then.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the two things being held apart before you answer.

payload.sentence: Rainfall in the Verdon valley is similar to rainfall further inland.
payload.question: Are the two areas close on this measure?

feedback.why_key: Similar claims a short distance between two figures. It stops well short of claiming they match.
feedback.feed_forward: Read similar as close, never as equal.

payload.context: A draft paragraph on a table of district rents.
payload.sentence: Rents in Brackenfield are different than rents in Sandmouth.
reasons: different does not take than
the two districts cannot be weighed this way
the sentence is missing its second as
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Than belongs after an ending or after more. Different asks for from and will not take anything else.
feedback.feed_forward: Pair different with from before you write the second half.

payload.context: From a report weighing up two regions.
payload.stem: Water use in the south is ___ same as water use in the east.

expected: the

feedback.why_key: Same is an ordinary describing word and needs the in front of it. An as will not do that job.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the same as as one three-word block.

payload.context: Two colleagues weighing up two places to eat near the depot.
payload.stem: The café gets as ___ customers at lunchtime as the canteen does.

expected: many

feedback.why_key: Customers arrive one at a time and can be counted, so the frame takes many. Much is for what you measure instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether you could count them before choosing.

payload.given: Rail moved 40 million tonnes in 2006. Rail moved 40 million tonnes in 2016.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence saying the two years came out level.

expected: as much freight in 2016 as it did in 2006
as much freight in 2016 as in 2006
the same amount of freight in 2016 as in 2006
as much in 2016 as it did in 2006

feedback.why_key: Two identical figures have no winner between them. The frame sets them side by side and says so in one clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for the frame whenever two numbers match.

payload.context: Build one sentence about visitor numbers on the island.

expected: the island is not as popular as it was in 2010

feedback.why_key: Not sits in front of the whole frame, and the describing word stays plain between the two ases.
feedback.feed_forward: Put not before the frame, never inside it.

payload.audio_text: It's not as quiet as the place we had before.

expected: it's not as quiet as the place we had before
its not as quiet as the place we had before
it is not as quiet as the place we had before

feedback.why_key: Both ases are unstressed and the second almost disappears. Learners write not quiet as and lose half the frame.
feedback.feed_forward: Count two ases every time you hear this frame.

payload.sentence: The fee for an evening class is as same as the daytime fee.

expected: the same as
identical to
no different from

feedback.why_key: Same needs the in front of it, and a single as behind is enough to carry the second half.
feedback.feed_forward: Change the first as to the whenever same follows.

payload.context: A paragraph arguing about the cost of keeping fit.
payload.sentence: Swimming at the council pool is as cheaper as running in the park.
reasons: the describing word should stay plain inside the frame
the two activities are too different to weigh
the sentence needs from instead of the second as
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The frame is already doing the comparing. An ending on top of it makes the sentence compare twice over.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip the ending off the word between the two ases.

payload.prompt_text: A chart shows household recycling in two towns. In 2018 both of them recycled 44 out of every hundred tonnes. Write one sentence reporting that, without naming a winner.

feedback.why_key: Figures meet all the time, and a writer with no way of saying so has to invent a difference that is not there.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the two are level, then give the year.

payload.prompt_text: Open your recycling chart answer. Find a place where two figures are level or nearly level, and rewrite that sentence so it reports the level instead of ranking them. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure every sentence turns into a ranking, and a reader who checks two of them stops trusting the rest.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each comparison for a winner that is not really there.

title: Keeping will out of the half of the sentence that starts with when, until or as soon as

point_json.grammar_name: Present forms after when, as soon as, before, after, until, once and by the time

teach.can_do: I can join two future events with when, until or as soon as, and put will in only one of them.
teach.why_it_matters: One of the most common errors at this level, and invisible to the person making it, because the broken version sounds perfectly logical in their head.
teach.meaning: Some sentences carry two future events: one is the moment, and the other is what happens at that moment. English marks the future only once. The half that starts with when, until, before, once, after, as soon as or by the time is the moment, and English treats a fixed future moment as though it were already here, so it uses the ordinary present shape. All the pointing forward is done by the other half. Saying it twice does not make the sentence more future; it makes it wrong.

form.pattern: when / before / after / until / once / as soon as / by the time + ordinary present shape ... will + plain verb
notes: the two halves can go in either order; whichever half starts with one of those words keeps the present shape
when the joining half comes first, a comma follows it: Once the results are in, we will decide.
the same words after a verb of knowing or asking are a different job, and there will is normal: nobody knows when it will reopen
form.negative: the joining half goes negative in the ordinary present way: until the road doesn't flood any more.
form.question: What will you do when the contract ends? — the asking half keeps will, the joining half does not.

left.text: when the funding arrives — ordinary present shape, no will

right.text: we will start the second phase — will lives here

spec.caption: One future, marked once. The half with the joining word never gets to carry it.

worked_example.sentence: As soon as the tide drops, the divers will go back down.
worked_example.why_this_form: The dropping tide is the moment the sentence is pointing at, and a moment is treated as fixed. The going down is the news, so that is where the pointing forward happens.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: As soon as the tide will drop would leave the reader waiting for a main piece of news that never comes, because both halves would be busy announcing the future.

notice_set.sentence: We will move the equipment once the floor dries.
notice_set.question: Has the floor dried yet?
notice_set.why: Both events are still ahead. The drying is simply being treated as the fixed point the moving hangs on.

notice_set.sentence: Ring me when you reach the depot.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking about now or about later?
notice_set.why: The arrival has not happened. The sentence borrows the everyday shape for a moment that is still ahead.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody knows when the crossing will reopen.
notice_set.question: Is the sentence about the moment something else happens, or about the reopening itself?
options: About the moment something else happens
notice_set.why: Here the reopening is the whole point of the sentence, not the peg another event hangs on.

notice_set.sentence: By the time the inspectors get here, we will have the paperwork ready.
notice_set.question: Which happens first, in the world?
notice_set.why: By the time sets a deadline, so everything the other half describes has to be done before it.

notice_set.sentence: I won't sign anything until the surveyor sends the report.
notice_set.question: Will the speaker sign if the report never comes?
notice_set.why: Until makes the report the condition, and the sentence says plainly what happens without it.

teach.rule_line: Mark the future once. The half with when, until or as soon as never carries it.
teach.false_rule: That a sentence about the future needs a future word in both halves. English marks it once and lets the joining word do the rest.

errors.wrong: I'll ring you when I will get to the station.
errors.right: I'll ring you when I get to the station.
errors.why_it_happens: Both events are genuinely in the future, so marking both feels honest and complete. Nothing in the sentence sounds odd afterwards, which is why it survives every re-reading.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.
errors.l1_note: Many languages do mark the future in both halves, so this transfers straight across.

errors.wrong: As soon as the figures will arrive, the committee will publish them.
errors.right: As soon as the figures arrive, the committee will publish them.
errors.why_it_happens: The joining half comes first, so the learner starts the sentence in future mode and stays there. By the time the real news arrives, the future has already been announced once.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: We can't begin until the surveyor will arrive on site.
errors.right: We can't begin until the surveyor arrives on site.
errors.why_it_happens: Until feels like a word about waiting, and waiting feels like the future, so the future gets marked again inside the waiting half where it does not belong.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: By the time the auditors get here, we finish the whole review.
errors.right: By the time the auditors get here, we will have finished the whole review.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has learned to strip the future out of the joining half, and strips it out of the other half too. The rule has been over-applied rather than misunderstood.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: will.

pays_in.note: Any argument about what must happen before something else improves needs it.
pays_in.model: Charging schemes will only work once the alternatives are genuinely usable.

pays_in.note: Answers about conditions and consequences are built on these joins.
pays_in.model: People will give up their cars when the buses run often enough to trust.

pays_in.note: Instructions and arrangements are sequenced with these words.
pays_in.model: Wait in the foyer until the previous group comes out.

used_in.quote: The whole argument turns on what has to happen first, which is this join made five or six times.
Talking about how people plan means sequencing two future events in one sentence, over and over.

payload.sentence: Text me when you land and I'll come out to the car park.
payload.question: Has the landing happened?

feedback.why_key: Nothing in this sentence has happened. The everyday shape is being used for a moment that is still ahead.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the whole sentence before you place it in time.

payload.sentence: Once the ring road opens, traffic in the old town will drop sharply.
payload.question: Which of the two happens first?
options: they happen at the same moment

feedback.why_key: Once names the moment everything else waits for, so the opening has to come first for the sentence to make sense.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the joining word and put its event first.

payload.context: Somebody explaining what they intend to do at the end of a contract.
payload.sentence: I'll take a fortnight off when I will finish this contract.
reasons: the future is marked twice in one sentence
the contract has already finished
the two halves are in the wrong order
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One sentence gets one mark for the future, and the half beginning with when has already given up its claim to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip will out of the half beginning with when.

payload.context: From a note on a river restoration scheme.
payload.stem: The fish will return as soon as the water ___ (clear).

expected: clears

feedback.why_key: The clearing is the moment the return hangs on, so it is treated as a fixed point rather than announced as news.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the ordinary present shape after as soon as.

payload.context: Somebody giving instructions in a kitchen.
payload.stem: Take it out of the oven before the top ___ (start) to darken.

expected: starts

feedback.why_key: Before names a moment that has not arrived, and English still treats that moment as a fixed point on the clock.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the present shape after before.

payload.given: The grant money arrives in June. After that, the workshops reopen.
payload.instruction: Join them into one sentence, marking the future once, with the joining half first.

expected: the grant money arrives in june, the workshops will reopen
the grant money arrives, the workshops will reopen
the grant money arrives in june the workshops will reopen

feedback.why_key: The arrival becomes the peg and the reopening becomes the news, which is why only one half is left pointing forward.
feedback.feed_forward: Put will in the half that carries the news.

payload.context: Build one sentence stating what happens at the end of a trial.

expected: we will publish the data when the trial ends

feedback.why_key: Will sits in the first half with the news, and the half after when keeps its plain ending and nothing else.
feedback.feed_forward: Place will before when, never after it.

payload.audio_text: I'll let you know as soon as I hear back.

expected: i'll let you know as soon as i hear back
ill let you know as soon as i hear back
i will let you know as soon as i hear back

feedback.why_key: One small sound at the front carries the future for the whole sentence, and the second half has nothing at all on it.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the first half's small sound, then leave the second bare.

items.decision_cue: until the charging network will be

payload.context: From a body paragraph about electric vehicles.
payload.sentence: Sales will stay flat until the charging network will be dense enough to rely on.
reasons: the future has been marked in both halves of the sentence
the two events are in the wrong order
the sentence is about something already finished
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The first half is already pointing forward. The half after until only has to name the moment, and naming a moment needs no extra machinery.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the second will and leave the first alone.

items.decision_cue: before the new rota will come

payload.sentence: The team needs training before the new rota will come into force in March.
payload.error_span: before the new rota will come

expected: before the new rota comes

feedback.why_key: March is doing all the work of pointing forward already. The extra word adds nothing and breaks the join.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete will from the half that starts with before.

payload.context: Two lines from the same report on a delayed instrument.
sentences: We will start the tests when the equipment arrives.
Nobody knows when the equipment will arrive.
meanings: The arrival is the peg the tests hang on, so it is treated as a fixed point.
The arrival is the thing being asked about, so the sentence leaves it pointing forward.

feedback.why_key: The same word does two different jobs. In one line it hangs an event on a moment; in the other it is the question itself.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the joining word is naming a moment or asking one.

payload.prompt_text: Think of something in your work or your studies that you are waiting on. Say in one sentence what you will do at the moment it finally happens.

feedback.why_key: You are naming a moment and hanging a plan on it, which is the exact shape this point exists for.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the future once, in the half with the plan.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences for an essay on free public transport, each saying what has to happen before the policy could work. Use a different joining word in each. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: An argument about conditions is nothing but these joins, and a reader who meets two broken ones stops following the order of events.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the condition first, then the consequence with will.

title: Saying what will be going on at a moment later, and asking without pressing

point_json.grammar_name: Future continuous: will be + the -ing verb

teach.can_do: I can say what will already be going on at a particular moment later, and I can ask about someone's plans without sounding as though I want a favour.
teach.why_it_matters: The second job is the one nobody teaches and the one that saves you socially: it lets you ask about somebody's afternoon without them hearing a request coming.
teach.meaning: Pick a moment in the future and stand in it. This shape says that the thing was already under way when you arrived and had not finished. It is the difference between arriving and starting. There is a second job, and in speech it is the more useful one: because the sentence describes a situation rather than a decision, it takes all the pressure out of a question. Asking somebody what they will be doing on Friday enquires about their afternoon. Asking what they will do on Friday sounds like the beginning of a favour.

form.pattern: will be + the -ing verb
notes: the small word be never changes and is never dropped, however fast the sentence is said
in speech the whole opening runs together as one blurred sound before the -ing verb
verbs that describe a state rather than an activity stay out of this shape, exactly as they do everywhere else
form.negative: won't be + the -ing verb: The office won't be taking deliveries over the holiday.
form.question: Will + person + be + the -ing verb: Will you be using the van on Thursday?

marks.label: the moment you are talking about

spec.caption: You arrive in the middle of it. It did not start when you got there and it does not stop.

worked_example.sentence: At six on Friday we will still be loading the last of the samples.
worked_example.why_this_form: Six o'clock is a moment the speaker is standing in, and the loading is neither beginning nor ending there. It is simply in progress around it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: We will load the last of the samples at six would say the loading begins at six, which is a promise about a start rather than a picture of a moment.

notice_set.sentence: At eleven tomorrow the surveyors will be walking the north boundary.
notice_set.question: Do they begin at eleven?
notice_set.why: Eleven is a moment inside the walk, not the start of it. They set off earlier.

notice_set.sentence: Will you be using the meeting room this afternoon?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking for something, or just checking?
notice_set.why: The question describes a situation rather than requesting a decision, so nobody feels pushed by it.

title: Saying whether a small amount is enough or is a shortage

point_json.grammar_name: a few and few, a little and little, and the language of proportion

pays_in.note: Proportion language is most of what a chart answer needs above the numbers themselves.
pays_in.model: The majority of journeys were made on foot, and a significant proportion by bicycle.

pays_in.note: The difference between conceding a point and dismissing it is one word.
pays_in.model: A few schemes have worked, but little of that success has been repeated elsewhere.

pays_in.note: Discussion answers need a way to grant part of a case without granting all of it.
pays_in.model: A few people manage it, but not many, and that's the whole problem.

pays_in.note: A true or false stem often turns on whether the passage said few or a few.
pays_in.model: Few of the original buildings survived the redevelopment.

teach.can_do: I can say that a small amount is enough, or that it is a shortage, and be understood the way I meant.
teach.why_it_matters: One missing word turns good news into a complaint. It is the cheapest meaning reversal in English and nobody warns learners about it.
teach.meaning: A few and few describe the same quantity and take opposite views of it. A few looks at what there is: some, enough to work with. Few looks at what there is not: hardly any, and the sentence is a complaint. A little and little do the same job for measured nouns. Nothing else in the sentence changes, so the only thing telling the reader which way you meant it is one small word at the front.

form.pattern: a few / few + counted noun  ·  a little / little + measured noun
notes: with the a, the sentence is positive: a few stalls stayed open, a little time is left
without it, the sentence is negative: few stalls stayed open, little time is left
the bare versions are formal and belong in writing rather than in conversation
for a large share without a number: the majority of, a significant proportion of, plenty of
the majority of takes its verb from the noun after of: the majority of households were, the majority of the money was
form.negative: few of the stalls stayed open, and little of the money was spent locally
form.question: How many of the stalls stayed open?

ends: there is enough to work with

worked_example.sentence: A few of the older traders are still there, so the market has kept some of its character.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second half of the sentence is positive, so the first half has to be too. The a is what makes the two halves agree.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Take the a away and the opening becomes a complaint, and the sentence then argues with itself halfway through.

notice_set.sentence: A few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
notice_set.question: Did the market keep going?
notice_set.why: The speaker is pointing at what survived, which is why the sentence feels like good news.

notice_set.sentence: Few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
notice_set.question: Did the market keep going?
notice_set.why: The same number, and the speaker is pointing at the shortage instead.

notice_set.sentence: There is a little time left before the tender closes.

notice_set.why: Enough is left to act on, which is the whole message of this version.

notice_set.sentence: There is little time left before the tender closes.
notice_set.question: Can the bid still go in?
notice_set.why: The same clock, and this version is telling you to give up on it.

notice_set.sentence: The majority of the households in the district were on the old tariff.
notice_set.question: Roughly what share of households is being described?
notice_set.why: It is the useful way to report a large share when the exact number is not worth giving.

teach.rule_line: The a turns a shortage into a supply. Nothing else in the sentence changes.
teach.false_rule: That few and a few are one word with an optional article. They point in opposite directions, and a reader follows whichever one you wrote.

contrast.question: Am I saying there is some, or am I saying there is almost none?

fork.answer: Some, enough to work with, and I am pleased about it
Almost none, and I am pointing at the shortage
A large share, and I do not want to give a number
fork.selects: the majority of, a significant proportion of

a.text: A few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
a.means: Some stayed open. The market kept going and the sentence is pleased about it.

b.text: Few of the stalls stayed open through the winter.
b.means: Almost all of them shut. The market emptied and the sentence is reporting a loss.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Writing few when you meant a few does not read as a slip. It reads as a complaint, and the rest of your paragraph then argues against a shortage you never intended to report.

edge_case.text: Without the a, both words are formal and suit writing. In conversation people reach for hardly any or not many, and that is the right choice there, not a lesser one.

contrast.stronger_test: Put but on the end and see which way the sentence wants to go. A few stayed open, but... expects a problem. Few stayed open, but... expects a consolation.

worked_pairs.a: A few of the older traders are still there.
worked_pairs.b: Few of the older traders are still there.
worked_pairs.gloss: One sentence is about survival and the other is about loss, and the difference between them is two letters and a space.

worked_pairs.a: There is a little money left in the maintenance budget.
worked_pairs.b: There is little money left in the maintenance budget.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first sentence lets you order the repair. The second tells you to write the letter explaining why you cannot.

worked_pairs.b: The majority of the money was spent on the old tariff.
worked_pairs.gloss: The verb follows the noun after of, not the word majority, which is why the two sentences take different verbs.

errors.wrong: Few of the funding reached the smaller schools.

errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored few as the negative word and reaches for it whatever kind of noun follows. The positive and negative pair exists twice, once on each side of the noun system.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: few becomes little.

errors.wrong: Few people came to the meeting, which was a good turnout for a wet evening.
errors.right: A few people came to the meeting, which was a good turnout for a wet evening.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the number was small and picks the word for a small number, without noticing that the second half of their own sentence is pleased about it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: a.

errors.wrong: The majority of the households in the district was on the old tariff.
errors.right: The majority of the households in the district were on the old tariff.
errors.why_it_happens: Majority looks singular and it is five words from the verb, so it wins the argument over the plural noun that actually decides the verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: was becomes were.

used_in.quote: Reporting six modes without repeating a number six times is exactly what this proportion language is for.

title: Running one three-question check in front of every noun I write

point_json.grammar_name: The article decision: a, the, or nothing

pays_in.note: You will run this check forty or fifty times in one answer.
pays_in.model: A degree taught in a second language costs students time before it saves them any.

pays_in.note: Chart language moves constantly between categories and particular figures.
pays_in.model: Cycling accounted for a small share of journeys, and the share fell after 2018.

pays_in.note: General claims in a discussion need the empty space, and examples need the pointer.
pays_in.model: People generally trust a doctor more than they trust the health service as a whole.

pays_in.note: A passage signals whether a claim is general or particular with these words alone.
pays_in.model: The scheme described in the previous section was never repeated.

teach.can_do: I can run one short check in front of any noun and come out with the right word every time.
teach.why_it_matters: Articles are among the last things any learner gets reliable, so what you need is not a feeling but a procedure you can run in three seconds under pressure.
teach.meaning: You have met the three choices separately. Putting them together is one question asked in a fixed order, and the order matters, because the first question that gets a yes ends the check. Ask whether you mean the category as a whole. If not, ask whether your reader can pick out which one you mean. If not, you are introducing one of several, and what happens then depends only on whether the noun is one English counts.

form.pattern: Q1 category? nothing.  Q2 identifiable? the.  Q3 otherwise: a with a singular counted noun, nothing with a plural or a measured one
notes: question one: renewable energy is expensive to store
question two: the storage problem described above is the reason
question three, singular counted: a battery lasts about ten years
question three, plural or measured: batteries lose capacity, storage costs money
a singular counted noun can never stand alone: not battery lasts ten years
form.negative: a battery does not last for ever
form.question: How long does a battery last?

rungs.text: Q1  Do I mean the whole category?  ->  nothing
Q2  Can my reader pick out which one?  ->  the
Q3  Neither: singular counted  ->  a, otherwise nothing

worked_example.sentence: Renewable energy is expensive to store, and a battery big enough for a house still costs more than the roof it sits under.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first noun is a whole category, so nothing goes in front. The second is one of many, so it takes a. The third is narrowed by the words after it, so it takes the.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The renewable energy would point at one particular supply, which is not a claim anybody could check, and battery on its own is a shape English does not have.

notice_set.sentence: Renewable energy is expensive to store.
notice_set.question: Is this about one supply or about the whole idea?
notice_set.why: The first question gets a yes, so the check stops there and the space stays empty.

notice_set.sentence: The storage problem described above is the main obstacle.
notice_set.question: Can a reader tell which problem is meant?
options: Only if they know the subject
notice_set.why: The words after the noun narrow it to one, which is the second question answered yes.

notice_set.sentence: A battery large enough for a house costs about as much as a small car.
notice_set.question: Is one particular battery meant?
options: No, any one of that kind
notice_set.why: Neither of the first two questions gets a yes, the noun is singular and counted, so it takes the third answer.

notice_set.sentence: Batteries lose capacity as they age.
notice_set.question: How many batteries are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The first question again, and a plural noun making a general claim takes nothing in front.

notice_set.sentence: Battery lasts about ten years.
notice_set.question: Does this sound like something an English speaker would write?
notice_set.why: A singular counted noun cannot stand on its own, whichever of the three answers you were aiming at.

teach.rule_line: Category, then identifiable, then one of several. Stop at the first yes.
teach.false_rule: That articles are a feel you pick up by reading. Reading helps and is not enough: the decision is taken faster than noticing works, so you need a check.

contrast.question: Whole category, one my reader can pick out, or one of several?

fork.answer: The whole category, with a plural or a measured noun
One my reader can pick out from what they already have
One of several, singular and counted

a.text: Buses in Marlow run every ten minutes.
a.means: This is what bus travel in Marlow is like, as a general fact about the town.

b.text: The buses in Marlow run every ten minutes.
b.means: The particular service we have been discussing, which the reader already has in mind.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: Both versions are correct English and they answer different questions. If your paragraph is about what the town is like, the pointer narrows a general claim into a timetable, and your reader takes away a smaller point than you made.

edge_case.text: Two places where the check does not help: fixed phrases like at home, by car, in bed and at school, and names, which have to be learned one at a time. Neither is worth arguing with. Learn them as words.

contrast.stronger_test: If the noun is singular and counted, something has to go in front of it, whatever the rest of the check said. That one fact catches more mistakes than the whole of the rest of the procedure.

worked_pairs.a: Renewable energy is expensive to store.
worked_pairs.b: The renewable energy generated at Verdon is stored in an old mine shaft.
worked_pairs.gloss: Question one is yes for the first sentence and no for the second, because the words after the noun have pinned it to one place.

worked_pairs.a: A battery lasts about ten years.
worked_pairs.b: The battery in the loft was replaced in March.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both nouns are singular and counted, so both need something. Which word depends only on whether the reader can pick it out.

worked_pairs.a: Students who commute pay more for housing.
worked_pairs.b: The students who commute pay more for housing.
worked_pairs.gloss: Words after the noun do not automatically call for the pointer. The first sentence is about all commuting students anywhere; the second is about a group already under discussion.

errors.wrong: Battery large enough for a house still costs a great deal.
errors.right: A battery large enough for a house still costs a great deal.
errors.why_it_happens: The check has been run and answered correctly at question three, and then the answer itself is left off, because a bare noun looks complete to a writer whose first language allows it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: A.

errors.wrong: The renewable energy is expensive to store.
errors.right: Renewable energy is expensive to store.
errors.why_it_happens: Question two is answered before question one, so a general claim gets treated as though the reader could pick out which supply is meant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: The.

errors.wrong: Storage problem described above is the main obstacle to any of this.
errors.right: The storage problem described above is the main obstacle to any of this.
errors.why_it_happens: The words after the noun already identify it, so the pointer at the front feels redundant. It is the pointer, not the description, that English requires.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: The.

errors.wrong: A research into tidal power has been going on for thirty years.
errors.right: Research into tidal power has been going on for thirty years.
errors.why_it_happens: Question three has been reached and answered as though the noun were one English counts. The check is only as good as the countability judgement it sits on.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: A.

used_in.quote: Every sentence of this answer contains at least two nouns, and every one of them needs the check run on it.

payload.sentence: Renewable energy is expensive to store.
payload.question: Is one particular supply meant?
options: No, it is the whole idea

feedback.why_key: The first of the three questions gets a yes, so the check ends there and nothing goes in front.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask the category question first, every time.

title: Saying whether somebody went and came back, or is still there

point_json.grammar_name: has been to and has gone to

teach.can_do: I can say whether someone went somewhere and came back, or is there at this moment.
teach.why_it_matters: One syllable decides whether your listener expects to see the person this afternoon. It is a small point and it goes wrong constantly.
teach.meaning: Both sentences describe a journey that has already started, and they disagree about where the traveller is standing while you read them. Been says the journey is finished in both directions: they went, they came back, and the trip is now part of what they have done. Gone says the journey is only half over: they set off and they have not returned, which is usually the reason they are being mentioned at all.

form.pattern: have / has been to + a place, or have / has gone to + a place
notes: been to takes to when you mean the trip: I have been to Marlow, not I have been in Marlow
you can count trips that are over, so been to takes twice, three times, several times; gone to cannot
been is also the plain third form of be, so it turns up in sentences with no travel in them at all
form.negative: haven't been to is the everyday negative; hasn't gone to usually means they never set off.
form.question: Have you ever been to ...? Where has she gone?

left.role: been to: the journey is finished both ways
left.text: Halida has been to the site office.

right.role: gone to: the journey is only half done
right.text: Halida has gone to the site office.

spec.caption: The difference is not where they went. It is where they are standing while you read the sentence.

worked_example.sentence: Two of the surveyors have been to the Norland reserve, so they know the access track.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence needs them back at the table, because it is using what they learned out there. Only the completed round trip leaves them in the room.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Gone would put both surveyors out at the reserve right now, and the second half of the sentence would have nobody left to know anything.

notice_set.sentence: Marek has gone to the harbour office.
notice_set.question: Can you speak to him where you are?
notice_set.why: The half-finished journey leaves him at the other end of it, which is why somebody said this to you in the first place.

notice_set.sentence: Marek has been to the harbour office.
notice_set.question: Can you speak to him where you are?
notice_set.why: The round trip is complete, so the office visit is behind him and he is back where you are.

notice_set.sentence: Have you ever been to a night market?
notice_set.question: What is the question about?
options: whether it has ever happened in your life
notice_set.why: Ever throws the question across a whole life, and only the completed round trip can be counted that way.

notice_set.sentence: Half the crew has gone to the yard.
notice_set.question: What is the office like at this moment?
notice_set.why: Half of them are at the other end of an unfinished journey, so the room they left is emptier than normal.

notice_set.sentence: It has been cold since the weekend.
notice_set.question: Is this sentence about a journey?
notice_set.why: Been here is just the plain third form of be. The travelling meaning only appears when to and a place follow it.

teach.rule_line: Been means they went and came back; gone means they are still at the other end.
teach.false_rule: That been and gone are two spellings of one idea. They put the traveller in two different places, and only one of them is in the room with you.

contrast.question: Is the person back, or are they still at the other end?

fork.answer: Back, and the trip is now part of what they have done
Still there, and that is exactly why they are not in front of you

a.text: Halida has been to the site office.
a.means: She went and she is back. You could turn round and ask her about it.

b.text: Halida has gone to the site office.
b.means: She is at the site office now, which is why you cannot find her.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote has gone. Your listener now expects an empty chair and starts planning round it. If she is sitting two desks away, been is the word that says so, and the whole difference is one syllable.

edge_case.text: Been is also the plain third form of be, so it appears in sentences with no travelling in them: it has been cold all week. And in speech been to happily takes a place that is really an appointment: I've been to the dentist.

contrast.stronger_test: Try adding and she's back now on the end. If the sentence takes it without complaint, been was the word you wanted. Gone refuses it outright.

worked_pairs.a: Kester has been to the Verdon gorge twice.
worked_pairs.b: Kester has gone to the Verdon gorge for the weekend.
worked_pairs.gloss: You can count trips that are over. A trip somebody is still on has no count yet, only a length.

worked_pairs.a: Half the team has been to the new depot and they say it is enormous.
worked_pairs.b: Half the team has gone to the new depot, so the office is quiet.
worked_pairs.gloss: The report needs them back in the room. The quiet office needs them out of it.

worked_pairs.a: I have been to Sandmouth, so I know the coast road.
worked_pairs.b: She has gone to Sandmouth, so she will not be in until Thursday.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so I know the coast road
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so she will not be in until Thursday
worked_pairs.gloss: One sentence uses the journey as knowledge. The other uses it as an absence.

errors.wrong: Nuala isn't at her desk. She has been to the wholesaler.
errors.right: Nuala isn't at her desk. She has gone to the wholesaler.
errors.why_it_happens: Been is the word learners meet first, in the question about experience, so it becomes the default for anything involving travel. Nothing in the sentence corrects it, and the result is a clear sentence saying the wrong thing.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: been becomes gone.

errors.wrong: I went to Sandmouth three times, so I know the coast road well.
errors.right: I have been to Sandmouth three times, so I know the coast road well.
errors.why_it_happens: The three trips are over, so the past simple looks right. The point of the sentence is what the speaker knows today, and a finished form leaves that connection hanging.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: went becomes have been.

errors.wrong: Have you ever gone to the Norland reserve?
errors.right: Have you ever been to the Norland reserve?
errors.why_it_happens: The question asks about a whole life of chances, but gone insists the person is away at this exact moment, which cannot be true of somebody standing in front of you answering it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: gone becomes been.

pays_in.note: Describing a place you visited runs on the completed round trip.
pays_in.model: I've been to the coast at Sandmouth two or three times.

pays_in.note: Everyday answers about family and colleagues need the other one constantly.
pays_in.model: My sister's gone to Marlow for a training week.

pays_in.note: Whether somebody is available this afternoon can turn on one syllable.
pays_in.model: She's gone to the depot, so try her tomorrow.

used_in.quote: Describing a place from childhood needs the completed round trip in nearly every sentence, and one slip puts the speaker back there.
Answers on this card swing between trips that are over and people who are away right now.

feedback.why_key: The journey is half over, so he is at the far end of it. That is the only reason anyone would tell you this.

payload.sentence: Marek has been to the harbour office.

payload.audio_text: She's gone to the depot, so try her tomorrow.

expected: she's gone to the depot so try her tomorrow
she has gone to the depot so try her tomorrow

feedback.why_key: The 's is almost inaudible and the whole message about where she is rides on the word after it.

title: Talking about an activity that has been running up to now and still shows

point_json.grammar_name: Present perfect continuous

teach.can_do: I can talk about an activity that has been running up to now and still shows.
teach.why_it_matters: It answers how long you have been doing something, and it explains the state you or a place are in without your having to name the state.
teach.meaning: This form points at the activity rather than at anything the activity produced. It says something has been going on across a stretch reaching up to this moment, and it very often exists to explain something the listener can see: the mud on the boots, the empty shelf, the tiredness. It makes no promise that the activity is finished, and quite often the whole point is that it is not.

form.pattern: have / has been + the -ing form
notes: Three parts and all three are needed: the helper, been, and the -ing form
've been and 's been in speech, and both are short enough to disappear entirely
Verbs about states rather than activities refuse this form: know, own, belong, mean
form.negative: haven't been + the -ing form: I haven't been sleeping properly.
form.question: How long have you been + the -ing form ...?

marks.label: and runs all the way along here
which is why things look like this

spec.caption: The arrow is the activity. The mark at the end is the state it has left behind, and that state is usually why anybody said it.

worked_example.sentence: The team have been sampling the estuary since first light, which is why the boat is filthy.
worked_example.why_this_form: The sentence is about the work itself and the mess it made, not about a finished set of samples. Nobody is counting anything here.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Have sampled would put a finished set of samples on the table and leave the state of the boat out of the sentence entirely.

notice_set.sentence: Idris has been repainting the survey hut.
notice_set.question: Is the hut finished?
notice_set.why: The form points at the work rather than at a result, so whether it is done is simply not part of the claim.

notice_set.sentence: Idris has repainted the survey hut.
notice_set.question: Is the hut finished?
notice_set.why: Without been and the -ing, the sentence hands you the finished hut and says nothing about the afternoon that produced it.

notice_set.sentence: The pump has been running since Tuesday.
notice_set.question: Is it running at this moment?
notice_set.why: The activity is drawn as a line reaching the present moment, and nothing in the sentence cuts it off before then.

notice_set.sentence: You've been working outside, haven't you?
notice_set.question: How does the speaker know?
options: they can see the result on the person
notice_set.why: This is the form's commonest job: reading backwards from a state you can see to the activity that caused it.

notice_set.sentence: We have been waiting for the results for three weeks.
notice_set.question: Have the results come?
notice_set.why: The waiting is drawn as still running, and waiting that is still running has nothing at the end of it yet.

teach.rule_line: Use it for the activity itself, running up to now and often still going.
teach.false_rule: That it simply means for a long time. A three-minute activity takes it perfectly well when the activity is the thing you are pointing at.

errors.wrong: I have been knowing the family since I was small.
errors.right: I have known the family since I was small.
errors.why_it_happens: The stretch really does run up to now, and this is the form that draws a stretch, so it is a reasonable guess. Knowing is not an activity anyone performs, so English refuses to view it as one.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: have been knowing becomes have known.

errors.wrong: The clinic has been treating four hundred patients this month.
errors.right: The clinic has treated four hundred patients this month.
errors.why_it_happens: A counted total is a result, and this form is not looking at results. The number makes the sentence sound like a report while the verb is still pointing at the activity behind it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: has been treating becomes has treated.

errors.wrong: I've written since two o'clock and I still have two sections left.
errors.right: I've been writing since two o'clock and I still have two sections left.
errors.why_it_happens: The simple form has been learned as the safe one and gets used everywhere. Here the sentence is about the afternoon and the state it has left behind, and the simple form throws both of those away.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word and one ending: written becomes been writing.

pays_in.note: It answers how long questions and explains why things look as they do.
pays_in.model: I've been commuting right across the city for about two years now.

pays_in.note: Describing a long project needs the activity, not only the result.
pays_in.model: I've been learning to sail since the spring and I am still nowhere near good.

pays_in.note: A trend that is still running wants the activity form.
pays_in.model: Governments have been subsidising rail travel for decades without closing the gap.

used_in.quote: Every answer on this card is about something still in progress, which is exactly what this form was built to say.
The speaker explains a delay by naming what has been going on, and the whole explanation rides on one unstressed been.

payload.sentence: Idris has been repainting the survey hut.
payload.question: Is the hut finished?

feedback.why_key: The form is looking at the work, not at what came out of it, so a finished hut is neither promised nor ruled out.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the sentence is looking at doing or at done.

payload.sentence: You've been working outside, haven't you?
payload.question: How does the speaker know?
options: they can see the result on the person

feedback.why_key: This is the form's commonest job: reading backwards from a state in front of you to the activity that produced it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for the visible state the sentence is explaining.

reasons: this verb is not something you do, so it refuses the activity form
the helper is the wrong one
the stretch of time is already finished

she has been covering the late shift all week

payload.prompt_text: Think of something you have been doing for a while and have not finished. Say one sentence about the activity and one about how anyone could tell.

feedback.why_key: Naming the activity and then the state it left is the natural two-sentence shape this form lives in.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the activity, then the evidence for it.

payload.prompt_text: Talk for one minute about something you have been learning at work, and make at least two sentences about the activity rather than the result.

feedback.why_key: An answer about learning that only names finished results sounds like a list. The activity form is what turns it into a story.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the activity in view for at least two sentences.

title: Choosing between pointing at the finished thing and pointing at the doing

point_json.grammar_name: Present perfect simple vs continuous

teach.can_do: I can choose between pointing at a finished result and pointing at the activity behind it.
teach.why_it_matters: Both forms are correct English and they answer different questions. The wrong one tells your listener the job is finished when it is not, or the reverse.
teach.meaning: Both forms reach from an earlier moment up to now, and when they arrive they look at different things. The simple form looks at what the activity produced: the finished thing, the total, the number done. The continuous looks at the activity itself: how long it has run, whether it is still going, and what state it has left everything in. Ask what you are pointing at and the choice makes itself.

form.pattern: simple: have / has + third form. continuous: have / has been + the -ing form
notes: A counted result pushes you towards the simple: I have sent four emails
A length, or an explanation of how things look, pushes you towards the continuous: I have been sending emails since eight
State verbs have no continuous at all, so the choice never arises with know, own, belong or mean
form.negative: haven't + third form for the result; haven't been + the -ing form for the activity.
form.question: How much have you done? asks for the simple. What have you been doing? asks for the continuous.

left.role: the simple: look at what came out of it
left.text: I have marked twelve essays.

right.role: the continuous: look at the doing and the state it left
right.text: I have been marking essays since six.

spec.caption: Same evening, same essays. One sentence hands you the pile and the other hands you the person.

worked_example.sentence: I have been marking essays since six, and I have finished eleven of them.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first half explains the state of the room and the person, so it takes the activity. The second half hands over a number, so it takes the result.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Swap them and the sentence claims the evening produced nothing, and that eleven essays were somehow an activity rather than a total.

notice_set.sentence: The council has repaired the footbridge.
notice_set.question: Can you walk over it this morning?
notice_set.why: The simple form hands you the finished bridge, and a finished bridge is one you can cross.

notice_set.sentence: The council has been repairing the footbridge.
notice_set.question: Can you walk over it this morning?
notice_set.why: This one reports the work rather than the bridge. Whether the barriers have come down is outside what it claims.

notice_set.sentence: Halida has been writing her report.
notice_set.question: Is the report finished?
notice_set.why: The activity is in view and the document is not, so the sentence is silent about it either way.

notice_set.sentence: Halida has written her report.
notice_set.question: Is the report finished?
notice_set.why: The simple form exists to hand over the product, and here the product is a finished report.

notice_set.sentence: We have owned the shop for eleven years.
notice_set.question: Why is there no continuous version of this sentence?
options: owning is not something you do
the sentence is in the wrong tense
notice_set.why: The continuous draws activities. Owning is a state that is simply true, so there is no activity for it to draw.

teach.rule_line: Point at the result with the simple; point at the doing with the continuous.
teach.false_rule: That the continuous means unfinished and the simple means finished. The continuous does not say either way. It is simply not looking at that.

contrast.question: Am I pointing at what is done, or at the doing?

fork.answer: At what is done: a result, a total, a number, a finished thing
fork.selects: the simple, as in have marked

fork.answer: At the doing: how long it ran, whether it is still going, why things look like this
fork.selects: the continuous, as in have been marking

a.text: Idris has marked the essays.
a.means: Every essay is done and the pile is ready to hand back.

b.text: Idris has been marking the essays.
b.means: That is what he has been doing, which is why he looks like that. Whether the pile is finished is not said.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose has been marking. Your reader now expects an unfinished pile and asks how far you got. If every essay is done, the simple form says so and stops there.

edge_case.text: With live, work and study the two forms mean almost exactly the same thing and nobody will notice which you chose. Verbs about states, like know, own and belong, refuse the continuous outright, and that is a rule rather than a preference.

contrast.stronger_test: Try dropping a number into the sentence. If a count sits comfortably, you are in the simple. The continuous does not want counting; it wants a length.

worked_pairs.a: I have read three of the six chapters.
worked_pairs.b: I have been reading since the train left.
worked_pairs.gloss: A count belongs to a result. A length belongs to an activity.

worked_pairs.a: The council has repaired the footbridge.
worked_pairs.b: The council has been repairing the footbridge.
worked_pairs.gloss: One says you can walk across it this morning. The other says the barriers may well still be up.

worked_pairs.a: Halida has written her report and left it on your desk.
worked_pairs.b: Halida has been writing her report, so do not disturb her.
worked_pairs.gloss: The second half of each sentence tells you which form the first half needed.

errors.wrong: I have been reading three of the six chapters.
errors.right: I have read three of the six chapters.
errors.why_it_happens: The reading really has gone on across a stretch, so the activity form feels honest. The counted chapters are a result, and a result cannot sit inside a form that refuses to look at results.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: have been reading becomes have read.

errors.wrong: Sorry about the flour everywhere. I have baked since lunchtime.
errors.right: Sorry about the flour everywhere. I have been baking since lunchtime.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reaches for the shorter and safer form. The sentence exists to explain the mess, and only the activity form points back at the afternoon that made it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word and one ending: baked becomes been baking.

errors.wrong: The same family have been owning the shop for eleven years.
errors.right: The same family have owned the shop for eleven years.
errors.why_it_happens: Eleven years is a stretch running up to now, which is exactly what the continuous draws, so it is a fair guess. Owning is not something anybody performs; it is a state that is simply true.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: have been owning becomes have owned.

pays_in.note: Questions about length and questions about progress want opposite forms.
pays_in.model: I've been taking an evening course, and I've finished two of the four modules.

pays_in.note: A trend still running and a total already reached are two sentences.
pays_in.model: Councils have been cutting rural routes for a decade and have removed nearly half of them.

pays_in.note: Whether a job is done or still in progress can turn on the word been.
pays_in.model: They've been resurfacing the road, so expect delays.

used_in.quote: Talking about something you have been getting to grips with needs both forms in the same minute, one for the effort and one for what you can now do.
The essay has to separate what has been going on from what has actually been achieved, and that separation is this choice.

payload.sentence: The council has been repairing the footbridge.
payload.question: Can you walk over it this morning?

feedback.why_key: This form reports the work rather than the bridge, so the state of the barriers is simply outside the claim.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether you are being handed a thing or an activity.

payload.sentence: The council has repaired the footbridge.
payload.question: Can you walk over it this morning?

feedback.why_key: The simple form hands over the finished bridge, and a finished bridge is one you can cross.
feedback.feed_forward: The simple form gives you the product.

payload.sentence: The same family have been owning the shop for eleven years.

the helper is the wrong one

've marked

feedback.feed_forward: A number in the sentence pulls you to the simple.

've been marking

have been rising steadily since 2019

expected: they've been resurfacing the road so expect delays
they have been resurfacing the road so expect delays
theyve been resurfacing the road so expect delays

payload.context: A colleague is holding out a stapled document across the desk.

That writing is what she has been doing, with nothing claimed about a finished report.

feedback.why_key: There is a document in somebody's hand, so the sentence is about the product rather than about the hours behind it.

options.why_this_means: That the report exists as a finished thing you could pick up.

expected: has been writing

feedback.why_key: A shut door and a warning are about a person mid-activity, and the activity form is the one that leaves the outcome open.

feedback.feed_forward: Handing something over calls for the simple form.

payload.stem: We ___ the survey data.

options.why_this_means: That the checking is done and the data can be relied on.

feedback.why_key: The sentence is explaining where the evening went, not delivering a verdict, and only the activity form does that job.
feedback.feed_forward: Explaining the evening means drawing the activity.

items.decision_cue: the same evening in the workshop

payload.context: Kester is telling a friend about the same evening in the workshop.
payload.stem: I ___ on the boat.

That the evening went on it, with nothing said about whether anything is finished.

follow_up.question: Which one leaves it open whether the boat is finished?

feedback.why_key: Both sentences are true about the same evening. They differ in whether anybody is being promised a result at the end of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether you are promising a result.

payload.context: Two messages left by the same person on the same evening.
sentences: I have written to the landlord.
I have been writing to the landlord.

This has been going on for a while and it is plainly not over.

feedback.why_key: One message closes a job and the other opens a complaint. The words in between them are identical.

payload.context: From a form filled in by a site inspector.
payload.sentence: I have been visiting four of the six sites on the list.
reasons: a counted total belongs to the other form
the helper is the wrong one
the stretch of time is already finished
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Four out of six is a score, and a score is a result. This form is not looking at results, so the number has nowhere to go.
feedback.feed_forward: Counted things take the simple form.

payload.sentence: Sorry about the flour everywhere. I have baked all afternoon.

expected: i have been baking
i've been baking

feedback.why_key: The sentence exists to account for the flour, and only the activity form reaches back to the afternoon that spread it about.

feedback.why_key: Putting both forms side by side in one answer is what shows you are choosing between them rather than defaulting to one.
feedback.feed_forward: Activity first, then the count.

payload.prompt_text: Talk for a minute about a piece of technology you have been getting to grips with. Use the activity form at least twice and give one total. One minute.

feedback.why_key: An answer that separates the effort from what was actually achieved sounds honest, and it happens to demonstrate the whole point at the same time.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what you have been doing, then what you have done.

title: Showing that one past event happened before another one

point_json.grammar_name: Past perfect

teach.can_do: I can show my listener which of two past events happened first, without having to spell the order out.
teach.why_it_matters: Stories and explanations both double back at some point. Without this form the reader has to guess the order and usually guesses wrong.
teach.meaning: Ordinary past tense lays events down in the order you say them. The past perfect breaks that arrangement. It reaches back behind a moment the telling has already fixed and puts an earlier event there. You need it when you have walked your listener to a point in the past and then have to explain something that was already true, already finished, or already going wrong before that point arrived. It is not about distance. It is about which of two past moments you are measuring from.

form.pattern: had + past participle
notes: had never changes for the subject: I had gone, she had gone, they had gone
'd in speech and in a letter: she'd left before the call came
'd is also the short form of would, so the shape of the next word decides which one you heard
form.negative: had not / hadn't + past participle
form.question: Had you + past participle ... ?

marks.label: the moment the story has reached
now, which this form says nothing about

spec.caption: The past perfect is not further back on its own. It is further back than a point the telling has already fixed.

worked_example.sentence: When the relief driver reached the yard, the depot had sent the load out by road.
worked_example.why_this_form: The telling has stopped at the driver's arrival. The load went out behind that moment, so the sentence has to reach back past the point it is standing on.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Sent would line the two up in the order given: the driver turns up, and then the load goes out. That is a different afternoon.

notice_set.sentence: When we got to the platform, the Marlow train had left.
notice_set.question: Did we see the train go?
notice_set.why: The leaving is placed behind our arrival, so it was over before we were standing there.

notice_set.sentence: When we got to the platform, the Marlow train left.
notice_set.question: Did we see the train go?
notice_set.why: Both events sit on the same line in the order given, so the train went while we watched.

notice_set.sentence: The council cancelled the scheme. It had cost eleven million pounds.
notice_set.question: Which came first?
notice_set.why: The second sentence steps back behind the first one in order to explain it.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed was furious because nobody had told him about the change.
notice_set.question: Had anyone spoken to him before he found out?
notice_set.why: The conversation that never happened is placed behind the anger, which is what makes the anger make sense.

notice_set.sentence: The ferry had been out of service for three weeks when the storm hit.
notice_set.question: Was the ferry running on the day of the storm?
notice_set.why: The three weeks are measured backwards from the storm, so they were over by the time it arrived.

notice_set.sentence: Delia moved to Sandmouth in 2016. She had trained as a baker in Verdon.
notice_set.question: Where did she learn the trade?
notice_set.why: The training is set behind the move, so it belongs to the life she had before she arrived.

teach.rule_line: Ask: has my telling already reached a later moment that this event happened before?
teach.false_rule: That the past perfect means a long time ago. It says nothing about distance. It says only: earlier than the moment we are standing on.

errors.wrong: When the auditors arrived, the depot destroyed the old rotas.
errors.right: When the auditors arrived, the depot had destroyed the old rotas.
errors.why_it_happens: Both events are in the past, so one past tense feels like enough. The learner has fixed the time correctly and has simply not marked which of the two came first.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: had.

errors.wrong: First she had studied engineering at Verdon, and then she worked in Ashfield.
errors.right: First she studied engineering at Verdon, and then she worked in Ashfield.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been told the past perfect is the more advanced tense and reaches for it to sound stronger. Nothing in that instruction says it needs a later moment to lean on.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: had.

errors.wrong: The depot shut in March. The last two drivers had left in January, and the site had stood empty ever since.
errors.right: The depot shut in March. The last two drivers had left in January, and the site has stood empty ever since.
errors.why_it_happens: Once the step back is switched on it tends to stay on for the rest of the paragraph. The writer stops asking, clause by clause, which moment each verb is measured from.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: had becomes has.

errors.wrong: He said he never worked a night shift before that week.
errors.right: He said he had never worked a night shift before that week.
errors.why_it_happens: The reporting verb has already put the sentence in the past, so a second past-marked verb feels like repetition. The experience being reported is older than the saying, and nothing shows it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: had.

pays_in.note: Every Part 2 story about a decision or a mistake needs one step back behind the main event.
pays_in.model: I only found out at the gate. The last bus had gone and the depot was locked.

pays_in.note: Explaining why a policy failed means naming what was already true before it started.
pays_in.model: The scheme was abandoned in 2019, though its funding had been cut two years earlier.

pays_in.note: A question about the order of events is answered by the auxiliary, not by the order of the sentences.
pays_in.model: The council withdrew the subsidy. Passenger numbers had fallen for six straight years.

used_in.quote: A mistake only becomes a story when the listener learns what was already in place before it happened.
Body paragraphs on this prompt explain a move by naming what had gone wrong in the job before it.

payload.sentence: When I got to the stop, the last bus had gone.
payload.question: Was the bus still there when I arrived?

feedback.why_key: The going is placed behind my arrival, so the stop was empty by the time I reached it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read had plus the participle as one step backwards in time.

payload.sentence: The firm closed in 2018. It had lost money for six years.
payload.question: Where do the six loss-making years sit?
options: at the same time as the closure

feedback.why_key: The second sentence steps back behind the closure to explain it, so the losses ran up to that year and stopped.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the later event first, then place the had-clause behind it.

payload.context: From a first draft of a paragraph about a career change.
payload.sentence: First she had trained as an engineer, and then she moved into teaching.
reasons: nothing has been reached yet for the training to sit behind
the training happened after the teaching
the participle is the wrong form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: First and then have already put the two events in order. The step back has nothing to step back from.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete had when a time word already fixes the order.

payload.context: From a note on the Ashfield freight line.
payload.stem: By the time the new depot opened, three of the four sidings ___ (close) for good.

expected: had closed

feedback.why_key: The opening is the moment the sentence stands on, and the sidings went before it.
feedback.feed_forward: Locate the later moment, then push the earlier verb behind it.

payload.context: Two colleagues talking about a bad Monday.
payload.stem: I got in at seven and somebody ___ (take) my locker already.

expected: had taken

feedback.why_key: Getting in fixes the moment; the locker had gone before that, so the taking goes behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the earlier action into had plus the participle.

payload.context: Build one sentence about the Verdon channel survey.

expected: the survey team found that the reeds had spread across the channel

feedback.why_key: The finding is the later moment and the spreading sits behind it, which is why had comes in front of the participle.

payload.given: The council approved the tower in June. Two surveyors resigned in March.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that makes clear the resignations came first.
payload.starter: By the time the council approved the tower in June, ___

two surveyors had already resigned

feedback.why_key: June is now the moment the sentence stands on, and March is behind it, so the resigning takes the step-back form.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the later moment, then mark the earlier verb with had.

payload.audio_text: She'd moved out before the letter arrived.

expected: she'd moved out before the letter arrived
she had moved out before the letter arrived
shed moved out before the letter arrived

feedback.why_key: In speech had shrinks to a single sound stuck on the pronoun. Miss it and the sentence loses its order.

the closure should be in the present perfect

title: Deciding when you actually need to show which past event came first

point_json.grammar_name: Past perfect vs past simple in a sequence

teach.can_do: I can tell when the step back into the past perfect is doing work, and when it is only weight.
teach.why_it_matters: Learners are taught to use this form and never taught to stop. Sprinkling it through a story is as visible as leaving it out.
teach.meaning: The past perfect is not a courtesy you pay to every earlier event. It exists to fix an order the sentence would otherwise get wrong. If a time word, or the plain order of the telling, already puts the events in sequence, the reader has everything they need and the extra auxiliary adds nothing but drag.
