Reach for it when you are genuinely going back out of sequence: a flashback, an explanation found after the effect, a reason that was in place before anybody noticed it.

form.pattern: had + past participle, but only where the order is not already visible
notes: before, after and then carry the order themselves, so the past simple is usually enough beside them
a plain list of events told in the order they happened needs no step back at all
once the step back is made, the following clauses in the same flashback can go back to the past simple
form.negative: hadn't + past participle — the same test applies; a negative is not a reason to use it
form.question: Had it happened by then? — asked when you want the state of things at an earlier moment

left.text: She finished the report and then went home.

right.text: She went home. She had finished the report at four.

spec.caption: Same two events, same real order. Only one version needs an auxiliary to say so.

worked_example.sentence: The surveyor refused to sign. Someone had changed the figures on the second page.
worked_example.why_this_form: The refusal comes first in the telling and second in time. Without the step back the reader files the changing as the next thing that happened.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Changed would read as a reply to the refusal, as though the figures were altered afterwards to get round it.

notice_set.sentence: The driver checked the load and then locked the van.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Then does the whole job. Nothing needs marking, because the telling and the timing already agree.

notice_set.sentence: The van was empty when it reached Marlow. Somebody had unlocked it overnight.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: The telling has gone backwards, and the auxiliary is the only thing telling the reader so.

notice_set.sentence: After the funding stopped, the clinic reduced its opening hours.
notice_set.question: Can you tell which came first?
notice_set.why: After settles it on its own, which is why nothing else has to be marked.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed apologised at the meeting. He had read the wrong version of the report.
notice_set.question: Did he read the wrong version before or after apologising?
notice_set.why: The second sentence is the explanation, and explanations sit behind the thing they explain.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed apologised at the meeting. He read the wrong version of the report.
notice_set.question: Did he read the wrong version before or after apologising?
notice_set.why: With nothing marking a step back, the second sentence reads as the next thing he did.

discovery.prompt: Half of these would be worse with an extra auxiliary in them, and half would be wrong without one. What separates them?
pairs: The van was empty. Somebody had unlocked it overnight.
The driver checked the load and then locked the van.
She refused to sign. Someone had altered the figures.
She altered the figures and then refused to sign.
The clinic cut its hours. The grant had run out in April.
After the grant ran out, the clinic cut its hours.

candidate_rules.text: The left-hand sentences go back out of the order they are told in; the right-hand ones do not.
The left-hand sentences are about problems and the right-hand ones are about routine actions.
Use had whenever a sentence contains two past events.

teach.rule_line: Ask: would the reader get the order wrong without it?
teach.false_rule: That the earlier of two past events always takes the past perfect. Most of the time the order is already visible and the auxiliary is dead weight.

contrast.question: Would the order be clear without the auxiliary?

fork.answer: Yes — a time word, or the order of the telling, already fixes it
No — the telling has doubled back and nothing else marks it

a.text: The engineer left the site and the alarm went off.
a.means: She was gone, and then the alarm sounded. Two events in the order given.

b.text: The engineer left the site and the alarm had gone off.
b.means: The alarm sounded first, and her leaving is being explained by it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You reached back with had while the sentence was walking forwards. The reader now hunts for the later moment you are measuring from, fails to find one, and reads the sentence twice before giving up on it.

edge_case.text: In a long narrative you do not have to keep making the step. One past perfect opens the flashback and the past simple can carry the rest of it. Mark the door, not every room inside.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover the auxiliary and read the sentence again. If the order still comes out right, the auxiliary was decoration.

worked_pairs.a: The shop closed at six. The last delivery had arrived at four.
worked_pairs.b: The last delivery arrived at four and the shop closed at six.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: The last delivery had arrived at four
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: arrived at four and the shop closed at six
worked_pairs.gloss: The first tells the day backwards, so the step back is load-bearing. The second tells it forwards and needs nothing.

worked_pairs.a: Nobody was surprised when the depot shut. Freight had moved to the road years earlier.
worked_pairs.b: Freight moved to the road, and a few years later the depot shut.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: Freight had moved to the road years earlier
worked_pairs.gloss: Same two facts. The first explains backwards; the second lists forwards, and the listing does the work on its own.

worked_pairs.a: She apologised. She had misread the rota.
worked_pairs.b: She misread the rota and apologised.
worked_pairs.gloss: Put the cause second and it has to be marked as earlier. Put it first and the word and is enough.

errors.wrong: The team had arrived at eight and started the survey by nine.
errors.right: The team arrived at eight and started the survey by nine.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has learned that this form marks earlier events, and every event in a list is earlier than the next. Nothing in that rule says the list needs a later moment to lean on.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: had.

errors.wrong: First the council had cut the subsidy, and then the operator withdrew the route.
errors.right: First the council cut the subsidy, and then the operator withdrew the route.
errors.why_it_happens: First and then have already sequenced the sentence. The learner marks the earlier verb anyway, because the rule they carry is about order rather than about what the reader can already see.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: had.

errors.wrong: The inspector was annoyed. Nobody warned him about the change of shift.
errors.right: The inspector was annoyed. Nobody had warned him about the change of shift.
errors.why_it_happens: A second sentence usually reports the next thing that happened, and that is how the reader takes it. Its job here is to explain the first one, and only the auxiliary says so.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: had.

errors.wrong: By the time the audit began, two managers had resigned and the finance officer moved to another department.
errors.right: By the time the audit began, two managers had resigned and the finance officer had moved to another department.
errors.why_it_happens: The step back is made once and dropped halfway through the sentence, because the second verb is chosen on its own rather than against the moment the sentence set up.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: had.

pays_in.note: A Part 2 story needs one step back, not six, and this is the test for which one.
pays_in.model: I only found out later. Someone had swapped the two boxes at the depot.

pays_in.note: Explaining a failure means one backward step into what was already true.
pays_in.model: The scheme was abandoned in 2019; its funding had been withdrawn two years before.

pays_in.note: Order questions turn on the auxiliary, and a passage that drops it is telling you the order is plain.
pays_in.model: The subsidy ended in March. Ridership had been falling since the depot closed.

used_in.quote: The card asks for a decision, and a decision needs one sentence about what was already true when it was taken.
The essay narrates a change and then explains it, which is one backward step and no more.

payload.sentence: Nobody said anything at the meeting. The decision had been taken on Friday.
payload.question: When was the decision taken?

feedback.why_key: The second sentence steps back to explain the silence, and the auxiliary is what puts it behind the meeting.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask which of the two sentences is explaining the other.

payload.sentence: The clinic opened at eight and closed again at four.
payload.question: Do you know which of the two happened first?

feedback.why_key: The order of the telling is the order of the day, so nothing needs marking and nothing is marked.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether the plain order already answers the question.

items.decision_cue: First the firm had cut overtime

payload.context: From a first draft about a company reorganisation.
payload.sentence: First the firm had cut overtime, and then it closed the second site.
reasons: the order is already fixed by first and then
the two events happened in the other order
the participle is wrong after had
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: First and then have done the sequencing. The auxiliary repeats information the reader already has.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the auxiliary and check the order still reads right.

payload.context: From a report on why a bus route was withdrawn.
payload.stem: The operator withdrew the route in June. Ridership ___ (fall) every quarter since the depot closed.

expected: had fallen

feedback.why_key: The withdrawal is the moment the paragraph stands on, and the falling ran up to it, so it goes behind.
feedback.feed_forward: Set the later moment, then mark what led up to it.

payload.context: Two colleagues talking about a shift that went badly.
payload.stem: I ___ (finish) the checks and then I went for a break.

expected: finished

feedback.why_key: Then puts the break after the checks, so the sentence needs no second marker saying the same thing.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the past simple alone when a time word already orders the clauses.

payload.given: The bank shut its Marlow branch in 2021. Its customer numbers dropped by half between 2015 and 2020.
payload.instruction: Report the closure, then add the customer numbers as something that was already true before it.
payload.starter: The bank shut its Marlow branch in 2021. Its customer numbers ___

expected: had dropped by half between 2015 and 2020
had halved between 2015 and 2020
had fallen by half between 2015 and 2020

feedback.why_key: The explanation arrives second in the telling and first in time, which is the one case that has to be marked.
feedback.feed_forward: When the reason comes second, push its verb behind with had.

payload.audio_text: They'd pulled the story before anyone noticed.

expected: they'd pulled the story before anyone noticed
they had pulled the story before anyone noticed
theyd pulled the story before anyone noticed

feedback.why_key: They'd and they take the same beat in speech, and the whole step back hangs on a sound you can miss.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a d on the end of the pronoun.

items.decision_cue: giving the reason the council acted

payload.context: A report on the youth centre, giving the reason the council acted when it did.
payload.stem: The council withdrew the grant, and the centre ___ its evening sessions.

options.why_this_means: That the cutting came after the withdrawal, as the next step in the story.
That the cutting came first, and the council's decision is a response to it.

expected: had cut

feedback.why_key: The paragraph is working backwards to a cause, so the earlier event has to be marked or the reader files it as a consequence.
feedback.feed_forward: When the second clause is the reason, push it behind with had.

items.decision_cue: listing what happened after the council's decision

payload.context: A report on the youth centre, listing what happened after the council's decision, in sequence.
payload.stem: The council withdrew the grant, and the centre ___ its evening sessions.

options.why_this_means: That the cutting came after the withdrawal, as the next step in the story.
That the cutting came first, and the council's decision is a response to it.

expected: cut

feedback.why_key: The clauses are being told in the order they happened, so nothing has doubled back and nothing needs marking.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the past simple when the telling runs forwards.

items.decision_cue: telling the story of the afternoon in the order it happened

payload.context: Priya is telling the story of the afternoon in the order it happened.
payload.stem: The manager came out of the meeting and the two of us ___ the figures again.

options.why_this_means: That the checking came after he came out, as the next thing the two of them did.
That the checking was finished before he came out, which is where his information came from.

expected: checked

feedback.why_key: Nothing in the telling has doubled back, so the two events sit on the same line in the order given.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the telling moved backwards before you reach for had.

items.decision_cue: walked in knowing the totals were wrong

payload.context: Priya is explaining why the manager walked in knowing the totals were wrong.
payload.stem: The manager came out of the meeting and the two of us ___ the figures again.

options.why_this_means: That the checking came after he came out, as the next thing the two of them did.
That the checking was finished before he came out, which is where his information came from.

expected: had checked

feedback.why_key: His knowledge has to come from somewhere earlier, so the checking is being placed behind the moment he walked in.
feedback.feed_forward: When a later moment needs explaining, mark the source as earlier.

payload.context: Two lines from different reports on the same wetland.
sentences: The channel was dredged in 2018. The reed beds had dried out.
The channel was dredged in 2018. The reed beds dried out.
meanings: The drying is the reason the dredging happened.
The drying is what the dredging led to.

feedback.why_key: One auxiliary decides whether the dredging is a response to the drying or the cause of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the second sentence explains the first or follows it.

items.decision_cue: two surveys of the same estate

payload.context: A housing officer is writing up two surveys of the same estate, six months apart.
payload.stem: The block was sold in March. Half the flats ___ empty for a year.

options.why_this_means: That the empty year is listed alongside the sale, as part of one forward account.
That the empty year ran up to the sale and is being offered as the reason for it.

follow_up.question: Which version gives the sale a reason?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct English about the same estate. One reports two facts; the other makes one of them explain the other.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether you are listing or explaining, then choose.

items.decision_cue: The firm had opened a second site in 2014

payload.context: From a Task 2 paragraph about small businesses.
payload.sentence: The firm had opened a second site in 2014, and it had taken on twenty staff over the following year.
reasons: there is no later moment for these events to sit behind
the two events are in the wrong order
the second verb needs a different participle
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The paragraph never fixes a moment for these to be earlier than, so the step back has nothing under it.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the later moment first; if there is none, drop had.

payload.sentence: The estate flooded twice in one winter, and it turned out that nobody surveyed the drains since the houses went up.

expected: nobody had surveyed the drains

feedback.why_key: The surveying that never happened runs up to the flooding, so it belongs behind it rather than beside it.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert had when the clause explains what was already the case.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about a project that was cancelled. Report the cancellation first, then give one thing that was true before it — and use the step back only where it is doing work.

feedback.why_key: One backward step, in the sentence that explains. Everything else stays on the line.
feedback.feed_forward: Use had once, in the explaining sentence, and nowhere else.

payload.prompt_text: Take one body paragraph from your last answer on changing careers. Rewrite it so that it makes exactly one backward step, and delete any auxiliary that is not earning its place. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: A paragraph with one marked step back reads as narrative. A paragraph with five reads as a learner demonstrating a tense.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep one had and cut the rest.

title: Saying what you had to do, could do and were allowed to do back then

point_json.grammar_name: Past modality: had to, could, was able to, was allowed to

teach.can_do: I can say what was compulsory, what I was capable of and what I was permitted to do at some time in the past.
teach.why_it_matters: Most modals have no past tense at all. When a story moves backwards, half of them must be swapped for something else, and that is where learners stall.
teach.meaning: Modals are one-shape words. Can has could, and that is the end of the list: must, may and had better have no past whatsoever. When a situation moves back in time, English swaps the modal for its longer partner — had to, was able to, was allowed to — and those partners take every shape an ordinary verb takes. Could is the exception that causes the trouble: it covers what somebody was generally capable of, not one occasion when they actually pulled it off.

form.pattern: had to + plain verb  ·  could + plain verb  ·  was / were able to + plain verb  ·  was / were allowed to + plain verb
notes: had to is the past of both must and have to; must itself never travels backwards
could covers a stretch of past ability; one occasion that came off takes was able to
was allowed to is the past of can, could and may whenever the sentence is about permission
have to keeps its ordinary-verb behaviour in the past: didn't have to, did you have to
the negative is the one place could still stretches — couldn't covers the whole period and the single occasion alike
form.negative: did not / didn't have to  ·  could not / couldn't  ·  was not able to  ·  was not allowed to
form.question: Did you have to ...?  ·  Could you ...?  ·  Were you able to ...?  ·  Were you allowed to ...?

left.role: the word you use about now
left.text: must · have to · can · may

right.role: the word it becomes about back then
right.text: had to · had to · could or was able to · was allowed to

spec.caption: Four words go in on the left and three come out on the right. Two of them collapse into one, and one of them splits in two.

worked_example.sentence: The depot lost its power for two days, so we had to log every delivery by hand.
worked_example.why_this_form: Must has no past shape. The two days are finished, so the obligation is carried by had to, which has all the shapes an ordinary verb has.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Must log would drag the sentence forward and claim the paperwork is still done by hand today, which is not what the story is about.

notice_set.sentence: Rasheed could read a wiring diagram before he left school.
notice_set.question: Did he read a diagram on his last day at school?
notice_set.why: Could reports a capacity that sat there for years. Whether he used it on any one day is outside what the sentence claims.

notice_set.sentence: The pump kept cutting out, but Rasheed was able to restart it before the shift ended.
notice_set.question: Did the restart actually happen?
notice_set.why: Was able to reports one occasion that came off, and it carries the result with it. That is the job could cannot do.

notice_set.sentence: We had to sign the visitors' book every morning.
notice_set.question: Could a worker skip it if they were in a hurry?
notice_set.why: Had to shuts the question exactly the way must does. The only thing that has changed is the time.

notice_set.sentence: We didn't have to sign the visitors' book at the Norland site.
notice_set.question: Was it up to the worker whether they signed?
notice_set.why: Didn't have to takes the obligation away and puts nothing in its place. It forbids nothing.

notice_set.sentence: Apprentices weren't allowed to drive the forklift in their first year.
notice_set.question: Was somebody deciding this while the sentence was being spoken?
notice_set.why: Was allowed to reports an arrangement that was already in place. Nobody in the room is granting or refusing anything.

notice_set.sentence: Delia couldn't get the software to open the file.
notice_set.question: Did she get it open in the end?
notice_set.why: Couldn't works for a single occasion as happily as for a whole stretch. Only the positive side of could splits in two.

teach.rule_line: Must, may and had better cannot go back. Swap them for had to and was allowed to.
teach.false_rule: That could is simply the past of can. It is the past of general ability only. One occasion that actually came off takes was able to.

errors.wrong: The road was flooded, so we must take the long way round.
errors.right: The road was flooded, so we had to take the long way round.
errors.why_it_happens: Must is stored as a strength rather than as a tense, so nothing in the learner's rule tells them it cannot move. The first half of the sentence has already gone into the past and left the modal standing in the present.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: must becomes had to.
errors.l1_note: Many languages inflect their obligation verb for tense, so nothing warns the learner that English cannot.

errors.wrong: In the end I could persuade the supplier to hold the order.
errors.right: In the end I was able to persuade the supplier to hold the order.
errors.why_it_happens: Could has been learned as the past of can with no limit on its scope, so it gets used for a single occasion. To an English ear the sentence then reports a talent rather than a result, and the story loses its point.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: could becomes was able to.

errors.wrong: Apprentices were not allow to use the cutter.
errors.right: Apprentices were not allowed to use the cutter.
errors.why_it_happens: Allowed to is stored as one fixed lump meaning permitted, and in speech the ending is swallowed by the t of to, so there is nothing to remind the writer that a participle is in there at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Add two letters: allow becomes allowed.

errors.wrong: We hadn't to book the room in advance.
errors.right: We didn't have to book the room in advance.
errors.why_it_happens: Have to sits beside must in the learner's head, so it inherits must's behaviour and takes not directly. It is an ordinary verb wearing a modal's meaning, and its negative and question both need did.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: hadn't becomes didn't have.

pays_in.note: Every Part 2 story about a difficulty runs on had to and was able to.
pays_in.model: The lift was out, so we had to carry the stock up three floors, and even then we were able to open on time.

pays_in.note: Questions about school and childhood are answered almost entirely in past permission.
pays_in.model: We weren't allowed to use the science lab unless a teacher was in the room with us.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often swaps could for was able to and changes the claim.
pays_in.model: Engineers were able to reopen the tunnel within a week of the collapse.

used_in.quote: Describing something you achieved means saying what you had to do first and what you were finally able to do, and the two halves take different words.
A story about a mistake is a run of past obligations plus one thing the speaker could not do at the time.

payload.sentence: Nadia could handle the till on her own by the end of her first week.
payload.question: Is this about one particular busy afternoon?

feedback.why_key: Could reports what she was generally up to from that point on. A single afternoon would need a form that carries a result.
feedback.feed_forward: Read could as a stretch of time, not as one event.

payload.sentence: The crew were able to clear the loading bay before the inspection began.
payload.question: Did the clearing actually get done?

feedback.why_key: Were able to reports an occasion that came off and carries the outcome with it, which is exactly why could would not fit here.
feedback.feed_forward: Use were able to when the sentence has to say it worked.

payload.context: From a paragraph about how a delivery firm used to run.
payload.sentence: Before the new depot opened, drivers must load their own vans.
reasons: the sentence is set in the past and must cannot go there
the drivers did not load the vans themselves
the wrong kind of verb follows must
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Must has one shape and it belongs to now. The rest of the sentence has already moved into the past and left it standing.
feedback.feed_forward: When the sentence is set in the past, write had to.

payload.context: From a note about how the old Ashfield warehouse ran.
payload.stem: Every driver ___ (have) to sign the keys out before eight.

expected: had

feedback.why_key: The rule was in force then and is not now, so the obligation takes the past shape that have to provides and must cannot.
feedback.feed_forward: Put have to into the past; must will not follow you there.

payload.context: Two friends talking about their old school.
payload.stem: We weren't ___ (allow) to leave the site at lunchtime.

expected: allowed

feedback.why_key: Allowed to reports a rule that somebody else had already settled, and the ending is what makes it a report rather than an order.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the -ed on allowed; it vanishes in speech, not on paper.

payload.context: From an account of the night the ordering network went down.
payload.stem: The team ___ (be) able to rebuild the day's orders from a printed list.

expected: were
was

feedback.why_key: One night, one problem, one rebuild that actually happened. That is the slot could is not allowed to fill.
feedback.feed_forward: When the sentence reports a success, reach for was or were able to.

payload.given: The lift is out of service. Staff must carry the stock up by hand.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence about last month, when the lift was out, keeping both facts.

expected: the lift was out of service so staff had to carry the stock up by hand
the lift was out of service and staff had to carry the stock up by hand
the lift was out of service so the staff had to carry the stock up by hand

feedback.why_key: Moving the sentence into last month strands must, because it has no past shape to move into and had to has to take the load.
feedback.feed_forward: Change the time first, then check every modal still has a shape.

payload.context: Build one sentence about how the Ashfield line used to work.

expected: passengers did not have to book a seat on the early service

feedback.why_key: Have to builds its negative with did, exactly like any ordinary verb, because underneath the meaning that is what it is.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the negative of have to with did, never with a bare not.

payload.audio_text: I couldn't shift it on my own, so we had to wait for the second van.

expected: i couldn't shift it on my own so we had to wait for the second van
i could not shift it on my own so we had to wait for the second van
i couldnt shift it on my own so we had to wait for the second van

feedback.why_key: Had to is squashed to almost one sound in speech and couldn't loses its middle. Neither survives unless you already know it is there.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a flat d in front of to; that is had to.

payload.sentence: The line was blocked for six hours, but in the end the crew could clear it before the morning peak.

expected: were able to clear
was able to clear
managed to clear

feedback.why_key: One blockage, one crew, one clearance that actually came off. Could would only say they were the sort of crew who can clear blockages.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap could for were able to whenever the sentence reports a result.

payload.context: Two former students remembering their old college.
payload.sentence: We hadn't to wear a uniform after the second year.
reasons: have to builds its negative with did, like an ordinary verb
the students did wear a uniform after the second year
the wrong kind of verb follows to
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Have to only looks like a modal. Its negative and its question both need did, and the past tense is no exception to that.
feedback.feed_forward: Say didn't have to aloud until hadn't to sounds wrong.

payload.prompt_text: Think of a day at work or college when something went wrong and you sorted it out. Say one sentence covering what you were obliged to do and what you succeeded in doing.

feedback.why_key: The two halves of the story need different words: the obligation takes had to and the outcome takes was able to.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the obligation first, then the outcome, changing the form between them.

payload.prompt_text: Here is your body paragraph about how careers used to work. Rewrite one sentence so that it names something workers were once obliged to do and are no longer obliged to do. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: A before-and-after sentence needs had to on one side and don't have to on the other, and the pair is what shows the reader the change.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the old obligation and the present freedom in one sentence.

title: Choosing between an obligation you feel yourself and one someone else laid down

point_json.grammar_name: must vs have to

teach.can_do: I can show whether an obligation is one I have taken on myself or one that was handed to me.
teach.why_it_matters: In an essay this is the line between arguing for a measure and reporting one. Pick the wrong side and your own argument reads as somebody else's rule.
teach.meaning: Both of these say something has to happen, and they are equally strong. What separates them is who is behind the push. Must comes from inside the speaker: my decision, my conviction, or my notice that I am the one writing. Have to comes from outside: a timetable, an arrangement, a person with authority, a road under water. Nothing about the action changes. What changes is where the reader thinks the pressure is coming from.

form.pattern: subject + must + plain verb   ·   subject + have to / has to + plain verb
notes: have to changes shape like any ordinary verb: has to, will have to, do you have to
must has one shape and cannot go anywhere else in a sentence
in speech have to is spreading over must's ground; in writing must holds firm
have to is squashed to almost one word when spoken, which is why it is hard to hear
form.negative: the two negatives are opposites, not partners — that is the next point
form.question: Do you have to ...? is the everyday question; must I ...? sounds put upon

left.role: must — the push starts inside the speaker
left.text: I must stop driving out to the reserve.

right.role: have to — the push arrives from outside
right.text: I have to stop driving out to the reserve.

spec.caption: Same decision, two different people standing behind it.

worked_example.sentence: We must cut what the depot burns this winter, whatever the council decides.
worked_example.why_this_form: The second half says outright that nobody outside the room is deciding this, so the first half has to name the speaker as the source.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: We have to cut would hand the decision to somebody beyond the depot gates, which is exactly what the rest of the sentence goes on to deny.

notice_set.sentence: I must cut down on the driving — it is costing me a fortune.
notice_set.question: Whose idea is this?
notice_set.why: The reason given is the speaker's own money, and nobody else has been mentioned at all.

notice_set.sentence: I have to cut down on the driving — the parking permits have gone.
notice_set.question: Whose idea is this?
notice_set.why: The permits were withdrawn by somebody outside this sentence, and the speaker is living with the result.

notice_set.sentence: Everyone on site has to wear a hard hat.
notice_set.question: Did the speaker set this up?
notice_set.why: The speaker is passing on an arrangement that was already there when they arrived.

notice_set.sentence: You must see the reedbeds before the water drops.
notice_set.question: Is this an order or an enthusiastic recommendation?
notice_set.why: The speaker is the whole source and nothing follows a refusal, so the pressure turns into enthusiasm.

notice_set.sentence: I must remember to book the tickets tonight.
notice_set.question: Is anybody else pressing the speaker about this?
notice_set.why: The speaker is reminding themselves, so the pressure begins and ends inside their own head.

discovery.prompt: Both sides describe the same thing happening. Work out what changes about the speaker.
pairs: I must get the roof looked at.
I have to get the roof looked at.
We must cut what we burn.
We have to cut what we burn.
Staff must sign the log.
Staff have to sign the log.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the push comes from the speaker; on the right it arrives from outside them.
Must is for serious things and have to is for small everyday ones.
Use have to whenever the sentence is about work or a public arrangement.

teach.rule_line: Ask who is pushing. Me: must. Somebody or something else: have to.
teach.false_rule: That must is the formal or stronger version of have to. They are equally strong. What differs is who the reader thinks is behind it.

contrast.question: Who is this obligation coming from?

fork.answer: From me — my decision, my conviction, my notice
From outside me — a timetable, an arrangement, a person with authority, the weather

a.text: I must stop taking the car out to the depot.
a.means: I have decided it myself, and nobody has made me.

b.text: I have to stop taking the car out to the depot.
b.means: Something outside me has closed the option — the cost, the permits, a new arrangement.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote have to. That tells your reader somebody else made you, and it quietly removes you from your own decision. In an essay it turns a measure you are arguing for into a rule you are merely passing on.

edge_case.text: In everyday speech have to has spread across most of must's ground, and nobody will think you odd for using it. Must holds firm in writing, on notices, and wherever the speaker owns the claim. Write must; stop policing your own speech.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask who you would blame if it did not happen. If the answer is yourself, you want must. If you would point at somebody else, you want have to.

worked_pairs.a: I must get the boiler looked at before it fails completely.
worked_pairs.b: I have to get the boiler looked at before the inspection.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is the speaker's own worry about the winter. The second is somebody else's date in somebody else's diary.

worked_pairs.a: Councils must think further ahead than one election.
worked_pairs.b: Councils have to publish the figures every March.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: think further ahead than one election
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is the writer arguing. The second is the writer reporting something that would happen whether or not they approved of it.

worked_pairs.a: You must see the reedbeds while the water is high.
worked_pairs.b: You have to book a permit before you walk the reedbeds.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is enthusiasm with nobody behind it but the speaker. The second has a desk and a form behind it.

errors.wrong: Under the new arrangement, residents must sort their glass separately.
errors.right: Under the new arrangement, residents have to sort their glass separately.
errors.why_it_happens: Must is stored as the strong obligation word and this is a strong obligation. Nothing in that stored rule asks who is speaking, so a reported arrangement comes out sounding like the writer's own decision.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: must becomes have to.

errors.wrong: I have to say something about the state of the river, even though nobody has asked me to.
errors.right: I must say something about the state of the river, even though nobody has asked me to.
errors.why_it_happens: Have to is the everyday word in speech and it spreads by habit. Here the end of the sentence says there is no outside pressure, and the beginning has already claimed there is.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: have to becomes must.

errors.wrong: Every household have to put the bins out by seven.
errors.right: Every household has to put the bins out by seven.
errors.why_it_happens: Every household sounds like many households, so the ear counts the meaning instead of the word. Have to changes shape like an ordinary verb, which is exactly what makes it catchable in a way must never is.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: You must have to renew the permit each year.
errors.right: You have to renew the permit each year.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner wants the obligation to land firmly and stacks both words to be sure of it. Only one of them can hold the slot, and the second one is already doing the whole job.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: must.

pays_in.note: This is the line between arguing for a measure and reporting one that already exists.
pays_in.model: Coastal councils must plan for the worst case rather than the average one.

pays_in.note: Answers about your routine and your intentions use both sides in the same breath.
pays_in.model: I have to be on site by seven, so I must get into the habit of packing the night before.

pays_in.note: A passage reporting a regulation and a writer recommending one look alike until you read the verb.
pays_in.model: Operators have to log every discharge into the estuary within an hour.

used_in.quote: The essay has to report what farms are already required to do and argue for what they ought to be required to do, and the two need different words.
Answers here move between rules that exist and rules the speaker thinks should exist, several times a minute.

payload.sentence: I must stop driving out to the reserve every weekend.
payload.question: Whose idea is this?

feedback.why_key: Nobody else appears in the sentence at all, so the pressure has nowhere to come from except the speaker.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for who else is in the sentence before you decide.

payload.sentence: Operators have to log every discharge into the estuary.
payload.question: Did the operators set this up themselves?

feedback.why_key: The sentence reports a requirement that came from somewhere beyond the operators, which is the whole reason it is written this way.
feedback.feed_forward: Read have to as pressure arriving from outside.

payload.context: The opening of a body paragraph in an essay about flood defence.
payload.sentence: In my view, coastal towns have to be given money to move buildings back from the shore.
reasons: the opening claims the writer is the source and the verb hands it to somebody else
coastal towns cannot be moved back
money is not the issue in flood defence
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Three words in, the writer has claimed the argument as their own. Four words later they hand it to an authority they never name.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to whoever your opening says is speaking.

payload.context: From an essay. The writer is arguing for something nobody has yet required.
payload.stem: Cities ___ plant far more street trees than they currently do.

expected: must

feedback.why_key: Nothing outside the essay is requiring this. The only source of the pressure is the person writing the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Use must when you are the one making the case.

payload.context: A volunteer explaining the shift she was given at the bird hide.
payload.stem: I ___ (have) to be in the hide by six, before the birds move off the mud.

expected: have

feedback.why_key: The six o'clock start came with the shift; she is passing on an arrangement rather than announcing a decision.
feedback.feed_forward: Use have to for something arranged outside you.

payload.given: The council brought in a new arrangement in April. Households now separate their glass.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence reporting the arrangement rather than recommending it.

expected: have to separate their glass
have to separate their glass now
have to separate their glass from april

feedback.why_key: The council is named in the first sentence, so the pressure has a visible source and the verb has to point at it.
feedback.feed_forward: Point the verb at whoever brought the requirement in.

payload.context: Build the line for a leaflet reporting the new arrangement.

expected: every household has to separate its glass

feedback.why_key: One household at a time is what every counts, and the verb follows the word rather than the picture in your head.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the single word every introduces.

payload.audio_text: You have to leave the van at the top gate.

expected: you have to leave the van at the top gate
you've to leave the van at the top gate
youve to leave the van at the top gate

feedback.why_key: Have to is squashed into something close to one word in speech, which is why learners hear an instruction and write down a verb they never heard.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the f sound where have meets to.

payload.context: From a notice written and signed by the site manager herself.
payload.stem: All staff ___ report a spill within the hour.

expected: must

feedback.why_key: The person writing the notice is the person imposing it, so the sentence has an author standing right behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Use must when the writer is also the source.

items.decision_cue: nobody has said a word to her about it

payload.context: Silje has decided by herself to give up the drive out to the reserve; nobody has said a word to her about it.
payload.stem: I ___ stop taking the car out there.

options.why_this_means: That the decision started with you and you are the only one behind it.
That something beyond you has closed the option and you are living with the result.

expected: must

feedback.why_key: There is nobody else in the story to push her, so the push has to be coming from where the decision was made.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether anybody else appears in the situation.

payload.context: Silje has just been told the permits have been withdrawn and the visitor car park is closing.
payload.stem: I ___ stop taking the car out there.

options.why_this_means: That the decision started with you and you are the only one behind it.
That something beyond you has closed the option and you are living with the result.

expected: have to

feedback.why_key: The car park closing is not her idea and not in her gift, so she is reporting a change rather than making one.
feedback.feed_forward: Point the verb outwards when the situation decides for you.

items.decision_cue: arguing for a change nobody has made yet

payload.context: From an essay in which the writer is arguing for a change nobody has made yet.
payload.stem: Water companies ___ publish every discharge within the hour.

options.why_this_means: That the writer is making the case and asking the reader to agree with it.
That this is already the arrangement and the writer is merely passing it on.

expected: must

feedback.why_key: Nothing outside the essay requires this yet. The only pressure in the room is the writer's own argument.
feedback.feed_forward: Use must for the measure you are arguing for.

items.decision_cue: describing an arrangement that came into force last spring

payload.context: From an essay describing an arrangement that came into force last spring.
payload.stem: Water companies ___ publish every discharge within the hour.

options.why_this_means: That the writer is making the case and asking the reader to agree with it.
That this is already the arrangement and the writer is merely passing it on.

expected: have to

feedback.why_key: The requirement was in place before the essay was written, so the writer is reporting rather than arguing.
feedback.feed_forward: Use have to when the requirement already exists.

items.decision_cue: who wrote it is not stated anywhere on the board

payload.context: A line on a site notice where who wrote it is not stated anywhere on the board.
payload.stem: Contractors ___ wear high-visibility jackets beyond this point.

options.why_this_means: That whoever wrote the board is the one imposing it, and is speaking to you directly.
That the board is passing on a requirement someone else set, and is only the messenger.

follow_up.question: Which one sounds like the person who wrote the board speaking?

feedback.why_key: Both are ordinary English on a real site. One makes the board an author and the other makes it a messenger, and the jacket is the same either way.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether your sentence is authoring or reporting.

payload.context: Two things the same volunteer said on the same afternoon.
sentences: I must do something about the state of that hedge.
I have to do something about the state of that hedge.
meanings: Nobody has mentioned it to her; it has simply been bothering her every time she walks past.
Somebody has raised it with her, and she is now committed to dealing with it.

feedback.why_key: The hedge has not changed between the two sentences. What has changed is whether anybody else has noticed it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether a third person has entered the story.

payload.prompt_text: Farms near the Verdon already log their fertiliser use. You think they should also be measuring what leaves the fields. Write two short sentences: one reporting what happens now and one arguing for the change.

feedback.why_key: Putting the reported and the argued side by side is what shows a reader you know which one you are doing.
feedback.feed_forward: Report first, then argue, and change the verb between them.

payload.prompt_text: Open your essay on farm run-off. Find one sentence where you describe what farms already do and one where you argue for something new. Check that the two use different verbs, and rewrite whichever one is wrong. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: An essay that uses one verb for both jobs leaves the reader unable to tell your proposals from the situation you are describing.
feedback.feed_forward: Underline your proposals and check every verb in front of them.

title: Building a sentence around the thing something was done to

point_json.grammar_name: The passive: what it does to a sentence

pays_in.note: Process and map answers are written almost entirely in this shape.
pays_in.model: Seawater is drawn into the plant through a screen at the intake.

pays_in.note: It lets a paragraph hold one topic in the subject slot throughout.
pays_in.model: The scheme was funded out of the transport budget rather than from reserves.

pays_in.note: Question stems flip a passage sentence into this shape and back again.
pays_in.model: The ridge was replanted after the fire of 2019.

teach.can_do: I can build a sentence around the thing something happened to, instead of around whoever did it.
teach.why_it_matters: Every process description and a great deal of academic prose is built this way. The form is small; what it does to a sentence is not.
teach.meaning: An ordinary English sentence starts with the doer: the council, the machine, the storm. Sometimes the doer is not what you want to talk about. This shape lets you move the thing that was affected to the front and make it the subject, so the sentence is now about that thing. The event itself does not change. What changes is where the reader's attention starts, and whether the doer appears in the sentence at all.

form.pattern: be + past participle
notes: be carries the time, exactly as it does anywhere else: is checked, was checked, will be checked
the past participle after it never changes shape
the doer, if you still want it, goes at the end after by
form.negative: be + not + past participle: the gates are not opened at night
form.question: Is the channel dredged every autumn?

left.text: the maintenance crew

right.text: the sluice gates

spec.caption: The right-hand box moves to the front of the sentence and takes the subject slot. The left-hand box steps back, or leaves altogether.

worked_example.sentence: The sluice gates are checked twice a day.
worked_example.why_this_form: The note is about the gates and their upkeep, not about which crew is holding the spanner, so the gates take the front of the sentence.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two engineers check the sluice gates twice a day makes the engineers the subject, and a reader would then expect the next line to carry on about them.

notice_set.sentence: The old pumping station at Verdon was demolished last spring.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you who knocked it down?
notice_set.why: Nobody is named. The building stands at the front because the building is what the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: A contractor from Norland knocked the pumping station down.
notice_set.question: Which does this sentence put first, the building or the people?
notice_set.why: The doer is in front, so a reader expects the next line to carry on about the contractor.

notice_set.sentence: Rainwater is collected on the roof and piped to a tank under the yard.
notice_set.question: Does it matter here who installed the pipes?
options: Yes, the sentence depends on it
No, the sentence works without it
notice_set.why: The interest is in where the water goes. Naming an installer would add a person nobody asked about.

notice_set.sentence: The proposal was rejected six weeks later.
notice_set.question: What is this sentence about?
options: The people who turned it down
notice_set.why: Putting the proposal in the subject slot keeps a paragraph about the proposal about the proposal.

notice_set.sentence: Two thousand trees were planted along the Ashfield ridge.
notice_set.question: Could you say who planted them from this sentence alone?
notice_set.why: The number and the place survive; the planters do not. That is the trade this shape makes.

notice_set.sentence: The storm brought down forty of the new trees.
notice_set.question: Does this sentence name what caused the damage?
notice_set.why: When the cause is the news, English puts it at the front and the sentence stays in its ordinary shape.

teach.rule_line: Decide what the sentence should be about, then put that first.
teach.false_rule: That this shape is a way of making writing sound clever. It is a way of choosing the subject. Any formality is a side effect of that choice.

errors.wrong: The pumping station demolished last spring.
errors.right: The pumping station was demolished last spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Demolished looks like a finished verb on its own, so nothing feels missing to the writer until a reader asks what the station demolished.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: was.

errors.wrong: Forty of the young trees were broke in the storm.
errors.right: Forty of the young trees were broken in the storm.
errors.why_it_happens: Broke is the shape the learner uses in ordinary past sentences and it arrives first. The second form of an irregular verb is stored far more weakly than the first.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: broke becomes broken.

errors.wrong: The old mill was collapsed during the storm.
errors.right: The old mill collapsed during the storm.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has decided this shape belongs in reports and applies it to every verb in one. Collapse has nothing to move to the front, because the mill is already the thing that came down.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: was.

used_in.quote: Every stage of the heat-pump diagram is written in this shape, from the first sentence to the last.

payload.sentence: The reservoir above Verdon was drained over the summer.
payload.question: Does the sentence name anyone who did the draining?

feedback.why_key: The doer has been left out on purpose. What survives is the reservoir and what happened to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether a doer is named before deciding what the sentence is about.

items.decision_cue: what happened to the depot yard

payload.context: Sam is describing what happened to the depot yard.
payload.sentence: The yard resurfaced in June.
reasons: the yard is shown as doing the work
the time named is wrong
this verb cannot take an object
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: As written, the yard is out there resurfacing something. One short word puts it back on the receiving end.
feedback.feed_forward: Add be when the subject is on the receiving end.

payload.context: From a note on the Verdon water works.
payload.stem: Silt ___ (remove) from the intake channel every autumn.

expected: is removed

feedback.why_key: Silt does not remove anything. It is what gets removed, so the sentence is built round it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match be to the time and leave the participle alone.

payload.context: Two neighbours are talking about the flats behind the station.
payload.stem: The whole block ___ (paint) last year and it still looks new.

expected: was painted

feedback.why_key: Last year fixes when it happened, and the block is on the receiving end, so was carries the date.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the time on be, never on the word after it.

payload.given: The council widened the approach road in March.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that the sentence is about the road.

expected: was widened in march
was widened by the council in march
was widened in march by the council
the approach road was widened in march

feedback.why_key: Moving the road to the front leaves nothing for it to do, so be steps in and the road becomes what the sentence reports on.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the affected thing first, then add be.

payload.context: A warden explaining the routine at the Verdon channel.

expected: every autumn the channel is dredged
the channel is dredged every autumn

feedback.why_key: Both orders are ordinary English. What neither of them does is tell you who runs the dredger.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep is and the participle together, wherever the time phrase goes.

payload.audio_text: The roof was checked before the tenants moved in.

expected: the roof was checked before the tenants moved in

feedback.why_key: Was is one unstressed syllable in the middle of a sentence, and it is the only thing marking the roof as the thing that got checked.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a short be in front of the -ed word.

payload.sentence: The intake screen cleaned every morning, and the debris is carted away.

expected: the intake screen is cleaned

feedback.why_key: The second half of the line shows the shape the first half is missing. Debris does not cart itself and screens do not clean themselves.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the two halves against each other before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: At a recycling plant, glass is sorted by colour before it goes into a crusher. Write one sentence about what happens to the glass. Do not mention the staff.

feedback.why_key: Nobody reading a process wants to meet the staff. Holding the glass in the subject slot is the whole register.
feedback.feed_forward: Start with the material, not with the plant.

payload.prompt_text: Take the first two stages of the dried pasta diagram and write them again as two sentences, keeping the wheat as the thing each sentence reports on. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Two stages in a row in one voice is what a process answer sounds like, and it is what a single sentence cannot show you.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that both sentences still open with the wheat.

title: Putting a sentence of that kind into whatever time I need

point_json.grammar_name: The passive across the tenses

pays_in.note: A map answer moves between what stood there once and what stands there now.
pays_in.model: The old goods yard has been replaced by a park-and-ride.

pays_in.note: One topic can be held across several times inside a single paragraph.
pays_in.model: The charge was brought in during 2018 and has been increased twice.

pays_in.note: Travel announcements are almost all built this way, and the first word carries the news.
pays_in.model: The next two services have been cancelled.

teach.can_do: I can move this shape into any time, from what is happening now to what will happen next year.
teach.why_it_matters: There is one thing to learn here, not six. Learners who find this hard are finding be hard, and be is already known.
teach.meaning: Once you can build one sentence of this kind you can build all of them, because only one word does the work of placing it in time. Be moves exactly as it moves in an ordinary sentence, and the word after it sits still. So the difference between a job that is happening, a job that is finished and a job that is promised is carried entirely by the first word of the pair.

form.pattern: be, in any time you like, + past participle
notes: now, as a routine: is repaired, are repaired
in the past: was repaired, were repaired
happening as we speak: is being repaired
finished and still relevant: has been repaired
after will, must, can and to, be keeps its plain shape: will be repaired, to be repaired
form.negative: be + not + past participle: the line was not reopened until May
form.question: Has the line been reopened?

spec.caption: Only the first word travels. The word after it never leaves its place.

worked_example.sentence: The signal box at Sandmouth is being rebuilt.
worked_example.why_this_form: The work started and has not finished, and the speaker is standing in the middle of it, so being is what reports that.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Has been rebuilt would close the job and hand you a finished box, which is not what a passenger looking at the scaffolding would say.

notice_set.sentence: The signal box at Sandmouth is being rebuilt.
notice_set.question: Is the work finished?
notice_set.why: Being tells you the work is under way at the moment of speaking.

notice_set.sentence: The box at Sandmouth has been rebuilt.
notice_set.question: Is the work finished?
notice_set.why: Been closes the job and leaves the result standing in front of you.

notice_set.sentence: Three of the level crossings will be closed for good.
notice_set.question: Have those crossings shut yet?
notice_set.why: Will puts the whole event ahead of now, so nothing has happened so far.

notice_set.sentence: Freight was diverted through Brackenfield for eleven weeks.
notice_set.question: Is freight still going that way?
notice_set.why: Eleven weeks is named and closed, so the arrangement ended when they did.

notice_set.sentence: Tickets can be bought at the machine on platform two.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence say anybody has bought one?
notice_set.why: It reports what is possible, not what has happened.

teach.rule_line: Put the time on be and leave the word after it alone.
teach.false_rule: That each time has its own version to memorise. There is one version. Be does the moving, and you already know how be moves.

errors.wrong: The bridge has been rebuild since the flood.
errors.right: The bridge has been rebuilt since the flood.
errors.why_it_happens: Three words are stacked up and only the first two get any attention. After been, nothing is allowed to stay in its plain shape.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: rebuild becomes rebuilt.

errors.wrong: The branch line will reopened in the spring.
errors.right: The branch line will be reopened in the spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Will already feels like the whole of the future, so be looks like a spare part. It is the part that puts the line on the receiving end.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: be.

errors.wrong: The depot was extended in 2019. New sidings are laid the following winter.
errors.right: The depot was extended in 2019. New sidings were laid the following winter.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape stays identical across the two sentences, so the writer stops noticing that the time has to be carried across as well.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: are becomes were.

used_in.quote: Every change between the two maps is reported in this shape, and only the first word of the pair changes.

payload.sentence: The Ashfield line has been closed since the landslip.
payload.question: Are trains running on it today?

feedback.why_key: Been holds the closure against the present, so the line is still shut as you read.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the first word of the pair: it says where in time you are.

payload.context: Ravi is telling a friend about the flat he has just moved into.
payload.sentence: The kitchen was fitted last month, so everything in it is new.
reasons: the time is wrong
the word after was is wrong
be is missing
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Was carries a closed month and fitted is the right second form. There is nothing here to repair.
feedback.feed_forward: Check be and the word after it separately, then stop looking.

payload.context: From a notice on the Brackenfield branch.
payload.stem: The signal box ___ (rebuild) at the moment, so the branch is on single-line working.

expected: is being rebuilt

feedback.why_key: At the moment puts the work under way as you write, and being is what reports under way.
feedback.feed_forward: Use being when the job is still going on as you speak.

payload.context: A supervisor going through the rules on a first day.
payload.stem: Nobody goes up onto the gantry until the harness ___ (check).

expected: has been checked
is checked

feedback.why_key: The check has to be over before anyone climbs, so the version that closes the job is the safer one.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the job must be finished before the next thing starts.

payload.given: Contractors will remove the old filter beds next year.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the sentence reports on the filter beds.

expected: will be removed next year
will be removed by contractors next year
will be removed next year by contractors
the old filter beds will be removed next year

feedback.why_key: Will needs be after it before the beds can sit on the receiving end of anything.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep be in its plain shape whenever will comes first.

payload.context: A guide showing visitors round a small dairy.

expected: the cheese is turned by hand every morning
every morning the cheese is turned by hand

feedback.why_key: By hand here is not a person. It is how the job is done, and it stays put whichever order you choose.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the time phrase freely; keep is and the participle together.

payload.audio_text: The last two services have been cancelled.

expected: the last two services have been cancelled

feedback.why_key: Have been is two weak syllables that vanish at speed, and they are the difference between a delay you can wait out and a train that is not coming.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the pair have been in front of the -ed word.

payload.sentence: The depot was extended in 2019, and new sidings are laid the following winter.

expected: were laid

feedback.why_key: The two halves of the sentence sit in different years and only one of them says so.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the dates first, then read the first word of each pair.

payload.prompt_text: A square in Marlow held a car park in 1990 and holds a market hall today. Write one sentence reporting that change, keeping the square as the thing the sentence is about.

feedback.why_key: A change of use is something done to a place, and the place is what the reader is looking at on the map.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose the time first, then build be to match it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the second paragraph of the Sandmouth maps answer: three changes, all reported as things done to the village, all sitting in the same time. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Three sentences is where drift starts, because the shape stops feeling like a decision and starts feeling like a habit.
feedback.feed_forward: Read your three first words in a row and check they match.

title: Telling a piece of a sentence apart from a whole one

point_json.grammar_name: Main clauses, subordinate clauses, and what makes a fragment

teach.can_do: I can tell whether a group of words can stand alone as a sentence or needs to lean on another one.
teach.why_it_matters: Nearly every broken sentence in a written answer is one of these two pieces being used as if it were the other.
teach.meaning: A clause is a group of words with a subject and its own verb: the fare rose. That is the smallest thing English accepts as a sentence, and a clause that stands on its own like that is called a main clause. Now put one small word in front of it — because, although, when, if — and it can no longer stand up. It still has its subject and its verb, but it now leans on a main clause and cannot be left alone with a full stop after it. That leaning kind is called a subordinate clause.

form.pattern: main clause = subject + verb, able to stand alone. subordinate clause = joining word + subject + verb, unable to stand alone.
notes: The joining word is what makes the difference, not the length. Because it rained is short and still cannot stand alone.
A subordinate clause can come first or second: because the road flooded, the coach was late — or — the coach was late because the road flooded.
When it comes first, a comma marks where it ends. When it comes second, usually no comma is needed.
One sentence needs exactly one main clause. It may have none, one or several subordinate clauses hanging off it.
form.negative: Both kinds go negative in the ordinary way: although the road was not flooded, the coach was still late.
form.question: Ask of any group of words: could I put a full stop after this and walk away?

left.text: the coach was late

right.text: because the road flooded

spec.caption: Both have a subject and a verb. Only one of them can be left alone with a full stop.

worked_example.sentence: Although the college added an evening class, the waiting list did not get any shorter.
worked_example.why_this_form: Although turns the first clause into the leaning kind, so the sentence still needs the second clause to stand on. The comma shows where the leaning part stops.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Delete although and you have two clauses that can each stand alone, and a comma between them is no longer enough to hold them together.

notice_set.sentence: Because the grant was withdrawn.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: It has a subject and a verb, but because leaves it leaning on something that never arrives.

notice_set.sentence: The grant was withdrawn.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: Subject, verb, and nothing in front of it asking for more. That is a whole sentence.

notice_set.sentence: When the results came out, half the class had already left.
notice_set.question: How many clauses are in this sentence?
notice_set.why: Two subjects and two verbs, joined by when. One of them leans and one of them stands.

notice_set.sentence: The results came out. Half the class had already left.
notice_set.question: Is anything broken here?
options: Yes, one part cannot stand alone
No, both parts are whole sentences
notice_set.why: Nothing is leaning, so two full stops are perfectly correct. It simply does not tell you how the two facts relate.

notice_set.sentence: Which explains why the scheme was quietly dropped.
notice_set.question: Could this be a sentence on its own?
notice_set.why: Which is a joining word too, so this piece is still waiting to be attached to whatever it explains.

notice_set.sentence: Fewer students took physics last year, although the department had opened two new labs.
notice_set.question: Which part could stand alone?
notice_set.why: The second part has although in front of it, so it leans. Cover it and the first part is still a sentence.

discovery.prompt: Every group of words on the left can be a sentence. None of the ones on the right can, even though all of them have a subject and a verb. What has been done to them?
pairs: the ferry stopped running
because the ferry stopped running
the tunnel was widened in 2018
when the tunnel was widened in 2018
the fee was reduced
although the fee was reduced

candidate_rules.text: One extra word at the front takes away the clause's ability to stand alone.
The ones on the right are about reasons and times, and reasons and times are never sentences.
A group of words cannot stand alone if it begins with because, when or although.

teach.rule_line: Could I put a full stop after this and walk away? If not, it is leaning on something.
teach.false_rule: That a long group of words is a sentence and a short one is not. Length has nothing to do with it: I agree is a sentence, and although the entire scheme was funded from the outset is not.

errors.wrong: Because the tuition fee rose again in September. Many applicants withdrew.
errors.right: Because the tuition fee rose again in September, many applicants withdrew.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner puts the full stop where they would take a breath, and the first piece is long enough to feel finished. Nothing in it sounds incomplete until you cover the piece that follows.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the full stop becomes a comma.

errors.wrong: The department opened two new labs, fewer students took physics.
errors.right: Although the department opened two new labs, fewer students took physics.
errors.why_it_happens: Both facts are true and they clearly belong together, so a comma feels like enough. Making one of them lean is the move the learner has never been shown.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: although.

errors.wrong: The lab was refitted over the summer the equipment arrived in October.
errors.right: The lab was refitted over the summer, and the equipment arrived in October.
errors.why_it_happens: Two clauses were written straight through without the writer noticing there was a seam. There is no punctuation error to see, which is why proofreading rarely catches it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: and.

errors.wrong: Despite the department opened two new labs, applications fell.
errors.right: Although the department opened two new labs, applications fell.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although both signal that a turn is coming, so they feel interchangeable. Nobody has told the learner that only one of the two can have a subject and a verb after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: despite becomes although.

pays_in.note: Every complex sentence you will ever write is these two pieces in some arrangement.
pays_in.model: Although the fee was reduced, the number of applications barely moved.

pays_in.note: A long passage sentence unpacks the moment you find the clause that stands alone.
pays_in.model: Because funding was tied to enrolment, departments that shrank lost staff twice over.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers need reasons attached to claims, not listed after them.
pays_in.model: People commute less because the cost has gone up, not because they prefer being at home.

used_in.quote: The prompt invites a concession in every paragraph, and a concession is a leaning clause.
Several sentences in the passage carry three clauses, and only one of them is the claim being made.

payload.sentence: Although the college kept the evening class open.
payload.question: Is this a complete sentence?
options: Only if you add a comma

feedback.why_key: Although leaves the clause waiting for the part it leans on, and that part never comes.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the first word and see whether what is left could stand alone.

payload.sentence: The coach was late because the road flooded.
payload.question: How many of these two clauses could stand alone?

feedback.why_key: The coach was late stands up on its own. Because the road flooded leans on it and cannot be left by itself.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the clauses first, then ask which one is leaning.

items.decision_cue: Because the fee rose again in September.

payload.context: From a first draft about tuition costs.
payload.sentence: Because the fee rose again in September. Applications from mature students fell by a fifth.
reasons: the first piece cannot stand alone
the second piece cannot stand alone
the two pieces are unrelated
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The first piece has a subject and a verb, but because leaves it leaning, and a full stop gives it nothing to lean on.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a piece on its own before you put a full stop after it.

payload.context: Two facts about a college course, to be put into one sentence.
payload.stem: ___ the fee was reduced, the number of applications did not change.

expected: although
though
even though
while

feedback.why_key: One word at the front turns a stand-alone clause into a leaning one, and the comma then shows where the leaning part ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the joining word to the clause you want to lean.

payload.context: From a report on a rural bus route.
payload.stem: The 4.15 service was withdrawn in January, ___ the village has had no evening link since.

expected: and
so

feedback.why_key: Both halves stand alone, so the comma needs a joining word beside it before the sentence will hold together.
feedback.feed_forward: Two stand-alone clauses need a joining word, not just a comma.

payload.context: Build one sentence in which the leaning clause comes first.

expected: because the reservoir was already low the ban came in early

feedback.why_key: The leaning clause comes first and hands over to a clause that can stand alone. Without that second clause the sentence never finishes.
feedback.feed_forward: After a leaning clause, always finish with one that stands alone.

payload.given: The library extended its opening hours. Very few students came in after eight.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence in which the first fact leans on the second.

expected: the library extended its opening hours very few students came in after eight
the library extended its opening hours, very few students came in after eight

feedback.why_key: Although turns a stand-alone clause into a leaning one, and the sentence then needs the second clause to hold it up.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the joining word in front of the clause you want to lean.

payload.audio_text: When we'd finished the audit, the office was already shut.

expected: when we'd finished the audit the office was already shut
when we had finished the audit the office was already shut
when wed finished the audit the office was already shut

feedback.why_key: When is the word doing all the work, and in speech it is short and unstressed. Miss it and you write two sentences the speaker never said.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small word at the start that makes a clause lean.

payload.sentence: Because the fee rose again in September. Applications from mature students fell by a fifth.

expected: in september, applications
in september applications

feedback.why_key: One mark is wrong. The leaning clause has to be tied to the clause that follows it, not fenced off from it.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the full stop after a leaning clause with a comma.

payload.context: From a draft report on a college refit.
payload.sentence: The lab was refitted over the summer the equipment arrived in October.
reasons: two stand-alone clauses have been run together with nothing between them
the first clause cannot stand alone
the second clause cannot stand alone
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Both halves could take a full stop, and nothing at all has been put between them, so the reader has to find the seam unaided.
feedback.feed_forward: Put a joining word or a full stop at every seam between stand-alone clauses.

payload.context: Two lines taken from different drafts of the same survey report.
sentences: Because the river level dropped, the survey was postponed.
The river level dropped. The survey was postponed.
meanings: The sentence states that the drop is why the survey moved.
Two facts are reported and the reader is left to guess how they connect.

feedback.why_key: A leaning clause puts the relation on the page. Two separate sentences leave the relation in the writer's head.
feedback.feed_forward: Use a leaning clause when the relation matters as much as the facts.

payload.prompt_text: A school has made an hour of exercise compulsory every day, and the timetable has lost an hour of science. Write one sentence in which one of those facts leans on the other.

feedback.why_key: Putting one fact into a leaning clause tells the reader which of the two you think is the news.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide which fact is the news, then make the other one lean.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on daily school exercise. Check every full stop: could what comes before it stand alone? Rewrite the two weakest sentences. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: This one check catches both of the errors that make a reader go back a line: a piece used as a whole, and two wholes glued with a comma.
feedback.feed_forward: Check every full stop before you check anything else.

title: Pinning one event to another with when, while, before, after and until

point_json.grammar_name: Time clauses: when, while, as, before, after, until, as soon as

teach.can_do: I can attach a time clause to a sentence and keep the verb inside it in the right form.
teach.why_it_matters: Time clauses are where will turns up and should not, and where a whole sentence quietly loses the part that can stand alone.
teach.meaning: A time clause is a leaning clause whose joining word answers when. When, while, as, before, after, until and as soon as each fix the second event against the first: at the same moment, earlier, later, or right up to a point and no further. Because the clause leans, it always travels with a clause that stands. And there is one habit here that catches everybody: when the whole sentence is about the future, the time clause itself stays in the present.

form.pattern: when / while / as / before / after / until / as soon as + subject + verb, + main clause
notes: Future meaning, present form: I will call you when the results arrive — never when the results will arrive.
While and as suit an activity that was already running; when suits a single moment.
Until means right up to a point and stops there: we waited until the last train left.
The time clause can go first or second. A comma is needed only when it goes first.
form.negative: The clause goes negative in the ordinary way: while the office was not open, deliveries were left at the gate.
form.question: Questions ask about the main clause, not the time clause: what did you do while the line was down?

spec.caption: Each joining word pins the second event to a different place against the first.
