worked_example.sentence: We will move the servers as soon as the new room is ready.
worked_example.why_this_form: The whole sentence is about the future and the main clause already says so. The time clause takes the present because the future has been stated once and does not need saying twice.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: As soon as the new room will be ready is not a stronger or a politer version. It is simply not English, and it is one of the most visible errors at this level.

notice_set.sentence: As soon as the survey closed, the figures were published.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: As soon as puts the second event immediately after the first, with nothing in between.

notice_set.sentence: While the line was closed, the freight went by road.
notice_set.question: Did the freight move during the closure or after it?
notice_set.why: While covers a stretch of time, and the second event sits inside that stretch.

notice_set.sentence: The office had emptied before the storm reached the coast.
notice_set.question: Was anyone still in the office when the storm arrived?
notice_set.why: Before puts the emptying earlier, so the storm found the office already empty.

notice_set.sentence: I will send the file when the meeting ends.
notice_set.question: Is the meeting over?
notice_set.why: Ends looks like a present form, but the sentence is about the future. The time clause simply does not repeat it.

notice_set.sentence: We stayed until the last bus had gone.
notice_set.question: Did they leave before the last bus?
notice_set.why: Until marks the point at which the staying stopped, so they were still there when the bus went.

teach.rule_line: In a sentence about the future, the time clause stays in the present.
teach.false_rule: That every clause in a sentence about the future needs will. English states the future once, in the main clause, and the time clause does not repeat it.

errors.wrong: I will let you know as soon as the results will arrive.
errors.right: I will let you know as soon as the results arrive.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence really is about the future and the learner is being consistent, which is exactly the reasoning that produces it. Nothing in the usual teaching says the time clause is the one place where consistency is wrong.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: After the depot closed in March. The drivers were moved to Ashfield.
errors.right: After the depot closed in March, the drivers were moved to Ashfield.
errors.why_it_happens: The time clause is long enough to feel like a finished thought, and after is not heard as a word that leaves anything hanging.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the full stop becomes a comma.

errors.wrong: When the alarm went off, everyone is outside within a minute.
errors.right: When the alarm went off, everyone was outside within a minute.
errors.why_it_happens: The two clauses are chosen one at a time and nobody reads the sentence as a single unit. The main clause slips back to the form the learner uses most.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: is becomes was.

errors.wrong: We waited when the last train left.
errors.right: We waited until the last train left.
errors.why_it_happens: When and until both point at a moment and when is far commoner, so it arrives first. When names the moment something happened; until names the moment something stopped.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: when becomes until.

pays_in.note: A two-minute story is a chain of events, and time clauses are the links.
pays_in.model: While we were waiting for the parts to arrive, the whole line stood idle.

pays_in.note: Predictions almost always need a moment attached, and that is where will doubles up.
pays_in.model: Employers will only change their hiring once the shortage starts costing them contracts.

pays_in.note: An instruction in a talk is often a time clause, and the answer sits inside it.
pays_in.model: Before you submit the form, check that the reference number matches the letter.

used_in.quote: Any answer about what will happen next needs a moment pinned to it, and the extra will appears there every time.
Two of the answers are inside time clauses, and the speaker gives the moment before the fact.

payload.sentence: While the shop was being refitted, the staff worked from the unit next door.
payload.question: Where were the staff during the refit?

feedback.why_key: While covers the whole stretch of the refit, and the second clause tells you what filled it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read while as during the whole of that.

payload.sentence: The system will switch to the new server when the tests finish.
payload.question: Have the tests finished?

feedback.why_key: Finish looks present, but the whole sentence sits in the future and the time clause simply does not repeat it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a present-form time clause as future when the main clause is future.

items.decision_cue: when the new contract will start

payload.context: From an email about a change of supplier.
payload.sentence: We will move the accounts across when the new contract will start.
reasons: the future is stated twice
the time clause is in the wrong place
the main clause needs a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Will in the main clause has already put the whole sentence in the future. The time clause has nothing left to add.
feedback.feed_forward: State the future once, in the main clause.

payload.context: From a note to a team about an office move.
payload.stem: We will hand over the keys as soon as the survey ___ (finish).

expected: finishes
is finished
has finished

feedback.why_key: The main clause has already put the sentence in the future, so the time clause takes the plain present.
feedback.feed_forward: Never put will inside a time clause.

payload.context: Two colleagues talking about a bad week at the clinic.
payload.stem: When the second nurse ___ (arrive), the queue had gone right round the corner.

expected: arrived

feedback.why_key: The queue formed first, so the arrival is the later of the two events and takes the simple past.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the earlier event first, then choose the form for the later one.

payload.given: The last ferry left at six. We were still queuing on the slip road.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence beginning with a time clause that puts the queue at that exact moment.

expected: the last ferry left at six we were still queuing on the slip road
the last ferry left at six, we were still queuing on the slip road

feedback.why_key: The time clause pins the queue to the moment the ferry went, which two separate sentences leave the reader to work out.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the moment in the leaning clause and the news in the main one.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a flood warning system.

expected: the alarm will sound before the level reaches the top gauge

feedback.why_key: Will sits in the main clause and nowhere else. Before takes the plain present even though both events are still ahead of us.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep will out of any clause starting with before.

payload.audio_text: As soon as we'd signed it off, the invoice went out.

expected: as soon as we'd signed it off the invoice went out
as soon as we had signed it off the invoice went out
as soon as wed signed it off the invoice went out

feedback.why_key: The 'd is one small sound and it carries the whole order of events. Lose it and the two things start happening at once.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a 'd riding on the subject inside a time clause.

payload.sentence: The old system will stay in use until the licence will expire in June.

expected: until the licence expires
until the licence has expired

feedback.why_key: The sentence has already been put in the future once. Repeating it inside the time clause is the single most visible error in this area.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete will from any clause beginning when, until, before or after.

items.decision_cue: After the depot closed in March.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph on rural employment.
payload.sentence: After the depot closed in March. Forty drivers were moved to the Ashfield site.
reasons: the first piece cannot stand alone
the second piece cannot stand alone
the two pieces are in the wrong order
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: After leaves the first piece leaning, and a full stop takes away the very thing it needs to lean on.
feedback.feed_forward: Tie a time clause to its main clause with a comma.

payload.context: Two lines from different versions of the same file note.
sentences: We worked until the power came back.
We worked when the power came back.
meanings: The working stopped at the moment the power returned.
The working started at the moment the power returned.

feedback.why_key: Until marks the end point of the first event. When marks the moment the first event begins.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the joining word ends the action or starts it.

payload.prompt_text: A change is coming at your workplace next year. Say one thing you will do, and pin it to the moment something else happens.

feedback.why_key: The future goes in the main clause and the time clause holds the moment. That split is the whole of this point.
feedback.feed_forward: Say will once, and put the moment in a present-form clause.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on translation apps in schools. Add one sentence that says what will happen and pins it to a moment. Then count the wills. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Predictions in an essay almost always need a time clause attached, and that is exactly where the extra will appears.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the sentence back and count the wills.

title: Choosing the right word to attach a reason or a result

point_json.grammar_name: Reason and result: because, since, as, so, therefore, consequently

teach.can_do: I can attach a reason or a result to a sentence with the right kind of word, in the right place.
teach.why_it_matters: These words look interchangeable and are not: one joins two clauses, one starts a new sentence, and mixing them is where comma splices come from.
teach.meaning: Cause and effect can be written from either end: name the reason, or name the result. English gives you three different kinds of word for it and they are not swappable. Because, since and as go in front of a clause and make it lean; they introduce the reason. So goes between two clauses that both stand; it introduces the result. Therefore and consequently are not joining words at all — they are adverbs, and they need a full stop in front of them.

form.pattern: reason: because / since / as + clause. result: main clause + , so + clause. adverb: full stop + Therefore, + clause.
notes: Because introduces the reason and so introduces the result. They face in opposite directions and you never need both.
Since and as also mean because, but they suit a reason the reader already knows.
Therefore and consequently cannot hold two clauses together. Put a full stop in front and a comma after.
form.negative: The reason clause goes negative as usual: because the funding was not renewed, the class closed at half term.
form.question: Ask which half is the reason and which is the result before you choose the word.

left.text: because the funding was withdrawn

right.text: so the evening class closed

spec.caption: One arrow, two ways to write it. The word you choose depends on which end you are standing at.

worked_example.sentence: Because the funding was withdrawn in April, the evening class closed at half term.
worked_example.why_this_form: The withdrawal is the reason, and because is the word that puts a reason into a leaning clause. The comma marks where the leaning part ends.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: So in that slot would claim the withdrawal was the result of the closure, which turns the whole sentence round.

notice_set.sentence: The bridge was closed for repairs, so the diversion added twenty minutes.
notice_set.question: Which part is the result?
notice_set.why: So always introduces the result, and the result always comes second.

notice_set.sentence: Because the diversion added twenty minutes, the school bus arrived late.
notice_set.question: Which part is the reason?
notice_set.why: Because always introduces the reason, and here the reason has been put first.

notice_set.sentence: The rent rose again in March. Therefore, two of the shops did not renew.
notice_set.question: Could that full stop be a comma instead?
notice_set.why: Therefore is an adverb, not a joining word, so it cannot hold two clauses together across a comma.

notice_set.sentence: As the site had no drainage, the first winter flooded it.
notice_set.question: Does as mean at the same time here, or because?
notice_set.why: As has both meanings. The reason reading is the natural one when the second clause is plainly a consequence.

notice_set.sentence: Since the depot moved, the village has lost its only employer.
notice_set.question: Is since about time here, or about a reason?
notice_set.why: Since is genuinely ambiguous here, and that ambiguity is a good reason to write because when the reason is the point.

notice_set.sentence: The line was single track, so trains could not pass each other.
notice_set.question: Is the second clause the cause or the effect?
notice_set.why: After so, you are always reading an effect. Nothing else can follow it.

discovery.prompt: Each pair says the same thing twice. Work out what has to change when the word changes.
pairs: Because the fare rose, fewer people travelled.
The fare rose, so fewer people travelled.
Because the mill shut, the village lost its shop.
The mill shut, so the village lost its shop.
Because the survey was late, the report missed its date.
The survey was late, so the report missed its date.

candidate_rules.text: Because goes in front of the reason and so goes in front of the result, so the two clauses swap places.
Because goes at the start of a sentence and so goes in the middle of one.
Use because when the sentence is about the past and so when it is about the present.

teach.rule_line: Because points at the reason. So points at the result. Therefore needs a full stop.
teach.false_rule: That because, so and therefore are three ways of writing one word. They are three different grammatical classes and they sit in three different places.

contrast.question: Am I about to write the reason or the result?

fork.answer: The reason, and I want it in a leaning clause
fork.selects: because, since or as in front of the clause

fork.answer: The result, and both halves are staying as full clauses
fork.selects: so between them, after a comma

fork.answer: The result, and I want a fresh sentence for it
fork.selects: a full stop, then therefore or consequently

a.text: The evening class closed because the funding ran out.
a.means: The money went first. The closure is what followed from it.

b.text: The evening class closed, so the funding ran out.
b.means: The closure came first, and losing the money is what followed from that.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote so. That tells your reader the closure came first and the money went because of it. The facts are unchanged and the arrow has been turned round, which is far harder to spot than a broken form.

edge_case.text: As and since also mean because, and as also means at the same time. In a timed answer that ambiguity costs you nothing if you simply write because whenever the reason is the point.

contrast.stronger_test: Say the two halves out loud with and because of that between them. Whichever half sits second is the result, and that is the half so belongs in front of.

worked_pairs.a: Rents rose sharply, so two of the independent shops did not renew.
worked_pairs.b: Rents rose sharply because two of the independent shops did not renew.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so two of the independent shops did not renew
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: because two of the independent shops did not renew
worked_pairs.gloss: The first blames the rents for the closures. The second blames the closures for the rents, and that is a different town.

worked_pairs.a: The path floods every winter, so the council has fenced it off.
worked_pairs.b: Because the path floods every winter, the council has fenced it off.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so the council has fenced it off
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: Because the path floods every winter
worked_pairs.gloss: Same arrow, two ways of writing it. The second puts the reason first, which leaves the fencing as the news.

worked_pairs.a: The line was never electrified. Therefore, journey times have not moved since the 1980s.
worked_pairs.b: The line was never electrified, so journey times have not moved since the 1980s.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct. The first is two sentences and reads formally; the second is one and reads plainly. What you may never do is put therefore where so is.

errors.wrong: The rent rose again in March, therefore two of the shops did not renew.
errors.right: The rent rose again in March. Therefore, two of the shops did not renew.
errors.why_it_happens: Therefore means what so means, so it feels as though it can stand in the same place. Nobody has told the learner that meaning and grammatical class are two separate facts about a word.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the comma becomes a full stop.

errors.wrong: Because the mill shut, so the village lost its only shop.
errors.right: Because the mill shut, the village lost its only shop.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner marks the relation twice to be certain the reader sees it. Both words are correct on their own and in English exactly one of them has to go.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: so.
errors.l1_note: Marking the pair on both clauses is the standard pattern in several Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The evening class closed, so the funding ran out.
errors.right: The evening class closed because the funding ran out.
errors.why_it_happens: Under time pressure the learner writes the two facts in the order they thought of them and reaches for the commonest joining word. So then quietly reverses the cause and the effect without breaking anything.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: so becomes because.

errors.wrong: Because of the funding was withdrawn, the class closed.
errors.right: Because the funding was withdrawn, the class closed.
errors.why_it_happens: Because of is stored as one unit and comes out whole. It takes a noun, not a clause, and here a clause with its own subject and verb has been put after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: of.

pays_in.note: A problem-and-solution answer is a chain of reasons and results end to end.
pays_in.model: Because deliveries are now priced as free, the number of separate vans on each street has doubled.

pays_in.note: Part 3 asks why about everything, and a bare fact does not answer why.
pays_in.model: Rents went up faster than wages, so a lot of people my age are still at home.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often reverses the arrow the passage drew.
pays_in.model: The scheme was withdrawn because take-up never reached a third of the target.

used_in.quote: The prompt asks for causes and then for consequences, which is this point twice in each paragraph.
The passage explains a closure and one question turns on which of the two facts caused the other.

payload.sentence: Rents rose sharply, so two of the independent shops did not renew.
payload.question: Which came first?

feedback.why_key: So always puts the result second, so whatever sits in front of it is the earlier event.
feedback.feed_forward: Read so as and because of that.

payload.sentence: We moved out to Brackenfield because the rent went up twice in one year.
payload.question: Why did they move?

feedback.why_key: Because introduces the reason, and the reason here is the rent, not the place they went to.
feedback.feed_forward: The clause after because is always the reason.

items.decision_cue: in March, therefore two of the shops

payload.context: From a first draft on town centre shops.
payload.sentence: The rent rose again in March, therefore two of the shops did not renew.
reasons: therefore cannot hold two clauses together
therefore is the wrong meaning here
the comma is in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Therefore means exactly what so means, but it is an adverb, and an adverb cannot join two clauses across a comma.
feedback.feed_forward: Put a full stop in front of therefore.

payload.context: From a paragraph on farm run-off in the Verdon.
payload.stem: The run-off was never treated, ___ the fish stocks below the weir collapsed.

expected: so

feedback.why_key: The collapse is what followed, and so is the word that puts a result in the second half of a sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: If the second half is the consequence, use so.

payload.context: From a paragraph on independent shops.
payload.stem: ___ the business rate was cut, three empty units were taken within a month.

expected: because
since
as

feedback.why_key: The rate cut is the reason and the lettings are the result, so the reason clause is the one that leans.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the reason in the leaning clause.

payload.given: The line was never electrified. Journey times have not changed since the 1980s.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that presents the second fact as the result of the first.

expected: so journey times have not changed since the 1980s
so journey times have not changed since the eighties

feedback.why_key: So marks the second clause as what followed, and one sentence now carries the whole cause and effect.
feedback.feed_forward: Use so when both halves stay as full clauses.

payload.audio_text: The van hadn't turned up, so we'd started without it.

expected: the van hadn't turned up so we'd started without it
the van had not turned up so we had started without it
the van hadnt turned up so wed started without it

feedback.why_key: So is a single unstressed sound at the seam. If you do not hear it you write two sentences and the cause disappears.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small word at the seam between two clauses.

payload.context: The college lost its grant in March and the class stopped meeting in May.
payload.stem: The evening class closed, ___ the funding ran out.

options.why_this_means: That the closure came first and the money stopped as a result of it.
That the money stopped first and the closure followed from it.

expected: because

feedback.why_key: The grant went in March and the class stopped in May, so the money is the reason and the closure is what followed.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask which of the two facts happened first.

items.decision_cue: the college withdrew the grant in June

payload.context: Four students were left in March, the class stopped meeting at half term, and the college withdrew the grant in June.
payload.stem: The evening class closed, ___ the funding ran out.

options.why_this_means: That the closure came first and the money stopped as a result of it.
That the money stopped first and the closure followed from it.

expected: so

feedback.why_key: Here the closure came first and the money went afterwards, so the arrow runs the other way and only so shows it.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the order of events, not the order of your sentence, pick the word.

items.decision_cue: announced a fare freeze in January

payload.context: The mayor announced a fare freeze in January, and in December the operator reported its first rise in ridership for a decade.
payload.stem: Fares were frozen this year, ___ passenger numbers rose by eight per cent.

options.why_this_means: That the freeze came first and the extra passengers are what it produced.
That the passengers came first and holding the fares was the response to them.

expected: so

feedback.why_key: The freeze was announced at the start of the year and the rise was counted at the end of it, so the rise is what followed.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the dates before you choose the word.

items.decision_cue: asked the mayor to hold fares

payload.context: Ridership climbed all through last year, and in the autumn the operator asked the mayor to hold fares to keep the trend going.
payload.stem: Fares were frozen this year, ___ passenger numbers rose by eight per cent.

options.why_this_means: That the freeze came first and the extra passengers are what it produced.
That the passengers came first and holding the fares was the response to them.

expected: because

feedback.why_key: The rise came first and it is why the fares were held, so the second clause is the reason and not the result.
feedback.feed_forward: The clause after because is the earlier event.

items.decision_cue: does not say which came first

payload.context: A survey team and a funding decision arrived in the same month, and the report does not say which came first.
payload.stem: The dig at Brackenfield was extended, ___ the trust released a second grant.

options.why_this_means: That extending the dig is what persuaded the trust to release more money.
That the money arrived first and the extra weeks were paid for out of it.

follow_up.question: Which version says the money came first?

feedback.why_key: Both are ordinary English and both fit these events. The word you pick tells the reader which way the money and the digging pushed each other.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide the order of events first; the word follows from it.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph on small towns.
payload.sentence: Because the mill shut, so the village lost its only shop.
reasons: the relation is marked twice
the two clauses are the wrong way round
the comma is unnecessary
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Because has already made the first clause the reason. So then tries to make the second one the result, and one of the two has nothing left to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the relation once and delete the spare word.

items.decision_cue: Because of the grant was withdrawn

payload.sentence: Because of the grant was withdrawn in April, the evening class closed at half term.
payload.error_span: Because of the grant was withdrawn

expected: because the grant was withdrawn
because of the withdrawal of the grant
because of the grant withdrawal

feedback.why_key: Because of takes a noun. What follows here is a clause with its own subject and verb, so the of has nothing to attach to.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete of when a subject and a verb follow.

payload.context: Two lines taken from different drafts of the same estuary report.
sentences: The silt had smothered the beds. Therefore, the beds were replanted in the spring.
The silt had smothered the beds, so the beds were replanted in the spring.
meanings: Two sentences, formal in tone, with the link carried by an adverb after a full stop.
One sentence, plainer in tone, with the link carried by a joining word after a comma.

feedback.why_key: The two versions claim exactly the same thing. What differs is the punctuation each word demands, and that is the whole lesson.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the punctuation to the class of word you have chosen.

payload.prompt_text: Half the shops on a high street have closed since a retail park opened outside the town. Write one sentence that names the reason and the result and makes clear which is which.

feedback.why_key: Naming both ends of the arrow inside one sentence is what turns a list of facts into an explanation.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the reason clause first, then check the arrow points the right way.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on town centre shops. Find every therefore, so and because and check that the punctuation around each one is what that word needs. Rewrite the two worst. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: The commonest punctuation error in a written answer is an adverb doing a joining word's job, and this one check finds all of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the punctuation on both sides of every linking word.

title: Stating what always happens once a condition is met

point_json.grammar_name: Zero conditional

teach.can_do: I can state a rule: once this is true, that follows, every time.
teach.why_it_matters: Describing a machine, a rule or a natural process needs this shape, and it is the cheapest two-part sentence English has.
teach.meaning: Some sentences are not reports about one occasion. They are claims about what the world reliably does. Put the tide below the marker and the ferry cannot dock — that is not a guess about Tuesday, it is a standing fact about the slipway. This shape allows no exceptions: it says that on every single occasion the first half is true, the second half follows. That is why it fits rules, machinery, procedures and natural processes, and why it sounds odd for a one-off.

form.pattern: If + present form, present form
notes: The two halves can swap places: the ferry cannot dock if the tide drops below the marker. When the if half comes second, no comma is needed.
When means almost exactly the same thing here, because you are talking about every occasion rather than one of them.
The if half never takes will, even though the sentence covers tomorrow as well as today.
form.negative: If the pump does not restart within a minute, the tank overflows.
form.question: What happens if the tide drops below the marker?

left.role: the condition, in a present form
left.text: If the tide drops below the marker

right.role: what follows, every occasion, also in a present form
right.text: the ferry cannot dock

spec.caption: No guess about one afternoon. A standing claim about every afternoon.

worked_example.sentence: If the river rises above the flood wall, the pumping station shuts itself down.
worked_example.why_this_form: Nothing is being predicted. The station is built so that this happens on every occasion the water gets that high, and both halves stay in a present form to say so.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting will into the second half would turn a standing fact about the station into a forecast about one particular flood the speaker has in mind.

notice_set.sentence: If the tide drops below the marker, the ferry cannot dock.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker talking about one particular afternoon?
notice_set.why: The sentence is describing how the slipway behaves, so it covers every afternoon the water gets that low.

notice_set.sentence: If the sample is left in daylight, the colour fades inside a day.
notice_set.question: Would the colour fade on a sample left out next month?
notice_set.why: A rule about samples carries forward. Next month's sample is covered by it without being mentioned.

notice_set.sentence: If the outside air falls below about minus five, the backup heater takes over.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know whether it will be that cold tonight?
notice_set.why: The sentence is about the heating system, not about tonight. Tonight has not been mentioned at all.

notice_set.sentence: If you do not rinse the rice, it sticks to the base of the pan.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker giving a warning about one particular meal?
notice_set.why: This is what rice does. Nobody's dinner tonight is being discussed.

notice_set.sentence: The gritters go out at four if the road surface freezes overnight.
notice_set.question: Is this what the council does every cold night, or only tonight?
notice_set.why: Both halves stay in a present form, which is how English says that this is the standing arrangement.

discovery.prompt: Two of these describe how something always behaves. One is about a single occasion. Work out what tells you which is which.
pairs: If the tide drops below the marker, the ferry cannot dock.
If the tide drops below the marker tonight, the ferry will stay out.
If you do not rinse the rice, it sticks to the base of the pan.
If you do not rinse this rice, it will stick to the pan.
The gritters go out at four if the road surface freezes overnight.
The gritters will go out at four if the road freezes tonight.

candidate_rules.text: On the left both halves stay in a present form because the sentence covers every occasion, not one.
The left-hand sentences are about machines and weather, and the right-hand ones are about people.
Whenever a sentence contains the word if, the second half needs will.

teach.rule_line: Ask: is this true every time, or only this time?
teach.false_rule: That if points at the future and therefore drags will in behind it. Here if points at every occasion, and will has nothing to add.

errors.wrong: If the temperature will fall below zero, the sensors stop reporting.
errors.right: If the temperature falls below zero, the sensors stop reporting.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reads the sentence as being about the future, and English usually marks the future with will, so it lands in the first half where nothing needs it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will fall becomes falls.

errors.wrong: If the tank would fill past the upper mark, the overflow pipe opens.
errors.right: If the tank fills past the upper mark, the overflow pipe opens.
errors.why_it_happens: Would has been stored as the word that keeps if company, so it arrives on its own. Nothing here is being imagined; the sentence is describing what the tank does.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would fill becomes fills.

errors.wrong: If the pressure drops below two bar. The valve closes automatically.
errors.right: If the pressure drops below two bar, the valve closes automatically.
errors.why_it_happens: The first half is long enough to feel finished, so a full stop arrives. On its own it names a condition and never says what follows from it, which leaves the reader waiting.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one punctuation mark: the full stop becomes a comma.

pays_in.note: Nearly every process description states what happens at a stage once a condition is met.
pays_in.model: If the salt content rises too far, the membrane is flushed and the cycle begins again.

pays_in.note: Science passages state their mechanisms in this shape and questions turn on them.
pays_in.model: If the surface water cools quickly enough, the layers beneath it stop mixing.

pays_in.note: Explaining how something normally works is a Part 3 staple.
pays_in.model: If a town loses its last bank, older residents stop going into the centre altogether.

used_in.quote: A process diagram is a chain of conditions, and describing it without this shape means writing every stage twice.
The passage explains a mechanism, and one question depends on reading a stated rule as a rule rather than as an event.

payload.sentence: If the barrier is down, the level crossing lights stay red.
payload.question: Is this about one particular morning?

feedback.why_key: Both halves sit in a present form, which is how English says that this is how the crossing behaves on every occasion.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the sentence as a claim about all occasions before you look for a date.

payload.sentence: If a soil sample dries out completely, the count of living organisms in it collapses.
payload.question: Would the same thing happen to a sample collected next spring?

feedback.why_key: The sentence is a claim about soil samples in general, so it reaches forward to samples nobody has collected yet.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the claim covers cases the sentence never names.

payload.context: From a description of how a flood scheme is meant to work.
payload.sentence: If the water level will rise above the wall, the pumping station shuts itself down.
reasons: the first half is describing every occasion, so it needs no will
the pumping station has not been built yet
the halves have been written the wrong way round
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The sentence is describing a permanent arrangement, and will would narrow it to one flood the writer has in mind.
feedback.feed_forward: Take will out of the if half whenever you are stating a rule.

payload.context: From a note on how a heat pump behaves in cold weather.
payload.stem: If the outside air ___ (fall) below about minus five, the backup heater takes over.

expected: falls

feedback.why_key: This is what the system does every cold night, so the first half stays in its plain present form.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the if half present when you are describing normal behaviour.

payload.context: From a card pinned above a bakery worktop.
payload.stem: If you ___ (not chill) the dough first, the biscuits spread right across the tray.

expected: do not chill
don't chill
dont chill

feedback.why_key: The negative changes nothing about the shape. Both halves keep a present form because this is what dough does.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the negative on do, then leave the rest of the sentence alone.

payload.context: Two colleagues comparing morning routines.
payload.stem: If I ___ (skip) breakfast, I get a headache by about eleven.

expected: skip

feedback.why_key: The speaker is describing what her body reliably does, not planning tomorrow morning.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the plain present when you are describing your own regular pattern.

payload.context: Build one sentence about what happens on still evenings near the Verdon works.

expected: if the wind drops the smoke settles over the valley
the smoke settles over the valley if the wind drops

feedback.why_key: Both orders are ordinary English and mean the same thing. Only the punctuation changes when the if half moves to the back.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the two halves in either order, then check that both have a verb.

payload.given: Ice forms on the overhead wires. The trains then run at half speed all day.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that states this as a standing rule rather than as news.

expected: forms on the overhead wires the trains run at half speed all day
forms on the overhead wires, the trains run at half speed all day
forms on the overhead wires the trains run at half speed
forms on the overhead wires, the trains run at half speed

feedback.why_key: Folding the two into one turns a report about a particular morning into a claim about every icy morning.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the condition to the result and keep both verbs in a present form.

payload.audio_text: If you don't rinse the rice, it sticks to the pan.

expected: if you don't rinse the rice it sticks to the pan
if you do not rinse the rice it sticks to the pan
if you dont rinse the rice it sticks to the pan

feedback.why_key: Don't and sticks are both squeezed almost flat in speech, and a listener who misses them hears a completely different claim.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small ending on the second verb, not just the first.

payload.context: From a paragraph explaining a safety valve.
payload.sentence: If the pressure would drop below two bar, the valve closes automatically.
reasons: nothing is being imagined here, so would has no work to do
the valve is described in the wrong half
the sentence needs a full stop rather than a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Would tells a reader that a situation is being imagined. This valve really does close, several times a week.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete would from the if half when the sentence states a fact.

payload.sentence: If a road surface will freeze overnight, the gritters go out at four in the morning.

expected: freezes

feedback.why_key: The second half already tells you this is the standing arrangement, so the first half must describe every cold night too.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the two halves: if one states a rule, so must the other.

payload.prompt_text: A recycling scheme only collects glass from households that put the bin out before seven. Write one sentence stating what happens, every week, to a household that misses that time.

feedback.why_key: Stating the rule once is what lets a reader work out every particular case without being told about each one.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the rule, not the story of one household.

payload.prompt_text: Take the process answer you wrote about turning sea water into drinking water. Rewrite one stage so that it states what happens on every occasion the salt level climbs too high. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: A process answer that never states a condition has to list occasions instead, and it runs out of words before it runs out of stages.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace one listed event with the rule behind it.

title: Saying what will follow if something that might happen does happen

point_json.grammar_name: First conditional

teach.can_do: I can say what will follow if something I think might really happen does happen.
teach.why_it_matters: Argument is mostly this shape. You cannot say a policy will work without saying what happens if it is brought in.
teach.meaning: Here the speaker is not describing a rule. They have one particular future occasion in mind and they genuinely do not know how it will go. The first half puts a real possibility on the table: the strike may go ahead, the funding may arrive, the water may rise again. The second half says what the speaker expects to follow from it. The whole sentence is a bet the speaker is prepared to make, which is why it carries weight in an argument.

form.pattern: If + present form, will + verb
notes: In the second half, may, might, can, should and an instruction all work in place of will: if the alarm sounds, leave by the side door.
In speech will is almost always squeezed down to 'll, and it disappears entirely if you are not listening for it.
The halves can swap: the depot will close for two days if the strike goes ahead.
form.negative: If the funding does not arrive by June, the centre will stay shut.
form.question: What will happen if the strike goes ahead?

ends: I think this could really happen

marks.label: If the strike goes ahead, the depot will close.
If the strike goes ahead, the depot may close.
reserved for the shape taught later in this unit

worked_example.sentence: If the reservoir drops below a quarter full, the council will bring in a hosepipe ban.
worked_example.why_this_form: The speaker has this summer in mind and does not know how dry it will get. The drop is a live possibility, and the ban is what they expect to follow from it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting the second half into a present form would turn this into a standing rule of the council's, true every year, rather than a forecast about the summer in front of them.

notice_set.sentence: If the strike goes ahead, the depot will close for two days.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know whether the strike is happening?
notice_set.why: Putting the strike after if is how the speaker says it is still open. If it were settled they would not have hedged it.

notice_set.sentence: If the funding arrives before June, the centre will open in September.
notice_set.question: Is the centre opening in September?
notice_set.why: The opening has been tied to the money. Nothing has been promised about the money.

notice_set.sentence: The path will stay shut if the tide comes over the wall again.
notice_set.question: Has the tide come over the wall before?
notice_set.why: Again is doing quiet work: it tells you this has happened at least once already, which is why the speaker treats it as a live risk.

notice_set.sentence: If the bus is late, ring the office and someone will come out for you.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker giving an instruction or making a prediction?
notice_set.why: The second half tells you what to do and then what to expect. Both live comfortably after if.

notice_set.sentence: If nobody objects by Friday, the plan goes to the committee.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker talking about one particular Friday?
notice_set.why: A named deadline pins the sentence to one occasion, and that is what separates this from a standing rule.

discovery.prompt: Each pair uses the same words about the same situation. Work out what the speaker on the right is doing differently.
pairs: If the reservoir drops below a quarter full, the council brings in a hosepipe ban.
If the reservoir drops below a quarter full, the council will bring in a hosepipe ban.
If the tide comes over the wall, the coast path shuts.
If the tide comes over the wall again, the coast path will shut.
If nobody objects, a plan goes to the committee.
If nobody objects by Friday, the plan goes to the committee.

candidate_rules.text: The right-hand speaker has one particular occasion in mind and is saying what they expect on it.
The right-hand sentences are the polite versions.
A sentence needs will as soon as it mentions a day of the week.

teach.rule_line: One occasion you cannot call yet: keep if plain and let will do the predicting.
teach.false_rule: That a sentence about the future needs will in both halves. Only the half that predicts takes it; the half that supposes stays plain.

errors.wrong: If the strike will go ahead, the depot will close for two days.
errors.right: If the strike goes ahead, the depot will close for two days.
errors.why_it_happens: The whole sentence is about the future, so the learner marks the future in both halves. English marks it once, in the half doing the predicting, and treats the supposing half as settled ground.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will go becomes goes.
errors.l1_note: Plenty of languages put a marker of futurity inside the condition as well, so the habit arrives fully formed.

errors.wrong: If the funding would arrive in time, the centre will open in September.
errors.right: If the funding arrives in time, the centre will open in September.
errors.why_it_happens: Would has been learned as a softener, and the learner is being cautious about money nobody has promised. The caution is already carried by if, and would drags the sentence into imagining instead.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would arrive becomes arrives.

errors.wrong: If the council approved the scheme, work will start in April.
errors.right: If the council approves the scheme, work will start in April.
errors.why_it_happens: A past form has been reached for to signal doubt, but the second half still predicts flatly. The two halves now disagree about whether any of this is expected to happen.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: approved becomes approves.

pays_in.note: A body paragraph arguing for a policy is a chain of these sentences.
pays_in.model: If councils charge for parking in the centre, shoppers will simply drive to the retail parks instead.

pays_in.note: Part 3 asks what will happen next, and the honest answer is conditional.
pays_in.model: If house prices keep climbing, younger people will just stop moving out of their parents' homes.

pays_in.note: Arrangements in Part 1 recordings arrive as conditions, with the detail parked after the comma.
pays_in.model: If the coach is full, we'll put on a second one at half past.

used_in.quote: Arguing about free transport means saying what will follow if fares are abolished, which is this shape used ten times over.
Every follow-up on this card asks what happens next, and none of it can be answered flatly.

payload.sentence: If the strike goes ahead, the depot will close for two days.
payload.question: Does the speaker know whether the strike is happening?

feedback.why_key: Putting the strike after if is how a speaker says it is still open. Somebody who knew would not have hedged it.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat what sits after if as something still undecided.

payload.sentence: If the grant arrives before June, the evening classes will run again from September.
payload.question: Are the evening classes running in September?

feedback.why_key: The classes have been tied to the money, and nothing at all has been promised about the money.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace what the promise is hanging on before you treat it as news.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about land for new homes.
payload.sentence: If the government will build on green land, small towns will lose the fields around them.
reasons: the half that supposes should stay plain
the two halves are about different countries
the sentence needs a full stop rather than a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: English marks the future once, in the half that predicts. The half after if is treated as settled ground for the sake of argument.
feedback.feed_forward: Strip will out of the if half and leave the plain verb.

payload.context: From a note circulated before a dry summer.
payload.stem: If the reservoir ___ (drop) below a quarter full, the council will bring in a hosepipe ban.

expected: drops

feedback.why_key: The ban is the prediction; the drop is the supposition, and English keeps suppositions plain.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the verb after if in its plain present form.

payload.context: From a letter about a proposed park-and-ride site.
payload.stem: If the site opens next spring, traffic through the village ___ (fall) sharply.

expected: will fall
'll fall
ll fall

feedback.why_key: The writer thinks the site really may open, so the second half is a forecast about one particular spring.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the prediction in the half that is not after if.

payload.context: A supervisor on the phone to a driver.
payload.stem: If the yard ___ (be) still blocked at six, take the load round to the Ashfield gate.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: An instruction sits perfectly happily where a prediction would go, and it leaves the first half untouched.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the if half plain even when the second half is an order.

payload.given: The clinic may lose one of its two nurses. Waiting times would then double.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence treating the loss as something that could genuinely happen this year.

expected: loses one of its two nurses waiting times will double
loses one of its two nurses, waiting times will double
loses one of its two nurses waiting times will double this year
loses one of its two nurses, waiting times will double this year

feedback.why_key: Treating the loss as real is what turns a piece of speculation into a warning somebody can act on.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the supposition plain and let will carry the consequence.

payload.context: Build one sentence for an essay about the cost of public transport.

expected: if fares rise again passengers will drift back to cars
passengers will drift back to cars if fares rise again

feedback.why_key: Whichever half comes first, will stays with the consequence and never crosses into the supposition.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the halves freely, but leave will where it started.

payload.audio_text: If the coach is full, we'll put on a second one at half past.

expected: if the coach is full we'll put on a second one at half past
if the coach is full we will put on a second one at half past
if the coach is full well put on a second one at half past

feedback.why_key: We'll and we sound almost identical at speed, and losing the 'll turns a plan into a claim about now.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a soft l riding on the pronoun.

payload.context: From a first draft of a funding letter.
payload.sentence: If the grant would arrive in time, the centre will open in September.
reasons: the caution is already carried by if, so would pulls the sentence into imagining
the centre has already opened
September is too far away for this shape
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The second half still predicts flatly, so the two halves end up disagreeing about whether any of this is expected.
feedback.feed_forward: Let if do the hedging and keep the verb after it plain.

payload.sentence: If the council approved the scheme next month, work will start on the first block in April.

expected: approves

feedback.why_key: Next month and will start both treat this as a live plan, so the first half cannot quietly step back from reality.
feedback.feed_forward: Make both halves agree about whether this is expected.

payload.prompt_text: A town is considering scrapping bus fares altogether next year. Write one sentence saying what you expect to follow if it goes ahead.

feedback.why_key: Naming the consequence is what turns an opinion about a policy into an argument a reader can weigh.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what follows, not whether you like it.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked what would help most with air quality in your nearest city. In forty-five seconds, name one measure and say what you expect to follow if it is actually brought in.

feedback.why_key: An answer that names a measure and stops is half an answer. The consequence is the part that shows you have thought about it.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the measure, then finish the sentence with what follows.

title: Admitting a fact that works against you and still keeping your point

point_json.grammar_name: Contrast clauses: although, even though, though, while, whereas

teach.can_do: I can put a fact that works against my point inside the same sentence and still keep my point.
teach.why_it_matters: Conceding something and then holding your ground is the shape of a strong body paragraph, and it is one leaning clause away.
teach.meaning: Sometimes two facts are both true and one of them makes the other surprising. Although, even though, though, while and whereas put the surprising fact into a leaning clause, so the reader knows immediately which of the two you are actually arguing for: the main clause always wins. Whereas is slightly different from the rest. It sets two things side by side and compares them, rather than admitting one in order to keep the other.

form.pattern: although / even though / though / while / whereas + clause, + main clause
notes: The main clause is the one you mean. The leaning clause is the fact you are giving away.
Even though is the strong version of although; though is the informal one and often comes at the end in speech.
Whereas compares two different subjects: online sales rose, whereas footfall fell.
One contrast word per sentence. Although at the front and but in the middle is one too many.
form.negative: The leaning clause takes its negative in the ordinary way: although the trial did not finish, the results were published.
form.question: Ask which of the two facts you want your reader to walk away with. That one goes in the main clause.

left.role: the concession, in the leaning clause
left.text: although the app was free

right.role: the point you are making, in the main clause
right.text: very few people kept it past a week

spec.caption: Both facts are true. The one in the main clause is the one you are arguing for.

worked_example.sentence: Although the app was free to download, very few people kept it past the first week.
worked_example.why_this_form: The free download is the fact that works against the point, so it goes into the leaning clause and the abandonment is left standing as the news.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Swap the two clauses over and the sentence becomes an argument for the app: the abandonment turns into a detail and the free download becomes the point.

notice_set.sentence: Although the tablets were handed out in September, the reading scores did not move.
notice_set.question: Which fact is the writer arguing for?
notice_set.why: The main clause carries the point; the leaning clause holds the fact being conceded.

notice_set.sentence: Even though the trial ran for three years, the findings were never published.
notice_set.question: Is three years a long time for this writer's argument?
options: Yes, and that is the job even though is doing
notice_set.why: Even though marks the concession as a strong one, which makes the main clause more surprising.

notice_set.sentence: Online sales rose by a fifth, whereas footfall in the shops fell.
notice_set.question: Are these two facts about the same thing?
options: No, two different things are being compared
notice_set.why: Whereas sets two subjects side by side rather than conceding one in order to keep the other.

notice_set.sentence: While the software was easy to install, the training took a fortnight.
notice_set.question: What does while mean here?
notice_set.why: While has a time meaning and a contrast meaning. Nothing here is happening at the same time, so only the contrast reading is available.

notice_set.sentence: The training took a fortnight, though the software installed in an hour.
notice_set.question: Where has the contrast word gone?
notice_set.why: Though is happy to sit in the middle, and in speech it will even come at the very end of the sentence.

teach.rule_line: The fact you are conceding goes in the leaning clause. Your point stays in the main one.
teach.false_rule: That although and but are two spellings of one word. Although makes a clause lean; but joins two clauses that both stand. Use one or the other, never both.

errors.wrong: Although the app was free, but almost nobody kept it.
errors.right: Although the app was free, almost nobody kept it.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner marks the turn twice so the reader cannot miss it, and in several languages that doubling is the correct pattern. In English one of the two words is always redundant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.
errors.l1_note: The doubled pattern is standard in several South and East Asian languages.

errors.wrong: Although the high cost, the scheme went ahead.
errors.right: Although the cost was high, the scheme went ahead.
errors.why_it_happens: Although has been stored as a contrast word rather than as a clause word, so it is put in front of whatever the contrast is about. What follows here is a noun phrase with no verb in it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: was.

errors.wrong: Although the reading scores did not move, the tablets were handed out in September.
errors.right: Although the tablets were handed out in September, the reading scores did not move.
errors.why_it_happens: Both clauses are true, so the sentence sounds fine when it is read back. The learner has put the news in the leaning clause and the concession in the main one, and the argument now runs backwards.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: although goes in front of the other clause.

errors.wrong: The software installed in an hour, the training took a fortnight.
errors.right: Although the software installed in an hour, the training took a fortnight.
errors.why_it_happens: The contrast between the two facts is obvious to the writer, so it feels as though it has been stated. Nothing on the page states it, and a comma cannot hold two stand-alone clauses together.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: although.

pays_in.note: A paragraph that never concedes anything reads as if the other side was never considered.
pays_in.model: Although phones are a genuine distraction in class, a blanket ban moves the problem to the school gate.

pays_in.note: Part 3 rewards an answer that admits the obvious objection before answering it.
pays_in.model: Even though it costs more up front, you get the money back over about four years.

pays_in.note: The writer's real claim is always in the clause without the contrast word.
pays_in.model: While the scheme met its recycling target, the cost per tonne doubled.

used_in.quote: A discussion answer has to state the other view fairly before it disagrees, and that is a leaning clause.
The follow-up questions push for both sides, and the neat answer concedes one and keeps the other.

payload.sentence: The pay is better, though the shifts are a lot longer.

the contrast word is the wrong one

feedback.feed_forward: Use whereas to compare and although to concede.

feedback.why_key: A paragraph that never concedes anything reads as though the writer has not thought about the other side at all.

title: Saying why something was done, and choosing between to and so that

point_json.grammar_name: Purpose: to, in order to, so as to, so that

teach.can_do: I can say why something was done, and pick the right shape depending on who does the second thing.
teach.why_it_matters: For to improve and for improving are among the most stubborn errors at this level, and the fix is one question about who does what.
teach.meaning: A purpose answers why. English has two shapes for it and the choice between them is mechanical. If the same person does both things, the second one goes into a bare to-infinitive: the council widened the path to slow the cyclists down. If somebody else does the second thing, a to-infinitive has nowhere to put that new subject, so you need so that and a full clause: the council widened the path so that walkers could pass safely. The deciding question is not formality. It is whether the subject changes.

form.pattern: same subject: main clause + to / in order to / so as to + verb. different subject: main clause + so that + subject + verb.
notes: In order to and so as to are the formal versions of to. They add no meaning at all.
The clause after so that almost always carries can, could, will or would.
For + -ing says what a thing is for, not why somebody acted: this valve is for releasing pressure.
form.negative: The negative purpose is so as not to or in order not to: we left early so as not to miss the last bus.
form.question: Ask who does the second action. The same person means to; a different person means so that.

left.text: the clinic opened on Saturdays to reach shift workers

right.text: the clinic opened on Saturdays so that shift workers could attend

spec.caption: Who does the second action decides the shape. Nothing else does.

worked_example.sentence: The clinic began opening on Saturdays so that shift workers could see a nurse without losing pay.
worked_example.why_this_form: The clinic opens and the shift workers do the seeing. Two different subjects, so the purpose needs a clause of its own with could inside it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: To see a nurse would attach the seeing to the clinic, and the sentence would end up claiming the clinic wanted to be examined.

notice_set.sentence: The council widened the path to slow the cyclists down.
notice_set.question: Who slows the cyclists down?
notice_set.why: A to-infinitive has no subject of its own, so it borrows the one standing in front of it.

notice_set.sentence: The council widened the path so that walkers could pass safely.
notice_set.question: Who passes safely?
notice_set.why: So that opens a full clause with its own subject, which is exactly why the subject is allowed to change.

notice_set.sentence: The hospital extended its opening hours to reduce the queue.
notice_set.question: Could so that replace to here without changing the meaning?
options: Yes, if a subject is added
notice_set.why: So that the queue would be shorter says the same thing in more words. Both are correct; to is shorter.

notice_set.sentence: We left an hour early so as not to miss the ferry.
notice_set.question: What does so as not to mean here?
options: We wanted to avoid missing it
notice_set.why: So as not to is the standard negative purpose, and it is what keeps for not missing off the page.

notice_set.sentence: This valve is for releasing pressure.
notice_set.question: Is this a purpose clause?
options: Yes, it says why somebody did something
No, it says what a thing is for
notice_set.why: For plus -ing describes a function. It cannot say why an action was taken.

notice_set.sentence: The trust bought two vans in order to reach the outlying villages.
notice_set.question: How does in order to differ from plain to here?
options: It is more formal, and nothing else
It changes who does the reaching
notice_set.why: In order to is a longer, more formal to. It adds no meaning whatsoever.

discovery.prompt: Three of these six are correct and three are not. Work out what the correct ones have in common.
pairs: The clinic opened late to reach shift workers.
The clinic opened late for reaching shift workers.
The clinic opened late so that shift workers could attend.
The clinic opened late to shift workers could attend.
We left early so as not to miss the ferry.
We left early for not missing the ferry.

candidate_rules.text: To takes a bare verb when the subject stays the same; so that takes a full clause when the subject changes.
For plus an -ing form is always wrong after a main clause.
Use to in short sentences and so that in long ones.

teach.rule_line: Same person doing both things? Use to. A different person? Use so that.
teach.false_rule: That for plus an -ing form is the way to say why. For plus -ing says what something is for. Why somebody acted needs to or so that.

contrast.question: Does the same person do both actions?

fork.answer: Yes — one subject does both of them
fork.selects: to, in order to or so as to, plus a bare verb

fork.answer: No — somebody else does the second one
fork.selects: so that plus a full clause, usually with can or could

a.text: The clinic opened on Saturdays to see more patients.
a.means: The clinic does the seeing. It wanted a bigger caseload.

b.text: The clinic opened on Saturdays so that more patients could be seen.
b.means: The patients are the ones who get seen. The clinic did it for them.

minimal_pair.only_difference: to see / so that ... could be seen

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote to see more patients. That hands the seeing to the clinic and turns a service into an ambition. If the people you are writing about are the ones who benefit, the purpose needs a subject of its own.

edge_case.text: So that will drop its that in speech, and in order that survives in very formal writing. Neither changes the decision, which is only ever about whether the subject stays the same.

contrast.stronger_test: Put a subject in front of the second verb and see whether it is the same one as the first. If you had to write a new subject, you have to write so that.

worked_pairs.a: The trust bought two vans to reach the outlying villages.
worked_pairs.b: The trust bought two vans so that the outlying villages could be reached.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so that the outlying villages could be reached
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first the trust does the reaching. In the second the villages are reached, and the sentence needs a clause to say so.

worked_pairs.a: The council fenced the path to keep walkers off the cliff edge.
worked_pairs.b: The council fenced the path so that walkers would keep off the cliff edge.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so that walkers would keep off
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct and they credit the keeping-off to different people: the council in the first, the walkers themselves in the second.

worked_pairs.a: We left an hour early so as not to miss the ferry.
worked_pairs.b: We left an hour early so that the children would not miss the ferry.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so that the children would not miss
worked_pairs.gloss: The negative works the same way. As soon as the subject changes, the infinitive cannot carry it and a clause has to.

errors.wrong: The clinic opened on Saturdays for reaching shift workers.
errors.right: The clinic opened on Saturdays to reach shift workers.
errors.why_it_happens: For is the everyday purpose word in most languages, and for plus -ing is a shape English really does use, for what a thing is for. The learner is generalising a pattern that genuinely exists.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: for reaching becomes to reach.
errors.l1_note: Almost universal where the first language uses one preposition for purpose.

errors.wrong: The council widened the path for to slow the cyclists down.
errors.right: The council widened the path to slow the cyclists down.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows the purpose word is for and also knows the verb needs to, so both arrive together. Only one of them is doing any work.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: for.

errors.wrong: The clinic opened on Saturdays so that to reach shift workers.
errors.right: The clinic opened on Saturdays to reach shift workers.
errors.why_it_happens: Both shapes are known and neither has been chosen, so they are stitched together. So that is waiting for a subject that never arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: so that.

errors.wrong: The trust bought two vans so that reach the outlying villages.
errors.right: The trust bought two vans so that the villages could be reached.
errors.why_it_happens: So that has been treated as a longer spelling of to, and the clause it opens has therefore been left with no subject in it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one subject: the villages.

pays_in.model: Councils could subsidise evening buses so that shift workers were not forced to drive.

pays_in.note: Any answer beginning why do people is a purpose clause waiting to happen.
pays_in.model: A lot of people cycle in now to avoid the cost of parking rather than for the exercise.

pays_in.note: Who benefits from a measure is usually carried by the shape of its purpose clause.
pays_in.model: The gates were fitted so that residents could reach the towpath after dark.

used_in.quote: Every proposal in the answer has to state what it is meant to achieve, and for whom.
The examiner asks why schemes are set up, and the answer is a purpose clause with a subject in it.

feedback.why_key: So that opens a clause with its own subject, and that is the only way the subject is allowed to change.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the subject inside the so that clause before you decide who benefits.

title: Saying how much of something there was and what it led to

point_json.grammar_name: Degree and result: so ... that, such ... that, too ... to, enough ... to

teach.can_do: I can say that there was so much of something that it produced a result, or so much that it blocked one.
teach.why_it_matters: It turns a bare adjective into a claim with a consequence attached, which is the difference between describing a problem and arguing about one.
teach.meaning: Very tells your reader the amount. So, such, too and enough tell them what the amount did. So and such report an amount that produced a result: the hall was so cold that half the class went home. Too reports an amount that blocked one: the hall was too cold to sit in, and nobody sat in it. Enough reports an amount that was sufficient, and the result did happen. Choosing between them is not about strength of feeling. It is about whether the thing happened or not.

form.pattern: so + adjective / adverb + that + clause | such + a / an + adjective + noun + that + clause | too + adjective + to + verb | adjective + enough + to + verb | enough + noun + to + verb
notes: So goes in front of an adjective or an adverb. Such goes in front of a noun phrase: so cold, but such a cold hall.
Enough goes after an adjective and in front of a noun: warm enough, but enough chairs.
Too and enough take a bare to-infinitive with no that: too cold to sit in, warm enough to sit in.
So and such take a full clause after that, and in speech the that is often dropped.
form.negative: Too already carries a negative result, so the clause after it stays positive: it was too cold to sit in, never too cold not to sit in.
form.question: Did the thing happen? If it did not, the sentence needs too.

spec.label: how much, and what the amount did

steps.text: not enough space to seat them
steps.gloss: there was too little, so it did not happen
there was too much of the wrong thing, so it did not happen
the amount was sufficient, and it happened

steps.text: so big that it seated them twice over
steps.gloss: the amount was striking, and here is what it produced

worked_example.sentence: The lecture hall was so cold that a third of the group left before the break.
worked_example.why_this_form: Something did happen because of the cold, and the sentence names it. So plus that is the shape for an amount that produced a result.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Too cold to stay would say that nobody stayed at all. The cold would have blocked the sitting rather than merely driving some people out.

notice_set.sentence: The hall was too small to take the whole year group.
notice_set.question: Did the whole year group fit in?
notice_set.why: Too always reports something that did not happen. The size is what stopped it.

notice_set.sentence: The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
notice_set.question: Was one boiler enough?
notice_set.why: Enough reports an amount that was sufficient, and what follows it did happen.

notice_set.sentence: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
notice_set.question: Did anyone finish it?
notice_set.why: So plus that reports a result that really happened, and most is not all.

notice_set.sentence: It was such a long reading list that most students never finished it.
notice_set.question: What is different from the sentence before?
options: Only the shape, because the adjective now sits in front of a noun
notice_set.why: Such is what you use when the adjective has a noun attached to it. The claim is unchanged.

notice_set.sentence: There were not enough chairs to seat the whole group.
notice_set.question: Did everyone get a chair?
notice_set.why: Enough in front of a noun counts the things, and not enough says the count fell short.

discovery.prompt: Each pair uses the same adjective about the same hall. Work out what changes between the left and the right.
pairs: The hall was too small to take the year group.
The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
The list was too long to finish in a term.
The list was so long that most students never finished it.
It was too cold to sit through the lecture.
It was so cold that a third of them left early.

candidate_rules.text: On the left the amount stopped it happening; on the right something did happen.
Too is used for bad things and enough for good ones.
Too goes with an infinitive and so goes with that, so the shape decides the meaning.

teach.rule_line: Did it happen? If it did not, you need too. If it did, you need so, such or enough.
teach.false_rule: That too is simply a stronger very. Very reports an amount and claims nothing else. Too reports that the amount stopped something from happening.

contrast.question: Did it happen, or did the amount stop it happening?

fork.answer: It happened, and I want to say how striking the cause was
fork.selects: so + adjective + that, or such + a + noun + that

fork.answer: It did not happen: there was too much of something in the way
It happened because there was as much as was needed
fork.selects: adjective + enough + to, or enough + noun + to

a.text: The hall was too small to heat on one boiler.
a.means: One boiler was not used, because the size ruled it out.

b.text: The hall was small enough to heat on one boiler.
b.means: One boiler was used, and the size is exactly why it worked.

minimal_pair.only_difference: too small to / small enough to

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote too small to heat on one boiler. That says the heating never happened and blames the size for it, which is the opposite of what you meant. Too always reports a failure, whatever the adjective in front of it.

edge_case.text: Enough goes after an adjective and in front of a noun: warm enough, but enough chairs. It is the one placement rule in this area and it catches everybody exactly once.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask whether the thing actually took place. If it did not, the sentence needs too. If it did, it needs so, such or enough, and nothing else will do.

worked_pairs.a: The reading list was too long to finish in one term.
worked_pairs.b: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: so long that most students never finished it
worked_pairs.gloss: The first says nobody finished it, as a matter of arithmetic. The second says most did not, as a matter of fact, and leaves room for the ones who did.

worked_pairs.a: It was so cold in the hall that a third of them left early.
worked_pairs.b: It was such a cold hall that a third of them left early.
worked_pairs.gloss: Identical claims. So sits in front of a bare adjective; such sits in front of an adjective with a noun behind it.

worked_pairs.a: There were not enough places to take everyone who applied.
worked_pairs.b: There were too few places to take everyone who applied.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct and both report the same shortfall. Not enough counts up from nothing; too few counts down from what was needed.

errors.wrong: The hall was enough warm to work in all afternoon.
errors.right: The hall was warm enough to work in all afternoon.
errors.why_it_happens: Every other word of this kind goes in front of the adjective — very warm, too warm, quite warm — so enough is put there too. It is the one that goes behind.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: enough goes after warm.

errors.wrong: It was so a cold hall that a third of them left early.
errors.right: It was such a cold hall that a third of them left early.
errors.why_it_happens: So is the commoner word and it has already been learned as the degree word. Nothing in the way it is taught says that a noun after the adjective switches it to such.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: so becomes such.

errors.wrong: The reading list was too long that most students never finished it.
errors.right: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
errors.why_it_happens: Too and so both report a striking amount, so they feel interchangeable, and that is dragged across from the so pattern. Too never takes that.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: too becomes so.

errors.wrong: The hall was too big to hold the whole year group, so everyone got a seat.
errors.right: The hall was big enough to hold the whole year group, so everyone got a seat.
errors.why_it_happens: Too is heard as a strong very and the writer means the size was impressive. The sentence then reports a failure in its first half and a success in its second.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: too big becomes big enough.

pays_in.note: It states a problem and its consequence in one sentence instead of two.
pays_in.model: Class sizes are now so large that a new teacher rarely learns every name in a term.

pays_in.note: It is the natural shape for the why part of a two-minute answer.
pays_in.model: The queue was so long that we gave up and went to the market instead.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often turns on whether the passage said something happened or did not.
pays_in.model: The samples were too degraded to date accurately.

used_in.quote: The answer has to say what the shortage has actually produced, not simply that it is large.
Saying why you would recommend it is a degree and a result held together in one sentence.

feedback.why_key: Too always reports something that did not happen, and the size is what stopped it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read too as and therefore it did not happen.

payload.sentence: The reading list was so long that most students never finished it.
payload.question: Did anybody finish it?

feedback.why_key: So plus that reports a result that actually happened, and most students is not the same as all of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the clause after that as a fact, not as an exaggeration.

the wrong adjective has been chosen
the infinitive should be an -ing form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.feed_forward: Say the adjective first, then enough.

feedback.why_key: The adjective has a noun behind it — a large group — and a noun phrase takes such rather than so.

payload.context: The same paragraph, written a second way.

expected: the flat was warm enough to work in all winter
