feedback.feed_forward: Put enough after the adjective, then to.

expected: the queue was so long we'd given up before we got to the door
the queue was so long we had given up before we got to the door
the queue was so long wed given up before we got to the door

feedback.why_key: The that is dropped in speech, so all that marks the result is a small so earlier in the sentence and a change of voice.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for so before the adjective when no that arrives.

The adjective now has a noun behind it, and a noun phrase takes such.

payload.sentence: The reading list was too long that most students never finished it.

expected: so long that most students
such a long list that most students

so is the wrong joining word here
the hall cannot be described as big

feedback.why_key: A bare adjective states a fact. A degree word with a result attached states a consequence, and the second one is an argument.
feedback.feed_forward: Attach a result to every claim about size.

title: Using a whole statement as the subject or object of a sentence

point_json.grammar_name: That-clauses as subject and object

teach.can_do: I can put a whole statement into a sentence as if it were a single noun.
teach.why_it_matters: It is how you state a position without opening with I think. Every stance sentence in an essay is built on it.
teach.meaning: Most sentences take a noun as their subject and another noun as their object. A that-clause lets a whole statement do either job. The claim that the scheme saved money can be the thing you are talking about; that the scheme saved money can be the thing somebody shows, argues or doubts. Nothing changes inside the statement — it keeps its own subject and its own verb — but the sentence around it now handles it as one lump, and can hang a verb on it.

form.pattern: that + subject + verb, filling a noun-sized slot
notes: as the object of a reporting verb, that can be dropped in speech: he says the road is closed
as the subject the clause is usually pushed to the end, and it holds the front: it is clear that costs have risen
the fact that turns the clause into a noun phrase, which is what lets it follow a preposition
form.negative: The negative goes inside the clause: it is clear that costs have not fallen.
form.question: Is it clear that ...? — the question is asked of the main verb, never of the clause.

left.role: a noun in the object slot
left.text: The report showed a sharp rise.

right.role: a whole statement in the same slot
right.text: The report showed that costs had risen sharply.

spec.caption: One slot, two things that can fill it. The clause is doing a noun's job.

worked_example.sentence: It is widely accepted that class size matters less to results than teacher quality does.
worked_example.why_this_form: The claim is the thing being discussed, so it needs a noun slot, and it carries too much to be squeezed into a noun phrase.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The effect of class size on results names the topic but drops the claim, and the sentence stops asserting anything at all.

notice_set.sentence: The audit showed that the figures had been copied from the previous year.
notice_set.question: What did the audit show?
notice_set.why: The whole statement is the thing the audit showed, which is why it sits where a noun would.

notice_set.sentence: That the trial was stopped early surprised nobody.
notice_set.question: What surprised nobody?
notice_set.why: The clause is the subject here. It is what the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: It is unlikely that the funding will be renewed.
notice_set.question: Is the funding expected to continue?
notice_set.why: It holds the subject slot for the clause, and the clause carries the whole prediction.

notice_set.sentence: The fact that two departments measure the same thing differently has never been raised.
notice_set.question: How many departments measure it?
notice_set.why: The clause has been packed into a noun phrase so that the sentence can hang a verb on it.

notice_set.sentence: She admitted the deadline was impossible.
notice_set.question: Whose view was it that the deadline was impossible?
notice_set.why: That has been left out, but the clause is still doing the same job in the same slot.

teach.rule_line: A that-clause fills a noun slot: subject, object, or after the fact.
teach.false_rule: That you can drop that anywhere. Drop it after a reporting verb in speech; keep it when the clause is the subject or the sentence is long.

errors.wrong: The fact that many graduates leave the region within two years.
errors.right: The fact that many graduates leave the region within two years has worried the council for a decade.
errors.why_it_happens: The fact that feels like an opening move, and by the time the clause has finished the writer has spent their sentence. The noun phrase is still waiting for a verb to hang on.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one main verb after the clause.

errors.wrong: Most researchers agree with that the effect is small.
errors.right: Most researchers agree that the effect is small.
errors.why_it_happens: Agree with is stored whole as a chunk, and it collides with a clause that already carries its own joining word. Two joiners end up in the same gap.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: with.

errors.wrong: The fact that costs have risen in three of the four regions mean the scheme is unaffordable.
errors.right: The fact that costs have risen in three of the four regions means the scheme is unaffordable.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb ends up next to regions and agrees with it. The real subject is the fact, several words back, and it stays singular however long the clause it carries.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: mean becomes means.

errors.wrong: Is clear that the current system cannot be funded much longer.
errors.right: It is clear that the current system cannot be funded much longer.
errors.why_it_happens: In the learner's first language the subject slot may be allowed to sit empty. English keeps it filled, and here it is holding the place for a clause arriving at the end.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: it.
errors.l1_note: Common where the first language allows a verb with no subject.

pays_in.note: It is how an essay names a claim it wants to argue with rather than assert.
pays_in.model: It is often argued that university places should follow demand rather than tradition.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers report a view and then take a position on it.
pays_in.model: I think the fact that people work later in life changes the whole picture.

pays_in.note: Paraphrase questions turn on which claim is inside the clause and which is outside it.
pays_in.model: The passage states that the decline began well before the subsidy ended.

used_in.quote: A discussion essay has to report each side's claim before answering it, and that reporting is this structure.
The follow-up questions ask what people believe about experts, which is a claim inside a clause.

feedback.why_key: The clause is too heavy for the front, so it goes to the end and something has to hold the subject slot.

feedback.feed_forward: Pack the statement first, then give it a verb.

payload.given: Fewer people pay for news. Editors find this difficult to accept.

expected: it's been argued that the rules are already out of date
it has been argued that the rules are already out of date

title: Choosing whether to treat something as settled or as still open

point_json.grammar_name: What the first conditional does: warning, promise, offer, negotiation, argument

teach.can_do: I can warn, promise, offer and argue by saying what follows from something, and show whether I think it is settled.
teach.why_it_matters: The form is easy and the choice is not. Using when for something you cannot know turns an arguable point into a claim a reader will not accept.
teach.meaning: This shape does far more than describe the future. Attach a consequence to a condition and you have a warning, a promise, an offer, an opening bid in a negotiation, or the backbone of an argument, depending on who the consequence lands on and whether they want it. The one word you have to get right is the one at the front. If leaves the condition open and hands the other person a real choice. When closes it and says the only question left is the timing.

form.pattern: If / When + present form, will + verb
notes: If keeps the condition open. When treats it as certain and only leaves the timing unsettled.
Neither word lets will into its own half, however far into the future the sentence reaches.
The job the sentence does comes from who the consequence lands on: a consequence the listener wants is an offer, one they do not want is a warning, and one you control is a promise.
form.negative: If the yard is not clear by six, nothing will get loaded before morning.
form.question: What will you do if the inspectors turn up on Thursday?

rungs.text: If you send the figures today, I'll have the draft ready by Friday. — an offer
If we drop the delivery charge, will you take the whole batch? — a negotiation
If the yard is still blocked at six, nothing gets loaded tonight. — a warning
If the charge comes in, traffic through the village will fall. — an argument

spec.top_label: the consequence is something they want
spec.bottom_label: the consequence is something they do not want

worked_example.sentence: If the committee agrees on Thursday, we will start advertising the post the same week.
worked_example.why_this_form: The writer does not know how the vote will go and says so by leaving the condition open. What follows is an offer of speed, not a boast about it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opening with when would tell the committee that their agreement is already assumed, which reads as pressure and invites somebody to disagree just to prove it is not.

notice_set.sentence: If the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we will move the vans out of the yard.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker expecting the inspectors?
notice_set.why: Leaving the visit open is how the speaker says nobody has confirmed it.

notice_set.sentence: When the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we will move the vans out of the yard.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker expecting the inspectors?
notice_set.why: The visit has been treated as settled, so the only thing left in doubt is the hour.

notice_set.sentence: If you send the figures across today, I will have the draft ready by Friday.
notice_set.question: Who benefits from the second half of this sentence?
notice_set.why: The consequence is something the listener wants, which is what makes the sentence an offer rather than a threat.

notice_set.sentence: If the yard is still blocked at six, nothing will get loaded before morning.
notice_set.question: Who is likely to be unhappy about the second half?
notice_set.why: Exactly the same shape, but the consequence now lands on the listener as something to avoid, which turns it into a warning.

notice_set.sentence: If we drop the delivery charge, will you take the whole batch?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker giving something away or asking for something?
notice_set.why: A concession has been tied to a request in one sentence, which is what bargaining sounds like in English.

discovery.prompt: Each pair changes one word at the front. Work out what that word does to the rest of the sentence.
pairs: If the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we will move the vans out of the yard.
When the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we will move the vans out of the yard.
If the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
When the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
If the grant comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.
When the grant comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.

candidate_rules.text: If leaves the first half open; when says it is settled and only the timing is unknown.
When is used for things that happen soon and if for things further away.
Use when whenever the sentence names a day, and if when it does not.

teach.rule_line: If hands the other person a choice. When tells them the decision is already made.
teach.false_rule: That if and when are interchangeable in a sentence about the future. Swapping them does not change the timing; it changes what you are claiming to know.

contrast.question: Is the first half settled, or could it still go either way?

fork.answer: It could still go either way, and the other person can affect it
It is going to happen; only the hour or the date is unsettled

a.text: If the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
a.means: The reopening is still in doubt. The writer is showing what would be gained by it.

b.text: When the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
b.means: The reopening is going ahead. The writer is telling you what to expect once it does.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote when. That tells your reader the tunnel is definitely reopening and that you know it. If it is still a proposal, you have just claimed something you cannot support, and a reader who spots it stops trusting the rest of the paragraph.

edge_case.text: In a warm invitation, when is used on purpose for something that is not settled at all: come and see us when you are next over. The speaker is being generous about the odds, not reporting them. Recognise it and leave it out of an essay.

contrast.stronger_test: Put the words as far as I know in front of the first half. If the sentence now sounds contradictory, you needed if. If it sounds merely modest, when was fine.

worked_pairs.a: If the grant comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.
worked_pairs.b: When the grant comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first was written by somebody waiting to hear. The second was written by somebody who has already had the letter.

worked_pairs.a: If the appeal succeeds, the family will move back into the flat.
worked_pairs.b: When the appeal is heard, the family will find out about the flat.
worked_pairs.gloss: The hearing is in the diary, so it takes when. Winning it is not, so it takes if. The same appeal, two different halves of it.

worked_pairs.a: If councils charge for parking in the centre, small shops will lose their regulars.
worked_pairs.b: When councils charge for parking in the centre, small shops lose their regulars.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first is an argument about a proposal. The second claims the charge is already normal and the loss already documented, which is a much bigger thing to have to prove.

errors.wrong: When the appeal succeeds, the family will move back into the flat.
errors.right: If the appeal succeeds, the family will move back into the flat.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer wants the appeal to succeed and lets the hope into the grammar. When reports the outcome as settled, which is a claim nobody has made and nobody can support.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: When becomes If.

errors.wrong: When the results will come out in August, we will know whether the course runs.
errors.right: When the results come out in August, we will know whether the course runs.
errors.why_it_happens: August is clearly ahead, so the future gets marked twice. English marks it once and leaves the half that fixes the moment in a plain present form, exactly as it does after if.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: will.

errors.wrong: If the inspection is confirmed for Thursday, we'd move the vans out of the yard.
errors.right: If the inspection is confirmed for Thursday, we'll move the vans out of the yard.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer softens the promise out of politeness. Softening it that way says the whole thing is imaginary, so a firm commitment reads as an idle thought.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: we'd move becomes we'll move.

pays_in.note: An argument for a proposal has to stay conditional or it claims what it set out to prove.
pays_in.model: If the charge is introduced across the whole county, smaller towns will lose their bus links first.

pays_in.note: Part 3 rewards a speaker who separates what is settled from what is arguable.
pays_in.model: If firms keep hiring remotely, city centres will empty out during the week.

pays_in.note: Arrangements are announced with when and warnings with if, and the difference carries the answer.
pays_in.model: If the hall is being used, the session moves to the annexe behind it.

used_in.quote: Arguing either side means predicting what follows from a change nobody has made yet, and claiming it is coming would lose the argument in a sentence.
The follow-ups all ask what will happen to work in the next twenty years, which is a run of open conditions.

payload.sentence: When the new rota starts, we'll be finishing an hour earlier on Fridays.
payload.question: Has the new rota been agreed?

feedback.why_key: When treats the start as settled, so the only open question is which Friday is the first one.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the opening word as a claim about what is already decided.

payload.sentence: If the department keeps the evening slot, working students will stay on the course.
payload.question: Has the department decided about the evening slot?

feedback.why_key: The writer is arguing for the slot, and arguing for something means treating the decision as still available.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice whether the writer is reporting a decision or trying to influence one.

payload.context: The opening line of a body paragraph arguing that petrol cars should be phased out.
payload.sentence: When governments ban petrol cars altogether, air quality in cities will improve sharply.
reasons: the ban is the thing being argued for, so it cannot be reported as settled
air quality cannot be predicted at all
the second half needs a present form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A paragraph that assumes its own conclusion in the first word has nothing left to argue, and a reader notices immediately.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the thing you are arguing for inside an open condition.

payload.context: From a letter to staff. The move has already been announced.
payload.stem: When the office ___ (move) to the Ashfield site in March, everyone will be given a parking permit.

expected: moves

feedback.why_key: March is ahead of us, but the half that fixes the moment stays plain. Only the promise takes will.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the verb after when in its plain present form.

payload.context: A driver offering to help a colleague who has no lift home.
payload.stem: If the yard clears before seven, I ___ (drop) you at the station on my way.

expected: will drop
'll drop
ll drop

feedback.why_key: The consequence is something the listener wants, and a firm form is what makes it an offer rather than a musing.
feedback.feed_forward: Use will for a promise you intend to keep.

payload.given: The council is thinking about scrapping bus fares. Nobody has voted yet. The writer expects passenger numbers to double.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that predicts the effect without claiming the decision has been taken.

expected: scraps bus fares passenger numbers will double
scraps bus fares, passenger numbers will double
scraps the fares passenger numbers will double
scraps the fares, passenger numbers will double

feedback.why_key: Keeping the vote open is what lets the sentence argue. Reporting it as done would make the prediction unnecessary.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with if whenever the decision has not been taken.

payload.audio_text: When the audit's over, they'll tell us about the second shift.

expected: when the audit's over they'll tell us about the second shift
when the audit is over they will tell us about the second shift
when the audits over theyll tell us about the second shift

feedback.why_key: When and if are both single unstressed syllables at speed, and mishearing one for the other reverses what the speaker claims to know.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen hard to the first word of a two-part sentence.

payload.context: From a residents' newsletter about a building already under contract.
payload.stem: When work ___ (begin) on the old mill in April, the lane will be closed to traffic for six weeks.

expected: begins

feedback.why_key: The contract is signed, so the start is settled and the sentence is telling residents what to expect around it.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the moment with a plain verb and predict with will.

items.decision_cue: the day the appeal was lodged

payload.context: From a letter written on the day the appeal was lodged, before any hearing.
payload.sentence: When the appeal succeeds, the family will move back into the flat above the shop.
reasons: the outcome is being reported as settled before anyone has heard the case
the family does not want to move back
the second half should be in a present form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Wanting an outcome badly is exactly when the wrong opening word slips in, and it commits the writer to something nobody can support.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that the opening word matches what you actually know.

items.decision_cue: a rumour going round that an inspection is due

payload.context: There is a rumour going round that an inspection is due at the depot this week, but nothing has arrived in writing.
payload.stem: ___ the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we'll move the vans out of the yard.

options.why_this_means: That nobody has confirmed the visit and the plan only matters should it happen.
That the visit is booked and the only thing left to sort out is the hour.

expected: if

feedback.why_key: A rumour is not a booking, and the opening word is where a speaker admits the difference.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what you have actually been told before you pick the first word.

items.decision_cue: A letter confirming the inspection date

payload.context: A letter confirming the inspection date arrived at the depot on Monday morning.
payload.stem: ___ the inspectors turn up on Thursday, we'll move the vans out of the yard.

options.why_this_means: That nobody has confirmed the visit and the plan only matters should it happen.
That the visit is booked and the only thing left to sort out is the hour.

expected: when

feedback.why_key: Once the date is in writing, hedging it reads as if the speaker has not read their own post.
feedback.feed_forward: Use when for anything already in the diary.

items.decision_cue: the trustees have been told the money has been signed off

payload.context: At the last meeting the trustees have been told the money has been signed off and is on its way to the account.
payload.stem: ___ the funding comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.

options.why_this_means: That the money is still in doubt and the hiring is a plan for one of two futures.
That the money is coming and the sentence is simply saying what happens on arrival.

expected: when

feedback.why_key: Hedging money that has already been signed off makes the writer sound less informed than the people reading it.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the opening word to what the reader already knows.

items.decision_cue: waiting to hear whether the application was successful

payload.context: The trustees sent the application off in January and are still waiting to hear whether the application was successful.
payload.stem: ___ the funding comes through, the centre will take on two more staff.

options.why_this_means: That the money is still in doubt and the hiring is a plan for one of two futures.
That the money is coming and the sentence is simply saying what happens on arrival.

expected: if

feedback.why_key: Same sentence, same money, and the opposite claim about it, because the trustees have not heard yet.
feedback.feed_forward: Do not let hope choose the first word for you.

items.decision_cue: a Friday train that usually runs to time

payload.context: Priya has booked a Friday train that usually runs to time, though the line has been patchy all month.
payload.stem: ___ I get in before six, I'll come straight to the office.

options.why_this_means: That she is not counting on the train and the office visit depends on it.
That she is treating the arrival as settled and simply saying what she will do next.

follow_up.question: Which version treats her arrival time as already settled?

feedback.why_key: Both are ordinary English. One promises a visit that depends on the railway, and the other promises the visit outright.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide how much you are willing to promise, then choose.

items.decision_cue: two newsletters about the same tunnel

payload.context: Two lines taken from two newsletters about the same tunnel, six months apart.
sentences: If the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
When the tunnel reopens, the journey drops to forty minutes.
meanings: The reopening is still a proposal, and this is what would be gained by it.
The reopening has been agreed, and this is what to expect once the work is done.

feedback.why_key: One newsletter is campaigning and the other is announcing, and the only visible difference is the first word.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the first word as a statement about what is settled.

payload.prompt_text: A hospital is thinking about opening its clinics on Saturdays. No decision has been taken. Say one thing you expect to follow, in a way that keeps the decision open.

feedback.why_key: Leaving the decision open is what lets you predict without pretending to have inside information.
feedback.feed_forward: Open the sentence with the condition, then predict.

parts: The county is considering a charge for driving into the centre.
Nobody has voted on it yet.
Shoppers would go to the retail parks on the ring road instead.
model_combinations: If the county introduces a charge for driving into the centre, shoppers will simply take their money out to the retail parks on the ring road.
Shoppers will drift out to the ring road if a charge for driving into the centre is ever agreed.
If a charge is brought in, and the vote has not been taken yet, the retail parks on the ring road will pick up the trade the centre loses.

feedback.why_key: The middle fact is the one that decides the grammar: an unvoted proposal has to stay inside an open condition.
feedback.feed_forward: Fold the doubt into the first half rather than adding a sentence about it.

payload.prompt_text: Go back to your paragraph on the shorter working week. Find the sentence where you predicted an effect and rewrite it so the change stays a proposal rather than a fact. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: An essay that treats its own proposal as already in force has stopped arguing and started reporting a world that does not exist.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the proposal back inside an open condition.

title: Signalling that what you are describing is not the case

point_json.grammar_name: The unreal past: one step back means one step away from reality

teach.can_do: I can show that I am describing something that is not the case, without saying so.
teach.why_it_matters: This one move is behind six different structures. Learn it here and the rest of the unit costs almost nothing.
teach.meaning: English has a quiet way of saying this is not so. You move the verb one step further back than the time you are actually talking about. I know her name is a report about now. I wish I knew her name is also about now, but the backward step tells the listener that the knowing is missing. The step is not about time at all. It is distance from what is true, and once you can see it you will start seeing it everywhere: in wishes, in regrets, in advice, in polite requests, and in every sentence about a world the speaker is only imagining.

form.pattern: one step further back than the time you actually mean
notes: About now or about the future, take a step back to the past simple: I wish I lived nearer the coast.
About the past, take a step back to had plus the past participle: I wish I had asked her at the time.
Were is available for every subject inside these sentences: I wish it were simpler. Was is also very common in speech and nobody will stop you.
The step happens after wish, if only, it's time, would rather, suppose and imagine, and it is what powers the two shapes coming next in this unit.
form.negative: The step survives a negative without changing: I wish I didn't have to drive in every day.
form.question: Would it help if I sent the figures over this afternoon?

marks.label: I know her name — plain present form
I wish I knew her name — a step back, still about now
I wish I had known her name — two steps back, about that evening

worked_example.sentence: I wish the shop took cards, because I never carry cash any more.
worked_example.why_this_form: The speaker is talking about the shop as it is today. Took, rather than takes, is the whole message: the card machine does not exist, and that is what is being complained about.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: I wish the shop takes cards is not a gentler way of making the same complaint. It leaves the listener with no signal that the machine is missing, and the sentence falls apart.

notice_set.sentence: I wish the shop took cards.
notice_set.question: Can you pay by card in that shop?
notice_set.why: The backward step is the speaker's way of saying the card machine is not there.

notice_set.sentence: I wish I had asked her about the deposit at the time.
notice_set.question: Did the speaker ask about the deposit?
notice_set.why: Two steps back reaches an occasion that is over, and says the asking did not happen on it.

notice_set.sentence: It's time we left for the airport.
notice_set.question: Have they left yet?
notice_set.why: Left points at a departure that has not taken place, and the sentence is a nudge to make it take place now.

notice_set.sentence: I'd rather you didn't mention the figures until Monday.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker want the figures mentioned today?
notice_set.why: The step back keeps the request off the table as a demand and puts it forward as a preference instead.

notice_set.sentence: I was wondering whether you had a few minutes this afternoon.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking about this afternoon or about earlier today?
notice_set.why: Nothing here is in the past. The step back is doing politeness, putting a little space between the speaker and the ask.

discovery.prompt: The left-hand and right-hand sentences are both about today. Work out what the change of verb is telling you.
pairs: The shop takes cards.
I wish the shop took cards.
We are leaving for the airport.
It's time we left for the airport.
Do you have a few minutes?
I was wondering whether you had a few minutes.

candidate_rules.text: The step backwards marks distance from what is true, not distance in time.
The right-hand sentences are about things the speaker regrets.
A verb in a past form always means the event happened before now.

teach.rule_line: Move the verb one step back and the listener hears: this is not the case.
teach.false_rule: That a past form always means past time. Here it means distance from reality, and the sentence can be about this afternoon.

errors.wrong: I wish I know more about how the scheme is funded.
errors.right: I wish I knew more about how the scheme is funded.
errors.why_it_happens: The sentence is about now, so a present form arrives on time and sounds right. The learner has never been told that the backward step is what carries the meaning, so nothing stops it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: know becomes knew.

errors.wrong: I wish I would have asked about the deposit at the time.
errors.right: I wish I had asked about the deposit at the time.
errors.why_it_happens: Would has been learned as the marker of an imagined world, so it is added to make the sentence sound unreal. The step backwards has already done that job, and would jams a second signal on top of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would have asked becomes had asked.
errors.l1_note: Speakers of several languages hear this version regularly in informal English, which keeps it alive.

errors.wrong: I'd rather you don't mention the figures until Monday.
errors.right: I'd rather you didn't mention the figures until Monday.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reads would rather as a polite way of saying please, and a polite request naturally takes a present form. The structure asks for the step back on the second verb, not the first.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: don't becomes didn't.

pays_in.note: Part 3 keeps asking about worlds that do not exist, and this is how English marks them.
pays_in.model: I wish public transport were reliable enough that people gave up their second car.

pays_in.note: Softening a request or an opinion in Part 1 runs on exactly this step.
pays_in.model: I was wondering whether there was somewhere quiet to work near the flat.

pays_in.note: Any argument about what ought to change needs a way of marking the imagined version.
pays_in.model: It is high time councils treated cycle lanes as roads rather than as decoration.

used_in.quote: Every answer on this card describes something that did not happen, which is this step used over and over.
A solution paragraph is a description of a world that does not exist yet, and it needs a way of saying so.

payload.sentence: I wish the corner shop took cards.
payload.question: Can you pay by card there?

feedback.why_key: The backward step is the whole message. It says the card machine is not there, and that is what the speaker minds.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a step backwards as a claim about what is missing now.

payload.sentence: I wish I had asked about the deposit before I signed anything.
payload.question: Where does this sit?
options: something that did not happen at a moment now past
something that is not happening now

feedback.why_key: Two steps back reaches an occasion that is over and tells you the asking did not take place on it.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the steps back to find which moment is being reported as missing.

payload.context: Talking about how often she gets home to see her grandmother.
payload.sentence: I wish I have more time with my grandmother.
reasons: a wish about now needs the verb a step further back
the grandmother is no longer alive
wish cannot be used about people
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Without the step back, nothing in the sentence says the time is missing, and the complaint quietly disappears.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back whenever wish comes in front of it.

payload.context: A commuter grumbling about the last bus of the evening.
payload.stem: I wish the last bus ___ (run) half an hour later than it does.

expected: ran

feedback.why_key: The timetable is a fact about today, and the step back is how the speaker says it is the wrong fact.
feedback.feed_forward: Take one step back for anything you are wishing about now.

payload.context: From a note written at the end of a course.
payload.stem: If only I ___ (start) the reading list in September rather than in January.

expected: had started
'd started
d started

feedback.why_key: September is over, so the step goes one further back than the past and lands on a September that never happened.
feedback.feed_forward: Use had plus the participle when the missed moment is already past.

payload.context: A manager glancing at the clock during a long meeting.
payload.stem: It's high time we ___ (move) on to the budget.

expected: moved

feedback.why_key: Nobody has moved on yet, and the step back is what turns a description into a nudge.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back after it's time and let the impatience do the rest.

payload.given: Please don't send the figures round until Monday.
payload.instruction: Say the same thing as a preference rather than an instruction, using would rather.

expected: didn't send the figures round until monday
did not send the figures round until monday
didnt send the figures round until monday

feedback.why_key: The step back lifts the sentence off the table as an order and puts it forward as something the listener may still refuse.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the second verb back and leave would rather alone.

payload.given: Do you have the account details somewhere?
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so it sounds less direct, keeping it about right now.

expected: had the account details somewhere
had the account details anywhere

feedback.why_key: Nothing in this sentence is about the past. The step back is buying the listener room to say no.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back to make an ask easier to refuse.

payload.audio_text: I'd rather we left before the traffic builds up.

expected: i'd rather we left before the traffic builds up
i would rather we left before the traffic builds up
id rather we left before the traffic builds up

feedback.why_key: The 'd is a single consonant riding on the pronoun, and a listener who loses it hears a report about a journey already taken.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a d on the pronoun before the main verb.

payload.context: From a letter about a flat the writer turned down two years ago.
payload.sentence: I wish I would have taken the flat above the bakery when it was offered.
reasons: the step backwards already marks this as unreal, so would has no work left
the flat is still available
wish cannot be used about the past at all
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two signals for one meaning is one too many, and the second one is the one that sounds wrong to a reader.
feedback.feed_forward: Use had plus the participle after wish about the past.

payload.sentence: It is high time councils treat cycle lanes as roads rather than as decoration.

expected: treated

feedback.why_key: The councils are not doing it, which is the writer's whole complaint, and the step backwards is where that complaint lives.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back after it is high time.

payload.prompt_text: Think of one thing about where you live that you would change tomorrow if you could. Write one sentence saying you want it changed, without saying the words I want.

feedback.why_key: The step backwards is doing something no other part of the sentence can do: it says the thing is not so, while the sentence talks about now.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what is not the case by stepping the verb back once.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked whether a bad decision teaches a person more than a good one. In forty-five seconds, describe one choice you would take differently, marking clearly that you did not take it that way.

feedback.why_key: Speaking about a decision you did not take is the commonest place this step is needed and the commonest place it is dropped under pressure.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for had plus the participle when the moment has gone.

title: Describing a situation that is not the case and what would follow from it

point_json.grammar_name: Second conditional: the unreal present and future

teach.can_do: I can build a situation that is not true and say what would come out of it.
teach.why_it_matters: Half of every discussion question asks about a world that does not exist. Without this you can only describe the world that does.
teach.meaning: You already have the step backwards from the last lesson. Here it goes inside an if half, and the result half answers it with would. The whole sentence sets up a situation the speaker does not expect: the city has no tram, the fares are not free, you are not me. Nothing in it is a prediction. It is an experiment run out loud, and the listener understands from the very first verb that they are being shown a world rather than told about this one.

form.pattern: If + the step-back form, would + verb
notes: Could and might take the place of would when the result is less certain: if the fares were free, more people might walk into town instead.
In speech would collapses to 'd and is easy to miss altogether.
Were is normal for every subject inside the if half: if the site were closer to the station. Was is common in speech and nobody will correct you for it.
The halves swap freely: nobody would use the car park if the tram ran until midnight.
form.negative: If the council did not own the land, nothing would get built on it at all.
form.question: What would happen if the tram ran until midnight?

marks.label: If the tram runs until midnight, fewer people will drive. — a live proposal
If the tram ran until midnight, fewer people would drive. — a world being shown

worked_example.sentence: If the tram ran until midnight, half the late-night traffic through the centre would disappear.
worked_example.why_this_form: The tram stops at eleven and the speaker has no reason to think that is changing. Ran and would disappear together tell the listener the whole sentence is a picture, not a forecast.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: If the tram runs until midnight, half the traffic will disappear would tell a councillor that the later service is genuinely on the table and that the speaker is arguing for a decision, not painting one.

notice_set.sentence: If the tram ran until midnight, half the late-night traffic would disappear.
notice_set.question: Does the tram run until midnight?
notice_set.why: The step backwards in the first half is the speaker's way of saying the late service does not exist.

notice_set.sentence: If I lived nearer the depot, I would walk in every morning.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker walk to work?
notice_set.why: The walking is tied to a house the speaker does not live in, so it is not happening either.

notice_set.sentence: If bus fares were free, town centres might fill up again on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: How sure is the speaker about the Saturday crowds?
options: Treating it as possible rather than certain
notice_set.why: Might in place of would keeps the result loose, and the speaker is showing a world without promising what it contains.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody would use the multi-storey if parking on the street were free.
notice_set.question: Is street parking free at the moment?
notice_set.why: The signal sits in the second half of the sentence here, but it says exactly the same thing about the world.

notice_set.sentence: If the council did not own that land, nothing would get built on it at all.
notice_set.question: Who owns the land?
notice_set.why: A negative inside an unreal half flips the world twice: the sentence supposes away an ownership that really exists.

discovery.prompt: Both sentences in each pair are about the same town. Work out which speaker expects something to change.
pairs: If the tram runs until midnight, half the late-night traffic will disappear.
If the tram ran until midnight, half the late-night traffic would disappear.
If bus fares are free, town centres will fill up on Saturdays.
If bus fares were free, town centres would fill up on Saturdays.
If I live nearer the depot, I will walk in every morning.
If I lived nearer the depot, I would walk in every morning.

candidate_rules.text: The right-hand speaker is showing a world that is not the case; the left-hand speaker is arguing about a real decision.
The right-hand sentences are about things that are impossible.
Would is the polite version of will, so the right-hand sentences are simply more formal.

teach.rule_line: Step the if half back, answer it with would, and the listener knows none of it is so.
teach.false_rule: That this shape is for the future and the last one was for the present. Both can be about tomorrow; only one of them expects tomorrow to look like that.

errors.wrong: If the council would ban cars from the centre, air quality would improve within a year.
errors.right: If the council banned cars from the centre, air quality would improve within a year.
errors.why_it_happens: Would is the most visible sign that a sentence is imaginary, so the learner puts it in both halves to make sure the reader sees it. English marks the world once and marks it in the answering half.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would ban becomes banned.

errors.wrong: If the city built a tram line, congestion will fall by a third.
errors.right: If the city built a tram line, congestion would fall by a third.
errors.why_it_happens: The two halves are written a few seconds apart and only the first one gets thought about. By the time the writer reaches the result they are predicting again, and the sentence ends up in two worlds at once.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will fall becomes would fall.

errors.wrong: If fares were free, far more people would to use the evening buses.
errors.right: If fares were free, far more people would use the evening buses.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is treating would like an ordinary verb, and ordinary verbs take to in front of the next one. Would belongs to a small family that refuses it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

pays_in.note: What would happen if is a Part 3 question type, and the answer must match the question.
pays_in.model: If cities charged drivers by the mile, people would think much harder about short journeys.

pays_in.note: A counter-argument often runs on a world the writer does not expect to arrive.
pays_in.model: If universities dropped their entry tests, admissions offices would have nothing left to compare.

pays_in.note: A speaker weighing options in Part 3 marks each imagined one this way.
pays_in.model: If we moved the session to the annexe, we would lose the projector.

used_in.quote: The follow-ups ask what a town would look like under conditions that do not hold, and the grammar has to say so.
The strongest paragraphs describe a centre without cars, which is a place that does not exist yet.

payload.sentence: If the tram ran until midnight, half the late-night traffic through the centre would disappear.
payload.question: Does the tram run until midnight?

feedback.why_key: The step backwards in the first half says the late service does not exist, and the whole sentence is a picture of a town that would be different if it did.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a stepped-back if half as a claim about what is missing.

payload.sentence: If I lived nearer the depot, I'd walk in every morning.
payload.question: How does the speaker get to work at the moment?

feedback.why_key: The walking is tied to a house the speaker does not live in, so it is not happening either. The sentence never says what she does instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow the imagined half through to what it cancels.

payload.context: From a paragraph imagining a city with no private cars at all.
payload.sentence: If the city banned cars from the centre altogether, emissions will fall by a third within a year.
reasons: the two halves disagree about whether any of this is expected
emissions cannot be measured that precisely
the ban should come second in the sentence
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The first half sets up a world that is not so and the second half predicts flatly, which leaves the reader in two places at once.
feedback.feed_forward: Answer a stepped-back if half with would, not will.

payload.context: From an essay about towns with no evening transport.
payload.stem: If the tram ___ (run) until midnight, the multi-storey would empty out.

expected: ran

feedback.why_key: The result half has already told you this is a world being shown, so the if half has to step back to match it.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb in the if half back and leave would where it is.

payload.context: From an essay about a scheme nobody has proposed.
payload.stem: If bus fares were dropped altogether, town centres ___ (fill) up again on Saturdays.

expected: would fill
'd fill
d fill

feedback.why_key: Were dropped sets the sentence in a world that is not so, and the answering half has to stay in the same world.
feedback.feed_forward: Answer with would and keep both halves in one world.

payload.context: Two friends talking about rents they cannot afford.
payload.stem: If I ___ (have) somewhere cheaper to live, I'd think about going part-time.

expected: had

feedback.why_key: The speaker has nowhere cheaper, which is why the part-time job stays imaginary as well.
feedback.feed_forward: Step have back to had inside the if half.

payload.given: The town does not have a bypass. Lorries go through the market square all day.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence showing what the square would be like in a town that had one.

expected: had a bypass lorries would stop going through the market square
had a bypass, lorries would stop going through the market square
had a bypass the lorries would not go through the market square
had a bypass, the lorries would not go through the market square

feedback.why_key: Both facts are true today, and the sentence has to cancel one of them before it can describe the other differently.
feedback.feed_forward: Suppose the missing thing into place, then say what changes.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a town where street parking is charged for.

expected: if parking were free nobody would use the multi-storey
nobody would use the multi-storey if parking were free

feedback.why_key: Would sits with the result whichever end of the sentence the result lands on, and it never crosses into the if half.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep would out of the half that begins with if.

payload.audio_text: If the yard were bigger, we'd load two lorries at once.

expected: if the yard were bigger we'd load two lorries at once
if the yard were bigger we would load two lorries at once
if the yard were bigger wed load two lorries at once

feedback.why_key: We'd and we are almost the same sound at speed, and losing the d turns a picture of a bigger yard into a claim about this one.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the d clinging to the pronoun.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph on air quality.
payload.sentence: If the council would ban lorries from the high street, the air outside the school would clear within months.
reasons: the world is marked twice, and the if half is the wrong place for it
the council has no power over lorries
the school should be named in the first half
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One would is enough to tell a reader the whole sentence is imagined, and the one in the if half reads as a complaint about the council's willingness instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the imagined world once, in the answering half.

payload.sentence: If the city built a tram line along the river, congestion in the centre will fall by about a third.

expected: would fall

feedback.why_key: Built has already put the reader in a city that does not exist, and a flat prediction drags them back out of it mid-sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the sentence in the world you opened it in.

payload.prompt_text: Nobody has suggested closing your nearest city centre to private cars, and nobody is going to. Write one sentence describing what such a centre would be like on an ordinary Tuesday.

feedback.why_key: Describing a place that does not exist is a different job from arguing for one, and the grammar is how a reader tells which you are doing.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the if half back and answer it with would.

payload.prompt_text: You are asked how towns will look different in fifty years. In forty-five seconds, describe one change nobody is planning and say what would follow from it, keeping both halves in the same imagined world.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure the second half is where speakers fall back into predicting, and the listener hears two different claims about the same town.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that both halves are still in the imagined world.

title: Choosing whether to argue about a real decision or show an imagined one

point_json.grammar_name: Using the unreal present: advice, softened requests and imagined policy

teach.can_do: I can pick between arguing about something that may really happen and showing something that will not.
teach.why_it_matters: Both shapes are correct English and only one is honest about what you know. Get it wrong and a firm plan sounds idle, or a stray thought sounds binding.
teach.meaning: The two shapes you now have look similar and claim opposite things. The plain one puts a real decision on the table and argues about it: somebody could still act on your sentence. The stepped-back one takes the decision off the table and shows a picture instead: nobody is expected to act, and that is precisely why it is safe to use for advice, for softening what you want, and for the imagined worlds a discussion question keeps asking about. Choosing between them is choosing what you are claiming to know.

form.pattern: If + present form, will + verb   OR   If + step-back form, would + verb
notes: The two halves move together. Stepping the first half back and leaving will in the second is the single commonest wreck in this unit.
If I were you is fixed advice, and nobody expects the listener to become the speaker. The stepped-back form is what makes it advice rather than an order.
It would help if you could send the figures is a request, not a hypothesis. The step back is buying the other person room to refuse.
form.negative: If the funding did not run out in June, none of this would be urgent.
form.question: What would you do if you were running the department?

left.role: on the table: somebody could act on this
left.text: If the college drops the evening slot, working students will have to travel in.

right.role: off the table: a picture, or a piece of advice
right.text: If the college dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel in.

spec.caption: Same college, same students. Only one of these sentences is asking anybody to do anything.

worked_example.sentence: If I were running the department, I would protect the evening slot before anything else.
worked_example.why_this_form: The speaker is not running the department and everybody in the room knows it. The step backwards is what turns a criticism of the person who is running it into a piece of advice they can take without losing face.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: If I am running the department, I will protect the evening slot would announce a plan for a job the speaker has apparently been offered, which is a very different meeting.

notice_set.sentence: If the college drops the evening slot, working students will have to travel in three nights a week.
notice_set.question: Is dropping the slot something the college is actually considering?
notice_set.why: The plain forms put the decision on the table, which is why the sentence works as a warning to the people taking it.

notice_set.sentence: If the college dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel in three nights a week.
notice_set.question: Is dropping the slot something the college is actually considering?
notice_set.why: The step backwards takes the decision off the table and leaves a picture of what would be lost.

notice_set.sentence: If I were you, I would ask for the figures in writing.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker expect the listener to become the speaker?
notice_set.why: Nobody takes this half literally. The impossible opening is what makes the second half advice rather than an instruction.

notice_set.sentence: It would help enormously if you could send the figures across before Friday.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker describing an imaginary situation or asking for something?
notice_set.why: This is a request wearing the clothes of a hypothesis. The step backwards leaves the listener room to say no.

notice_set.sentence: If the grant were renewed, the department would keep both evening tutors.
notice_set.question: Is the grant being renewed?
options: Not as far as the speaker knows
notice_set.why: Somebody who had heard the grant was safe would have written this the other way, and the reader is entitled to read the step back as bad news.

discovery.prompt: Each pair is about the same decision. Work out which sentence expects somebody to do something about it.
pairs: If the college drops the evening slot, working students will have to travel in.
If the college dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel in.
If the firm wins the contract, we will take on four more drivers.
If the firm won the contract, we would take on four more drivers.
If the grant is renewed, the department keeps both evening tutors.
If the grant were renewed, the department would keep both evening tutors.

candidate_rules.text: The left-hand sentences treat the decision as live; the right-hand ones show a picture nobody is expected to act on.
The right-hand sentences are the polite ones, so they belong in formal writing.
Would is used for the more distant future and will for the nearer one.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether anybody could act on your sentence. If nobody could, step it back.
teach.false_rule: That the stepped-back version is just the polite one. Politeness is a side effect; the sentence is claiming that none of this is expected to happen.

contrast.question: Could anybody actually act on this sentence?

fork.answer: Yes, the decision is live and somebody is weighing it right now
No, I am showing a picture, giving advice, or softening a request

a.text: If the firm wins the Ashfield contract, we will take on four more drivers.
a.means: The bid is in and the result is coming. Four people may genuinely be hired.

b.text: If the firm won the Ashfield contract, we would take on four more drivers.
b.means: The firm is not going to win it. The four drivers are a way of saying how big the contract is.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You stepped it back. To a manager reading it, that says the bid is hopeless and the hiring plan is a daydream. If the tender is genuinely open, you have just told your own team not to bother preparing for it.

edge_case.text: A speaker sometimes steps a live possibility back on purpose, to be modest or to avoid jinxing it: if we won it, we'd need four more drivers, said by somebody who thinks the bid is strong. Hear it, enjoy it, and keep it out of an essay where the reader cannot see your face.

contrast.stronger_test: Ask what the sentence would sound like if the person who takes the decision were standing behind you. If it would embarrass you to be overheard treating their decision as already lost, you needed the plain forms.

worked_pairs.a: If the mill site is cleared, forty homes go up on it next year.
worked_pairs.b: If the mill site were cleared, forty homes would go up on it.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first belongs in the section of the report on agreed schemes. The second belongs in the section on what the town is missing.

worked_pairs.a: If you take the earlier train, you will get an hour with the family before dinner.
worked_pairs.b: If I were you, I would take the earlier train.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: If you take the earlier train
worked_pairs.gloss: The first lays out a consequence and leaves the decision alone. The second reaches into the decision, and only the impossible opening keeps it friendly.

worked_pairs.a: If you can send the figures before Friday, I will finish the draft over the weekend.
worked_pairs.b: It would help enormously if you could send the figures before Friday.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: If you can send the figures
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: if you could send the figures
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are asking for the same spreadsheet. The second has stepped back so that saying no costs the other person nothing.

errors.wrong: If I were in charge of the budget, I will spend it on the evening classes.
errors.right: If I were in charge of the budget, I would spend it on the evening classes.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening is a fixed phrase the learner has memorised whole, so it comes out right without being thought about. The second half is built from scratch a moment later, and the default for a future statement is will.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: will spend becomes would spend.

errors.wrong: If the college would drop the evening slot, working students would have to travel in.
errors.right: If the college dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel in.
errors.why_it_happens: Both halves are imagined, so the learner marks both. The result is a sentence that reads as a complaint about whether the college is willing, rather than a picture of what would follow.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: would drop becomes dropped.

errors.wrong: If I were you, I must ask for the figures in writing.
errors.right: If I were you, I would ask for the figures in writing.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner wants the advice to sound serious and reaches for the strongest word available. Must turns a suggestion into an order and cancels the softening the opening phrase was chosen for.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: must becomes would.

pays_in.note: Part 3 mixes live issues with imagined ones, and the examiner hears which is which.
pays_in.model: If schools taught cooking to everybody, families would waste far less food.

pays_in.note: A concession is usually a picture of a world the writer does not expect.
pays_in.model: If tuition were free at the point of use, universities would still have to choose between applicants somehow.

pays_in.note: A polite letter softens its central request with exactly this step.
pays_in.model: It would help a great deal if the repairs could be finished before the end of the month.

used_in.quote: Giving advice out loud without sounding like a supervisor is exactly what the stepped-back form is for.
The prompt asks about a funding arrangement that does not exist, and every body paragraph has to say so in its grammar.

payload.sentence: If the college dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel in three nights a week.
payload.question: Is the college considering dropping the slot?
options: Not as far as the writer knows

feedback.why_key: The step backwards takes the decision off the table and leaves a picture of what would be lost with it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the sentence expects anybody to act.

payload.sentence: If I were you, I'd ask for the figures in writing.
payload.question: What is the speaker doing?

feedback.why_key: Nobody takes the opening half literally. Its impossibility is what keeps the second half friendly instead of bossy.
feedback.feed_forward: Read an impossible opening as a softener, not as a claim.

payload.context: From an early draft of an essay on how a town spends its transport budget.
payload.sentence: If I were the council, I will put the whole budget into the buses instead.
reasons: the second half has climbed out of the imagined world the first half set up
a writer cannot mention the council in an essay
the budget should come first in the sentence
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The opening admits the writer is not the council, and then the second half makes a firm promise on the council's behalf.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the sentence in the world you opened it in.

payload.context: The department has just been told the grant is being renewed for three years.
payload.stem: If the grant ___ (be) renewed, the department keeps both evening tutors.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: The renewal is real news, so nothing in the sentence should suggest the tutors are a fantasy.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep both halves plain when the decision is already taken.

payload.context: The same department a year earlier, when the grant had already been refused twice.
payload.stem: If the grant were renewed, the department ___ (keep) both evening tutors.

expected: would keep
'd keep
d keep

feedback.why_key: Were renewed has put the reader in a year that did not arrive, and the tutors have to stay in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Answer a stepped-back opening with would.

payload.context: A colleague asking for help with a difficult email.
payload.stem: If I ___ (be) you, I would leave the last paragraph out altogether.

expected: were
was

feedback.why_key: Both spellings are heard every day. What matters is that the opening is impossible, because that is what makes the advice easy to refuse.
feedback.feed_forward: Open advice with an impossible half and follow it with would.

payload.given: Send me the figures before Friday.
payload.instruction: Turn the instruction into a request the other person could comfortably refuse.

expected: if you could send the figures before friday
if you could send me the figures before friday
a great deal if you could send the figures before friday

feedback.why_key: Stepping the request back is not decoration. It is what leaves the other person a way out that does not cost either of you anything.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the asking verb back to make refusing easy.

payload.audio_text: If I were you, I'd take the earlier train.

expected: if i were you i'd take the earlier train
if i were you i would take the earlier train
if i were you id take the earlier train

feedback.why_key: Advice arrives at speed and the 'd is the only thing separating it from an announcement about the speaker's own travel plans.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the d before the advice verb.

payload.context: From a paragraph about land nobody has any intention of releasing.
payload.sentence: If the council would build on the old airfield, two thousand families would have somewhere to live.
reasons: the imagined world is marked twice, and the first half is the wrong place for it
the airfield is too small for two thousand homes
the families should be named in the first half
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: As written, the sentence complains that the council is unwilling. Stepping the first half back instead simply shows what the land could do.
feedback.feed_forward: Mark the imagined world once, in the answering half.

items.decision_cue: the bid went in last week and the result is due on Friday

payload.context: The firm is one of three bidders for the Ashfield haulage work; the bid went in last week and the result is due on Friday.
payload.stem: If the firm ___ take on four more drivers.

options.why_this_means: That the result is genuinely open and the hiring is something to start planning for.
That nobody expects the firm to win, and the drivers are a way of describing the size of the job.

expected: wins the contract, we will

feedback.why_key: A bid that is already in and due on Friday is a live decision, and the sentence should let the team prepare for it.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the forms plain while the decision is still open.

items.decision_cue: far too small to bid for the Ashfield work and never has

payload.context: The firm is far too small to bid for the Ashfield work and never has; the owner is describing the size of the contract to a visitor.
payload.stem: If the firm ___ take on four more drivers.

options.why_this_means: That the result is genuinely open and the hiring is something to start planning for.
That nobody expects the firm to win, and the drivers are a way of describing the size of the job.

expected: won the contract, we would

feedback.why_key: Same sentence, same four drivers, and no bid at all. The step backwards is how the owner keeps the boast honest.
feedback.feed_forward: Step back anything nobody is going to act on.

items.decision_cue: on the agenda for next month's meeting

payload.context: Cutting the evening slot is on the agenda for next month's meeting and two of the five governors have already said they support it.
payload.stem: If the college ___ into the city three nights a week.

options.text: drops the evening slot, working students will have to travel
options.why_this_means: That the cut is being weighed now and the sentence is a warning to the people weighing it.

options.text: dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel
options.why_this_means: That the cut is not on anybody's list, and the sentence is showing what the slot is worth.

expected: drops the evening slot, working students will have to travel

feedback.why_key: Governors who are about to vote can act on this sentence, and stepping it back would tell them there is nothing to decide.
feedback.feed_forward: Write to the people who can still change it.

items.decision_cue: protected by a funding agreement that runs for another decade

payload.context: The evening slot is protected by a funding agreement that runs for another decade, and a tutor is explaining to a new colleague why it matters.
payload.stem: If the college ___ into the city three nights a week.

options.text: drops the evening slot, working students will have to travel
options.why_this_means: That the cut is being weighed now and the sentence is a warning to the people weighing it.

options.text: dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel
options.why_this_means: That the cut is not on anybody's list, and the sentence is showing what the slot is worth.

expected: dropped the evening slot, working students would have to travel

feedback.why_key: Nothing is under threat, so the plain forms would frighten a new colleague about a decision that cannot be taken.
feedback.feed_forward: Step it back when there is no decision left to influence.

items.decision_cue: thinks it is a real option, though the funders may still say no

payload.context: The team could move the trial to the Sandmouth site, and the manager thinks it is a real option, though the funders may still say no.
payload.stem: If we ___ the results by spring.

options.text: move the trial to Sandmouth, we'll have
options.why_this_means: That the move is something the team is preparing for and spring is a working deadline.

options.text: moved the trial to Sandmouth, we'd have
options.why_this_means: That the move is being thought about out loud, and spring is what it would buy them.

follow_up.question: Which version treats the move as something the team is likely to do?

feedback.why_key: Both are honest sentences about the same trial. One of them commits the team to a deadline and the other only weighs it.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide how much you are committing to, then choose.

payload.context: Two sentences from a housing report: one from the section on agreed schemes and one from the section on missed opportunities.
sentences: If the mill site is cleared, forty homes go up on it next year.
If the mill site were cleared, forty homes would go up on it.
meanings: The clearance is agreed and the writer is describing the timetable.
The clearance is not happening, and the homes are a measure of what the town is losing.

feedback.why_key: The same forty homes appear in both halves of the report, but only one of them will have anybody living in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the verb forms to work out which section you are in.

payload.prompt_text: Nobody is proposing to make university free in your country and nobody is going to. Write one sentence describing what admissions offices would have to do in that world.

feedback.why_key: A concession works because the reader can see you are describing a world, not demanding one, and the verb forms are the only thing that says so.
feedback.feed_forward: Step both halves back together.

parts: A friend is thinking of taking a job two hours from home.
You are not the one taking the decision.
You think the commute will wear them out inside a year.
model_combinations: If I were in your position, I would ask them whether any of the week could be done from home.
If it were me, I would work out what two hours each way does to a Tuesday before saying yes.
If I had that commute in front of me, I would want the offer to be a lot better than the one you have.

feedback.why_key: The middle fact decides the grammar. You are not taking the decision, so the sentence has to leave your friend room to ignore you.
feedback.feed_forward: Open from a position you do not hold, then advise.

payload.prompt_text: Return to your essay on who should pay for a degree. Find the paragraph where you described an arrangement that does not exist and rewrite its first sentence so that both halves sit in that imagined world. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Halfway through a long sentence is exactly where a writer forgets which world they are in, and the reader feels the join.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the two halves back and check they match.

title: Saying which person or thing I mean by hanging a clause on it

point_json.grammar_name: Defining relative clauses

teach.can_do: I can add a clause after a noun to say exactly which person or thing I mean.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the cheapest complex sentence in English and the safest one to risk. Two short sentences become one, and the reader stops asking which one you meant.
teach.meaning: This kind of clause does one job: it narrows a noun down until only the right thing is left. Say the driver and your listener has a whole depot to choose from. Say the driver who took the Ashfield run and there is one. The clause is not decoration you could lift out. Take it away and the sentence stops identifying anything, which is why nothing is allowed to separate it from its noun.

form.pattern: noun + who / which / that + the rest of the clause
notes: who for people, which for things, and that for either of them in this kind of clause
the relative word stands in for the noun inside the clause, so the noun is never said twice
the verb inside the clause agrees with the noun outside it, however far back that noun is
form.negative: The inside of the clause goes negative in the ordinary way: the driver who does not take the Ashfield run.
form.question: Ask which one? about the noun. Turn the answer into who took it or which arrived late, and hang it straight on the noun.

left.text: the driver

right.role: the clause that narrows it to one
right.text: who took the Ashfield run

spec.caption: Nothing comes between the two boxes. No comma, no pause, no breath.

worked_example.sentence: The engineer who checked the Ashfield line has written the report.
worked_example.why_this_form: On its own, the engineer could be any of nine people on that team. The clause cuts nine down to one, and then the sentence can get on with its news.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two separate sentences would still be true, but they make the reader hold a person in mind and wait to find out which one was meant.

notice_set.sentence: The drivers who finished the safety course start on the new route in April.
notice_set.question: Do all the drivers start on the new route in April?
notice_set.why: Only the drivers picked out by the extra words start. The others are outside what the sentence is talking about.

notice_set.sentence: The lift that serves the north platform is out of order.
notice_set.question: Can you use a different lift?
notice_set.why: One lift has been picked out. Whether the station has any others is simply left open.

notice_set.sentence: The road that runs along the Verdon floods twice a winter.
notice_set.question: Does the road beside the river flood?
notice_set.why: The added words are how you know which road is meant, and that road is the one beside the river.

notice_set.sentence: Passengers who booked online can board first.
notice_set.question: Can a passenger who paid at the desk board first?
notice_set.why: The permission is attached to one group only, and paying at the desk puts you outside it.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic treats patients who live inside the county.
notice_set.question: Would the clinic treat someone from three counties away?
notice_set.why: Living inside the county is what makes someone one of the patients the sentence means.

teach.rule_line: If taking the words out leaves the reader asking which one, weld them on.
teach.false_rule: That who is for people and that is only for things. That works for people too here, and speakers use it constantly.

errors.wrong: The engineer who I trained him last year has taken over the depot.
errors.right: The engineer who I trained last year has taken over the depot.
errors.why_it_happens: Plenty of languages keep the pronoun inside the clause. The learner builds a complete clause and then adds the relative word in front of it, and nothing feels missing, because nothing is.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: him.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Arabic, Persian and several South Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The inspector which signed the report has retired.
errors.right: The inspector who signed the report has retired.
errors.why_it_happens: Which arrives first because it is the word learners meet most in written English. The check for whether the noun is a person happens later, once the sentence is already moving.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: which becomes who.

errors.wrong: The reports that covers the Sandmouth crossing arrive on Friday.
errors.right: The reports that cover the Sandmouth crossing arrive on Friday.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb inside the clause has to agree with a noun that is now several words behind, and the last thing the learner heard in their head was a singular word.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on covers.

errors.wrong: The scheme which the council approved in March. It has already run over budget.
errors.right: The scheme which the council approved in March has already run over budget.
errors.why_it_happens: The added clause makes the first group of words long enough to feel like a whole sentence, so a full stop goes in and the real news is left stranded in a new one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one full stop and let the sentence carry on.

pays_in.note: Every sentence in a body paragraph that defines who you are talking about.
pays_in.model: The households that struggle most with fuel bills are the ones least able to pay for insulation.

pays_in.note: It is how you identify a person or a place inside a long turn.
pays_in.model: The teacher who taught me to swim was the one everybody at the pool was frightened of.

pays_in.note: Passages define their key terms this way, and the questions test the definition.
pays_in.model: The technique that the survey team adopted had been abandoned almost everywhere else.

used_in.quote: You cannot argue about which services a small town should keep without a sentence that says which services you mean.
The passage introduces its central term and then narrows it with a clause, which is exactly what the first question turns on.

payload.sentence: The trains that stop at Brackenfield are always the slow ones.
payload.question: Is every train on this line slow?

feedback.why_key: Only one group of trains has been picked out, and it is the group that stops at Brackenfield.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the added words as a filter on the noun, not as extra news.

payload.sentence: Staff who work nights are offered a free eye test each year.
payload.question: Does a day-shift nurse get the free eye test?

feedback.why_key: Working nights is what makes someone one of the staff the sentence is about, so the offer stops at the edge of that group.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who is inside the group before you decide what is being promised.

payload.context: From a first draft of a report on shift patterns.
payload.sentence: The supervisor who I interviewed her last week runs the whole night team.
reasons: the person is named twice inside the same clause
the wrong relative word has been chosen
the two halves need a comma between them
nothing wrong, it's fine
