feedback.why_key: Who already stands in for the supervisor. Her says it again, and the clause ends up with one person too many in it.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause on its own and delete anything that repeats the noun.

payload.context: From a paragraph about small towns losing their bus routes.
payload.stem: The residents ___ rely on the last bus have no other way of getting home.

expected: who
that

feedback.why_key: Residents are people, so who is the natural choice, and that is equally at home in this kind of clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether the noun is a person before you reach for which.

payload.context: A student explaining how her course is organised.
payload.stem: The modules that ___ (run) in the evening fill up first.

expected: run

feedback.why_key: The verb inside the clause points back to modules, which is plural, even though evening is the nearest word to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look back to the noun the clause hangs on, not to the nearest word.

payload.context: Build one sentence about equipment on the Verdon survey.

expected: the sensors that the team installed in march have already failed

feedback.why_key: The clause sits straight after sensors and stops there. The main verb of the sentence is still waiting behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the clause next to its noun, then finish the sentence you started.

payload.given: Some passengers change at Marlow. Those passengers lose forty minutes.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that says which passengers lose the time.

expected: who change at marlow lose forty minutes
that change at marlow lose forty minutes
changing at marlow lose forty minutes

feedback.why_key: One sentence now does both jobs: it says which passengers are meant and it says what happens to them.
feedback.feed_forward: Fold the second sentence into the noun it describes.

payload.audio_text: The neighbours who've just moved in keep the yard gate open.

expected: the neighbours who've just moved in keep the yard gate open
the neighbours who have just moved in keep the yard gate open
the neighbours whove just moved in keep the yard gate open

feedback.why_key: In speech who've is a single syllable. If you never hear it you will write who just moved in and lose the link.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small extra sound riding on the relative word.

payload.sentence: The software which the depot ordered it last spring has never been switched on.

expected: which the depot ordered
that the depot ordered
the depot ordered

feedback.why_key: Which is already the software. Saying it again gives the clause two objects and one of them has to go.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the pronoun that repeats the noun in front of the clause.

payload.context: Two lines from a timetable notice at Sandmouth.
sentences: The ferries that serve the islands run all winter.
The ferry that serves the islands runs all winter.
meanings: Several boats do this crossing, and none of them stops for the season.
One boat does this crossing, and it does not stop for the season.

feedback.why_key: Both verbs agree with the noun the clause hangs on, so the endings tell you how many boats there are.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the verb endings backwards to the noun to count the things.

payload.prompt_text: A college wants to charge a small fee for evening classes. Write one sentence that says exactly which students would be hit hardest.

feedback.why_key: Naming the group precisely is the whole move here, and it is how a bare opinion becomes an argument a reader can follow.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the group, then narrow it with a clause before the main verb arrives.

payload.prompt_text: Take the body paragraph you wrote on rural services. Rewrite one sentence so that it names the exact group of people affected and finishes with the main point. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: The commonest way this goes wrong under time pressure is a full stop after the clause, leaving the sentence with nothing to say.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that the sentence still has a main verb after the clause ends.

title: Leaving out who, which or that when the clause already has a subject

point_json.grammar_name: Omitting the relative pronoun (contact clauses)

teach.can_do: I can drop who, which or that when someone else is already doing the verb in the clause.
teach.why_it_matters: It makes your English sound like English rather than like a grammar drill, and it is the shape most people are actually listening for.
teach.meaning: The relative word has a job inside its own clause. Sometimes it is the one doing the verb, and then it cannot leave, because the clause would have nobody in it. Sometimes another subject is already there, doing the verb, and the relative word is only the thing the verb happens to. Then it is carrying no weight, and English quietly drops it. The meaning does not change at all. Only the number of words does.

form.pattern: noun + (who / which / that) + subject + verb ...
notes: keep the word when nothing follows it but a verb: the tutor who marked my essay
drop it when a new subject follows: the essay the tutor marked
a preposition left at the end of the clause is normal and stays where it is: the flat we looked at
form.negative: Nothing changes when the clause is negative: the essay the tutor did not mark.
form.question: Put your finger on the word straight after who, which or that. Is it a verb, or is it somebody new?

ends: nobody else in the clause, so the word has to stay
somebody else is already doing the verb, so the word can go

marks.label: the tutor who marked my essay
the bus that goes past the school
the essay that the tutor marked

worked_example.sentence: The form I filled in on Tuesday has gone missing.
worked_example.why_this_form: I is already doing the filling in, so the relative word has nothing left to do in the clause, and English lets it disappear without a trace.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Putting that back in front of I changes nothing about the meaning. It only slows the sentence down by a syllable and makes it a shade more careful.

notice_set.sentence: The engineer the depot hired last month starts on Monday.
notice_set.question: Who did the hiring?
notice_set.why: The depot sits between the engineer and the verb, which puts the depot in charge of the hiring.

notice_set.sentence: The engineer who hired the new drivers starts on Monday.
notice_set.question: Who did the hiring?
notice_set.why: Nobody else appears before the verb, so the engineer is the one doing it.

notice_set.sentence: The report the council rejected ran to ninety pages.
notice_set.question: Who rejected it?
notice_set.why: The council has slipped straight in after the noun, and that is your signal about who acted.

notice_set.sentence: The tutor I emailed twice has finally replied.
notice_set.question: Who sent the emails?
notice_set.why: I is doing the emailing. The tutor is only on the receiving end of it.

notice_set.sentence: The parcel that arrived this morning is still on the desk.
notice_set.question: Did something arrive this morning?
notice_set.why: Nothing stands between that and arrived, so the parcel itself is what arrived.

teach.rule_line: Look at the word after the relative word. If it is a new subject, you can drop it.
teach.false_rule: That leaving it out is lazy or too informal for an essay. Careful written English drops it exactly as readily as conversation does.

errors.wrong: The bus goes past the school leaves at ten past eight.
errors.right: The bus that goes past the school leaves at ten past eight.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored the rule as the word is optional and applies it everywhere. Nothing in that stored version mentions who is doing the verb, so nothing fires to stop it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: that.

errors.wrong: The flat we looked at it on Saturday has already gone.
errors.right: The flat we looked at on Saturday has already gone.
errors.why_it_happens: With the relative word gone, the clause looks unfinished, so the learner puts an object back in to repair it. The repair is what creates the error.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: it.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for speakers of Arabic, Persian, Hebrew and several South Asian languages.

errors.wrong: The route the drivers complain about most. It has three level crossings.
errors.right: The route the drivers complain about most has three level crossings.
errors.why_it_happens: With no relative word to signal that the sentence has not finished, the run of words feels complete, a full stop goes in, and the actual news is stranded in the next sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one full stop and run the two halves together.

pays_in.note: Short answers about your own life run on these almost continuously.
pays_in.model: The course I signed up for last autumn turned out to be mostly practical.

pays_in.note: It shortens a clumsy sentence without costing you any complexity.
pays_in.model: The measures governments announce most loudly are rarely the ones that change behaviour.

pays_in.note: Nothing marks the join, so a listener has to hear the second subject.
pays_in.model: The building the college bought last year is still empty.

used_in.quote: Describing a book you recommend needs a run of these: the book I read, the part I liked, the friend I lent it to.

payload.sentence: The tutor my sister recommended has a waiting list until March.
payload.question: Who did the recommending?

feedback.why_key: My sister has arrived before the verb, which means she is the one doing the recommending and the tutor is what she recommended.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the first subject after the noun and give the verb to it.

payload.sentence: The editor who commissioned the piece has since left the paper.
payload.question: Who commissioned the piece?

feedback.why_key: Nothing stands between who and commissioned, so the editor is doing the commissioning rather than receiving it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether a new subject appears before the verb.

payload.context: From a letter to a local paper.
payload.sentence: The service runs through Brackenfield was cut without any warning.
reasons: nobody else is doing the verb, so the word cannot be dropped
the object of the clause has been repeated
a comma is needed after the noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Runs has no subject of its own here, so the sentence gives the reader two main verbs and no way to sort them out.
feedback.feed_forward: Restore the word whenever a verb follows the noun directly.

payload.context: A tenant writing to a landlord. Put in the missing word only if the sentence needs one.
payload.stem: The damp ___ appeared in the back bedroom has now spread to the hallway.

expected: that
which

feedback.why_key: Appeared has nobody else to belong to, so the word has to stay and hold the clause together.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the word whenever a verb comes straight after the noun.

payload.given: The college bought a building last year. It is still empty.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence, and leave out the relative word if you are allowed to.

expected: the college bought last year is still empty
that the college bought last year is still empty
which the college bought last year is still empty

feedback.why_key: The college is already doing the buying, so nothing is lost when the relative word goes.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the word once a second subject is in place.

payload.given: One instrument failed in the first week. That instrument had been borrowed.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence. Decide whether the relative word can go.

expected: that failed in the first week had been borrowed
which failed in the first week had been borrowed

feedback.why_key: The instrument is the thing doing the failing, so there is nobody to take the word's place and it has to stay.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who fails, who buys, who writes, before you delete anything.

payload.context: Say one sentence about a recipe in your family.

expected: the dish my grandmother taught me takes two days

feedback.why_key: My grandmother slides in straight after dish with nothing to introduce her, and the sentence still finds its main verb at the end.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the second subject next to the noun and keep going.

payload.audio_text: The shift I'd swapped with him fell on the bank holiday.

expected: the shift i'd swapped with him fell on the bank holiday
the shift i had swapped with him fell on the bank holiday
the shift id swapped with him fell on the bank holiday

feedback.why_key: Nothing marks where the clause begins, so the only clue is the new subject arriving with a squashed auxiliary attached to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a new subject appearing straight after a noun.

payload.sentence: The path the guides recommend it in summer is closed for repairs.

expected: the guides recommend
that the guides recommend
which the guides recommend

feedback.why_key: The path is already the thing being recommended. Adding it gives the clause a second object and one of them has no home.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete any pronoun that repeats the noun the clause hangs on.

payload.context: Two lines from a court report.
sentences: The officers the magistrate criticised have been moved to other duties.
The officers who criticised the magistrate have been moved to other duties.
meanings: The magistrate did the criticising and the officers were on the receiving end.
The officers did the criticising and the magistrate was on the receiving end.

feedback.why_key: The same six words in a different order swap who acted and who was acted on, and only the position of the subject tells you which.
feedback.feed_forward: Locate the subject of the inner verb before you decide who did what.

payload.prompt_text: Think of something you were given as a child and still own. Say one sentence about it, and leave out the relative word.

feedback.why_key: Because someone else did the giving, the relative word is doing no work and the sentence sounds lighter without it.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the thing, add who acted on it, then finish the sentence.

payload.prompt_text: You have one minute on the long-turn card about a book you would recommend. Identify the book, the person who lent it to you and the part you remember, using three of these clauses. Speak it, do not write it.

feedback.why_key: Under real speaking pressure the object slips back in, because the clause feels unfinished without it. That is the habit this turn is hunting.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the clause once, then stop; do not repeat the thing.

title: Putting a question inside a sentence without it behaving like a question

point_json.grammar_name: Embedded questions and other noun clauses

teach.can_do: I can drop a question into the middle of a sentence and keep the word order straight.
teach.why_it_matters: It is one of the most visible errors a listener notices, it happens in almost every polite request, and the repair is a single move.
teach.meaning: A clause can do the job of a noun. Instead of naming a thing, it names a piece of information: where the office is, whether the funding will continue, what the council intends. When a question goes into that slot it stops being a question and becomes a thing your sentence is talking about, so it loses the swapped word order that questions carry. The question word stays. The swap goes.

form.pattern: verb / adjective + question word or whether + subject + verb ...
notes: no swapping: where the office is, not where is the office
no do, does or did inside the clause: how much it cost, not how much did it cost
when there is no question word, use whether or if: I am not sure whether it is worth it
the clause can also be the subject of the sentence: what the council intends is anybody's guess
form.negative: The negative sits on the outer sentence or inside the clause, not on both: I do not know why they left.
form.question: Ask what the sentence is about. If the answer is a piece of information, that information is behaving like a noun.

left.text: Where is the ticket office?

right.role: the same question sitting inside a sentence
right.text: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?

spec.caption: Once the question is inside another sentence, it stops behaving like a question.

worked_example.sentence: Nobody can tell me how long the repairs will take.
worked_example.why_this_form: The question has become the thing the sentence is about, so it sits where a noun would sit and takes ordinary subject-before-verb order.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: How long will the repairs take is a question being asked out loud. Inside this sentence it leaves the reader waiting for a question mark that never comes.

notice_set.sentence: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?
notice_set.question: Is the speaker asking for directions?
notice_set.why: The whole sentence is a request, even though the part about the office has stopped looking like a question.

notice_set.sentence: She asked me whether the office was open on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: Did she already know the answer?
notice_set.why: Asking is what you do when the information is missing, and whether marks the gap as a yes-or-no one.

notice_set.sentence: I can't remember how much the repairs cost.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know the figure?
notice_set.why: The missing piece of information is the amount, and the sentence is a statement about not having it.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody has explained why the meeting was moved.
notice_set.question: Was the meeting moved?
notice_set.why: The clause takes the move for granted. What is missing is only the reason for it.

notice_set.sentence: It is not clear whether the funding will continue.
notice_set.question: Has a decision been announced?
notice_set.why: Whether marks an open question, so nothing has been settled either way.

teach.rule_line: Once a question sits inside a sentence, put the subject before the verb.
teach.false_rule: That a question word always brings question order along with it. The question word stays; the swapped order is left behind.

errors.wrong: Could you tell me where is the ticket office?
errors.right: Could you tell me where the ticket office is?
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is asking a question, so the question shape fires automatically. The shape belongs to the outer sentence, which already has it, and the inner clause never needed it.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: is goes to the end.

errors.wrong: Nobody knows how much did it cost.
errors.right: Nobody knows how much it cost.
errors.why_it_happens: Did is stored as part of the question, not as a signal of question order, so it travels inside with the question word and nothing flags it as redundant.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: did.

errors.wrong: She asked me if would I be free on Thursday.
errors.right: She asked me if I would be free on Thursday.
errors.why_it_happens: If already feels like the start of a question, so the swap comes with it. The learner is repeating the shape of the original question rather than reporting its content.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: would goes after I.

errors.wrong: I explained her where the office was.
errors.right: I explained to her where the office was.
errors.why_it_happens: Explain looks like tell and behaves like say, and nothing about its meaning warns the learner that it refuses a person straight after it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: to.

pays_in.note: Hedged answers about your own life are built out of these clauses.
pays_in.model: I'm not really sure why my parents chose that school, to be honest.

pays_in.note: It states a question the essay will answer without asking one.
pays_in.model: What is less clear is whether stricter rules would change anybody's behaviour.

pays_in.note: Requests and enquiries in a booking dialogue are almost all of this shape.
pays_in.model: Could you let me know whether the afternoon session still has places?

used_in.quote: Answers on this card keep reaching for it is hard to say whether and nobody really knows why.

payload.sentence: Do you know whether the library takes cards?
payload.question: Is the speaker asking a question?

feedback.why_key: The outer sentence is the question. The part about cards has become a piece of information the speaker is short of.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at the outer sentence to see who is asking what.

payload.sentence: The report does not say how many staff were consulted.
payload.question: Were any staff consulted?

feedback.why_key: What is missing is the number. Whether anyone at all was asked is left entirely open by the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the clause for what is missing, not for what is claimed.

items.decision_cue: when does the last bus leave

payload.context: At the enquiry desk in Sandmouth.
payload.sentence: Could you tell me when does the last bus leave?
reasons: the inner clause has kept the shape of a question
the wrong question word has been chosen
the outer sentence is not a question at all
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Could you tell me is already doing the asking, so the second half only has to deliver the information in ordinary order.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete does and put the subject in front of the verb.

payload.context: Ask somebody at the station.

expected: do you know where the night bus stops

feedback.why_key: The swap happens once, at the front, in do you know. Everything after where runs in plain order.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap the outer sentence only, never the inner one.

payload.context: Build the last line of a formal letter.

expected: i should be grateful if you could confirm whether the post is still open

feedback.why_key: Whether opens a yes-or-no gap, and the clause after it runs in the same plain order as any statement.
feedback.feed_forward: Follow whether with a subject, then a verb.

payload.given: How much does the evening course cost?
payload.instruction: Turn this into a polite request inside one sentence.

expected: how much the evening course costs
how much the evening course costs?

feedback.why_key: Does disappears and its ending moves back onto the main verb, which is exactly what happens whenever a question goes inside.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the auxiliary and put its ending back on the verb.

payload.given: Will the landlord replace the boiler?
payload.instruction: Say that you have no information about this.

expected: whether the landlord will replace the boiler
if the landlord will replace the boiler

feedback.why_key: There is no question word here, so whether or if has to open the gap, and the subject then comes before the verb as usual.
feedback.feed_forward: Reach for whether when the missing answer is yes or no.

payload.audio_text: I'm not sure where they've put the spare keys.

expected: i'm not sure where they've put the spare keys
i am not sure where they have put the spare keys
im not sure where theyve put the spare keys

feedback.why_key: The subject and its squashed auxiliary come straight after where, and that order is the whole difference between a statement and a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the subject arriving directly after the question word.

items.decision_cue: why do so many new teachers leave

payload.sentence: The study does not explain why do so many new teachers leave within five years.
payload.error_span: why do so many new teachers leave

expected: why so many new teachers leave

feedback.why_key: The sentence is a statement about a gap in the study, so nothing inside it needs the shape of a question.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the auxiliary whenever the clause is reporting, not asking.

payload.context: From a draft about newspapers and their audiences.
payload.sentence: The editorial explained readers why the paper had changed its position.
reasons: explain will not take a person immediately after it
the question inside has kept its swapped order
the wrong question word has been chosen
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The clause after why is built correctly. The trouble is one word earlier, where explain needs to before the person.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert to before the person after explain, describe and suggest.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody has asked you whether people will still write letters in twenty years. Answer in one sentence that admits you do not know.

feedback.why_key: Admitting uncertainty is a real answer, and this clause is what lets you do it without sounding as though you have nothing to say.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with it is hard to say, then keep plain order.

payload.prompt_text: Take the Part 3 card about advice and experts. Give a forty-second answer that uses two of these clauses to hedge, and keep the order plain in both. Record it and listen back for a stray auxiliary.

feedback.why_key: Under speaking pressure the question shape comes back first, because it is the older and stronger habit. Hearing it in your own recording is what breaks it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen back and mark every place an auxiliary slipped in.

title: Saying why you did something, without using because

point_json.grammar_name: Infinitive of purpose vs for + noun

teach.can_do: I can say what something is for, and pick the marker the sentence actually wants.
teach.why_it_matters: For plus an -ing form to express a person's purpose is one of the commonest errors in the module, and it survives all the way up to band 7.
teach.meaning: English has two ways of saying what something is for, and they are not swappable. To plus a bare verb answers why did you do it: it names an action you were aiming at. For plus a noun answers what is it for: it names the function of a thing or the group it is meant for. The difference is not formality and it is not length. It is whether what follows is an action somebody performed or a job something does.

form.pattern: to + base verb (an aim) / for + noun (a function or a beneficiary)
notes: never for to: for cannot introduce an infinitive at all
for plus -ing names what a thing is generally used for, not why a person acted once
in order to and so as to are the same structure, longer and more formal
form.negative: so as not to + verb, or in order not to + verb; a bare not to is ambiguous
form.question: What did you go there to do?

left.text: She went to Verdon to study engineering.

right.text: The back room is for storage.

spec.caption: One names the aim of a person. The other names the function of a thing.

worked_example.sentence: Many students take an extra year to improve their English before applying.
worked_example.why_this_form: Improving is what the students were aiming at, so the sentence needs an action, and to plus a verb is how English attaches one.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: For improving would turn the year into a piece of equipment with a stated function, and the student disappears from their own sentence.

notice_set.sentence: She moved to Ashfield to look after her mother.
notice_set.question: Why did she move?
notice_set.why: To plus a verb names the aim behind the move.

notice_set.sentence: This card is for the staff car park.
notice_set.question: Is the card doing something, or being used for something?
notice_set.why: For plus a noun names the job the object does.

notice_set.sentence: He took the early train to avoid the roadworks.
notice_set.question: What was the point of the early train?
notice_set.why: The infinitive gives the reason behind the choice.

notice_set.sentence: The hall is used for exams in June.
notice_set.question: Who sits the exams, according to this sentence?
options: People, though the sentence does not name them
notice_set.why: For plus a noun names a function and leaves the people out of it.

notice_set.sentence: She rang the office to check the closing time.
notice_set.question: What did she want?
options: To find out when it closes
To tell them when it closes
notice_set.why: The infinitive gives her aim, not a fact about the office.

discovery.prompt: Each pair describes the same situation from two sides. Work out what the marker in front is doing.
pairs: He joined the club to meet people.
The club is for people new to the town.
She saved for a year to buy a van.
The fund is for equipment, not wages.
They rebuilt the shed to store the tools.
The shed is for tools.

candidate_rules.text: To plus a verb names an action somebody was aiming at; for plus a noun names the job a thing does.
To is used with people and for is used with buildings.
Use for whenever the word after it ends in -ing.

teach.rule_line: If what follows is an action you were aiming at, use to plus a verb.
teach.false_rule: That for and to are two ways of saying the same thing and you pick whichever sounds better. For will not carry an infinitive at all.

contrast.question: Is what comes next an action somebody aimed at?

fork.answer: Yes — somebody did it in order to achieve something
No — it is the function of a thing, or the group it is meant for

a.text: I came to the centre to learn Spanish.
a.means: Learning Spanish is my aim, and I am the one doing it.

b.text: I came to the centre for Spanish lessons.
b.means: Lessons are the service I came for. What I do there is not stated.

minimal_pair.only_difference: to learn Spanish / for Spanish lessons

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote for learning Spanish. That reads as a label on a room or a line in a budget, not as something you set out to do. Your own aim has quietly turned into a category of use.

edge_case.text: For plus -ing is perfectly correct when you are naming what a tool or a space is used for: this knife is for boning fish. It is only wrong when it has been put in the place of a person's aim.

contrast.stronger_test: Put in order in front of it. If in order to works, the sentence wanted an infinitive, because in order for is not English here.

worked_pairs.a: She stayed late to finish the accounts.
worked_pairs.b: She stayed late for the overtime.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first names what she was doing. The second names what she was after.

worked_pairs.a: The council widened the path to reduce accidents.
worked_pairs.b: The council widened the path for cyclists.
worked_pairs.gloss: An aim and a beneficiary are different things, and each takes its own marker.

worked_pairs.a: I use this app to track my spending.
worked_pairs.b: I use this app for budgeting.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both are correct. The first says what I do with it; the second names the category of use.

errors.wrong: I came to this college for to improve my writing.
errors.right: I came to this college to improve my writing.
errors.why_it_happens: For and to both feel necessary because the learner's first language marks purpose with a single word that covers both. English uses one marker at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: for.
errors.l1_note: Very common where one word covers both markers.

errors.wrong: She took the extra module for improving her chances of a place.
errors.right: She took the extra module to improve her chances of a place.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows that a preposition takes an -ing form and applies that rule correctly. The problem is a step earlier: a person's aim is not a function, so the preposition should not be there at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: for improving becomes to improve.

errors.wrong: This room is used to storage.
errors.right: This room is used for storage.
errors.why_it_happens: Used to is stored whole as a phrase about past habits and arrives instead of the preposition the sentence actually needs.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: to becomes for.

errors.wrong: The gate was locked for prevent people crossing the yard.
errors.right: The gate was locked to prevent people crossing the yard.
errors.why_it_happens: For is being treated as a joining word that can take a verb. It is a preposition, and prepositions take nouns or -ing forms, never a bare verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: for becomes to.

pays_in.note: Part 1 asks why you are studying English, and the answer is one infinitive.
pays_in.model: I'm doing the course to get onto a masters next year.

pays_in.note: Recommendations need an aim attached without a second clause.
pays_in.model: Councils could cut fares to make the network worth using outside rush hour.

pays_in.note: A letter states its purpose in the first line.
pays_in.model: I am writing to ask about the repairs promised in March.

used_in.quote: The opening line of the letter has to state a purpose, which is this structure doing its clearest job.
Why are you doing that course is a Part 1 question whose natural answer is an infinitive of purpose.

payload.sentence: I signed up for the evening class to meet a few people locally.
payload.question: What was the speaker after?

feedback.why_key: The infinitive names the aim behind signing up, and the aim here is the people, not the course.
feedback.feed_forward: Read to plus a verb as the reason somebody acted.

payload.sentence: The lower floor is for bicycles and prams.
payload.question: Is the sentence naming an aim or a function?

feedback.why_key: For plus a noun says what the space is used for and never names anyone who decided it.
feedback.feed_forward: Take for plus a noun as a label on a thing.

payload.context: From a first draft of a paragraph about tuition fees.
payload.sentence: Several universities raised their entry grades for to raise the standard of the intake.
reasons: two purpose markers have been stacked and English wants one
the verb after for should be an -ing form
the main verb should be in the present
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: For cannot carry an infinitive, so one of the two markers has to go, and it is the one that cannot take a verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete for and keep to in front of the verb.

payload.context: From a paragraph about adult learners.
payload.stem: Many people take an evening course ___ (widen) the range of jobs open to them.

expected: to widen

feedback.why_key: Widening is what the learners are aiming at, and an aim takes to plus the bare verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Put to in front of the verb when a person is aiming at something.

payload.context: From a notice on a shared office kitchen.
payload.stem: The upper cupboard is ___ storage, not for anything that needs refrigerating.

expected: for

feedback.why_key: A cupboard has a function rather than an aim, and a function takes for with a noun after it.
feedback.feed_forward: Use for plus a noun when you are labelling a thing.

payload.given: The town put in a second footbridge. They wanted to keep walkers away from the level crossing.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that attaches the aim to the action without a second clause.
payload.starter: The town put in a second footbridge ___

expected: to keep walkers away from the level crossing
to keep walkers off the level crossing
in order to keep walkers away from the level crossing

feedback.why_key: The aim folds into an infinitive and the sentence loses a clause without losing any of its meaning.
feedback.feed_forward: Attach the aim with to plus the bare verb.

payload.audio_text: I've moved to the early shift to see the kids in the evening.

expected: i've moved to the early shift to see the kids in the evening
i have moved to the early shift to see the kids in the evening
ive moved to the early shift to see the kids in the evening

feedback.why_key: The purpose to is unstressed and sounds like the to of the first phrase, so the two are easy to merge.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a second to arriving before a bare verb.

items.decision_cue: The library is open to everyone on Sundays

payload.context: A press release explaining the council's reasons for the change. The library is open to everyone on Sundays.
payload.stem: The council reopened the library on Sundays ___ revising for exams.

options.why_this_means: That helping those students is the aim the council had, while anyone else may still walk in.
That the Sunday hours are set aside for that group, and other people are not covered by them.

expected: to help students

feedback.why_key: Everyone can use the building, so naming a group as what the day is for would shut a door the council left open.
feedback.feed_forward: Use to plus a verb when you are naming an aim, not a group.

payload.context: A notice on the library door. On Sundays the building is open only to one group and everyone else waits until Monday.
payload.stem: The council reopened the library on Sundays ___ revising for exams.

options.why_this_means: That helping those students is the aim the council had, while anyone else may still walk in.
That the Sunday hours are set aside for that group, and other people are not covered by them.

expected: for students

feedback.why_key: The day is reserved, and reserving is what for plus a group does. An aim would leave the door open to everyone.
feedback.feed_forward: Use for plus a noun when you are naming who something is set aside for.

items.decision_cue: After six the rooms are restricted

payload.context: A tutor is reading out a sign on the door. After six the rooms are restricted and a card is needed to get in.
payload.stem: The college keeps two computer rooms open late ___ on the evening programme.

options.why_this_means: That supporting them is the aim behind the late opening, which anybody may use.
That the late hours belong to that group and other students are not admitted.

expected: for students

feedback.why_key: A card on the door means the hours are allocated, and allocation is what for plus a group says.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether anybody else may walk in before you choose.

items.decision_cue: Any student may use the rooms at any hour

payload.context: A tutor is describing the prospectus. Any student may use the rooms at any hour, and one group was in mind when the hours were extended.
payload.stem: The college keeps two computer rooms open late ___ on the evening programme.

options.why_this_means: That supporting them is the aim behind the late opening, which anybody may use.
That the late hours belong to that group and other students are not admitted.

expected: to support students

feedback.why_key: Nothing is reserved here, so the sentence has an aim and no allocation, and only one marker can carry an aim.
feedback.feed_forward: When nobody is shut out, name the aim rather than the group.

payload.context: Two lines from a leaflet about a walk-in clinic.
sentences: The Thursday clinic opened to reach the over-sixties.
The Thursday clinic opened for the over-sixties.
meanings: Reaching that group was the aim, and anybody can still walk in.
That group is who the day belongs to, and others come on another day.

feedback.why_key: One marker names an aim and leaves the door open. The other names a group and closes it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether you are naming an aim or naming who it is for.

items.decision_cue: an app that is free to download

payload.context: A charity is describing an app that is free to download and open to any user.
payload.stem: The app was built ___ energy use in older houses.

options.why_this_means: That tracking energy use is what the developers set out to make it do.
That tracking energy use is the job it does, stated as a function rather than as anyone's aim.

follow_up.question: Which version tells you what the developers were trying to achieve?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct, because a built thing has an aim behind it and a function in front of it. They are two true sentences.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose an aim when the maker is the point, a function when the tool is.

items.decision_cue: for reducing traffic in the centre

payload.context: From a draft essay paragraph.
payload.sentence: Several cities have raised parking charges for reducing traffic in the centre.
reasons: an aim behind an action needs to plus a verb
the main verb should be in the past
the preposition should be with
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The cities acted with something in mind. For reducing labels a function, and a city council is not a function.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap for plus -ing to to plus a verb when a person or a body acted.

payload.sentence: Many learners join a conversation group for to practise speaking outside class.

expected: to practise
to practice
in order to practise

feedback.why_key: Two purpose markers are stacked, and English keeps the one that can carry a verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete for and keep to.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody asks why you are studying English. Answer in one sentence that names an aim rather than a subject.

feedback.why_key: An aim turns a flat fact about your timetable into a reason the listener can follow.
feedback.feed_forward: Attach to plus a verb to the thing you did.

payload.prompt_text: Open your letter to the landlord with one sentence stating why you are writing, using an infinitive of purpose. Then add one sentence naming what a particular repair is needed for. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: The first line of a letter is the purest use of this structure anywhere in the exam.
feedback.feed_forward: State your purpose in the first sentence, then the function in the second.

title: Choosing between to work and working after the verb in front

point_json.grammar_name: Verb + to-infinitive vs verb + -ing

teach.can_do: I can pick the right shape, to do or doing, for the verbs I use most often.
teach.why_it_matters: The sentence still makes sense when this is wrong, so nobody stops you. It just leaks a small error through every paragraph you write.
teach.meaning: Most of the time this carries no meaning at all. The verb standing in front reaches for one shape or the other, and which one it reaches for is a fact about that verb rather than a fact about the world. Enjoy takes doing. Decide takes to do. Nothing about enjoying is longer or less finished than deciding. So the verb and its shape are learned together, as one piece, the way the word itself was learned.

form.pattern: verb + to + base verb   |   verb + verb-ing
notes: Reaches for to: decide, want, hope, plan, agree, offer, refuse, learn, manage, afford, promise, seem, tend, fail, expect
Reaches for -ing: enjoy, avoid, finish, suggest, mind, keep, practise, consider, risk, deny, admit, involve, imagine, delay
Takes either, with no change of meaning: begin, start, continue, prefer, like, hate, love
There is no third list to work out. A verb that is not in one of the first two has to be looked up once and then stored
form.negative: The word not goes in front of the shape, never inside it: we decided not to renew the contract; she admitted not checking the figures.
form.question: Ask the verb, not the sentence: what does this verb take?

left.text: decided to move, agreed to pay, managed to finish, refused to sign

right.text: avoided moving, suggested paying, finished writing, denied signing

spec.caption: Two piles, and no rule running between them. The verb on the left of the gap tells you which pile you are standing in.

worked_example.sentence: The Marlow depot managed to cut its fuel bill without losing a single route.
worked_example.why_this_form: Manage is one of the verbs that arrives with to already attached, the way depend arrives with on. The choice was made by the word manage, not by the situation.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Managed cutting means nothing at all. That is the useful half of this point: the wrong shape here is not a different meaning, it is no meaning.

notice_set.sentence: The council avoided closing the Marlow library.
notice_set.question: Did the library close?
notice_set.why: Avoid says the thing was kept from happening, and the verb after avoid always turns up in the -ing shape.

notice_set.sentence: The crew managed to repair the pump before the tide turned.
notice_set.question: Was the pump repaired?
notice_set.why: Manage says the hard thing was actually done. Manage always takes to, whatever the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: Our neighbours have offered to drive us to the station.
notice_set.question: Have they driven you to the station yet?
notice_set.why: An offer points forward, so nothing has happened yet. Offer is one of the to verbs.

notice_set.sentence: She kept apologising for the delay.
notice_set.question: How many times did she apologise?
notice_set.why: Keep says the action came round again and again, and keep is one of the -ing verbs.

notice_set.sentence: The firm denied causing any lasting damage to the river.
notice_set.question: Does the firm say it damaged the river?
notice_set.why: Deny pushes the thing away from the speaker, and deny takes the -ing shape every time.

notice_set.sentence: We cannot afford to lose another driver this winter.
notice_set.question: Has a driver left this winter?
notice_set.why: The sentence is about what would be too costly, not about what has happened. Afford is a to verb.

discovery.prompt: Every sentence below is correct English. Try to find the rule that puts a sentence in the left column rather than the right one.
pairs: They enjoy walking to work.
They want to walk to work.
We finished repairing the roof.
We agreed to repair the roof.
He avoided answering the question.
He refused to answer the question.

candidate_rules.text: There is no rule to find. The verb on the left of the gap belongs to a list, and the list is learned rather than worked out.
Verbs about liking or disliking something take the -ing shape.
The -ing shape is used when the action goes on for longer.

teach.rule_line: Ask the verb in front, not the sentence. Store each verb with its shape attached.
teach.false_rule: That -ing here means a longer or unfinished action. It does not. Finish takes -ing, and finishing is exactly what is over.

errors.wrong: The council suggested to build a second footbridge.
errors.right: The council suggested building a second footbridge.
errors.why_it_happens: Suggest means roughly what advise and recommend mean, and those feel like to verbs, so to is supplied by analogy. Meaning is doing the choosing here, and meaning has no vote.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: to build becomes building.

errors.wrong: We are considering to move the depot to Verdon.
errors.right: We are considering moving the depot to Verdon.
errors.why_it_happens: Consider points at something not yet done, and a not-yet action feels as though it should take the forward-looking to shape. Consider simply refuses it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: to move becomes moving.

errors.wrong: She enjoys to cycle along the towpath at the weekend.
errors.right: She enjoys cycling along the towpath at the weekend.
errors.why_it_happens: To do is the shape a learner meets first, so it becomes the default filling for every gap. Enjoy is one of the commonest verbs that will not take it.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: to cycle becomes cycling.

errors.wrong: They decided to moving the market to Tuesdays.
errors.right: They decided to move the market to Tuesdays.
errors.why_it_happens: Both shapes have been half-learned and both arrive at once. It is the signature of a chunk that was never stored whole, only as two loose pieces.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete three letters: moving becomes move.

pays_in.note: Every policy sentence has one verb sitting on top of another.
pays_in.model: Councils that plan to cut bus subsidies rarely consider replacing them with anything.

pays_in.note: A two-minute answer is a chain of verbs following verbs.
pays_in.model: I kept going back because I enjoyed working with people who had done the job for years.

pays_in.note: Whether the second action happened is carried by the first verb.
pays_in.model: The company denied withholding the survey results for eight months.

used_in.quote: Both sides of this essay are built from verbs like plan, expect, avoid and involve, each dragging its own shape behind it.
Saying what you enjoy, what you have decided and what you keep doing uses three different shapes in one answer.

payload.sentence: My manager has offered to swap my Friday shift.
payload.question: Has the shift been swapped?

feedback.why_key: An offer is something put on the table and not yet taken up. Offer is one of the verbs that arrives with to attached.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the first verb for what happened, and take its shape as given.

payload.sentence: The report avoided naming the firm responsible for the spill.
payload.question: Does the report name the firm?

feedback.why_key: Avoid says the naming was kept from happening. The -ing shape after it is not adding anything; avoid always takes it.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the first verb tell you what happened, not the shape of the second.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a college trying to save money.
payload.sentence: The college suggested to reduce the number of evening classes.
reasons: suggest takes the -ing shape, not to
the sentence needs a person after suggested
reduce is the wrong verb here
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Suggest sits in the -ing pile. Nothing about the meaning of this sentence is wrong, which is exactly why the error survives so long.
feedback.feed_forward: Check suggest against the list before you write the second verb.

payload.context: From a letter about the last bus out of Verdon.
payload.stem: Passengers who miss it cannot afford ___ (wait) an hour for a taxi.

expected: to wait

feedback.why_key: Afford is a to verb, and it stays a to verb after cannot. The negative changes nothing about the shape.
feedback.feed_forward: Look past the negative to the verb that owns the shape.

payload.context: A cook talking about a busy Saturday.
payload.stem: I have finally finished ___ (plan) the menu for the weekend.

expected: planning

feedback.why_key: Finish sits in the -ing pile. The planning is over, so if -ing meant an unfinished action this sentence could not exist.
feedback.feed_forward: Store finish and its -ing shape as one chunk.

payload.context: From a maintenance note on the Verdon sensor trial.
payload.stem: The team keeps ___ (find) the same fault, and has agreed ___ (replace) the whole batch.

expected: finding, to replace
finding to replace

feedback.why_key: One sentence, two verbs, two different piles. Keep takes -ing and agree takes to, and neither choice is about the meaning.
feedback.feed_forward: Handle each verb separately; the sentence has no single setting.

payload.given: The landlord will not repair the boiler. He has said so twice.
payload.instruction: Write it as one sentence that starts with the landlord and uses refuse.

expected: to repair the boiler
to repair the boiler twice
twice to repair the boiler

feedback.why_key: Refuse belongs to the to pile, and it stays there whatever tense is wrapped round it.
feedback.feed_forward: Fix the shape from the verb, then worry about the tense.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a delay to the Ashfield recycling scheme.

expected: the council has postponed replacing the recycling bins

feedback.why_key: Postpone takes the -ing shape, and that shape sits directly against the verb with nothing between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the second verb straight after the first, in the shape the first one wants.

payload.audio_text: They've agreed to look at it, but they keep putting the meeting off.

expected: they've agreed to look at it, but they keep putting the meeting off
they have agreed to look at it, but they keep putting the meeting off
theyve agreed to look at it but they keep putting the meeting off

feedback.why_key: In speech the to after agreed is almost swallowed. If you never hear it you will never write it, and the sentence will come out as agreed look.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small unstressed to riding between the two verbs.

payload.sentence: Most students avoid to ask questions in a full lecture theatre.

expected: avoid asking

feedback.why_key: Avoid is in the -ing pile. Nothing in the sentence signals it, which is why this one has to be retrieved rather than reasoned out.
feedback.feed_forward: When the fix is a list fact, retrieve it; do not argue from meaning.

payload.context: Someone talking about their shifts at the hospital.
payload.sentence: I've decided cutting down on nights, but I don't mind to work weekends.
reasons: both verbs have taken the wrong shape
only the first verb has taken the wrong shape
only the second verb has taken the wrong shape
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Decide belongs with to and mind belongs with -ing, so the sentence has them the wrong way round twice over.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each verb against its own pile before you move on.

payload.prompt_text: A town is about to start collecting food waste from every street. Write one sentence saying what households will have to stop doing and what the council has agreed to provide.

feedback.why_key: The prompt forces one verb from each pile into the same sentence, which is where the error normally appears.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the first verb, then ask it what shape it wants.

payload.prompt_text: Take the body paragraph you wrote on the four-day week. Rewrite two sentences so that each one has a verb sitting on top of another verb, and check both shapes before you stop. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Under time pressure the default shape wins, and the default shape is to. Two sentences is enough to catch that habit in the act.
feedback.feed_forward: On the reread, look only at pairs of verbs standing next to each other.

title: Saying what one thing gets somebody else to do

point_json.grammar_name: Verb + object + to-infinitive

teach.can_do: I can say that one thing causes, allows or persuades somebody else to act.
teach.why_it_matters: Most of an essay about policy is sentences about what a rule makes people do. Without this pattern you write two clauses where one carries more.
teach.meaning: A group of very common verbs takes two things after it: a person or thing, and then an action with to in front of it. Allow, encourage, force, enable, persuade, require, expect, remind, cause. The object names who acts; the infinitive names what they do. Between them they pack a cause and its effect into one clause, and the reader sees the link instead of having to build it. The object is part of the pattern, not an optional extra.

form.pattern: verb + object + to + base verb
notes: the object is never dropped: allow people to work, not allow to work
the passive keeps the to: drivers are encouraged to use the park-and-ride
make and let break this pattern by dropping the to — they are handled in their own point
form.negative: The negative sits on the infinitive: the rules allow staff not to attend.
form.question: What does the scheme encourage people to do?

left.text: encourages commuters

right.text: to leave the car at home

spec.caption: The verb names the pressure. The object names who feels it. The infinitive names the result.

worked_example.sentence: Charging for the centre encourages commuters to leave the car at the edge of town.
worked_example.why_this_form: The charge and the behaviour are one causal move, and the pattern keeps them in one clause where the reader can see the join.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The centre charges drivers, so they leave the car states two facts and hands the reader the job of connecting them.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme allows residents to park free after six.
notice_set.question: Who parks?
notice_set.why: The object after the verb is the one who acts, and the infinitive is the action.

notice_set.sentence: The council required the developer to rebuild the footpath.
notice_set.question: Who did the rebuilding?
notice_set.why: Required names the pressure; the developer is the one under it.

notice_set.sentence: Poor lighting caused two drivers to miss the turning.
notice_set.question: Was the lighting driving?
notice_set.why: The subject supplies the cause. The object supplies the person who actually did the thing.

notice_set.sentence: Staff are expected to report faults the same day.
notice_set.question: Who reports faults?
notice_set.why: In the passive the object has moved to the front, but it is still the one who acts.

notice_set.sentence: The grant enabled the clinic to open on Saturdays.
notice_set.question: Was the clinic open on Saturdays before the grant?
notice_set.why: Enable says the action became possible, so it was not happening before.

teach.rule_line: Name the pressure, then who feels it, then what they do.
teach.false_rule: That you can say allow to do something. This group of verbs will not skip the person; the object is part of the pattern, not an option.

errors.wrong: The new rules allow to work from home two days a week.
errors.right: The new rules allow staff to work from home two days a week.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner is treating allow as a one-word permission verb, which is how the equivalent verb works in many first languages. English wants to know who is being allowed before it will take the action.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: staff.
errors.l1_note: Common where the equivalent verb takes only an action.

errors.wrong: The council encouraged residents recycle more of their waste.
errors.right: The council encouraged residents to recycle more of their waste.
errors.why_it_happens: The object arrives correctly and then the action follows bare, on the model of make and let. Those two are the exception; everything else in this group needs the to.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: to.

errors.wrong: Higher fares caused many passengers switching to the bus.
errors.right: Higher fares caused many passengers to switch to the bus.
errors.why_it_happens: Result in takes an -ing form, and cause sits beside it in the learner's mental list of result verbs. The two look interchangeable and take different shapes.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: switching becomes to switch.

errors.wrong: A policy which requires every household to separate food waste.
errors.right: A policy which requires every household to separate food waste has been in place since 2019.
errors.why_it_happens: The pattern is long enough to feel like a finished sentence, and the writer runs out of attention before the main verb ever arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one main verb after the pattern.

pays_in.note: Every policy sentence in an essay is this pattern.
pays_in.model: Free evening travel would encourage older residents to use the network more.

pays_in.note: Part 3 asks what governments should do, and the answer takes this shape.
pays_in.model: It would help if schools encouraged children to cook for themselves.

pays_in.note: Cause-and-effect questions often turn on which noun is the object of the verb.
pays_in.model: The subsidy enabled two operators to keep the rural routes running.

used_in.quote: The whole answer is a series of claims about what closing the centre would make or let people do.
The follow-up questions are about who persuades whom, which is this pattern used aloud.

payload.sentence: The new charge forces delivery firms to use smaller vans in the centre.
payload.question: Who uses the smaller vans?

feedback.why_key: The object of the verb is the one who acts, and the infinitive after it names what they do.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the word after the verb as the person or thing that acts.

payload.sentence: The grant enabled the workshop to take on two apprentices.
payload.question: Could the workshop have taken them on without the grant?

feedback.why_key: Enable says the money is what made the action possible, so it was out of reach until then.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what the subject did to the object before the action happened.

payload.context: From a first draft of a paragraph about recycling rules.
payload.sentence: The scheme would allow to sort their waste at the kerbside.
reasons: the verb has no object, so nobody is being allowed
the infinitive should be an -ing form
the verb should be in the past
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Their has nothing to refer back to, because the person doing the sorting was never named.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the person straight after the verb, before the to.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a park-and-ride scheme.
payload.stem: Cheaper parking on the edge of town encourages drivers ___ (leave) the car outside the centre.

expected: to leave

feedback.why_key: Encourage names the pressure, drivers names who feels it, and the action has to arrive with to in front of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put to before the base verb after this group of verbs.

payload.context: From a note on a new attendance policy.
payload.stem: The rules require ___ to give notice of any absence in writing.

expected: students
staff
parents
pupils

feedback.why_key: Require will not take the action alone. Somebody has to be named between the verb and the to.
feedback.feed_forward: Name who is under the requirement before the infinitive.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a clinic that extended its hours.

expected: longer opening hours allowed the clinic to see forty more patients

feedback.why_key: The cause is the subject, the clinic is the one that acts, and the action comes last with its to.
feedback.feed_forward: Order it as cause, then actor, then action.

payload.given: The council cut the fares. As a result, more people started using the evening buses.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that puts the cause and the behaviour in a single clause.

expected: more people to use the evening buses
people to use the evening buses
more passengers to use the evening buses

feedback.why_key: Two sentences and a linker collapse into one clause, and the causal link is now inside the grammar.
feedback.feed_forward: Fold the result into an infinitive after the object.

payload.given: My manager talked me into it. In the end I applied for the supervisor's job.
payload.instruction: Say it in one clause, naming who was persuaded and what they did.

expected: me to apply for the supervisor's job
me to apply for the supervisors job
me to apply for the job

feedback.why_key: Persuade wants the person first and the action second, which is exactly the order the story happened in.
feedback.feed_forward: Say who was persuaded, then what they did.

payload.audio_text: Residents are expected to separate food waste from packaging.

expected: residents are expected to separate food waste from packaging
residents are expected to separate food waste from the packaging

feedback.why_key: Expected to runs together into one unstressed lump, and the to is the part that disappears first.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a to between the participle and the next verb.

payload.sentence: Better cycle lanes would enable to move around the city without a car.

expected: enable people to move
enable residents to move
enable commuters to move

feedback.why_key: Enable has a cause and an action and nobody in between, so the sentence never says who gets the benefit.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert the person between the verb and the to.

payload.prompt_text: A city is thinking of closing its centre to cars. Write one sentence saying what the change would get one named group of people to do.

feedback.why_key: Naming the group and the behaviour in one clause turns an opinion into a claim somebody could argue with.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the pressure, the group, then the behaviour.

payload.prompt_text: Write the solutions paragraph of the car-free centres essay. Use this pattern twice, with two different groups of people, and check that each one names who acts. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: A solutions paragraph is a chain of these clauses, and the chain falls apart wherever the actor is missing.
feedback.feed_forward: After each verb, check that a person is named before the to.

title: Putting the -ing shape after every preposition, with no exceptions

point_json.grammar_name: The -ing form after a preposition

teach.can_do: I can put a verb after by, without, after, instead of or good at without stopping to think.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the one place in the whole area where a real rule exists, it never has exceptions, and it repairs a very common written error at the same time.
teach.meaning: A preposition is a word that expects a thing after it: after lunch, without a ticket, good at maths. When what follows is an action rather than a thing, English turns the action into a thing by adding -ing. That is all -ing is doing here. It is not saying the action is long, or repeated, or still running. It is the shape a verb wears when it has to stand where a noun would stand.

form.pattern: preposition + verb-ing
notes: Common ones: by, without, after, before, instead of, on, in, for, about, of, at, with, since, apart from
Despite and in spite of are prepositions, so they take -ing or a noun and never a full clause
A few phrases end in the word to and that to is a preposition: look forward to, object to, be used to, be committed to, in addition to. The verb after them is -ing
A preposition can never be followed by to plus the base verb. There is no sentence in English where it can
form.negative: The word not goes between the preposition and the -ing: she apologised for not telling us sooner.
form.question: Is the word in front of the gap a preposition? Then the question is already answered.

left.role: the word before the gap is a preposition
left.text: by / without / after / instead of / good at / look forward to

right.role: so the verb can only wear -ing
right.text: closing, saying, finishing, replacing, fixing, hearing

spec.caption: One arrow, no branches. This is the only part of the unit where knowing the rule is enough.

worked_example.sentence: The depot cut its emissions by replacing the two oldest vans.
worked_example.why_this_form: By is a preposition, so whatever follows it has to stand where a noun stands. Replacing is the verb replace wearing the shape that lets it do that.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: By to replace has no meaning available to it. The preposition has asked for a thing and been handed something that cannot be one.

notice_set.sentence: They cut costs by closing the two smallest depots.
notice_set.question: How were the costs cut?
notice_set.why: By names the method, and the action that is the method turns up in the -ing shape because by needs a thing after it.

notice_set.sentence: She left the meeting without saying anything.
notice_set.question: Did she say anything?
notice_set.why: Without is a preposition, so the action it rules out arrives as saying rather than as to say.

notice_set.sentence: After finishing the river survey, the team drove back to Verdon.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: After puts one thing before the other, and the thing it puts first is an action in the -ing shape.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme went ahead in spite of costing twice the estimate.
notice_set.question: Did the scheme cost more than expected?
notice_set.why: In spite of is a preposition, so the cost comes in as a thing. This is why despite cannot be followed by a full clause.

notice_set.sentence: I am looking forward to hearing from the housing office.
notice_set.question: Has the housing office written back yet?
notice_set.why: The to in look forward to is a preposition, not the to of to do. That is why hearing and not hear follows it.

notice_set.sentence: He apologised for arriving forty minutes late.
notice_set.question: Did he arrive late?
notice_set.why: For is a preposition, so the thing being apologised for is an action wearing the -ing shape.

discovery.prompt: One of these columns is impossible English. Work out what the left-hand words have in common.
pairs: We saved money by cycling.
We saved money to cycle.
She went out without locking up.
She went out without to lock up.
I object to paying twice.
I object to pay twice.

candidate_rules.text: By, without and object to all end in a preposition, and a preposition can only be followed by -ing.
Short linking words like by and without take -ing.
When the sentence contains the word to, the verb goes in its base form.

teach.rule_line: If the word before the gap is a preposition, the verb after it must be -ing.
teach.false_rule: That the word to is always followed by the base verb. In look forward to, object to and be used to, to is a preposition.

errors.wrong: Despite the survey was finished on time, the report arrived in June.
errors.right: Despite finishing the survey on time, the report arrived in June.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite means what although means, so it inherits although's grammar. Nobody mentions that one is a preposition and the other joins clauses, and the meaning gives no clue.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: was finished becomes finishing, and the subject goes.

errors.wrong: I look forward to hear from you about the tenancy.
errors.right: I look forward to hearing from you about the tenancy.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner sees to and applies the only rule they have for it. The to in look forward to is a preposition and looks identical to the other one.
errors.smallest_fix: Add three letters: hear becomes hearing.

errors.wrong: The council reduced waste by to collect food scraps separately.
errors.right: The council reduced waste by collecting food scraps separately.
errors.why_it_happens: To do is the default shape for a second verb, and it goes in even after a preposition that has no room for it. The result is a shape English cannot read at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word and add three letters: by to collect becomes by collecting.

errors.wrong: She is used to work nights, so the shift does not bother her.
errors.right: She is used to working nights, so the shift does not bother her.
errors.why_it_happens: Be used to and used to look the same and are learned at the same time. One is a preposition phrase about being accustomed; the other is a past habit and takes the base verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Add three letters: work becomes working.

pays_in.note: Every sentence about method, cause or concession runs through a preposition.
pays_in.model: Cities have cut congestion by charging for road space rather than by widening it.

pays_in.note: The standard closing line of a formal letter turns on this rule.
pays_in.model: I look forward to receiving confirmation that the repairs have been booked.

pays_in.note: Explaining how something could be done needs by plus -ing.
pays_in.model: You could cut most of that waste just by planning the week's meals in advance.

pays_in.note: A concession clause built on despite compresses a whole claim.
pays_in.model: Despite falling steadily since 2016, the figure remains above the national average.

used_in.quote: Every solution sentence in this task is built on by plus an action, and the action has to be a thing before by will take it.

payload.sentence: We got the bill down by turning the heating off at night.
payload.question: What brought the bill down?

feedback.why_key: By points at the method, and the method is an action that has been turned into a thing so that by can hold it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read by as how, then expect an -ing straight after it.

payload.sentence: Despite cutting its staff by a third, the depot met every delivery slot.
payload.question: Did the depot lose staff?

feedback.why_key: Despite is a preposition, so the staff cut arrives as a thing. The sentence still asserts it happened.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat despite plus -ing as a fact the writer accepts.

payload.context: The last line of a letter to a letting agency.
payload.sentence: I look forward to hear from you before the end of the month.
reasons: the to in look forward to is a preposition, so it needs -ing
look forward is the wrong verb for a letter
the sentence needs a subject after hear
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two identical-looking words are doing different jobs. This to is the kind that ends a phrase, not the kind that starts a verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the to belongs to the phrase in front of it.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a town-wide recycling trial.
payload.stem: Ashfield halved its landfill waste by ___ (sort) glass at the kerbside.

expected: sorting

feedback.why_key: By is a preposition and there is no second option. This is the one gap in the unit you can fill without knowing the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Spot the preposition first; the shape follows automatically.

payload.context: Someone describing their commute since the tram opened.
payload.stem: I am used to ___ (stand) now, and I leave without ___ (check) the timetable.

expected: standing, checking
standing checking

feedback.why_key: Both gaps sit behind a preposition, and the to in am used to is one of them. Neither gap has a choice to make.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether to belongs to a phrase before you treat it as an infinitive.

payload.given: Although the college raised its fees, applications went up.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it starting with despite, keeping the same meaning.

expected: raising its fees, applications went up
raising its fees, the college's applications went up
raising its fees applications went up

feedback.why_key: Despite cannot hold a clause, so the clause has to be squeezed into an -ing shape before it will fit.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap although for despite and the verb loses its subject and gains -ing.

payload.context: Build one sentence for a report on a small savings scheme.

expected: the fund grew without taking on any new risk

feedback.why_key: Without has to sit directly in front of the -ing shape. Nothing can come between a preposition and the thing it holds.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the preposition and the -ing word next to each other.

payload.audio_text: We cut the waste right down by planning the week's meals before shopping.

expected: we cut the waste right down by planning the week's meals before shopping
we cut the waste right down by planning the weeks meals before shopping

feedback.why_key: Two prepositions and two -ing shapes in one short sentence. In speech the endings are light, and light is exactly what learners stop writing.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the -ing ending even when you barely hear it.

payload.sentence: Many households now rent tools instead of to buy them outright.

expected: instead of buying

feedback.why_key: Instead of ends in the preposition of, and of will not hold an infinitive. The fix is the ending, not the word.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at the last word before the gap, not the first.

payload.sentence: Despite the rent was rising every year, most tenants stayed in the district.

expected: despite rising rents
although the rent was rising
despite the rising rent
despite the rent rising

feedback.why_key: Despite is holding a full clause, which it cannot do. Either the clause shrinks to a thing or the word changes to one that takes clauses.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide which side to move: shrink the clause or swap the connector.

payload.context: Someone talking about training for a half marathon.
payload.sentence: I used to running before work, but now I go at lunchtime.
reasons: this used to is the past habit one, so it takes the base verb
used to always takes -ing
the sentence needs but replaced with and
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Used to on its own is a past habit and takes run. It is only be used to, with a form of be in front, that ends in a preposition.
feedback.feed_forward: Look for a form of be before used to before you reach for -ing.

payload.prompt_text: Someone asks how an ordinary household could cut its water use. Answer in one sentence that begins with a method, using by.

feedback.why_key: By plus -ing is the fastest way to answer a how question, and it is available before you have decided how the sentence ends.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with by, then let the -ing word carry the idea.

payload.prompt_text: Go back to your food-waste answer. Rewrite one solution sentence so it names the method with by plus -ing, and one concession sentence so it opens with despite plus -ing. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Despite plus a full clause is the error that survives longest, because it only appears when the sentence is long enough to forget how it started.
feedback.feed_forward: After writing despite, check that no subject follows it.

title: Deciding between despite and although by looking at what comes next

point_json.grammar_name: despite / in spite of + noun or -ing, versus although + clause

teach.can_do: I can choose between despite and although by looking at what I am about to write next.
teach.why_it_matters: Despite he was tired is one of the most common written errors at this level, and the fix is a question about the next four words, not about meaning.
teach.meaning: Despite, in spite of and although all mark the same turn, and almost no learner ever gets the meaning wrong. What goes wrong is the grammar on the right of the word. Although is a clause word: a subject and its verb must follow it. Despite and in spite of are prepositions: a noun, a pronoun or an -ing form must follow them, and never a subject with a verb. So the decision is not about what you mean at all. It is about what shape the next few words are going to take.

form.pattern: although + subject + verb ... | despite / in spite of + noun phrase or -ing form ...
notes: In spite of is three words and despite is one. There is no despite of.
To put a clause after despite you have to wrap it first: despite the fact that the cost rose. Correct, and four words longer than although.
Either can start the sentence or sit in the middle. The comma goes in only when the concession comes first.
form.negative: Negatives change nothing about the choice: although the funding was not renewed, or despite the loss of funding.
form.question: Ask what the word straight after the linker is going to be: a subject, or a noun?

left.role: although: a subject and a verb follow
left.text: although the cost rose

right.role: despite: a noun or an -ing form follows
right.text: despite the rising cost

spec.caption: Same meaning, two different shapes on the right-hand side. The shape is the whole decision.

worked_example.sentence: Despite the rise in fuel duty, freight traffic on the motorway kept growing.
worked_example.why_this_form: What follows the linker is a noun phrase — the rise — with no verb of its own, and a noun phrase is exactly what despite takes.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Although the rise in fuel duty is not a milder version of the same sentence. It is an unfinished clause, and the reader waits for a verb that never arrives.

notice_set.sentence: Despite the heavy rain, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after despite?
notice_set.why: The heavy rain has no verb in it, so it is a noun phrase, and that is what despite requires.

notice_set.sentence: Although it rained heavily, the survey went ahead.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after although?
notice_set.why: It rained is a subject and its verb, which is exactly what although requires.

notice_set.sentence: Despite losing two days to the weather, the team finished the survey.
notice_set.question: What comes straight after despite?
notice_set.why: Losing is an -ing form, and despite takes those as happily as it takes nouns.
