used_in.quote: Each solution in this essay is an activity, and each one reads better as the subject of its own sentence.
The passage opens several paragraphs with an activity as the subject, which is where the topic of each one sits.

payload.sentence: Insulating older houses cuts more carbon than any new build ever will.
payload.question: What is being compared with new building?

feedback.why_key: The activity holds the subject slot, so the activity is what the comparison is between.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the whole -ing phrase as one thing before you look for the verb.

payload.sentence: Marking two hundred scripts a week leaves very little room for anything else.
payload.question: How many things is the verb agreeing with?

feedback.why_key: The subject is the marking, not the scripts, and one activity takes a singular verb however big it is.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the head of the subject before you check the ending.

items.decision_cue: Replanting the hillsides above the reservoir

payload.context: From a first draft of an essay paragraph.
payload.sentence: Replanting the hillsides above the reservoir over the next fifteen years.
reasons: the subject is there but nothing is said about it
the -ing form should be a bare verb
the sentence needs an article at the front
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The phrase names an activity and then stops. A subject on its own is not a sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Give the -ing subject a verb before the full stop.

payload.context: From a paragraph about household energy.
payload.stem: Replacing old boilers across a whole street ___ (cost) less than most people assume.

expected: costs

feedback.why_key: The subject is the replacing, which is one activity, so the verb takes the singular ending.
feedback.feed_forward: Agree the verb with the activity, not with the nearest noun.

payload.context: From a paragraph about workplace health.
payload.stem: ___ (walk) part of the commute makes more difference than an hour in a gym.

expected: walking

feedback.why_key: A bare verb cannot be a subject, so it has to become a thing first, and -ing is how English does that.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn the verb into an -ing form before you put it in the subject slot.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a city-centre housing scheme.

expected: converting empty offices into flats has housed four hundred families

feedback.why_key: The whole activity comes first as one block, and only then does the sentence get its verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the subject phrase before you start the verb.

payload.given: When councils close rural bus routes, they save very little money.
payload.instruction: Rewrite so that the closing itself is the subject of the sentence.

expected: rural bus routes saves very little money
rural bus routes saves councils very little money
rural bus routes saves very little

feedback.why_key: The councils have left the sentence and the activity has taken their place, which is what the argument was about anyway.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the activity into the subject slot and drop the human subject.

payload.given: People work from home two days a week now. It has changed how the city centre feels.
payload.instruction: Say it in one sentence with the activity as the subject.

expected: has changed how the city centre feels
two days a week has changed how the city centre feels
has changed the way the city centre feels

feedback.why_key: One activity is doing the changing, so the verb stays singular even though it took a crowd of people to do it.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the verb singular after an -ing subject.

payload.audio_text: Raising wages hasn't closed the gap on its own.

expected: raising wages hasn't closed the gap on its own
raising wages has not closed the gap on its own
raising wages hasnt closed the gap on its own

feedback.why_key: Hasn't and haven't sound close at speed, and the one you write says whether you heard the subject as one thing or many.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the singular auxiliary after an -ing subject.

items.decision_cue: in the two largest cities have

payload.sentence: Banning older diesel vehicles in the two largest cities have made almost no difference to roadside readings.

expected: cities has made

feedback.why_key: The subject is the banning, not the cities. Two cities sit next to the verb and steal the agreement.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to the -ing form before choosing its ending.

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence about a way of cutting household waste, making the activity itself the subject and saying what it achieves.

feedback.why_key: Putting the activity first makes the sentence a claim about the activity, which is what a body paragraph argues over.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the activity, then say what it does.

payload.prompt_text: Rewrite the solutions paragraph of your sedentary-working-day answer so that two sentences open with an activity as the subject. Check the verb after each one. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: A solutions paragraph built on activities argues about what works. One built on people argues about who to blame.
feedback.feed_forward: Open two sentences with an activity, then check both verbs.

title: Getting the small word right after an adjective

point_json.grammar_name: Adjective + preposition + -ing

teach.can_do: I can put the right preposition after an adjective and the right verb form after that preposition.
teach.why_it_matters: Two mistakes stacked inside three words, and both are visible. They cost lexical marks as well as grammar marks, which is why fixing them pays twice.
teach.meaning: Many adjectives will not stand next to a verb on their own. They need a preposition first, and which preposition is decided by the adjective rather than by the meaning: responsible for, capable of, committed to, involved in, aware of, keen on, dependent on. Once the preposition is in place, whatever follows it has to be a noun or an -ing form, because that is all a preposition will take. The two rules meet inside the same three words, which is why the errors come in pairs.

form.pattern: adjective + its own preposition + -ing
notes: the preposition belongs to the adjective and has to be learned with it, like a second syllable
committed to and dedicated to end in to, and that to is a preposition, so -ing follows it
aware of, capable of, guilty of; responsible for, famous for, known for; involved in, interested in, successful in
form.negative: Not responsible for cutting — the not goes in front of the adjective, never in front of the preposition.
form.question: Who is responsible for approving the budget?

left.role: the adjective and its own preposition
left.text: responsible for

right.text: cutting the waiting list

spec.caption: Two fixed choices in a row: which preposition, and then which verb form.

worked_example.sentence: The trust is responsible for cutting the waiting list by a third this year.
worked_example.why_this_form: Responsible carries for wherever it goes, and once for is in place the verb has no choice left: it becomes cutting.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Responsible to cut is not a different meaning. It is a sentence that stops making sense at the preposition and has to be reread.

notice_set.sentence: She is capable of running the whole depot on her own.
notice_set.question: Is she running it now?
notice_set.why: Capable of names an ability, not a current arrangement.

notice_set.sentence: The firm is committed to reducing packaging by 2030.
notice_set.question: What has the firm promised?
notice_set.why: Committed to takes what follows as a thing promised, which is why the verb turns into an -ing form.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody was aware of the change until Friday.
notice_set.question: Did people know before Friday?
notice_set.why: Aware of takes a thing, and the thing here is the change.

notice_set.sentence: Two departments are involved in checking the figures.
notice_set.question: How many departments do the checking?
notice_set.why: Involved in takes the activity, and the -ing form is what the preposition allows.

notice_set.sentence: The town is famous for making rope.
notice_set.question: Is the town doing something, or known for something?
notice_set.why: Famous for names what the place is known for, and for takes an -ing form.

teach.rule_line: Learn the preposition with the adjective, then let it force the -ing.
teach.false_rule: That the preposition can be worked out from the meaning. It cannot. Good at and skilled in mean nearly the same thing and take different words.

errors.wrong: The department is responsible of approving new contracts.
errors.right: The department is responsible for approving new contracts.
errors.why_it_happens: Of is the commonest preposition after an adjective, so it arrives by default whenever the stored pair is missing. Nothing about the meaning would warn the learner off it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: of becomes for.

errors.wrong: The company is committed to reduce its packaging by a third.
errors.right: The company is committed to reducing its packaging by a third.
errors.why_it_happens: The to looks like the to of an infinitive, and every instinct the learner has says a bare verb follows it. Here it is a preposition, and prepositions do not take bare verbs.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: reduce becomes reducing.

errors.wrong: She is very good in explaining things to new staff.
errors.right: She is very good at explaining things to new staff.
errors.why_it_happens: In is right after successful and skilled, and the learner generalises across a group of adjectives that look interchangeable and are not.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: in becomes at.

errors.wrong: They are responsible for the reduce of waste on site.
errors.right: They are responsible for reducing waste on site.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows a noun can follow a preposition and goes looking for one, but reduce is not a noun. The -ing form is the noun this verb already has.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: the reduce of becomes reducing.

pays_in.note: Responsibility and capability sentences are the spine of a solutions paragraph.
pays_in.model: Employers are capable of cutting commuting without cutting anybody's hours.

pays_in.note: Part 3 keeps asking who should be responsible for what.
pays_in.model: Schools are better at teaching this than most parents are, honestly.

pays_in.note: A letter of complaint has to name who is responsible for what.
pays_in.model: I understand the agency is responsible for arranging repairs of this kind.

used_in.quote: The essay has to say who is capable of what and who is responsible for what, which is this pattern half a dozen times.
Questions about who should give advice are answered with adjectives that all carry their own preposition.

payload.sentence: The site manager is responsible for checking every load before it leaves.
payload.question: Who does the checking?

feedback.why_key: Responsible for names the duty, and the person carrying it is the subject of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the adjective and its preposition as one unit.

payload.sentence: The operator is committed to cutting its water use by a fifth.
payload.question: Has the cut already happened?

feedback.why_key: Committed to names a promise, so the cutting is still in front of them rather than behind them.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat the to in committed to as a preposition, not an infinitive.

payload.context: From a first draft of a paragraph about staff retention.
payload.sentence: The firm says it is committed to increase pay for its lowest-paid staff.
reasons: the to here is a preposition, so an -ing form has to follow it
the adjective needs a different preposition
the verb should be in the past
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Committed carries to as its own preposition, and prepositions never take a bare verb.
feedback.feed_forward: After committed to, write the -ing form.

payload.context: From a note on who signs off what.
payload.stem: The finance team is responsible ___ approving anything over five thousand pounds.

expected: for

feedback.why_key: Responsible carries for and nothing else, which is why the pair has to be stored as one item.
feedback.feed_forward: Store responsible for as a single chunk.

payload.context: From a paragraph about coastal defences.
payload.stem: Older sea walls are simply not capable of ___ (hold) back a surge of that size.

expected: holding

feedback.why_key: Of is a preposition, and a preposition takes the -ing form whatever the verb happens to be.
feedback.feed_forward: Put -ing on the verb straight after the preposition.

payload.context: Someone talking about a course they are on.
payload.stem: I've always been quite good ___ picking up the grammar, it's the speaking that goes.

expected: at

feedback.why_key: Good takes at, and no amount of thinking about ability will produce it. It has to be remembered.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn good at as one chunk, like a two-word adjective.

payload.given: The trust will reduce waiting times by a third. It has said so publicly.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence using committed and the right two words after it.

expected: to reducing waiting times by a third
to cutting waiting times by a third

feedback.why_key: The to belongs to committed rather than to the verb, so the verb has to arrive as an -ing form.
feedback.feed_forward: Write committed to, then add -ing to the verb.

payload.audio_text: We're not really involved in running the site any more.

expected: we're not really involved in running the site any more
we are not really involved in running the site any more
were not really involved in running the site any more

feedback.why_key: The preposition is unstressed and sits between two longer words, which is exactly where a small word goes missing.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the little word between the adjective and the -ing.

payload.sentence: The whole restoration project is dependent of continued funding from the regional authority.

expected: dependent on
dependent upon

feedback.why_key: Depend on is known, but the adjective is stored separately and picks up of from the crowd around it.
feedback.feed_forward: Carry the preposition across from the verb you already know.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about how firms recruit.
payload.sentence: Line managers are now responsible of hiring their own teams.
reasons: the adjective takes a different preposition
the verb after the preposition is the wrong form
the subject and verb do not agree
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The -ing form after the preposition is right. It is the preposition itself that the adjective refuses.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the preposition first, then the verb form.

payload.sentence: Far more adults are interested in learn a second language than actually enrol.

expected: interested in learning

feedback.why_key: The preposition is right and the verb form is not, which is the other half of the same three-word problem.
feedback.feed_forward: Add -ing to any verb that follows a preposition.

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence about who should deal with long working hours, using responsible for or capable of and an -ing form after it.

feedback.why_key: Naming who is responsible and for what is how a solutions paragraph stops being a wish list.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the adjective, its preposition, then the -ing form.

payload.prompt_text: Write the solutions paragraph of the sedentary-working-day essay using three different adjective-plus-preposition pairs. Underline each preposition and check the form after it. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Three pairs in one paragraph is where the habit either holds or comes apart, and it comes apart in the same two places every time.
feedback.feed_forward: Check every preposition, then every verb form after it.

title: Saying who made, let or helped somebody do something

point_json.grammar_name: make, let, have, get and help + object + verb form

teach.can_do: I can use make, let, have, get and help correctly, even though each one takes a different form after its object.
teach.why_it_matters: Five extremely common verbs, five different shapes, and no rule joining them. Getting one wrong is audible in the first minute of a speaking test.
teach.meaning: This is a closed set, and it has to be memorised rather than worked out. All five say that one person brings about an action by somebody else, and they differ in how much pressure is applied and in what form the second verb takes. Make and let take a bare verb. Have takes a bare verb when you are arranging something as a matter of course. Get takes to, because it means persuading. Help takes either, and nobody minds which one you pick.

form.pattern: make / let / have + object + bare verb; get + object + to + verb; help + object + (to) + verb
notes: make somebody do, let somebody do, have somebody do — no to anywhere
get somebody to do is the only member of the group that keeps the to
help somebody do and help somebody to do are both correct English
in the passive, make picks the to back up: staff were made to sign
form.negative: Let does not go negative comfortably; use not allow instead: the rules do not allow staff to leave early.
form.question: What made you change your mind?

spec.label: how much pressure is being applied?

steps.gloss: you permit it
you make it easier
you persuade
you arrange it as a matter of course
they have no choice

worked_example.sentence: The head let the sixth form run the open evening themselves.
worked_example.why_this_form: Let takes the bare verb, with nothing standing between the students and the running, and that bareness is part of what the verb means: no pressure applied.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Let the sixth form to run is not a softer version of the same sentence. It is a sentence the reader stumbles over and has to repair before carrying on.

notice_set.sentence: The school made every pupil sit the test again.
notice_set.question: Did the pupils have a choice?
notice_set.why: Make is the strongest of the five, and the bare verb goes straight after the object.

notice_set.sentence: She got two colleagues to check the figures.
notice_set.question: Did she check them herself?
notice_set.why: Get names persuading somebody else, and it is the one verb here that keeps its to.

notice_set.sentence: They had the surveyor come back on Friday.
notice_set.question: Who came back?
notice_set.why: The object is the person who acts, and the verb after it arrives bare.

notice_set.sentence: He helped his sister move the boxes.
notice_set.question: How many people moved boxes?
notice_set.why: Help means both were involved, and the verb after the object can go bare.

notice_set.sentence: Staff were made to sign a new contract.
notice_set.question: Did they want to?
notice_set.why: The passive of make brings the to back, and the sentence reports pressure without reporting anyone's feelings.

teach.rule_line: Make, let and have take a bare verb; get takes to; help takes either.
teach.false_rule: That these five behave alike because they mean nearly the same thing. Meaning does not decide the pattern here. The individual verb does, and there are only five to learn.

errors.wrong: The new rules make staff to log every visitor.
errors.right: The new rules make staff log every visitor.
errors.why_it_happens: Make is being treated like force and require, which do take to. The learner has generalised from a much larger group onto one of the few exceptions.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: Her supervisor let her to leave an hour early.
errors.right: Her supervisor let her leave an hour early.
errors.why_it_happens: Let sits in the mind right next to allow, and allow takes an object and to. The two verbs are near-synonyms with different shapes, and nothing in the meaning warns you.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: We finally got the landlord fix the boiler.
errors.right: We finally got the landlord to fix the boiler.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has stored make and let correctly and extends the bare verb across the whole group. Get is the one member that wants its to kept.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: to.

errors.wrong: The scheme helps students to finding work in the region.
errors.right: The scheme helps students find work in the region.
errors.why_it_happens: Two patterns are being merged: help plus to plus a verb, and a preposition plus an -ing form. Only one of them can be right at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one phrase: to finding becomes find.

pays_in.note: Part 1 answers about school and family run on made me and let me.
pays_in.model: My parents let me choose the subjects, which not everyone gets.

pays_in.note: Policy sentences need the difference between making people act and helping them.
pays_in.model: Fining drivers makes them slow down; better lighting helps them see the junction.

pays_in.note: A speaker's attitude often sits in which of the five they reach for.
pays_in.model: They had the whole team come in on the Saturday.

used_in.quote: Answers about what a course or a job requires of you come out as made me, let me and got me to.
The essay has to distinguish between forcing drivers out of the centre and helping them leave the car behind.

payload.sentence: My parents let me drop chemistry after the first year.
payload.question: Did the speaker want to drop it?

feedback.why_key: Let means permission was given for something the speaker was after, which is why no pressure is anywhere in the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Read let as permission and make as pressure.

payload.sentence: The auditor got two of the managers to reopen the files.
payload.question: Who reopened the files?

feedback.why_key: Get names persuading, so the work was done by the people named after the verb rather than by the person applying the pressure.
feedback.feed_forward: The object of these verbs is always the one who acts.

payload.context: From a first draft of a paragraph about shift patterns.
payload.sentence: Some contracts still make employees to work six days in a row.
reasons: make does not take to before the second verb
the object should come after the second verb
the main verb should be in the past
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Make takes the bare verb. The to has arrived from force and require, which are not in this group.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete to after make and let.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a change to the timetable.
payload.stem: The new rule makes every pupil ___ (choose) a practical subject in the third year.

expected: choose

feedback.why_key: Make takes the verb bare, with nothing at all between the pupil and the choosing.
feedback.feed_forward: After make, write the verb with no to in front of it.

payload.context: Someone talking about growing up in a big household.
payload.stem: It took us weeks to get my father ___ (agree) to a shared calendar.

expected: to agree

feedback.why_key: Get is the one verb in the group that keeps its to, and weeks of persuading is exactly what it means.
feedback.feed_forward: After get, keep the to.

payload.context: From a letter about work on a flat.
payload.stem: I would like to have an engineer ___ (inspect) the boiler before the winter.

expected: inspect

feedback.why_key: Have used for arranging something takes the bare verb, the same as make and let.
feedback.feed_forward: After have, leave the verb bare.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a depot training week.

expected: the training helped the new drivers read the route cards faster

feedback.why_key: Help takes the object first and then the verb, and the verb can go bare with nothing lost.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the person straight after help, then the verb.

payload.audio_text: They wouldn't let us take the books home.

expected: they wouldn't let us take the books home
they would not let us take the books home
they wouldnt let us take the books home

feedback.why_key: Let us take runs together at speed, and if you hear a to that is not there you will write one.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the gap where a to would be, and leave it empty after let.

payload.sentence: The agency would not let us to move in until the certificate had come through.

expected: let us move

feedback.why_key: Let refuses the to, however much it looks like allow. The two verbs mean the same and are built differently.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete to after let.

items.decision_cue: got the whole department fill in

payload.sentence: In the end she got the whole department fill in the same form twice.

expected: department to fill in

feedback.why_key: Getting a department to do anything is persuasion, and persuasion is the one meaning in this group that keeps its to.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert to after the object when the verb is get.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a work-placement scheme.
payload.sentence: The scheme helps students to finding paid work in their final year.
reasons: two patterns have been mixed and the verb form is wrong
help cannot take an object at all
the subject and the verb do not agree
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Help takes find or to find. What it will not take is a to with an -ing form behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: After help, choose the bare verb or to plus the verb, never both patterns at once.

payload.prompt_text: Say one thing your family made you do as a child and one thing they let you do. Two clauses, one sentence.

feedback.why_key: Made and let side by side is where the shared bare verb becomes obvious, and where a stray to would stand out.
feedback.feed_forward: Use the bare verb after both made and let.

payload.prompt_text: Answer the Part 1 questions about your work or studies. Somewhere in your answers, use make, let and get about the people around you, and keep the form right on each one. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: These three arrive early in a speaking test and they arrive fast, which is the only condition under which the pattern really has to be automatic.
feedback.feed_forward: Bare verb after make and let, to after get.

title: Deciding whether to move a reported verb back, instead of doing it automatically

point_json.grammar_name: Backshift as a choice

teach.can_do: I can decide whether a reported verb should step back, instead of stepping it back every time.
teach.why_it_matters: The step back is a claim about whether the thing is still true. Applied automatically it puts live facts quietly into the past.
teach.meaning: Moving the verb back is not a tax you pay for having written said. It is a small piece of distancing, and your reader feels it. The step back says: I am reporting this from outside the moment it was spoken, and I am not standing behind it as I write. Leaving the verb where it is says the opposite — the situation has not moved, and this is a statement that is still live. English offers you both, and whichever you take, the reader takes something from it.

form.pattern: said / told + (that) + [verb stepped back]  OR  said / told + (that) + [verb left alone]
notes: after a present-tense reporting verb — says, argues, claims, points out — nothing steps back at all
a past reporting verb makes the step available, never compulsory
will becomes would, can becomes could, may becomes might; must and should do not move
an event that finished before the speaking still steps back, because the order has to stay visible
form.negative: He said he did not think the figures were reliable. / He said he does not think the figures are reliable.
form.question: Before you write said, ask: is this still true as I write?

ends: still true as I write, and I will say so
sealed inside the moment it was spoken

marks.label: She said the fee is forty pounds — I am passing on a live fact
She said the fee was forty pounds — I take no position on today
She said the fee was forty pounds, though it has gone up since

worked_example.sentence: The tutor said the library opens at eight, so there is no rush.
worked_example.why_this_form: The opening time has not changed between her saying it and you passing it on, and the second half of your sentence is leaning on that.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Opened would seal the hours inside her sentence, and a reader would wonder whether they had since changed — which the rest of your sentence denies.

notice_set.sentence: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon is safe to drink.
notice_set.question: What has the person reporting committed themselves to?
options: that the water is safe as they write
that the water was safe only when Kemi spoke
notice_set.why: Leaving the verb alone hands the claim on as live, and the reporter has signed it on the way past.

notice_set.sentence: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon was safe to drink.
notice_set.question: Does this version say the water is unsafe today?
options: No, it simply declines to say
notice_set.why: The step back is a refusal to take a position, not a denial. It hands you Kemi's words and stops.

notice_set.sentence: The porter said the lift was out of order, but it seems fine to me.
notice_set.question: Why does the second half sit comfortably here?
options: because the report was sealed at the moment he spoke
notice_set.why: The step back left room for an update, and the second clause walks straight into it.

notice_set.sentence: The porter said the lift is out of order, so take the stairs.
notice_set.question: Is the lift broken as the speaker says this?
notice_set.why: The verb was left alone, so the report is a live instruction rather than a piece of history.

notice_set.sentence: The survey found that older houses lose more heat through the roof than through the walls.
notice_set.question: Is this claim tied to the moment of the survey?
options: No, it is offered as generally true
notice_set.why: Nothing about the claim has an end date, so there is nothing for the step back to mark.

notice_set.sentence: She said she was living in Marlow.
notice_set.question: Is she living in Marlow now?
notice_set.why: The stepped-back verb covers the moment she spoke and makes no offer about anything later.

discovery.prompt: Each pair reports exactly the same words. Work out what the right-hand version is refusing to claim.
pairs: Kemi said the tap water in Verdon is safe to drink.
Kemi said the tap water in Verdon was safe to drink.
The porter said the lift is out of order.
The porter said the lift was out of order.
The letter said the deposit is refundable.
The letter said the deposit was refundable.

candidate_rules.text: The left-hand version keeps the claim live as the writer writes; the right-hand version seals it inside the moment it was spoken.
The left-hand version is for facts and the right-hand version is for opinions.
A past reporting verb such as said forces every verb after it into a past form.

teach.rule_line: Ask whether it is still true as you write. If it is, you may leave the verb alone.
teach.false_rule: That said pushes every following verb one step back. It offers the step; it does not demand it, and taking it always tells your reader something.

contrast.question: Is what they said still true as I write this?

fork.answer: Still true, and I am content to stand behind it: leave the verb where it is
Over, changed, or not something I want to vouch for: step the verb back

a.text: The agent said the flat is available from the first of the month.
a.means: It is available as I write. I am passing on a fact I expect to hold.

b.text: The agent said the flat was available from the first of the month.
b.means: That is what he told me at the time. Whether it has since gone, I am not saying.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote was. A reader takes that as a deliberate step back: you are reporting what the agent said then and declining to say whether it holds now. If you meant the flat is there today, was has quietly withdrawn the only useful part of your sentence.

edge_case.text: After a reporting verb in the present — says, argues, claims, points out — nothing steps back at all, because there is no distance to mark and no choice to make. That is the single context where the question does not arise. Everything else you have read about compulsory shifts, leave it there.

contrast.stronger_test: Read the reported clause aloud on its own, as a statement of your own. If you would say it that way today, leave the verb alone. If saying it that way would make you a liar, step it back.

worked_pairs.a: The council said the footbridge is closed until the spring.
worked_pairs.b: The council said the footbridge was closed for most of last winter.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first closure is still running as you write. The second finished before you started, so there is nothing live left to keep.

worked_pairs.a: The letter said the deposit is refundable, so I have not paid the extra.
worked_pairs.b: The letter said the deposit was refundable, though the terms changed in April.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: so I have not paid the extra
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: though the terms changed in April
worked_pairs.gloss: In the first you are acting on the claim today, so you keep it live. In the second you already know it has expired.

worked_pairs.a: Dr Anand argues that rural bus funding is the cheapest lever available.
worked_pairs.b: Dr Anand argued that rural bus funding was the cheapest lever available.
worked_pairs.gloss: A present reporting verb leaves nothing to decide. Once the reporting verb itself goes back, the choice opens and you have to make it on purpose.

errors.wrong: My landlord said the boiler was fine, so I am not going to call anyone out.
errors.right: My landlord said the boiler is fine, so I am not going to call anyone out.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught that said pushes the next verb back, and applies it without reading on. The step back then withdraws the very claim the second half of the sentence is relying on.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: was becomes is.

errors.wrong: A guest on the programme said vaccines cause more harm than good.
errors.right: A guest on the programme said vaccines caused more harm than good.
errors.why_it_happens: Learners are told the unshifted form is for general truths and apply it to anything phrased like one. Leaving the verb alone reads as the writer signing a claim they never meant to sign.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: cause becomes caused.

errors.wrong: He said he was tired and he wants to go home.
errors.right: He said he was tired and he wanted to go home.
errors.why_it_happens: Both clauses came out of one breath in the original and only the first got re-anchored. Nothing in the situation justifies the split, since he is not tired-then and wanting-now.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: wants becomes wanted.

pays_in.note: Every essay that reports supporters and critics makes this choice.
pays_in.model: Critics of the charge said the savings were speculative; supporters say they are already visible.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers are full of what people say, and the choice shows where you stand.
pays_in.model: A lot of people said the app was a gimmick, but it is still the one everyone uses.

pays_in.note: A True or False stem often turns a sealed report into a live claim.
pays_in.model: The report said the pilot scheme was cheaper to run than the existing service.

used_in.quote: The essay has to report what each side says without accidentally agreeing with either, which is this choice made a dozen times.
Answers here report claims the speaker does not believe, and the stepped-back verb is how a speaker declines to endorse one.

payload.sentence: The surveyor said the roof is sound.
payload.question: What is the writer telling you about the roof today?
options: that it was sound only when the surveyor spoke

feedback.why_key: The verb was left alone, so the report arrives as a live fact and the writer has put their name to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read an unshifted verb as a claim the writer is making now.

payload.sentence: The driver said the coast road was flooded.
payload.question: Does the speaker claim the road is flooded as they speak?
options: No, only that the driver said so at the time
No, they say it is clear

feedback.why_key: The stepped-back verb seals the report inside the driver's moment and leaves the present entirely open.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat a stepped-back verb as a refusal to vouch, not a denial.

items.decision_cue: so I have cancelled my order

payload.context: From a message about a magazine subscription.
payload.sentence: They said the print edition was ending in June, so I have cancelled my order.
reasons: the ending has not happened yet, so the verb should not have moved
the writer has cancelled, so the report is sealed and the step back is fine
was ending is the wrong form of end
there should be a that after said

feedback.why_key: Both versions would work here. The step back reports what they told him without promising the reader that June is still the date.
feedback.feed_forward: Accept the step back whenever the writer is only relaying.

payload.context: You are writing to the department this morning and you need the reader to act on the fee. Original, spoken yesterday: "The late fee is thirty pounds."
payload.stem: Your colleague said the late fee ___ (be) thirty pounds, so I have enclosed a cheque for that amount.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: You are asking the reader to act on the figure today, so the report has to arrive as a live one.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep the verb live when the reader must act on it.

payload.context: Talking about a flat you looked at in the spring and did not take. Original: "The rent includes the water."
payload.stem: The agent told me the rent ___ (include) the water, but I never checked it.

expected: included

feedback.why_key: You are not living there and never verified it, so the report belongs sealed inside the viewing rather than offered as fact.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back when you would not vouch for it.

payload.given: The archive told us: "The recordings are open to the public." They are open as you write, and you want your reader to go.
payload.instruction: Report it so the reader can act on it.

expected: the recordings are open to the public
that the recordings are open to the public

feedback.why_key: The reader is being sent somewhere, so the claim has to be live. A stepped-back verb would leave them wondering whether it had closed.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the verb alone when the reader is meant to act.

payload.audio_text: He said he'd finish it tonight, so I'm not chasing him.

expected: he said he'd finish it tonight, so i'm not chasing him
he said he would finish it tonight, so i am not chasing him
he said hed finish it tonight, so im not chasing him

feedback.why_key: The 'd is the whole step back and it is one unstressed sound. Miss it and the report loses the distance the speaker put there.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the 'd, then decide what it is doing.

items.decision_cue: so please send the forms straight to me

payload.context: An email you are sending this morning, so please send the forms straight to me.
payload.stem: The agent said the flat ___ available from the first.

options.why_this_means: That it is available as you write, and you are prepared to be held to that.
That it was available when he spoke, and you take no position on today.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: You are asking someone to act, and an action needs a live fact. A sealed report would leave them chasing something that might have gone.
feedback.feed_forward: Before choosing, ask whether the reader must act on it.

items.decision_cue: though somebody else took it in the end

payload.context: An account of a flat hunt that ended in March, though somebody else took it in the end.
payload.stem: The agent said the flat ___ available from the first.

options.why_this_means: That it is available as you write, and you are prepared to be held to that.
That it was available when he spoke, and you take no position on today.

expected: was

feedback.why_key: Somebody else has it, so a live report would be untrue. The step back puts the claim safely back where it was made.
feedback.feed_forward: Seal the report once the situation has moved on.

items.decision_cue: and I am about to start there myself

payload.context: Talking about the depot where a friend works and I am about to start there myself.
payload.stem: Dev told me the shifts ___ eight hours long.

options.why_this_means: That this is how the depot runs, and you are passing it on as fact.
That this was how it ran when he told you, with no claim about the rota you will meet.

expected: are

feedback.why_key: You are describing the job you are walking into, so the shifts are a live arrangement and not a piece of Dev's history.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep an ongoing arrangement live.

items.decision_cue: before the whole rota was rewritten

payload.context: Describing the depot as it ran two years ago, before the whole rota was rewritten.
payload.stem: Dev told me the shifts ___ eight hours long.

options.why_this_means: That this is how the depot runs, and you are passing it on as fact.
That this was how it ran when he told you, with no claim about the rota you will meet.

expected: were

feedback.why_key: The rota has been rewritten since, so a live report would describe a depot that no longer exists.
feedback.feed_forward: Seal the report when the arrangement has been replaced.

items.decision_cue: an argument the writer goes on to build on

payload.context: From an essay paragraph, an argument the writer goes on to build on.
payload.stem: The panel argued that recycling rates ___ largely on collection frequency.

options.why_this_means: That the writer accepts the point and is taking it forward as their own.
That the writer is relaying the panel's view and reserving judgement on it.

expected: depend

feedback.why_key: The paragraph is built on this claim, so the writer has to hold it live. A sealed version would leave the argument standing on nothing.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep a claim live when your next sentence leans on it.

items.decision_cue: a view the writer spends the next paragraph dismantling

payload.context: From an essay paragraph, a view the writer spends the next paragraph dismantling.
payload.stem: The panel argued that recycling rates ___ largely on collection frequency.

options.why_this_means: That the writer accepts the point and is taking it forward as their own.
That the writer is relaying the panel's view and reserving judgement on it.

expected: depended

feedback.why_key: You are about to take the claim apart, so signing it in the previous sentence would leave you arguing with yourself.
feedback.feed_forward: Step back from a claim you are about to attack.

items.decision_cue: a documentary somebody watched last month

payload.context: Two people discussing a documentary somebody watched last month.
payload.stem: The programme said local papers ___ half their readers in ten years.

options.why_this_means: That the loss is a fact you are happy to repeat as your own.
That this was the programme's figure, and you are relaying it without checking it.

follow_up.question: Which version puts the figure on you rather than on the programme?

feedback.why_key: Both are correct English and they hand the reader a different author for the same number. That difference is the whole point of the choice.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whose figure it is before you pick the form.

payload.context: Two sentences from different parts of a prospectus.
sentences: The department said the placement is compulsory.
The department said the placement was compulsory.
meanings: You should plan on doing a placement; the prospectus is standing behind it.
That is what the department said at the time; check before you plan anything.

feedback.why_key: One version is advice you can act on. The other is a record of something somebody once said. The reader is entitled to know which.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask which version a reader could safely act on.

items.decision_cue: and the samples arrive on Thursday

payload.context: From a draft essay paragraph about a delayed study.
payload.sentence: The team said the first results were disappointing and the samples arrive on Thursday.
reasons: half the report was re-anchored and half was left alone for no reason
the results were not disappointing
arrive is the wrong form of the verb
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing in the situation separates the two clauses, so the split is an accident and the reader has to decide which frame is real.
feedback.feed_forward: Split the frames only when the meaning asks you to.

payload.prompt_text: Somebody told you last year that people would stop paying for news altogether. You think they were wrong. Write one sentence reporting them in a way that makes clear you do not agree.

feedback.why_key: The step back is how English lets you put somebody's claim on the page without adopting it, and that is exactly what you need here.
feedback.feed_forward: Step the verb back when you want the claim kept at arm's length.

payload.prompt_text: Open your last answer to this prompt and find one sentence reporting somebody else's view. Rewrite it twice: once so you are standing behind the claim, once so you are not. Then say which one the paragraph needs. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: Seeing both versions of your own sentence side by side is the fastest way to feel that the step back is a decision rather than a reflex.
feedback.feed_forward: In the final read-through, check every reported verb against your own position.

title: Choosing a reporting verb that says what you think of the claim

point_json.grammar_name: Reporting verbs and their patterns

teach.can_do: I can choose a reporting verb that shows what I think of a claim, and get its pattern right.
teach.why_it_matters: Said is neutral and free. Claimed, argued, admitted and pointed out each add a judgement, and the judgement lands whether you meant it or not.
teach.meaning: Every reporting verb does two jobs in one word. It reports, and it rates. Argue says the person is building a case. Claim says they have asserted something you are not signing. Admit says the statement cost them something. Point out says it was a fact already lying there. Concede says they gave ground under pressure. The second job is why this is essay grammar and not vocabulary. Each verb also carries its own pattern, which cannot be worked out from the meaning and has to be stored with the word.

form.pattern: verb + that-clause | verb + -ing | verb + object + to-infinitive | verb + preposition + -ing
notes: that-clause: argue, claim, point out, insist, deny, admit, concede, warn, suggest
-ing form: admit, deny, suggest — she denied seeing the email
object + to-infinitive: urge, advise, warn, remind — they urged the council to reopen it
preposition + -ing: accuse someone of, warn against, insist on, object to
suggest never takes an object with to: not suggest us to wait
form.negative: He denied that the figures had been changed. / He denied changing the figures.
form.question: Which verb says what I actually think of this claim?

spec.label: how far am I standing behind this?

steps.gloss: it is a fact and I am with them
they demonstrated it and I accept it
they are making a case; I am neutral
they float it, and so do I
they assert it; I am not signing
they assert it and I have doubts

worked_example.sentence: Supporters of the charge point out that the money is ring-fenced for buses.
worked_example.why_this_form: Point out treats the ring-fencing as a fact already sitting there, so the writer has quietly agreed with it before the argument even starts.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Claim would hold the same words at arm's length: the money may or may not be ring-fenced, and the writer is not vouching for it.

notice_set.sentence: The company admitted that the data had been stored abroad.
notice_set.question: Was this comfortable for the company?
notice_set.why: Admit is only used when the statement costs the person making it something.

notice_set.sentence: The company claimed that the data had been stored securely.
notice_set.question: Is the writer standing behind this?
options: No, the writer is only reporting it
The writer says it is false
notice_set.why: Claim reports an assertion and declines to endorse it. It does not say the assertion is false.

notice_set.sentence: Ms Oduya pointed out that the two figures had been measured differently.
notice_set.question: Is this presented as something already true?
notice_set.why: Point out treats the difference as a fact lying in plain sight that somebody has drawn attention to.

notice_set.sentence: The panel conceded that the first estimate had been too low.
notice_set.question: Whose estimate was it?
notice_set.why: Concede means giving ground, and you can only give ground on your own position.

notice_set.sentence: The union urged the trust to reopen the ward.
notice_set.question: Who would reopen the ward?
notice_set.why: Urge takes an object and a to-infinitive, and the object is the one who would act.

notice_set.sentence: The developer denied cutting the number of affordable flats.
notice_set.question: What does the developer say happened?
notice_set.why: Deny takes an -ing form and reverses it: the developer's position is that no cut took place.

discovery.prompt: The same report is written two ways. Work out what the second verb in each pair is doing besides reporting.
pairs: The minister said the scheme would pay for itself.
The minister claimed the scheme would pay for itself.
Researchers said the effect was small.
Researchers found the effect was small.
The council said the consultation had been rushed.
The council admitted the consultation had been rushed.

candidate_rules.text: The second verb adds the writer's rating of the claim on top of the report.
The second verb in each pair is simply more formal than said.
Any reporting verb can replace said as long as a that-clause follows it.

teach.rule_line: Pick the verb that says what you think of the claim, then check its pattern.
teach.false_rule: That these verbs are synonyms of said that make writing look academic. Swapping one in without meaning its judgement is how an essay accidentally takes a side.

contrast.question: Am I signing this claim, staying neutral, or holding it away from me?

fork.answer: Signing it — it is a checkable fact and I am with them
Neutral — they are making a case and I am reporting it
At arm's length — they assert it and I am not vouching for it

a.text: The developer pointed out that the flats would be built on brownfield land.
a.means: The brownfield land is a fact, and the writer has accepted it on the way past.

b.text: The developer claimed that the flats would be built on brownfield land.
b.means: That is the developer's assertion, and the writer is not standing behind it.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote claimed. In one word you have told your reader you do not believe the developer, and the rest of your paragraph now has to earn that. If you had no reason to doubt them, claimed has picked a fight you did not intend to pick.

edge_case.text: Suggest is the trap of the set. It takes a that-clause or an -ing form and never an object with to, so suggest us to wait is wrong however natural it feels next to advise us to wait. Store suggest that and suggest doing as two fixed chunks and stop reasoning about it.

contrast.stronger_test: Read your sentence back as if you were the person being reported. If they would object to the verb you chose, you have taken a position. Decide whether you meant to take it.

worked_pairs.a: Campaigners point out that both consultations closed in August, which the council's own diary confirms.
worked_pairs.b: Campaigners claim that both consultations were deliberately timed to be missed.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: which the council's own diary confirms
worked_pairs.gloss: A date anybody can check invites point out. A statement about somebody's intentions is exactly what claim is for.

worked_pairs.a: The trust admitted that it had missed the target for a third year.
worked_pairs.b: The trust insisted that it had missed the target only because of the strike.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_a: it had missed the target for a third year
worked_pairs.gloss: Admit is for something that costs the speaker. Insist is for a defence they are holding on to while somebody pushes.

worked_pairs.a: Drawing on three small trials, the report suggests that shorter shifts reduce errors.
worked_pairs.b: Drawing on a decade of hospital records, the report shows that shorter shifts reduce errors.
worked_pairs.gloss: The strength of the evidence picks the verb. Suggest is honest about thin evidence; show over-claims on it.

errors.wrong: The committee suggested us to postpone the vote.
errors.right: The committee suggested postponing the vote.
errors.why_it_happens: Suggest sits in the same meaning space as advise and urge, and both of those take an object with to. The pattern cannot be worked out from the meaning, so it has to be stored with the word.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: us to postpone becomes postponing.

errors.wrong: The report accused the operator to cut corners on maintenance.
errors.right: The report accused the operator of cutting corners on maintenance.
errors.why_it_happens: Accuse looks like a verb that should take to, because so many verbs in this family do. Its preposition is of, and after of English takes only an -ing form.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: to cut becomes of cutting.

errors.wrong: She denied to send the message from the shared account.
errors.right: She denied sending the message from the shared account.
errors.why_it_happens: Deny is stored as a refusal verb and refuse takes to. Deny takes an -ing form or a that-clause and never an infinitive, which is a fact about the word rather than about refusing.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one form: to send becomes sending.

errors.wrong: The survey proves that shoppers prefer independent shops.
errors.right: The survey suggests that shoppers prefer independent shops.
errors.why_it_happens: Proves feels like the strongest available word and therefore the most persuasive. The reader hears a promise the evidence cannot keep, and the whole paragraph loses credit for it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: proves becomes suggests.

pays_in.note: It is how an essay gets other voices in without agreeing with all of them.
pays_in.model: Critics argue that the levy is regressive; the review concedes that its early years were poorly targeted.

pays_in.note: Paraphrase questions turn on whether the writer signed the claim or only reported it.
pays_in.model: The author notes that the two surveys used different age bands.

pays_in.note: Referring to what people argue lifts an answer off your own opinion.
pays_in.model: A lot of people argue that streaming has killed the album, though the sales figures suggest otherwise.

used_in.quote: A discussion essay on funding has to report two sides fairly, and the verb chosen for each side is where fairness is won or lost.
The card asks who gets believed and why, so answers report claims the speaker rates very differently.
The passage reports several researchers with different verbs, and one question depends on noticing which one the author endorses.

payload.sentence: The broadcaster conceded that the interview had been edited before transmission.
payload.question: Was this something the broadcaster wanted to say?

feedback.why_key: Concede reports a position given up under pressure, which is information about the situation and not just about the words.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the reporting verb as information about the speaker.

payload.sentence: The team leader urged the depot to keep two vans on standby.
payload.question: Who would keep the vans on standby?

feedback.why_key: Urge puts the person being pushed straight after it, and that person is the one who would act.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the object after urge; that is the doer.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph resting on a single pilot study.
payload.sentence: The pilot study proves that shorter lessons improve retention.
reasons: the verb claims more than one pilot study can support
shorter lessons do not improve retention
proves is the wrong form of the verb
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The verb writes a cheque the evidence cannot cash, and a reader who notices stops trusting the rest of the paragraph.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb's strength to the evidence you have.

payload.context: Original: "We did not release anything into the river."
payload.stem: The plant denied ___ (release) anything into the river.

expected: releasing
having released

feedback.why_key: Deny takes an -ing form, which is a fact about the word and not something the meaning can tell you.
feedback.feed_forward: Store deny with an -ing form attached.

payload.context: Original: "The channel has been burying corrections."
payload.stem: The regulator accused the channel ___ burying corrections.

expected: of

feedback.why_key: Accuse comes with of welded to it, and the -ing form after it is there because of arrived first.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn accuse of as one unit, never as two words.

payload.given: The panel said: "Screening should start five years earlier."
payload.instruction: Report it with suggest, using the pattern suggest takes.

expected: that screening should start five years earlier
screening should start five years earlier
starting screening five years earlier

feedback.why_key: Suggest takes a that-clause or an -ing form. It never takes an object with to, however much it feels like advise.
feedback.feed_forward: After suggest, write that or an -ing form.

payload.audio_text: They've admitted deleting the footage, but they've denied doing it deliberately.

expected: they've admitted deleting the footage, but they've denied doing it deliberately
they have admitted deleting the footage, but they have denied doing it deliberately
theyve admitted deleting the footage, but theyve denied doing it deliberately

feedback.why_key: Two verbs, two -ing forms, and two completely different admissions. Miss one and the sentence says the opposite of what was said.
feedback.feed_forward: Catch the -ing form that follows each reporting verb.

payload.stem: The authors ___ that daylight lamps improve winter concentration.

options.why_this_means: That the finding leans one way and the evidence is thin.
That the finding is established and the writer is treating it as settled.

feedback.why_key: Hedging evidence this strong is its own kind of inaccuracy: the reader is told to doubt something the writer has no reason to doubt.
feedback.feed_forward: Do not hedge a finding the evidence fully supports.

items.decision_cue: which had been their own policy for years

payload.context: The board was defending a pay freeze which had been their own policy for years.
payload.stem: The board ___ that the freeze had held wages below inflation.

options.why_this_means: That the point went against them and they gave it up.
That they were holding a line while somebody pushed at it.

expected: admitted

feedback.why_key: The point damages their own policy, and a verb that damages the speaker is exactly what admit is for.

options.why_this_means: That the point went against them and they gave it up.
That they were holding a line while somebody pushed at it.

items.decision_cue: a long piece about local newspapers

payload.stem: The editor ___ that free distribution had kept the paper alive.

options.why_this_means: That she was making a case, and the writer is reporting it without judging it.
That she has held this view for a long time and has been challenged on it.

payload.context: Two sentences from different sections of the same review of a clinic.
sentences: The trust acknowledged that waiting times had risen.
The trust alleged that waiting times had been recorded incorrectly.
meanings: The trust accepted a point that did not help it, and the writer treats it as settled.
The trust made an accusation, and the writer is keeping well clear of it.

feedback.why_key: One verb records something conceded, the other records something asserted against somebody else. The writer's distance is different in each.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask who each claim damages before you read on.

payload.sentence: The waste review suggested residents to sort food waste separately, which most of them already did.

expected: suggested that residents sort
suggested that residents should sort
suggested sorting

feedback.why_key: Suggest will not take an object with to. The pattern has come across from advise, which means something similar and behaves differently.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the object and to with a that-clause after suggest.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about a change in how people get their news. In the first, report a view you accept. In the second, report a view you do not accept. Do not use said in either.

feedback.why_key: Two sentences of the same shape with two different verbs is the fastest way to feel how much of your position lives in the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Check each verb against what you actually think.

payload.prompt_text: Write one body paragraph for this prompt that reports both sides. Use three different reporting verbs, none of them said, and make sure each one shows where you stand. Eight minutes.

feedback.why_key: A discussion paragraph that reports both sides with the same verb has not discussed anything. The verbs are where the discussion actually happens.
feedback.feed_forward: Read back the three verbs alone and check the pattern of each.

title: Putting something near the top without claiming it is the top

point_json.grammar_name: one of the + superlative + plural noun; among the most

teach.can_do: I can put something near the top of a group without claiming it is the very top.
teach.why_it_matters: A top-of-the-list claim needs only one counter-example to fall over, and it takes the rest of your paragraph with it. This frame keeps the claim strong and keeps it survivable.
teach.meaning: A top ranking is the strongest claim English will let you make about a group: nothing else comes close, and one exception destroys it. Most of the time what you actually mean is weaker and more useful — that the thing sits in the small handful at the top. That is what this frame says. Because it reaches into a group and picks one member out, the group itself has to be named, and a group is always more than one.

form.pattern: one of the + -est / most + PLURAL NOUN  ·  among the + -est / most + PLURAL NOUN
notes: the noun after the frame is always plural, because it names the group, not the thing: one of the largest towns
the verb answers to one, not to the plural: one of the busiest stations is closed this week
among the takes no one and no a in front of it: among the cheapest options available
a clause hanging off the plural noun agrees with the group: one of the few schemes that have survived
it works on words describing how something is done too: one of the most heavily used crossings
the softer versions: among the busier crossings, one of the more expensive options — near the top, no ranking claimed
form.negative: not one of the cheapest puts the thing outside the top group without saying where it does sit.
form.question: Is it one of the busiest crossings on the river?

spec.label: how strong is the claim, and how easily does it fall over?

steps.text: the busiest crossing on the river
steps.gloss: alone at the top; one busier crossing sinks the sentence

steps.text: one of the busiest crossings on the river
steps.gloss: in the top handful; survives a reader who knows the river
above the middle, and nothing more is claimed
no claim about anything else at all

worked_example.sentence: Sandmouth is one of the wettest towns on this stretch of coast.
worked_example.why_this_form: The claim is strong enough to be worth making and small enough to survive a reader who knows a wetter town. The group at the top has several members, so towns is plural.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The wettest town would stand Sandmouth alone at the top, and a single rainier place anywhere along that coast would make the whole sentence untrue.

notice_set.sentence: Brackenfield has one of the oldest markets in the county.
notice_set.question: Could any market in the county be older?
notice_set.why: The frame reaches into a small group at the top and picks one member, so a handful of older markets is exactly what it expects.

notice_set.sentence: Brackenfield has the oldest market in the county.
notice_set.question: Could any market in the county be older?
notice_set.why: Nothing is left above it, so one older market anywhere in the county would make the sentence untrue.

notice_set.sentence: Cycling is among the cheapest ways of getting into town.
notice_set.question: Might something be cheaper than cycling?
notice_set.why: Among places cycling inside the cheap group and deliberately leaves room underneath it.

notice_set.sentence: One of the two lifts is out of service today.
notice_set.question: How many lifts are working?
notice_set.why: The sentence picks a single lift out of the pair and says nothing at all against the other one.

notice_set.sentence: The island is one of the few places on this coast that have kept a daily boat.
notice_set.question: Do other places still have a daily boat?
notice_set.why: Few places names a small surviving group, and the island is one member of it rather than the whole of it.

teach.rule_line: One of the always lands on a group, so the thing you name after it must be plural.
teach.false_rule: That one of means you are describing one thing, so the noun should be singular. One picks the item; the noun names the group it was picked out of.

errors.wrong: Marlow is one of the largest town in the district.
errors.right: Marlow is one of the largest towns in the district.
errors.why_it_happens: One is sitting right beside the noun and drags it into the singular. The noun is not describing Marlow, though — it is naming the group Marlow has just been lifted out of.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: town becomes towns.

errors.wrong: One of the busiest crossings are closed for repairs.
errors.right: One of the busiest crossings is closed for repairs.
errors.why_it_happens: Crossings stands next to the verb and wins the argument by being nearest. The thing that is actually shut is a single crossing, and that is the word the verb has to answer to.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: are becomes is.

errors.wrong: Traffic is the most serious problem any council has to deal with.
errors.right: Traffic is one of the most serious problems any council has to deal with.
errors.why_it_happens: The unhedged version sounds more forceful, and force feels like a virtue in an argument. The reader only has to think of one worse problem to stop believing the paragraph.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert three words: one of the.

errors.wrong: It is one of the few schemes that has survived the cuts.
errors.right: It is one of the few schemes that have survived the cuts.
errors.why_it_happens: The clause looks as though it belongs to the one, but it is doing its work on schemes: the survivors are the few, and one of them is being singled out afterwards.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: has becomes have.

pays_in.note: It lets you make a strong claim you can still defend in the next sentence.
pays_in.model: Housing is one of the hardest costs for a young household to absorb.

pays_in.note: It ranks a bar without pretending it stands alone at the top.
pays_in.model: Rail was among the fastest-growing categories across the period.

pays_in.note: Part 3 runs on claims that are strong without being absolute.
pays_in.model: It's one of the reasons people move away, though it isn't the only one.

used_in.quote: An answer about services in small towns has to rank several problems, and every ranking in it needs to survive a reader who lives in one.
A statement that turns the passage's hedged ranking into an outright top ranking is false on those three small words.

payload.sentence: The Norland reserve is one of the largest wetlands in the region.
payload.question: Might another wetland in the region be about the same size?

feedback.why_key: The frame puts the reserve in the top handful and leaves the other members of that handful standing.
feedback.feed_forward: Read one of the as top handful, not as top.

payload.sentence: That's one of the better places to eat near the station.
payload.question: Is the speaker saying nowhere else nearby is any good?

feedback.why_key: The frame names a group of decent places and picks one out, so the rest of the group is still there.
feedback.feed_forward: Notice how much the speaker is not claiming.

items.decision_cue: one of the fastest growing city

payload.context: A draft paragraph about towns that have grown quickly.
payload.sentence: Ashfield is one of the fastest growing city in the north.
reasons: the group being named has to be plural
the ranking is stronger than the evidence allows
the sentence needs among instead of one of
nothing wrong, it's fine

payload.context: From a paragraph on a table of district populations.
payload.stem: Ashfield is one of the fastest-growing ___ (district) in the county.

expected: districts

payload.audio_text: It's one of the cheapest streets in the whole district.

expected: it's one of the cheapest streets in the whole district
its one of the cheapest streets in the whole district
it is one of the cheapest streets in the whole district

payload.sentence: Class size is one of the biggest problem facing the college.

expected: one of the biggest problems
among the biggest problems
one of the bigger problems

the group named should be plural

title: Saying how big the difference is, not just that there is one

point_json.grammar_name: Grading a comparison: far, much, slightly, considerably, marginally, nowhere near

teach.can_do: I can say how big a difference is, in one word, and get the size right.
teach.why_it_matters: A bare comparison tells the reader a difference exists and leaves them to guess whether it matters. The guess is usually wrong, and it is the difference between describing a chart and reading one aloud.
teach.meaning: A comparison on its own reports a direction: one thing is higher than another. It says nothing about distance, so two figures a whisker apart and two figures miles apart come out as the same sentence. A grading word puts the distance back in. It is one word, it goes in front of the comparison, and it decides whether the reader treats the gap as noise or as the story.

form.pattern: GRADER + comparative + than  ·  GRADER + as + WORD + as
notes: big gap: far, much, considerably, significantly, substantially, a great deal
small gap: slightly, marginally, a little, somewhat, a fraction
next to nothing: barely, hardly, no higher than, little more than
the grader always goes in front of the comparison, never after it
it works on both builds: much higher, and much more expensive
with the level frame the graders change shape: nowhere near as high as, almost as high as, just as high as, not quite as high as
very will not grade a comparison. Very high is fine; very higher is not
a lot, loads, way and miles belong to speech; considerably, substantially and marginally belong to writing, and mixing them up is visible on the page
form.negative: no higher than, not much higher than, nowhere near as high as
form.question: How much higher is it — a little, or a great deal?

spec.label: how big is the gap between the two figures?

steps.gloss: the two are not in the same conversation
level, or below; there is no gap to report
a gap you would need the table to see
visible, and not worth building anything on
a gap of unstated size — the reader has to guess
one of the things the chart is about
the gap is the story

worked_example.sentence: Spending on rail was marginally higher at the end of the period than at the start.
worked_example.why_this_form: The two figures are a whisker apart. Marginally warns the reader not to build an argument on the gap, which is exactly what the numbers deserve.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Far higher would promise a gap worth explaining, and the reader would go looking in the figures for something that is not there.

notice_set.sentence: Fuel spending was marginally lower in the second year.
notice_set.question: Would you be able to see the change on a chart?
notice_set.why: Marginally says the distance between the two figures is about as small as a distance can be while still existing.

notice_set.sentence: Rents in the city are far higher than rents along the coast.
notice_set.question: Could somebody save real money by moving to the coast?
notice_set.why: Far stretches the gap out to the point where it changes what a household can afford.

notice_set.sentence: The tunnel is nowhere near as busy as the bypass on a Sunday.
notice_set.question: Which route would you take to avoid queues on a Sunday?
notice_set.why: Nowhere near drops the tunnel a long way below the bypass, and the quiet road is the one to take.

notice_set.sentence: Waiting times at the two clinics are slightly different.
notice_set.question: Is it worth travelling across town for the shorter wait?
notice_set.why: Slightly puts the two clinics close enough together that the journey would cost more than the wait it saves.

notice_set.sentence: The new pass is a fraction cheaper than the old one.
notice_set.question: How much would a traveller save?
notice_set.why: A fraction is at the small end of the scale, and the saving is being described as barely worth naming.

teach.rule_line: Look at the two numbers, then pick the one word that sizes the gap between them.
teach.false_rule: That dramatically, sharply and significantly make a description sound more academic. They make a claim about size, and the numbers underneath either back it or contradict it.

contrast.question: How big is the gap, and is the size worth saying?

fork.answer: Small — a point or two, a few units, something the reader would shrug at
fork.selects: slightly, marginally, a little, a fraction

fork.answer: Large — a gap that changes what the chart is about
fork.selects: far, considerably, substantially, a great deal

fork.answer: Unmeasured, or beside the point of the sentence

a.text: Rents in Marlow are slightly higher than rents in Ashfield.
a.means: A few pounds in it. Nobody would move house over the difference.

b.text: Rents in Marlow are far higher than rents in Ashfield.
b.means: A gap big enough to decide which of the two towns a household can live in.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote far higher for a two-pound gap. The sentence is correct English and wrong about the chart: your reader now pictures a gap the figures do not contain, and every number after it has to fight that picture.

edge_case.text: Very will not stretch a comparison — not very higher, not very more expensive. It strengthens the plain word instead: very high. Learn the pair much higher and very high together and the problem stops arising.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover the sentence and look only at the two numbers. If you had to describe the gap to somebody over the phone in a single word, which word would come out? That is the one the sentence needs.

worked_pairs.a: Unemployment in Sandmouth was marginally lower in 2016 than in 2015.
worked_pairs.b: Unemployment in Sandmouth was considerably lower in 2016 than it had been the year before.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first says the fall would be hard to spot on the chart. The second says the fall is what the chart is about.

worked_pairs.a: The coast route is slightly busier at weekends.
worked_pairs.b: The coast route is nowhere near as busy at weekends.
worked_pairs.gloss: One nudges the weekend above the weekday. The other drops it a long way below. The size word carries the entire claim.

worked_pairs.a: Fees at the college rose a little faster than fees at the school.
worked_pairs.b: Fees at the college climbed a great deal faster than the school's did.

errors.wrong: The bypass is very quicker at that hour of the morning.
errors.right: The bypass is much quicker at that hour of the morning.
errors.why_it_happens: Very is the word the learner reaches for to make anything stronger, and it has never failed them before. It will strengthen a plain describing word, but it cannot stretch a comparison.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: very becomes much.

errors.wrong: Spending on transport was way higher in the second half of the period.
errors.right: Spending on transport was considerably higher in the second half of the period.
errors.why_it_happens: Way, loads and miles do this job perfectly well and the learner has met them far more often than the written set. Nothing marks them as spoken until a reader flinches at them on the page.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: way becomes considerably.

errors.wrong: Rail use rose dramatically, from 41 in every hundred journeys to 43.
errors.right: Rail use rose marginally, from 41 in every hundred journeys to 43.
errors.why_it_happens: Dramatically is the first word most learners are handed for describing a graph, so it lands on every movement regardless of size. The figures then contradict the sentence in the same breath.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: dramatically becomes marginally.

errors.wrong: The fee is higher slightly than it was last term.
errors.right: The fee is slightly higher than it was last term.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows the word describes the comparison and puts it next to what it describes, which almost everywhere else in English means after it. These words lean on the front instead.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: slightly goes in front of higher.
