title: Saying that when one thing changes, another changes with it

point_json.grammar_name: the more ..., the more ...; increasingly

teach.can_do: I can say that two things move together, and which way each of them goes.
teach.why_it_matters: It packs a whole cause-and-effect sentence into eight words, and it is one of the few patterns that reads as fluent even when the rest of the paragraph is plain.
teach.meaning: Two things are moving, and they are tied to each other: whenever one goes up, the other follows it up or pulls the other way. Two separate sentences would report both movements and leave the reader to guess whether there is a link. This pattern states the link itself, and it does it without a single word for cause. The shape carries the meaning, which is why the shape has to be exact.

form.pattern: The + comparison + first half, the + comparison + second half
notes: both halves open with the, and the comparison jumps to the front of its own half: the longer the wait, the angrier the queue
in short halves the verb is often left out entirely: the sooner the better
the two halves have to be built the same way — a full clause on the left wants a full clause on the right
when a noun is involved the whole phrase moves forward: the more money a council spends, the fewer complaints it receives
use fewer with things you count and less with things you measure: the fewer complaints, the less paperwork
increasingly does a smaller version of the same job on one scale by itself: journeys are increasingly made by rail
increasingly goes in front of the word it stretches: increasingly crowded, increasingly hard to fund
form.negative: The less you book ahead, the more you pay — the pattern reverses simply by changing the comparison in either half.
form.question: Does one really move with the other, or do they just both happen to be moving?

left.text: the longer the wait at the clinic

right.text: the more people give up and go home

spec.caption: Two scales tied together. The pattern claims the tie; two separate sentences would only report the two movements.

worked_example.sentence: The later the train leaves, the fewer connections there are at the other end.
worked_example.why_this_form: Every extra minute takes another connection away, so the two are tied rather than merely both true. The sentence states the tie in one clause pair.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Two separate sentences would report a late train and a thin timetable and leave the reader to work out for themselves whether one of them causes the other.

notice_set.sentence: The longer the queue at the clinic, the more people give up and go home.
notice_set.question: What happens on a quiet morning?
notice_set.why: The two are tied, so a short queue pulls the other side of the sentence down with it.

notice_set.sentence: The more the council spends on street lighting, the fewer break-ins are reported.
notice_set.question: What would probably happen if the lighting budget were cut?
notice_set.why: The sentence ties the two scales together, so pulling one down pushes the other up.

notice_set.sentence: Cycling to work is increasingly common in Ashfield.
notice_set.question: Was it less common a few years ago?
notice_set.why: Increasingly reports movement along one scale, and movement has to start somewhere lower down.

notice_set.sentence: The earlier you book, the less you pay.
notice_set.question: Who ends up paying the most?
notice_set.why: Booking late is the far end of the first scale, and the second scale follows it in the opposite direction.

notice_set.sentence: The bigger the class, the harder it is to notice a quiet student.
notice_set.question: Are quiet students easier to spot in small classes?
notice_set.why: Small is the low end of the first scale, and the difficulty drops with it.

teach.rule_line: Two halves, each opening with the, each with its comparison pulled to the front.
teach.false_rule: That the here is the ordinary little word that goes in front of a noun. It is a different word doing a different job, and it turns up twice or not at all.

errors.wrong: The more the council spends, the less complaints it receives.
errors.right: The more the council spends, the fewer complaints it receives.
errors.why_it_happens: Less is the word that comes out when the meaning is downwards, and it works in front of almost everything the learner says out loud. Complaints arrive one at a time, and that is the one thing less will not sit in front of.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: less becomes fewer.

errors.wrong: More you wait, more it costs.
errors.right: The more you wait, the more it costs.
errors.why_it_happens: The pattern is usually met in speech, where the two small words are almost inaudible, so the learner stores it without them. What is left still looks balanced, so nothing feels missing.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert two words: the, at the front of each half.

errors.wrong: The busier the road, the more accidents happening.
errors.right: The busier the road, the more accidents happen.
errors.why_it_happens: The second half is doing a lot at once — pulling its comparison forward and keeping its own verb — and the verb is what slips. The half then has no working verb and stops being a clause.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: happening becomes happen.

errors.wrong: The centre of town is becoming crowded increasingly.
errors.right: The centre of town is becoming increasingly crowded.
errors.why_it_happens: Words ending in -ly usually settle at the end of a clause, and this one is treated the same way. It belongs in front of whatever it is stretching, exactly like the other size words.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: increasingly goes in front of crowded.

pays_in.note: It states a cause-and-effect claim without a single linking word.
pays_in.model: The longer a household waits for social housing, the harder it becomes to hold down steady work.

pays_in.note: Part 3 asks what happens if something changes, and this answers it in one breath.
pays_in.model: The earlier children start, the less nervous they seem about speaking.

pays_in.note: A statement that reverses one half of the pattern is false while looking almost identical.
pays_in.model: The steeper the fee, the fewer applications the course attracted.

title: Saying how many times bigger one figure is than another

point_json.grammar_name: twice as many, three times higher, more than double, a tenfold increase

teach.can_do: I can say how many times one figure fits into another, and get the direction right.
teach.why_it_matters: A chart description that can only report differences has to give every number twice. A multiple says the relationship once, in three words, and a reader who never sees the chart still gets it.
teach.meaning: There are two honest ways of describing the distance between two figures. One is the difference: subtract the smaller from the larger and report what is left. The other is the multiple: ask how many times the smaller one fits into the larger, and report that. They answer different questions. A difference of two hundred is enormous between two figures of three hundred and meaningless between two figures of a million, and a multiple carries its own scale with it.

form.pattern: twice / three times + as + many / much / WORD + as  ·  NUMBER times + comparative + than  ·  a NUMBERfold increase
notes: twice, not two times, in careful writing. From three upwards the number is used: three times, four times
as many with things you count, as much with things you measure: twice as many visitors, twice as much rain
the second half takes as after as high, and than after higher — three times as high as, or three times higher than, and never a mixture of the two
double and half attach straight to the noun: double the number of visitors, half the rainfall
the noun versions: a twofold increase, a threefold rise, a tenfold increase — written as one word, with the number spelt out
the verbs: double, treble, halve — demand doubled between 2005 and 2015
hedges go in front, not inside: almost twice as many, just over three times higher, more than double
form.negative: half as many as sends the multiple the other way, and so does a halving of.
form.question: How many times does the smaller figure fit into the larger one?

left.text: twenty thousand more visitors than the castle

right.text: twice as many visitors as the castle

spec.caption: Both describe the same two figures. Only the one on the right still means something to a reader who never sees the totals.

worked_example.sentence: The reserve drew twice as many visitors as the castle in 2015.
worked_example.why_this_form: Two visitors at the reserve for every one at the castle. The relationship survives without the totals, which is what a reader of an overview sentence actually needs.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Twenty thousand more visitors reports the same two figures and tells the reader nothing about whether that is a landslide or a rounding error.

notice_set.sentence: The reserve drew twice as many visitors as the castle.
notice_set.question: For every hundred people at the castle, how many were at the reserve?
notice_set.why: Twice puts two of the second figure into the first, so the reserve is the busier of the two sites.

notice_set.sentence: The castle drew half as many visitors as the reserve.
notice_set.question: Which of the two sites was busier?
notice_set.why: Half runs the multiple downwards, so the castle is the smaller figure and the reserve is the larger one.

notice_set.sentence: There was a threefold rise in applications between 2010 and 2014.
notice_set.question: If there were 200 applications in 2010, how many were there in 2014?
notice_set.why: A threefold rise multiplies the starting figure by three rather than adding three to it.

notice_set.sentence: Water use in the uplands was almost twice as much as on the coast.
notice_set.question: Was upland use quite double the coastal figure?
notice_set.why: Almost stops the multiple just short, so the upland figure had not quite reached double.

notice_set.sentence: Rail carried more than double the freight that water did.
notice_set.question: Did water carry less than half the rail figure?
notice_set.why: More than double turned round gives the same relationship from the other end: water is under half of rail.

teach.rule_line: Ask how many times the smaller figure fits into the larger, then hang that number on the larger one.
teach.false_rule: That three times more and three times as many are two names for one thing, so either will do. Say what fits into what and the question stops arising.

contrast.question: Is this relationship a multiple, or is it a difference?

fork.answer: One figure fits into the other a whole number of times — 20 and 40, 12 and 36
fork.selects: twice as many, three times as high

fork.answer: The two figures are close, and no multiple would be honest — 41 and 43
The two figures met
fork.selects: as many as, the same as

a.text: The reserve drew twice as many visitors as the castle.
a.means: Two people at the reserve for every one at the castle: forty thousand against twenty.

b.text: The reserve drew half as many visitors as the castle.
b.means: One person at the reserve for every two at the castle: twenty thousand against forty.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You wrote half as many where the figures say twice as many. Nothing in the sentence looks broken, so nobody will query it — the reader simply takes away the opposite chart from the one in front of you.

edge_case.text: Two times as many is not wrong and plenty of people say it. In writing, twice is the safe choice and it is one word shorter. Above two, nobody says thrice any more — use three times.

contrast.stronger_test: Say the smaller figure out loud and count how many of it you need to reach the bigger one. That count is your multiple, and it always hangs on the bigger thing.

worked_pairs.a: Rail freight was three times as high as road freight in 2010.
worked_pairs.b: Rail freight was three times higher than road freight in 2010.
worked_pairs.gloss: Both of these are standard. What you may never do is take the front of one and the back of the other and write three times as high than.

worked_pairs.a: The town recorded double the number of visitors it had in 2005.
worked_pairs.b: The town recorded a twofold rise in visitors between 2005 and 2015.
worked_pairs.gloss: One compares two points in time. The other turns the movement between them into a thing you can put a verb in front of.

worked_pairs.a: Almost twice as much water was used in the southern district.
worked_pairs.b: Almost twice as many households were connected in the southern district.
worked_pairs.gloss: Water is measured and households are counted, and the frame changes word for word to follow that.

errors.wrong: The site attracted twice as much visitors as the museum.
errors.right: The site attracted twice as many visitors as the museum.
errors.why_it_happens: Much and many mean the same thing to the ear, and nothing in the sentence's meaning separates them. Only many will sit in front of something that arrives one at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes many.

errors.wrong: Demand in the city was three times as high than in the villages.
errors.right: Demand in the city was three times as high as in the villages.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner holds two correct patterns and builds a sentence out of the front of one and the back of the other. Both halves feel familiar, so nothing sounds wrong on the way past.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: than becomes as.

errors.wrong: Road freight was half as high as rail freight, at 60 million tonnes against 30 million.
errors.right: Road freight was twice as high as rail freight, at 60 million tonnes against 30 million.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner reads the two numbers in the order they appear on the page instead of in the order the sentence needs, so the multiple lands on the smaller side and the whole claim inverts.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: half becomes twice.

errors.wrong: There was a ten fold increase in the number of applications.
errors.right: There was a tenfold increase in the number of applications.
errors.why_it_happens: Fold is not a word the learner meets on its own, so there is no reason to expect it to weld onto the number. On the page it looks like an ordinary two-word phrase.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one space: ten fold becomes tenfold.

pays_in.note: The arithmetic of a chart, said in words, is most of the marks in the body paragraphs.
pays_in.model: Road carried roughly three times as much freight as rail throughout the period.

pays_in.note: A multiple makes a claim about scale that a raw figure cannot.
pays_in.model: Rents have risen at more than double the rate of local wages.

pays_in.note: A statement that swaps twice for half is false, and it is the hardest kind to spot.
pays_in.model: The northern district used almost twice as much water as the coast.

used_in.quote: The bars stand in whole-number relationships to one another, and an answer that only ever subtracts them misses what the chart is showing.
The passage gives a relationship as a multiple and a statement gives it back reversed, which is invisible unless the reader does the arithmetic.

payload.sentence: The harbour museum took three times as many bookings as the gallery.
payload.question: For every ten bookings at the gallery, how many did the museum take?

feedback.why_key: A multiple multiplies rather than adds, so ten at the gallery becomes thirty at the museum.
feedback.feed_forward: Multiply the smaller figure, never add to it.

payload.sentence: The coastal plots received half as much rain as the uplands.
payload.question: Which area was wetter?

feedback.why_key: Half runs the multiple downwards, so the figure carrying it is the smaller of the two.
feedback.feed_forward: Check which side of the sentence the multiple is sitting on.

payload.context: A draft describing a chart of connections by district.
payload.sentence: The eastern district had twice as much households on the network.
reasons: households are counted, so this is the wrong word
the multiple has been put on the wrong district
the sentence is missing its second as
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Households arrive one at a time and can be counted, so the frame needs many. Much belongs in front of what you measure.
feedback.feed_forward: Test the noun for counting before you fill the frame.

payload.context: From a paragraph on a chart of water use by district.
payload.stem: The northern district used twice as ___ (much / many) water as the coast.

expected: much

feedback.why_key: Water is measured rather than counted, so the frame stretches with much.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the frame word to what the noun does.

payload.context: Earnings in the city stood at 900 a week; along the coast they stood at 300.
payload.stem: Earnings in the city were three times ___ high as earnings along the coast.

expected: as

feedback.why_key: As high is one half of the frame and it calls for the matching as behind it, not for than.
feedback.feed_forward: Finish the frame you opened.

payload.given: In 2004 the college had 400 laptops. In 2014 it had 4,000.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence reporting the change as a multiple rather than as a difference.
payload.starter: Between 2004 and 2014 the number of laptops ___

expected: rose tenfold
increased tenfold
grew tenfold
rose by a factor of ten
became ten times higher

feedback.why_key: Three thousand six hundred more laptops means nothing on its own. Tenfold carries the scale with it.
feedback.feed_forward: Divide the two figures before you write.

payload.context: Build one sentence from the freight chart.

expected: road carried almost four times as much freight as water

feedback.why_key: The hedge goes in front of the number, the number in front of the frame, and the frame closes with its second as.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the hedge outside the frame, never inside it.

payload.audio_text: It costs about twice as much as it did.

expected: it costs about twice as much as it did

feedback.why_key: Twice as much runs together into something close to one word, and the second as is the piece that disappears.
feedback.feed_forward: Write both ases even when you only hear one.

items.decision_cue: 40,000 at the reserve and 20,000 at the castle

payload.context: A chart records 40,000 at the reserve and 20,000 at the castle.
payload.stem: The reserve drew ___ visitors as the castle.

options.why_this_means: That two people came to the reserve for every one who went to the castle.
That one person came to the reserve for every two who went to the castle.

expected: twice as many

feedback.why_key: Twenty thousand fits into forty thousand twice, and the multiple hangs on the bigger of the two sites.
feedback.feed_forward: Divide the larger figure by the smaller one first.

items.decision_cue: 20,000 at the reserve and 40,000 at the castle

payload.context: A chart records 20,000 at the reserve and 40,000 at the castle.
payload.stem: The reserve drew ___ visitors as the castle.

options.why_this_means: That two people came to the reserve for every one who went to the castle.
That one person came to the reserve for every two who went to the castle.

expected: half as many

feedback.why_key: Same two figures, opposite sites. The reserve is now the smaller one, so the multiple has to run downwards.
feedback.feed_forward: Check which site the sentence has made its subject.

payload.context: A table gives what each district drew from the reservoir last year, measured in litres.
payload.stem: The north recorded ___ as the south.

options.why_this_means: That what is being counted is measured in quantity rather than in whole items.
That what is being counted arrives in separate items you could count on your fingers.

expected: twice as much

feedback.why_key: Litres are measured out rather than counted one by one, so the frame stretches with much.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at what the table is counting before you choose.

payload.context: A table gives the new connections signed off in each district last year.
payload.stem: The north recorded ___ as the south.

options.why_this_means: That what is being counted is measured in quantity rather than in whole items.
That what is being counted arrives in separate items you could count on your fingers.

expected: twice as many

feedback.why_key: Connections are signed off one at a time, so the frame takes many even though the sentence is otherwise identical.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the noun, not the number, choose the frame word.

payload.context: Two sentences from separate reports on the same cycling figures.
sentences: Journeys by bicycle doubled over the decade.
Journeys by bicycle rose by two thousand across the same ten years.
meanings: Whatever the starting figure was, the town finished on twice it.
The rise is fixed at two thousand, and how impressive that is depends entirely on where the line began.

feedback.why_key: One sentence carries its own scale and the other borrows it from a figure the reader may never see.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether the sentence still works without the totals.

items.decision_cue: 30 tonnes of glass in 2010 and 60 tonnes in 2020

payload.context: A chart records 30 tonnes of glass in 2010 and 60 tonnes in 2020.
payload.stem: Glass recycling ___ across the decade.

options.why_this_means: That the second figure is the first one multiplied by two, whatever those figures happen to be.
That thirty tonnes were added, which is only meaningful to somebody who knows the starting point.

follow_up.question: Which one still makes sense to a reader who never sees the totals?

feedback.why_key: Both are true of this chart. One of them survives on its own and the other needs the chart standing next to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Prefer the version that carries its own scale.

payload.sentence: Spending on housing was three times as high than spending on transport.

expected: three times as high as
three times higher than

feedback.why_key: Two good patterns have been welded together at the join. Either half is fine; the two halves are not compatible.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick one pattern and finish it before you move on.

payload.prompt_text: A chart shows export earnings: machinery 900 million, textiles 300 million, fish 150 million. Write one sentence that reports the relationship between all three as multiples rather than as totals.

feedback.why_key: These three figures stand in whole-number relationships to each other, and saying so is what an overview sentence is for.
feedback.feed_forward: Divide first, then write the sentence.

payload.prompt_text: Open your export earnings answer. Find one place where you subtracted two figures and rewrite it as a multiple, then check the direction by dividing. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: This is the sentence that separates a description from a transcription, and the direction is the part that goes wrong under a clock.
feedback.feed_forward: Divide the two figures again before you move on.

title: Keeping the verb matched when the subject gets long

point_json.grammar_name: Subject-verb agreement: the hard cases

teach.can_do: I can find the real subject inside a long noun phrase and match the verb to it.
teach.why_it_matters: Agreement errors climb sharply as sentences get longer, so they are the price of the complex sentences that lift a band, and they are avoidable.
teach.meaning: Once a subject grows past two words, the verb stops sitting next to the thing it answers to. English does not care what noun is nearest; it cares which noun the sentence is actually about. Everything between that noun and the verb is scenery. A short list of quantity words then overrides the count you would expect, and there is and there are look forward instead of back.

form.pattern: find the head noun → count that noun only → match the verb to it
notes: a phrase in between never changes it: the cost of the new defences has risen
a relative clause in between never changes it: the survey that produced these figures was funded locally
each and every are one, however many nouns follow: each of the schemes has failed
a number of takes a plural verb; the number of takes a singular one
neither ... nor and either ... or match whichever part sits nearest the verb
a collective noun (the government, the team, the committee) takes a singular verb when it acts as one body and a plural one when the members act separately
there is and there are match the first item in the list that comes after them
form.negative: The rule does not change under negation: the cost of the defences has not risen since April.
form.question: In a question the auxiliary comes first and still matches the head noun: has the cost of the defences risen?

left.role: the head of the subject, which the verb answers to
left.text: The cost

right.role: everything sitting in between, which it ignores
right.text: of the new flood defences

spec.caption: The verb reaches back over the second box and matches the first.

worked_example.sentence: The cost of the new flood defences has risen twice since the survey.
worked_example.why_this_form: One cost is the thing that rose. Defences is inside a phrase explaining which cost, and a phrase like that never gets a vote.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Have risen would make the defences themselves the thing that went up, which turns a budget sentence into a sentence about sea walls getting taller.

notice_set.sentence: The list of protected sites has grown again.
notice_set.question: What has grown?
notice_set.why: Has points back to a single thing, and the only single thing available is the list.

notice_set.sentence: A number of residents have objected to the plan.
notice_set.question: How many people objected?
notice_set.why: A number of is a way of saying several, and the verb follows the several rather than the word number.

notice_set.sentence: The number of complaints has fallen since March.
notice_set.question: What is the sentence measuring?
notice_set.why: The number of names one figure, and one figure is what has fallen.

notice_set.sentence: Each of the three schemes was funded separately.
notice_set.question: Were the schemes funded together?
notice_set.why: Each takes the group apart and looks at the members one at a time, which is why the verb is singular.

notice_set.sentence: There is a car park, two cycle racks and a bus stop outside.
notice_set.question: How many car parks are there?
notice_set.why: There is matches the first item on the list, and the first item is a single car park.

notice_set.sentence: The committee are still arguing about the wording.
notice_set.question: Is the group acting as one body here?
notice_set.why: Arguing needs more than one person, so the plural verb tells you the members are acting separately.

teach.rule_line: Cover everything between the subject and the verb, then read it again.
teach.false_rule: That the verb matches the nearest noun. It matches the noun the sentence is about, however far back that sits.

errors.wrong: The impact of rising sea levels are already visible on this coast.
errors.right: The impact of rising sea levels is already visible on this coast.
errors.why_it_happens: By the time the writer reaches the verb, the last thing in working memory is levels, and the verb is matched to whatever is still warm rather than to the head noun.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: are becomes is.

errors.wrong: The survey that produced these figures were funded by the council.
errors.right: The survey that produced these figures was funded by the council.
errors.why_it_happens: A relative clause reads like a complete sentence of its own, so its last noun feels like a fresh subject when the main verb finally arrives.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: were becomes was.

errors.wrong: Each of the proposals have been costed separately.
errors.right: Each of the proposals has been costed separately.
errors.why_it_happens: Each is about a group, so it feels plural. Its whole job is the opposite: it walks through the group one member at a time.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: There is several reasons why the scheme stalled.
errors.right: There are several reasons why the scheme stalled.
errors.why_it_happens: There is has been learned as a fixed opener rather than as a verb that still has to look forward at what follows it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: is becomes are.

errors.wrong: Neither the council nor the residents was consulted.
errors.right: Neither the council nor the residents were consulted.
errors.why_it_happens: Neither sounds negative and singular, so it seems to set the count for the whole subject. English lets the part nearest the verb decide instead.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: was becomes were.

pays_in.note: Long subjects are what an essay is made of, and they are where agreement breaks.
pays_in.model: The effect of these measures on household bills is harder to predict.

pays_in.note: The number of and a number of sit in almost every data description.
pays_in.model: The number of journeys made by bicycle rose steadily across the period.

pays_in.note: The verb tells you which noun a long subject is really about.
pays_in.model: The range of species recorded at the reserve has narrowed since 2015.

used_in.quote: Answers on this prompt run on long subjects such as the effect of fertiliser run-off on river life.

payload.sentence: The quality of the rivers around Marlow has improved since 2018.
payload.question: What has improved?

feedback.why_key: Has points back to one thing, and quality is the only single noun in the subject.
feedback.feed_forward: Let the verb tell you which noun the sentence is about.

payload.sentence: The number of households in the district has doubled.
payload.question: Is the sentence about a total or about the households themselves?

feedback.why_key: The number of names one figure, and the singular verb keeps the reader looking at that figure rather than at the houses.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the number of as one measurement.

items.decision_cue: The share of journeys made on foot

payload.context: A line from a description of a bar chart.
payload.sentence: The share of journeys made on foot rises sharply after 2019.
reasons: the verb has been matched to the wrong noun
the phrase in the middle needs a different preposition
the tense is wrong for a chart
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: One share is what rises. Journeys sits inside a phrase saying which share, so it never gets a vote.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the head noun first, then stop reading.

payload.context: From a paragraph about farm run-off in the Verdon.
payload.stem: The effect of these chemicals on river life ___ (be) still being measured.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: Effect is the head of the subject and there is one of it. Chemicals and life are both inside phrases describing which effect.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover everything after of and read the subject again.

payload.context: From a table description about rents across four districts.
payload.stem: A number of tenants ___ (pay) more than half their income in rent.

expected: pay

feedback.why_key: A number of is a quantity word meaning several, so the tenants are what the verb answers to.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a number of as several and the verb follows.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about tuition costs.
payload.stem: Each of the four proposals ___ (leave) graduates paying for longer.

expected: leaves

feedback.why_key: Each takes the four apart and looks at one at a time, so the verb answers to a single proposal.
feedback.feed_forward: Treat each and every as one, whatever follows them.

payload.context: Open a paragraph that will list what went wrong.

expected: there are three reasons for the decline in the reserve

feedback.why_key: There has no meaning of its own, so the verb looks forward to reasons and matches that.
feedback.feed_forward: After there, read on before you choose is or are.

payload.given: The findings are disputed. The findings come from a single study.
payload.instruction: Join them so that the second sentence sits inside the first as a relative clause.

expected: that come from a single study are disputed
which come from a single study are disputed
coming from a single study are disputed

feedback.why_key: Study is the last noun before the main verb but it is inside the clause, so are still answers to findings.
feedback.feed_forward: Bracket the relative clause off before you write the main verb.

payload.audio_text: The range of species recorded at the reserve has narrowed.

expected: the range of species recorded at the reserve has narrowed

feedback.why_key: Has is squashed almost to nothing in speech, and species gives no clue either way, so the head noun is the only guide.
feedback.feed_forward: Catch the head noun and let it predict the auxiliary.

items.decision_cue: The cost of these measures are

payload.sentence: The cost of these measures are passed straight on to households.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: One cost is what reaches the household bill. Measures is inside a phrase saying which cost, so it is scenery.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the of-phrase in your head and reread the subject.

payload.context: Two districts were surveyed and several households in each reported the same problem.
payload.stem: A number of households ___ reported damp in the same two blocks.

options.why_this_means: That one countable total is being reported as a single figure.
That several separate households did the reporting.

expected: have

feedback.why_key: A number of is a way of saying several, so the households themselves are doing the reporting and the verb follows them.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap in several and see whether the sentence still means the same.

payload.context: One figure was tracked across the survey period and it moved in a single direction.
payload.stem: The number of households ___ risen every year since 2019.

options.why_this_means: That one countable total is being reported as a single figure.
That several separate households did the reporting.

expected: has

feedback.why_key: The number of names one figure and the figure is the thing that moved, so the verb answers to it and not to the households.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask whether you are counting a total or the things themselves.

items.decision_cue: Neither the magistrates nor the police officer

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about community sentences.
payload.sentence: Neither the magistrates nor the police officer was told about the change.
reasons: the verb should match the first of the two
neither cannot be used with two people
the verb should be plural because two parties are named
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: With neither and nor the part nearest the verb decides, and the nearest part here is one officer.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at the noun immediately before the verb after nor or or.

payload.prompt_text: Write one sentence about river pollution whose subject is at least six words long and contains a plural noun that is not the head.

feedback.why_key: Building the trap yourself is the fastest way to stop walking into it, because you have to name the head noun before you write the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Say the head noun out loud before you write the verb.

payload.prompt_text: Take the prompt on farm run-off and river pollution. Write the problem paragraph, then spend two minutes on one pass that checks only the verbs whose subject runs to more than three words.

feedback.why_key: The check has to be a separate pass, because the same attention that builds a long subject is the attention that loses the verb at the end of it.
feedback.feed_forward: Run one pass for agreement alone, reading subject to verb.

title: Putting commas where they earn their place

point_json.grammar_name: Comma rules: fronted adverbial, extra clause, list, and the comma that must not appear

teach.can_do: I can place a comma because of what the sentence is doing, not because of where I would breathe.
teach.why_it_matters: Two of the four comma jobs change what a sentence claims, so a stray pair can hand a reader a number or a group you never meant.
teach.meaning: A comma has four jobs and one thing it must never do. It closes a piece of scenery placed in front of the main clause. It fences off a clause or a phrase that is extra rather than identifying, with one comma each side. It separates the items of a list. And it stands beside and, but or so when two whole clauses are joined. What it may never do is stand between a subject and its verb, however long the subject has grown.

form.pattern: front matter , main clause · noun , extra news , verb · a , b and c · clause , and clause
notes: a phrase in front of the main clause closes with a comma: in most European cities, cycling has grown
an extra clause takes commas on both sides, and once you open the fence you must close it
no comma before a defining clause, because that clause is telling the reader which one you mean
in a list the comma before and is optional in British English, and whichever you choose you keep
no comma between a subject and its verb, however long the subject: what the survey actually showed was something else
form.negative: A negative main clause is punctuated the same way: after the first year, the trial was not extended.
form.question: In a question the front matter still closes with a comma: after the first year, was the trial extended?

left.role: scenery, which closes with a comma
left.text: Since the paywall went up,

right.role: the sentence itself, which never takes one before its verb
right.text: local coverage has almost disappeared.

spec.caption: The comma marks where the scenery ends, not where you would take a breath.

worked_example.sentence: Since the paywall went up, the paper's local coverage, which had already been cut twice, has almost disappeared.
worked_example.why_this_form: The opening phrase is scenery and closes with a comma. The middle clause is extra news about coverage there is only one of, so it is fenced off on both sides.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Take the second pair of commas away and the clause starts identifying, which would claim there is some other local coverage that has not been cut.

notice_set.sentence: The reporters, who had covered the harbour, were moved to the news desk.
notice_set.question: Were all the reporters moved?
notice_set.why: The commas make the harbour a side note, so the sentence is about the whole group of reporters.

notice_set.sentence: The reporters who had covered the harbour were moved to the news desk.
notice_set.question: Were all the reporters moved?
notice_set.why: With no commas the clause picks a smaller group out of a bigger one, and only that group moved.

notice_set.sentence: After the paywall went up, sales fell for four months.
notice_set.question: Did sales fall before or after the paywall went up?
notice_set.why: The front phrase sets the time and the comma closes it, so everything after the comma sits inside that time.

notice_set.sentence: The paper covers sport, local politics and planning.
notice_set.question: How many areas does the paper cover?
notice_set.why: The comma and the final and mark off three separate items on one list.

notice_set.sentence: The editor who joined last year has already left.
notice_set.question: Has the paper had more than one editor recently?
notice_set.why: No commas means the clause is telling you which editor, and that only has a job to do if there was more than one.

teach.rule_line: A comma marks a boundary in the grammar, never a place to breathe.
teach.false_rule: That a comma goes wherever you would pause. Read a long subject aloud and you will pause; the comma still must not go there.

errors.wrong: Journalists, who work freelance, are paid for each piece.
errors.right: Journalists who work freelance are paid for each piece.
errors.why_it_happens: The clause feels like an aside, so it is fenced off out of politeness. The fence turns a claim about freelancers into a claim about every journalist alive.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two marks: both commas.

errors.wrong: The scheme, which the council approved in March has already stalled.
errors.right: The scheme, which the council approved in March, has already stalled.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening comma goes in correctly and the writer then reads on through the clause and forgets that a fence needs a second side.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one mark: a comma after March.

errors.wrong: What the survey actually showed, was a sharp fall in trust.
errors.right: What the survey actually showed was a sharp fall in trust.
errors.why_it_happens: The subject has grown long enough that the writer needs a breath, and the mark is placed where the breath falls rather than where the grammar allows one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one mark: the comma.

errors.wrong: In most European cities cycling to work has grown sharply.
errors.right: In most European cities, cycling to work has grown sharply.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening phrase is short enough to read smoothly without a mark, so nothing warns the writer that a reader has to guess where the scenery ends.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one mark: a comma after cities.

pays_in.note: Fronted phrases and extra clauses are how a body paragraph varies its shape.
pays_in.model: In most large cities, local reporting, which used to be funded by advertising, has thinned out.

pays_in.note: Every trend sentence opens with a time phrase that has to close.
pays_in.model: Between 2015 and 2019, the share of readers under thirty fell by half.

pays_in.note: A pair of commas tells you the clause inside is not narrowing anything down.
pays_in.model: The trial, which ran for six months, was never repeated.

used_in.quote: Answers on this prompt lean on fronted time phrases and on extra clauses about the newspapers themselves.

payload.sentence: The photographers, who were freelance, were paid a month late.
payload.question: Were all the photographers paid late?

feedback.why_key: The commas fence the clause off as a side note, so the sentence is about the whole group and being freelance is extra.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a fenced clause as extra news, never as a filter.

payload.sentence: The photographers who were freelance were paid a month late.
payload.question: Were all the photographers paid late?

feedback.why_key: With the fence gone the clause narrows the group, so the staff photographers were paid on time.
feedback.feed_forward: Count who is left outside the clause when there are no commas.

payload.context: The opening line of a description of a line graph.
payload.sentence: Between 2015 and 2019, the number of cycle journeys almost doubled.
reasons: the front phrase should not take a comma
a second comma is needed before the verb
the years should come at the end
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The time phrase is scenery and closes with one comma. Nothing then comes between the subject and its verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Close the front phrase and then leave the sentence alone.

payload.context: There is one paper in Marlow, and the fence is already in place around the clause.
payload.stem: The Marlow paper, ___ has covered the harbour since 1954, is closing in June.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: Inside a pair of commas the clause is extra news, and that is the one place where that cannot stand.
feedback.feed_forward: Use which once the clause is fenced off.

payload.context: Open the paragraph with a phrase that sets the place before the claim arrives.
payload.stem: ___ most European cities, cycling to work has grown steadily.

expected: in

feedback.why_key: The phrase is scenery placed in front of the sentence, and the comma after cities is what tells the reader the scenery has ended.
feedback.feed_forward: Close every fronted phrase with a comma.

payload.context: Build one sentence that opens with the time and then makes the claim.

expected: after the paywall went up local sales fell sharply

feedback.why_key: The mark belongs at the join between the scenery and the sentence, which is after up and nowhere else.
feedback.feed_forward: Drop the comma where the front phrase stops.

payload.given: The trial was never repeated. It ran for six months.
payload.instruction: Put the second fact inside the first as extra news, fenced off on both sides.

expected: which ran for six months, was never repeated
which ran for six months was never repeated

feedback.why_key: There is only one trial, so the length cannot be narrowing anything down and has to be presented as a side note.
feedback.feed_forward: Open the fence and close it in the same breath.

payload.audio_text: The editor, who's been there since 2019, is leaving in June.

expected: the editor, who's been there since 2019, is leaving in june
the editor who's been there since 2019 is leaving in june
the editor who has been there since 2019 is leaving in june
the editor whos been there since 2019 is leaving in june

feedback.why_key: In speech the fence is a small drop in the voice on either side of the clause, and that drop is what a comma is written for.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the dip in the voice around the extra clause.

payload.sentence: What the survey actually showed, was a sharp fall in trust.

expected: showed was

feedback.why_key: Everything up to showed is the subject and was is its verb, and nothing is allowed to stand between the two.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the verb, then check that nothing sits in front of it.

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a council planning decision.
payload.sentence: The scheme, which the council approved in March has already stalled.
reasons: the fence round the extra clause has only one side
which should be that
the date has been put in the wrong place
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The reader is told the clause is extra, then never told where it ends, so the main verb arrives with no subject in sight.
feedback.feed_forward: Once you open a comma fence, close it before the main verb.

items.decision_cue: only three of them went to the harbour

payload.context: The paper employs eight reporters, and only three of them went to the harbour.
payload.stem: The reporters ___ have been moved to the news desk.

options.why_this_means: That only the harbour reporters moved, and the others stayed where they were.
That every reporter moved, and that all of them had been at the harbour.

expected: who covered the harbour

feedback.why_key: Five reporters never went near the harbour, so the clause has real work to do: it says which three are meant.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the commas out whenever the clause is separating a group.

items.decision_cue: all eight spent the summer at the harbour

payload.context: The paper employs eight reporters, and all eight spent the summer at the harbour.
payload.stem: The reporters ___ have been moved to the news desk.

options.why_this_means: That only the harbour reporters moved, and the others stayed where they were.
That every reporter moved, and that all of them had been at the harbour.

expected: , who covered the harbour,

feedback.why_key: If all eight were at the harbour there is nobody left to narrow the group down to, so the clause can only be a side note.
feedback.feed_forward: Fence the clause off once the group is already complete.

payload.context: Two lines from different letters about the same college.
sentences: The tutors who trained abroad run the evening classes.
The tutors, who trained abroad, run the evening classes.
meanings: Some of the tutors trained abroad, and those are the ones on the evening timetable.
Every tutor trained abroad, and all of them are on the evening timetable.

feedback.why_key: The words are identical. The pair of marks is the whole difference between some of the staff and all of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the people before you punctuate the clause.

payload.prompt_text: Write two sentences about where you get your news. Open the first with a time or place phrase, and put an extra fenced-off clause inside the second.

feedback.why_key: The two shapes carry almost all the commas an essay needs, and building them deliberately is what stops the marks landing on breaths instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what each comma is doing before you leave it there.

payload.prompt_text: Take the two-part prompt on news and social media. Write one body paragraph, then take three minutes to point at every comma and say out loud which of the four jobs it is doing. Delete any that cannot answer.

feedback.why_key: Making each mark justify itself is faster than remembering the rules, and it catches the subject-verb comma that no rule ever seems to catch.
feedback.feed_forward: Make every comma name its job or lose its place.

title: The rest of the marks: semicolon, colon, apostrophe and capital letter

point_json.grammar_name: Semicolon, colon, apostrophe, capitalisation and quotation

teach.can_do: I can use a semicolon, a colon and an apostrophe for what each of them actually does.
teach.why_it_matters: These are the cheapest marks on the page: each error is one character, each is instantly visible, and none of them takes any thought once the job is named.
teach.meaning: A semicolon is a full stop that promises the next sentence is closely related, so what stands on either side of it must be a whole sentence. A colon announces that what follows is the thing just promised: an example, a list, an explanation. An apostrophe does two jobs only, belonging and a missing letter, and it never marks more than one. Capital letters belong to names, not to words that feel important.

form.pattern: clause ; clause · clause : the thing announced · noun + 's = belonging · it's = it is
notes: a semicolon needs a whole sentence on each side; a comma there is a splice
a colon needs a whole sentence in front of it, and can be followed by a list, a phrase or a clause
its means belonging to it; it's means it is or it has
plurals never take an apostrophe: the 1990s, three CVs, two buses
a plural owner takes the apostrophe after the s: the residents' committee
capitals go on people, places, institutions, months and days, not on subjects or job titles in general
form.negative: A negative second half changes none of it: the shop reopened in May; the owners have not taken a wage since.
form.question: A question can follow a colon: the report asks one thing: can the street survive another year?

left.text: the firm's account · it's closed

right.text: the 1990s · two CVs · the buses

spec.caption: If the word is only counting, it takes no mark at all.

worked_example.sentence: The firm's accounts were filed late: its finance team had lost three weeks to a software change.
worked_example.why_this_form: The first mark shows the accounts belong to the firm. The colon announces the explanation that was promised, and its is the belonging form, which never takes a mark.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: It's finance team would read as it is finance team, and a semicolon in place of the colon would drop the promise that a reason is on its way.

notice_set.sentence: The shop's owner has appealed against the decision.
notice_set.question: How many shops are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The mark sits in front of the s, and that is where English puts it when the owner is a single thing.

notice_set.sentence: The shops' owner has appealed against the decision.
notice_set.question: How many shops are being talked about?
notice_set.why: The mark has moved behind the s, which is what happens once the owner is already a group.

notice_set.sentence: Its front window was replaced last month.
notice_set.question: Whose window was replaced?
options: Somebody who has not been named
notice_set.why: Its with no mark means belonging, and what it belongs to is whatever the writing was already about.

notice_set.sentence: The report gives one reason: rents.
notice_set.question: How many reasons are given?
notice_set.why: The colon delivers exactly what the sentence in front of it promised, and one reason was promised.

notice_set.sentence: Sales fell every quarter; the owners blamed the new car park.
notice_set.question: Are the two facts offered as connected?
notice_set.why: A semicolon stops the first sentence and promises that the second belongs with it.

teach.rule_line: An apostrophe means belonging or a missing letter, and never means more than one.
teach.false_rule: That an apostrophe tidies up an s. Plurals never take one, not for decades, not for initials, not for prices.

errors.wrong: Its important to compare prices before buying anything large.
errors.right: It's important to compare prices before buying anything large.
errors.why_it_happens: The two sound identical, and everywhere else in English the belonging form is the one that carries the mark, so the mark is dropped exactly where it is needed.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one mark: an apostrophe in its.

errors.wrong: House prices rose sharply in the 1990's.
errors.right: House prices rose sharply in the 1990s.
errors.why_it_happens: The apostrophe has been stored as the mark that goes near an s, and a decade looks unusual enough on the page to invite one.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one mark: the apostrophe.

errors.wrong: The report blames: rising rents and online shopping.
errors.right: The report blames rising rents and online shopping.
errors.why_it_happens: A colon feels like a formal way of introducing a list, and nothing in that feeling says the colon needs a whole sentence standing in front of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one mark: the colon.

errors.wrong: Sales fell every quarter, the owners blamed the new car park.
errors.right: Sales fell every quarter; the owners blamed the new car park.
errors.why_it_happens: The two facts are so closely linked that a full stop feels too heavy, so the lighter mark is chosen. The semicolon is the mark that is light and strong at once.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one mark: the comma becomes a semicolon.

pays_in.note: A colon is the cheapest way to introduce an example without a linking phrase.
pays_in.model: One cost is rarely counted: the time people spend travelling to buy anything at all.

pays_in.note: Letters are full of names, dates and belonging, which is where these marks live.
pays_in.model: The landlord's agent has not replied to either of my emails.

pays_in.note: A colon tells you the next words are an unpacking rather than a new point.
pays_in.model: The findings point in one direction: the high street is losing its convenience trade.

used_in.quote: Answers here are dense with shops, owners and decades, so all three marks appear within a paragraph.

payload.sentence: The bakery's ovens were replaced last winter.
payload.question: How many bakeries are being talked about?

feedback.why_key: The mark sits in front of the s, and that is the position English uses when the owner is one thing.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the position of the mark as a count of owners.

payload.sentence: The traders' association has written to the council.
payload.question: How many traders are in the association?

feedback.why_key: The mark has moved behind the s, which only happens once the owner is already a group.
feedback.feed_forward: Look at which side of the s the mark is standing.

payload.context: A line from a finished report on a shopping street.
payload.sentence: The owners give one reason: the rent has trebled since 2019.
reasons: a colon cannot be followed by a whole sentence
the colon should be a semicolon
the first half is not a whole sentence
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A whole sentence stands in front of the colon and what follows is exactly the reason that sentence promised.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that the half before a colon could stand alone.

payload.context: Writing about a single shop that was damaged in a storm.
payload.stem: The shop lost ___ (it) front window and half a week of trade.

expected: its

feedback.why_key: The window belongs to the shop, and the belonging form of it is the one word in English that takes no mark at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Try reading it as it is; if that fails, write its.

payload.context: Everyone in the block belongs to the same committee.
payload.stem: The ___ (residents) committee meets on the first Tuesday of the month.

expected: residents'

feedback.why_key: The owners are already a group, so the s is doing the counting and the mark goes behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the plural first, then add the mark on the end.

payload.context: One firm, and the writer wants the reader to know whose figures these are.
payload.stem: The ___ (company) own figures show a fall of nine per cent.

expected: company's

feedback.why_key: One owner puts the mark in front of the s, and nothing about the word company changes that.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the owners before you place the mark.

payload.context: Hold two closely related facts in one sentence without a joining word.

expected: sales fell every quarter the owners blamed the car park

feedback.why_key: The mark can only stand where both sides are whole sentences, and there is only one such place here.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the semicolon where a full stop would also work.

payload.audio_text: It's the only shop on the street that has kept its opening hours.

expected: it's the only shop on the street that has kept its opening hours
it is the only shop on the street that has kept its opening hours

feedback.why_key: The two words sound the same, so the only way to write them apart is to ask which one can be stretched back out into it is.
feedback.feed_forward: Stretch each one into it is and see which survives.

payload.sentence: House prices rose faster than wages throughout the 1990's.

feedback.why_key: The decade owns nothing and nothing has been left out of it, so neither of the mark's two jobs applies.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask what is belonging or missing; if neither, take the mark out.

payload.context: From an early draft of an essay about town-centre shops.
payload.sentence: The report blames: rising rents, online shopping and parking charges.
reasons: there is no whole sentence in front of the colon
the list needs a comma before and
the three items are in the wrong order
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The report blames stops mid-thought, so the colon is announcing a promise the sentence never actually made.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover the colon and read what is left; it must stand alone.

items.decision_cue: One shop on the street lost its licence

payload.context: One shop on the street lost its licence last month and is fighting the decision.
payload.stem: The ___ owner has appealed against the ruling.

options.why_this_means: That one shop is being talked about and the owner belongs to that one.
That several shops are being talked about and they share one owner between them.

expected: shop's

feedback.why_key: There is a single shop in the situation, so the mark goes in front of the s where a single owner belongs.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the owners, then decide which side of the s to write on.

items.decision_cue: Four shops on the street are run by the same family

payload.context: Four shops on the street are run by the same family, and all four lost their licences.
payload.stem: The ___ owner has appealed against the ruling.

options.why_this_means: That one shop is being talked about and the owner belongs to that one.
That several shops are being talked about and they share one owner between them.

expected: shops'

feedback.why_key: Four shops share the owner, so the s is already counting and the mark has to stand behind it.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the plural first and add the mark afterwards.

payload.context: Two lines from different drafts of the same report.
sentences: The market closed in May; the car park was full within a week.
The market closed in May: the car park had been full for months.
meanings: Two related facts, with the second following the first in time.
A fact and then the reason behind it, which the colon promised.

feedback.why_key: A semicolon says these two belong together. A colon says the second one is the thing the first one was pointing at.
feedback.feed_forward: Use a colon only when the second half unpacks the first.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences about the shops in your area: one that uses a semicolon, one that uses a colon, and one containing a plural owner.

feedback.why_key: Each mark has to be chosen for its job here, which is the only way any of them ever becomes automatic.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the job the mark is doing as you write it.

payload.prompt_text: Take the two-part prompt on town-centre shops. Write the first body paragraph, then run one two-minute pass that looks only at apostrophes and asks of each one whether something belongs or something is missing.

feedback.why_key: These marks are never caught while you are writing, because writing is about the argument. They are caught in a pass that looks at nothing else.
feedback.feed_forward: Run a separate pass for apostrophes alone.

title: The prepositions that belong to a word and travel with it

point_json.grammar_name: Dependent prepositions on verbs, adjectives and nouns

teach.can_do: I can keep the right preposition attached to a word instead of guessing at it.
teach.why_it_matters: It is scored under vocabulary as often as under grammar, and it is one of the few errors that survives every other improvement a learner makes.
teach.meaning: Some prepositions are not chosen at all. They arrive attached to a particular word and stay with it wherever it goes: depend on, result in, aware of, an increase in, a solution to. No rule predicts which one, because the preposition is not being used for its meaning here. It is part of the word. That is why these are learned as pairs, inside sentences, the way a phrase is learned, rather than reasoned out at the moment of writing.

form.pattern: verb + its own preposition · adjective + its own preposition · noun + its own preposition
notes: the verb and the noun for one idea often disagree: it affects prices, but an effect on prices
the family usually keeps its preposition: depend on, dependent on, dependence on
a preposition is always followed by a noun or an -ing form: aware of losing, never aware of lose
an increase in names what is rising; an increase of names the size of the rise
some words take a preposition in one meaning and none in another: discuss the plan, but an argument about the plan
form.negative: The pair holds together under negation: the outcome does not depend on the weather.
form.question: The preposition stays with its word even when the question word moves: what does the outcome depend on?

left.text: an increase

right.role: the preposition that came with it
right.text: in rainfall

spec.caption: Store the two boxes as one item. Splitting them is what creates the error.

worked_example.sentence: The rise in flooding results from decades of drainage work upstream.
worked_example.why_this_form: Rise brings in with it and results brings from with it. Neither preposition is describing a place or a time; each one belongs to its word.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Rise of would push the reader towards the size of the change, and results in would turn the sentence round and make the drainage the outcome.

notice_set.sentence: Rainfall in the catchment rose by twelve per cent.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell us the figure it reached?
notice_set.why: By gives the size of the change and leaves the level it arrived at unstated.

notice_set.sentence: Rainfall in the catchment rose to twelve inches.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell us the figure it reached?
notice_set.why: To names the point the line arrived at, which is exactly the figure.

notice_set.sentence: The flooding resulted from years of drainage work.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: Result from looks backwards to the cause, so the drainage is the earlier of the two.

notice_set.sentence: Local groups are concerned about the river.
notice_set.question: Are the groups worried?
notice_set.why: Concerned about is worried; concerned with would only mean the river is what they work on.

notice_set.sentence: There has been a sharp increase in reported spills.
notice_set.question: Is the number of spills going up?
notice_set.why: Increase brings in with it, and whatever follows in is the thing that is rising.

teach.rule_line: Learn the preposition with the word, inside a sentence, never as a rule.
teach.false_rule: That you can work the preposition out from what it means. Here it carries no meaning of its own.

errors.wrong: The outcome depends of the weather in early spring.
errors.right: The outcome depends on the weather in early spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Of is the commonest preposition in the language and gets reached for as a default whenever the required one was never stored beside the verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: of becomes on.

errors.wrong: Rising temperatures have an effect in crop yields.
errors.right: Rising temperatures have an effect on crop yields.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb affect takes no preposition at all, so the learner's memory of the idea offers no clue about what the noun form demands.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: in becomes on.

errors.wrong: The council is aware about the state of the river.
errors.right: The council is aware of the state of the river.
errors.why_it_happens: About is the preposition for a topic and awareness does have a topic, so the wrong choice is the semantically reasonable one.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: about becomes of.

errors.wrong: There is no solution for this without national funding.
errors.right: There is no solution to this without national funding.
errors.why_it_happens: For marks purpose and a solution obviously has a purpose, which makes the wrong preposition the more logical of the two on the page.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: for becomes to.

pays_in.note: Rise in, rise by and rise to sit in almost every line of a data description.
pays_in.model: The increase in household demand was matched by a fall in industrial use.

pays_in.note: Depend on, result in and contribute to carry most causal sentences.
pays_in.model: Much of the damage results from decisions taken thirty years ago.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers are built on aware of, worried about and responsible for.
pays_in.model: Most people are aware of the problem, but very few feel responsible for it.

used_in.quote: Every trend line on this task needs a rise in something, by some amount, to some level.

payload.sentence: Household demand for water rose by nine per cent.
payload.question: Does the sentence give the level demand reached?

feedback.why_key: By gives the size of the step and says nothing about where the line started or finished.
feedback.feed_forward: Read by as the size of the change.

payload.sentence: The damage resulted from three decades of drainage work.
payload.question: Which happened first?

feedback.why_key: Result from looks backwards to the cause, so whatever follows from is the earlier event.
feedback.feed_forward: Let from and in tell you which way the causing runs.

payload.context: A Part 3 answer about who should pay for cleaning up rivers.
payload.sentence: Most people are aware of the problem but nobody wants to pay for it.
reasons: aware takes about rather than of
pay takes no preposition at all
the two halves need a different joining word
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Aware brings of with it and pay brings for with it, and both pairs are sitting intact.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the preposition against the word in front of it, not the word after.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about flood defences.
payload.stem: How well the scheme works depends ___ how much rain falls in March.

expected: on
upon

feedback.why_key: Depend carries on with it wherever it goes, in every tense and in every word class in its family.
feedback.feed_forward: Store depend on as one item, never as two.

payload.context: The opening line of a description of a line graph.
payload.stem: The graph shows a steady increase ___ the number of recorded spills.

expected: in

feedback.why_key: Increase brings in with it, and what follows in is the thing that is going up rather than the size of the rise.
feedback.feed_forward: Write an increase in whenever you name what is rising.

payload.context: From a paragraph arguing that the problem has no cheap answer.
payload.stem: There is no realistic solution ___ this without national funding.

expected: to

feedback.why_key: Solution takes to, even though a solution has a purpose and for would be the more logical guess.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn solution to as one word with a gap in the middle.

payload.given: Rising temperatures affect crop yields across the region.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so that the verb becomes a noun.

expected: an effect on crop yields across the region
an effect on crop yields

feedback.why_key: The verb needs no preposition and the noun demands one, which is why the two forms of the same idea have to be stored separately.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the preposition again every time you change word class.

payload.audio_text: It's led to a rise in flooding and a fall in water quality.

expected: it's led to a rise in flooding and a fall in water quality
it has led to a rise in flooding and a fall in water quality
its led to a rise in flooding and a fall in water quality

feedback.why_key: Every one of these prepositions is unstressed, so what you catch is the word in front of it and what you write is whatever was stored beside that word.
feedback.feed_forward: Catch the noun, then write the preposition it always takes.

payload.sentence: The council has been aware about the state of the river since 2019.

expected: aware of

feedback.why_key: About is what you would choose from the meaning, and aware simply does not take it.
feedback.feed_forward: Trust the stored pair over the meaning.

items.decision_cue: resulted in decades of poor drainage

payload.context: From a draft paragraph on why one river valley floods so often.
payload.sentence: The flooding resulted in decades of poor drainage upstream.
reasons: the preposition has reversed the cause and the outcome
result cannot be used with a time expression
the sentence needs a different tense
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Result in points forwards to what came out of something, so as written the flooding is causing the drainage rather than the other way round.
feedback.feed_forward: Ask which side of result the cause is standing on.

options.why_this_means: That four inches is the size of the step, not the level reached.
That four inches is the level the line arrived at.

options.why_this_means: That four inches is the size of the step, not the level reached.

feedback.feed_forward: Underline every preposition and name the word it belongs to.

title: Saying how a figure moved, how far it went and where it ended up

point_json.grammar_name: The grammar of change: rise in / rise to / rise by, from ... to, peak at, level off
signal_blocklist: as can be seen from the graph

teach.can_do: I can describe how a figure moved: how far it travelled, where it stopped and what shape the journey had.
teach.why_it_matters: A chart description is nothing but this. Every sentence reports a movement, and the small word after the verb is where the marks go.
teach.meaning: A chart hands you two kinds of number and English keeps them apart. One is the movement itself, which is how far the line travelled. The other is the level, which is where it stopped. The verb names the shape of the journey and the small word after it tells the reader which of those two numbers is coming next. Choose the right verb and the wrong preposition, and the reader still walks away with a different chart from the one in front of you.

form.pattern: rise / fall + by SIZE  ·  rise / fall + to LEVEL  ·  rise / fall + from START + to END  ·  a rise / fall + in WHAT  ·  a rise / fall + of SIZE  ·  peak / stand / remain + at LEVEL
notes: The three prepositions do three different jobs. By measures the movement: rose by four points. To names the level it reached: rose to eleven per cent. In names the thing that is moving: a rise in unemployment.
The verb takes by for the size; the noun takes of for the size and never by. Output fell by nine million. There was a fall of nine million.
from ... to ... gives both ends at once and wants nothing else with it: demand rose from twenty to thirty-five million litres.

The irregular past forms, which are the ones that get guessed: rise / rose / risen, fall / fell / fallen, grow / grew / grown. The rest are regular: increase, decrease, decline, double, fluctuate, plateau, peak.
rise never takes an object and never goes passive; raise does both. Prices rose. The council raised the fee. Never was risen, and never was increased when nobody did the increasing.
Verb and noun come in fixed pairs: rise / a rise, fall / a fall, grow / growth (there is no a grow), decline / a decline, fluctuate / a fluctuation, level off / a levelling off, peak / a peak.
The flat verbs report an absence of movement and take no figure at all: level off, plateau, remain stable, hold steady, fluctuate. Only peak, stand and remain take at.

Adverb after the verb, adjective in front of the noun, and they come in matched pairs: rose sharply / a sharp rise, fell dramatically / a dramatic fall, grew steadily / steady growth, dipped slightly / a slight dip.
The article is not optional in the noun version. There was a sharp rise, never there was sharp rise. Growth is the exception, because it is uncountable: steady growth, no article.
form.negative: The negative you almost never need is nothing fell. Reach instead for the flat verbs — remained stable, showed little change, held steady at — which say it without a negative.
form.question: Which number am I about to give: how far it moved, or where it ended up?

left.text: demand fell by nine million litres

right.text: demand fell to nine million litres

spec.caption: Same verb, same figure, two different charts. One small word is the only thing telling the reader which one you are looking at.

worked_example.sentence: Industrial water demand rose by a fifth between 2000 and 2010, peaking at just over ninety million litres a day.
worked_example.why_this_form: By measures the climb and at fixes the highest point. Two numbers doing two different jobs, and neither preposition will do the other one's work.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Rose to a fifth would put demand at twenty per cent of something. That is a level, not a climb, and it describes a different graph.

notice_set.sentence: Unemployment in the northern districts fell by four per cent between 2010 and 2014.
notice_set.question: What was unemployment in 2014?
options: four per cent lower than in 2010
notice_set.why: By measures the drop and nothing else. Without the 2010 figure there is no way to work out where it landed.

notice_set.sentence: Unemployment in the northern districts fell to four per cent by 2014.
notice_set.question: What was unemployment in 2014?
options: four per cent lower than in 2010
notice_set.why: To names the level the line stopped at, so four per cent is the destination rather than the distance travelled.

notice_set.sentence: Visitor numbers levelled off after 2016.
notice_set.question: Did visitor numbers go down after 2016?
notice_set.why: Levelling off is a line that stops moving. It is flat, not falling, and that is exactly why the verb exists.

notice_set.sentence: Rainfall in the catchment fluctuated between 2005 and 2012.
notice_set.question: Did rainfall end the period higher than it started it?
notice_set.why: Fluctuate reports repeated movement up and down and makes no claim at all about the two end points.

notice_set.sentence: Household spending on fuel peaked at eleven per cent in 2013.
notice_set.question: Was eleven per cent the highest figure anywhere in the period?
notice_set.why: A peak is the top of the whole graph, not just a local bump, and at pins it to one number.

notice_set.sentence: There was a slight rise in cycling, followed by a dramatic fall.
notice_set.question: Which of the two movements was the bigger one?
notice_set.why: Slight and dramatic are the two words carrying the sizes, and they sit in front of the nouns rather than after the verbs.

teach.rule_line: Ask which number is coming: how far it moved, or the level it reached.
teach.false_rule: That the little word after a change verb is decoration, so by, to, in and of are interchangeable. Each one points the reader at a different number.

errors.wrong: There was a sharp rise of unemployment in the northern districts after 2009.
errors.right: There was a sharp rise in unemployment in the northern districts after 2009.
errors.why_it_happens: Of is the all-purpose linking word and it arrives first. The learner has also met a rise of nine points, which is correct, and does not yet separate the thing that rises from the size of the rise.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: of becomes in.

errors.wrong: Freight moved by rail fell by nine million tonnes, a drop by almost a third.
errors.right: Freight moved by rail fell by nine million tonnes, a drop of almost a third.
errors.why_it_happens: By was correct three words earlier, so it is still loaded and fires again. The verb takes by for the size of a movement; the noun for that same movement takes of.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: the second by becomes of.

errors.wrong: A dramatically fall in rainfall followed the diversion of the river.
errors.right: A dramatic fall in rainfall followed the diversion of the river.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has drilled fell dramatically and stored the pair as one lump. Turning the verb into a noun leaves the adverb behind, and nothing in the meaning signals that it has to change shape too.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two letters: dramatically becomes dramatic.

errors.wrong: Visitor numbers rose between 2005 and 2010 sharply.
errors.right: Visitor numbers rose sharply between 2005 and 2010.
errors.why_it_happens: The dates feel like the important information, so they go straight after the verb and the adverb is left to trail on the end. English wants the manner word next to the verb it describes.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: sharply goes straight after rose.

errors.wrong: Rainfall in the uplands was decreased steadily after 2011.
errors.right: Rainfall in the uplands decreased steadily after 2011.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has been taught that the passive makes a description sound academic and applies it to a verb that has no object to promote. Nobody decreased the rainfall; it went down on its own.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: was.

pays_in.note: Every single sentence of a line graph or bar chart answer is built out of this.
pays_in.model: Demand from agriculture rose steadily from twenty million litres a day in 2000 to thirty-five million in 2020.
