spec.top_label: as much as one noun can carry

worked_example.sentence: The steady rise in weekend visitors that followed the new rail link has emptied the car parks by nine in the morning.
worked_example.why_this_form: Everything the reader needs about the rise is packed in before the verb, so the sentence makes one point instead of three and never has to name the rise twice.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three short sentences would carry the same facts and would make the reader hold the rise in mind while the other two arrived and joined on.

notice_set.sentence: The hostel by the harbour that the guidebooks recommend is shut all winter.
notice_set.question: Is every hostel in the town shut all winter?
notice_set.why: One hostel has been picked out with two pieces of detail. What the others do is outside the sentence altogether.

notice_set.sentence: The number of visitors staying more than two nights has fallen since 2019.
notice_set.question: What has fallen?
notice_set.why: Everything after number is describing it, so number is the word the verb belongs to.

notice_set.sentence: Cheap flights from the northern cities have filled the town every August.
notice_set.question: Where do the flights come from?
notice_set.why: The small phrase after flights says where they start, and the town is where they end up.

notice_set.sentence: The path along the cliff above the old lifeboat station floods at high tide.
notice_set.question: What floods?
notice_set.why: Two small phrases have stacked up behind path, but path is still the thing the sentence is about.

notice_set.sentence: A converted warehouse with twelve rooms and a shared kitchen opened last spring.
notice_set.question: How many rooms does it have?
notice_set.why: The rooms and the kitchen are both hanging off warehouse, so both belong to the same building.

teach.rule_line: Pack the detail behind the noun and keep the verb agreeing with the noun itself.
teach.false_rule: That range means long sentences. Long noun phrases show range; long sentences with three clauses show how many ways there are to break one.

errors.wrong: The number of visitors arriving at the coastal towns in August have doubled.
errors.right: The number of visitors arriving at the coastal towns in August has doubled.
errors.why_it_happens: Eight words separate the noun from its verb, and the last thing in the writer's ear was towns in August. The verb copies whatever plural was nearest.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: Increase in weekend visitors that followed the new line has strained the car parks.
errors.right: The increase in weekend visitors that followed the new line has strained the car parks.
errors.why_it_happens: The clause behind the noun has already identified exactly which increase is meant, so the phrase feels complete. English still wants the word at the front that says the reader can now find it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.
errors.l1_note: Frequent for learners whose first language marks no articles.

errors.wrong: The town offers cheap accommodation, good transport and it has a long beach.
errors.right: The town offers cheap accommodation, good transport and a long beach.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer runs out of the list shape halfway through and finishes the third item as a fresh sentence, because by then they are thinking about the beach rather than about the list.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one phrase: it has.

pays_in.note: It names a category exactly, in one phrase rather than a sentence.
pays_in.model: The share of households with no car rose in every district outside the centre.

pays_in.note: Complexity you can risk, because so little of it can go wrong.
pays_in.model: Towns dependent on a single summer season have the least room to absorb a bad year.

pays_in.note: A long subject hides the verb, which is often exactly what the question tests.
pays_in.model: The decision to close the two smallest sites was taken without any consultation.

used_in.quote: This prompt is about a kind of traveller and a kind of place, and both have to be named precisely before the argument can start.

payload.sentence: The ferry to the islands that runs twice a day was cancelled all week.
payload.question: What was cancelled?

feedback.why_key: Everything after ferry is describing it, so ferry is what the main verb at the end belongs to.
feedback.feed_forward: Find the noun everything else is hanging on.

payload.sentence: The little place by the station we found last year has closed.
payload.question: How does the speaker know the place?

feedback.why_key: We found last year is a second piece of detail stacked behind the noun, and it tells you how the place got into the conversation.
feedback.feed_forward: Read every phrase after the noun as more about that noun.

items.decision_cue: The cost of the ferry crossings during the summer months

payload.context: From a draft about island communities.
payload.sentence: The cost of the ferry crossings during the summer months are now beyond most families.
reasons: the verb has agreed with the wrong word
the word the is missing from the front
the list does not match itself
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Cost is what the sentence is about and it is one thing. Crossings and months are only describing it, however close they are to the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to the head noun before you write it.

payload.context: From a description of a chart on overnight stays.
payload.stem: The number of visitors booking more than three nights ___ (have) fallen every year since 2018.

expected: has

feedback.why_key: Number is one thing and it is what the sentence is about. Visitors and nights are only describing it from behind.
feedback.feed_forward: Cover everything after the head noun, then choose the verb.

payload.given: A hostel stands by the harbour. It is cheap. The guidebooks all recommend it.
payload.instruction: Write one noun phrase carrying all three facts, then finish the sentence.

expected: by the harbour that the guidebooks all recommend is shut in winter
by the harbour that the guidebooks recommend is full every august
by the harbour that all the guidebooks recommend is shut in winter

feedback.why_key: One phrase, one small phrase and one clause, and the whole of it is still just the subject waiting for its verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Stack the small phrase first, then the clause.

payload.given: The district has cheap rents. It has good transport. It also has a lot of empty units.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence with a list of three items in the same shape.

expected: cheap rents, good transport and a lot of empty units
cheap rents, good transport and plenty of empty units

feedback.why_key: Three noun phrases in a row read as one list. Two noun phrases and a clause make the reader start the sentence again.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that every item in a list is the same shape.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a coastal walk.

expected: the path along the cliff above the bay floods twice a month

feedback.why_key: Two small phrases stack up behind path in the order you would walk them, and the verb still belongs to path at the front.
feedback.feed_forward: Stack the phrases behind the noun in the order they narrow it.

payload.audio_text: The café by the harbour that we liked has closed.

expected: the café by the harbour that we liked has closed
the cafe by the harbour that we liked has closed

feedback.why_key: Two unstressed words are holding the whole phrase together, and losing either one leaves you with three nouns and no idea how they connect.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small joining words between the nouns.

items.decision_cue: The share of beaches meeting the water quality standard

payload.sentence: The share of beaches meeting the water quality standard have risen every year since 2017.

expected: has risen

feedback.why_key: Share is the head of the phrase and it is singular. Beaches is doing nothing but describing it from behind.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the first noun in the phrase.

items.decision_cue: Studies carried out before 2015 tend to

payload.context: From the opening of a research summary.
payload.sentence: Studies carried out before 2015 tend to report much larger effects than later ones.
reasons: this phrase needs the in front of it
the ending on the verb does not match the head noun
the detail should come before the noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: This is a claim about a class rather than about particular studies, and a class opens without the. The clause behind it narrows the class without identifying members.
feedback.feed_forward: Leave the off a class you are generalising about.

parts: A ferry serves the three outer islands.
It runs twice a day in summer.
It has carried the same number of passengers since 2015.
model_combinations: The ferry serving the three outer islands twice a day in summer has carried the same number of passengers since 2015.
The twice-daily summer ferry to the three outer islands has carried the same number of passengers since 2015.
Passenger numbers on the summer ferry to the three outer islands have not moved since 2015.

feedback.why_key: Two of the three facts are describing the ferry, so they belong inside the subject and only the third one needs a verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Put every describing fact inside the subject, then write one verb.

payload.prompt_text: A chart shows how many visitors to a coastal town stayed overnight rather than coming for the day. Write one sentence naming that group precisely and saying what happened to it.

feedback.why_key: Naming the group exactly is most of the work in a chart answer, and it all happens inside the subject before the verb arrives.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the verb against the first noun, not the last.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on photo-led travel. Find three consecutive short sentences that all describe one noun and pack two of them into the subject of the third. Then check the verb against the head noun. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: This is the safest way to raise the level of a paragraph under time pressure, because nothing in it depends on a clause you might not finish.
feedback.feed_forward: Fold the describing sentences into the subject, then reread the verb.

title: Keeping everything in a list the same shape as everything else

point_json.grammar_name: Parallel structure

teach.can_do: I can build a list where every item has the same shape, so my reader can take them in at one go.
teach.why_it_matters: Readers read a list by its pattern. Break the pattern in the third item and they go back to the beginning, which costs you far more than the words saved.
teach.meaning: When you join things with and, or, but or than, English expects the joined parts to be built the same way. Three nouns, or three -ing forms, or three whole clauses, but not two nouns and a clause. The shape is what tells a reader where each item ends and the next begins. When one item changes shape halfway through, the reader loses the thread and has to reread, and they will blame the sentence rather than themselves.

form.pattern: item + , + item + and / or + item, all built the same way
notes: the commonest break is the last item, because by then the writer is thinking about content and not about shape
the paired joiners are stricter still: both ... and, either ... or, not only ... but also, whether ... or
with the paired joiners, whatever follows the first half must match whatever follows the second
than and as are joiners too: better at running than at swimming, not better at running than to swim
form.negative: A negative list matches as well: the scheme covers neither travel nor equipment.
form.question: Read the joining word, then read each item on its own with the opening of the sentence. Do all of them fit?

left.role: the pattern breaks on the last item
left.text: fitness, concentration and it helps them sleep

right.text: fitness, concentration and sleep

spec.caption: A reader takes a list in by its shape. Change the shape and they start it again.

worked_example.sentence: The scheme pays for coaching, equipment and travel to away matches.
worked_example.why_this_form: Three nouns in a row let the reader take all three in one movement, because the shape itself says where each item begins and ends.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Coaching, equipment and it pays for travel turns the third item into a fresh sentence, and the reader goes back to check whether they missed something.

notice_set.sentence: The club offers coaching, equipment and transport to matches.
notice_set.question: How many things does the club offer?
notice_set.why: Three items of the same shape, so the counting happens without any effort at all.

notice_set.sentence: The club offers coaching, equipment and it will take children to away matches.
notice_set.question: How many things does the club offer?
notice_set.why: The third item has changed shape, so it no longer reads as part of the same list and the count comes apart.

notice_set.sentence: Children who play twice a week sleep better than those who play once.
notice_set.question: Which group sleeps better?
notice_set.why: Both sides of than are built the same way, so the comparison lines up and the answer falls out of it.

notice_set.sentence: The council will either build a new pool or refurbish the old one.
notice_set.question: How many of these will the council do?
notice_set.why: Either and or offer a choice of one, and the two matching verbs make it clear these are the two options.

notice_set.sentence: Not only does the club train children, but it also runs a holiday scheme.
notice_set.question: How many activities does the club run?
notice_set.why: The paired joiner promises a second item and delivers exactly one, in the same shape as the first.

teach.rule_line: Everything joined by and, or or than has to be built the same way.
teach.false_rule: That variety is a virtue, so items in a list should look different from one another. Variety belongs between sentences, never inside one list.

errors.wrong: The programme improves fitness, concentration and helps children sleep.
errors.right: The programme improves fitness and concentration, and helps children sleep.
errors.why_it_happens: By the third item the writer is thinking about what to say rather than about the shape they set up two items ago, and the sentence quietly changes gear.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one comma into and.

errors.wrong: Children learn more by playing regularly than to sit through a lesson about it.
errors.right: Children learn more by playing regularly than by sitting through a lesson about it.
errors.why_it_happens: Than feels like a link between two ideas rather than between two matching shapes, so the second half is built from scratch in whatever form comes to mind.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one form: to sit becomes by sitting.

errors.wrong: The club offers coaching, to hire equipment and free travel.
errors.right: The club offers coaching, equipment hire and free travel.
errors.why_it_happens: The middle item arrives as an action rather than as a thing, because that is how the writer thought of it, and nothing forces it back into the shape of its neighbours.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one item: to hire equipment becomes equipment hire.

errors.wrong: Not only the club trains children but also it runs a holiday scheme.
errors.right: The club not only trains children but also runs a holiday scheme.
errors.why_it_happens: Not only has been learned as a phrase that opens a sentence, so it goes to the front. From there it takes a whole clause on each side and the two halves stop matching.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one phrase: not only goes after the club.

pays_in.note: Any sentence listing reasons or benefits is a list, and lists break.
pays_in.model: Daily exercise improves concentration, attendance and behaviour in the afternoon.

pays_in.note: Chart answers list categories, and the categories have to match.
pays_in.model: Spending rose in housing, transport and education, and fell in everything else.

pays_in.note: A long turn is mostly lists, and a broken list is audible.
pays_in.model: It was cheap, easy to get to and open until quite late.

used_in.quote: The benefits paragraph on this prompt is one long list, which is exactly where a shape starts to slip.

payload.sentence: The centre runs classes in swimming, judo and climbing.
payload.question: How many activities does the centre run classes in?

feedback.why_key: Three items of the same shape count themselves, and the reader never has to stop and work anything out.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the items by their shape, not by the commas.

payload.sentence: She's better at running long distances than at sprinting.
payload.question: Which does she do better?

feedback.why_key: Both sides of than open with at and a verb form, so the two halves line up and the comparison is unmistakable.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that both sides of than start the same way.

payload.context: From a draft on school sport.
payload.sentence: Daily exercise improves concentration, attendance and it also builds confidence.
reasons: the last item is built differently from the first two
there are too many items in the list
the verb does not agree with the subject
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Two nouns set up a pattern and the third item arrives as a whole clause, so the reader loses the list and has to go back to the verb.
feedback.feed_forward: Make the last item match the shape of the first.

payload.context: From a paragraph about a village sports club.

title: Writing long sentences that hold together under time pressure

point_json.grammar_name: Control of the complex sentence

teach.can_do: I can write long sentences that stay in one piece, and I know which long sentences are worth the risk.
teach.why_it_matters: A higher score asks for more clean complex sentences, not for fewer mistakes. Writing short and safe is not the cautious option; it is a decision to score lower.
teach.meaning: Two things are being marked at once, and learners usually protect one at the expense of the other. Range means sentences that carry more than one idea and join them properly. Accuracy means those sentences arriving whole. The way to have both is not to write more carefully; it is to reach for structures that have very little in them to go wrong, use two of them per sentence at most, and check three specific things at the end. Long is not the risk. Uncontrolled is.

form.pattern: main clause + one or two supporting clauses, each doing exactly one job
notes: the low-risk workhorses are the relative clause, the because and although clause, the shortened clause and the loaded noun phrase
two supporting clauses in one sentence is plenty; a third rarely adds anything a reader notices
vary the length on purpose, because a short sentence after two long ones is the strongest thing on the page
the three end checks: does every sentence have a main verb, does each verb match its own subject, and did every clause you opened get closed
form.negative: A negative main clause changes nothing about the joins: because nobody else was free, my grandmother collected us.
form.question: Read your sentence back and find the main verb. If you cannot, the sentence has not finished.

spec.label: how much is there in this structure to get wrong?

steps.text: a relative clause, a because clause, an although clause
steps.gloss: one or two things to get right, so use them constantly

steps.text: a shortened clause, a loaded noun phrase
steps.gloss: two or three things, and safe once you have checked whose subject it borrowed

steps.text: an inverted opening, a mixed unreal sentence
steps.gloss: four things at once, under time pressure, for one sentence's worth of credit

worked_example.sentence: Because both my parents worked shifts, the person who actually raised me was my grandmother, who lived three streets away.
worked_example.why_this_form: Two supporting clauses, each doing one job, and both of the kinds that hardly ever break. The sentence is plainly long and has very little inside it that can fail.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three short sentences would carry every one of those facts and would leave a reader with no evidence that the writer can join anything at all.

notice_set.sentence: Because both my parents worked shifts, my grandmother was the one who actually raised me.
notice_set.question: Who raised the speaker?
notice_set.why: The opening explains why, and the part after the comma is the sentence's real news.

notice_set.sentence: My grandmother moved in when I was nine she stayed for eleven years.
notice_set.question: How many separate things is the speaker reporting?
notice_set.why: Nothing marks where the first report ends, so the reader has to hunt for the join and may find it in the wrong place.

notice_set.sentence: Although both my parents worked full time and my grandmother lived three streets away.
notice_set.question: What does the speaker end up telling you happened?
notice_set.why: Everything here is background. The part it was building towards never arrives, so the sentence makes no claim.

notice_set.sentence: We ate together every evening, a habit that has completely disappeared.
notice_set.question: Does the family still eat together?
notice_set.why: The noun after the comma names the practice and the clause behind it reports that it has gone.

notice_set.sentence: Having grown up in a house of six, I found sharing a room completely normal.
notice_set.question: Who grew up in a house of six?
notice_set.why: Nobody is named in the first half, so the reader waits for the comma and gives the growing-up to whoever turns up next, which here is the speaker.

teach.rule_line: Two supporting clauses per sentence, and check every sentence still has a main verb.
teach.false_rule: That a higher score means making fewer mistakes. It means more clean complex sentences, so short safe writing scores lower rather than higher.

errors.wrong: My grandmother moved in with us when I was nine she stayed for eleven years.
errors.right: My grandmother moved in with us when I was nine, and she stayed for eleven years.
errors.why_it_happens: One subordinate clause has already gone in, so the sentence feels complex enough and the second main idea gets attached with nothing joining it at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one joining word after nine.

errors.wrong: Although both my parents worked full time and my grandmother lived three streets away.
errors.right: Although both my parents worked full time, my grandmother lived three streets away.
errors.why_it_happens: Two clauses feel like enough for one sentence. Neither of them is the main one, because and pulled the second clause inside the although along with the first.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: and.

errors.wrong: We ate together every evening, that has completely disappeared now.
errors.right: We ate together every evening, a habit that has completely disappeared.
errors.why_it_happens: The comment plainly belongs with the sentence in front of it, so a full stop feels too heavy. A comma cannot hold two sentences, and there is nothing else in the sentence doing the work.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one noun: a habit, in front of that.

errors.wrong: Having grown up in a house of six, sharing a room felt completely normal.
errors.right: Having grown up in a house of six, I found sharing a room completely normal.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer is thinking about their own childhood, so the opening is anchored inside their head. On the page it borrows the subject that follows, and that subject is an activity rather than a person.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one subject: sharing a room becomes I.

pays_in.note: It is the difference between an answer that is correct and one that shows range.
pays_in.model: Because rents rose faster than wages, the young people who stayed had to live at home.

pays_in.model: The people who moved out were mostly the ones who had young children.

pays_in.note: Dense passages are two-clause sentences, and finding the main one is the skill.
pays_in.model: Although the scheme proved popular, the council that introduced it lost the following election.

title: Giving the other side one point on purpose so your own point lands harder

point_json.grammar_name: Concession structures: while it is true that, admittedly, granted

teach.can_do: I can hand the other side one point on purpose and then take the argument back.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the shape of a band-7 body paragraph. The risk is small: concede once and answer it. Concede twice with no answer and you have changed sides.
teach.meaning: A concession frame hands the other side one point, out loud, before you answer it. It is not politeness and it is not weakness. It tells your reader you have read the argument you are about to beat, which is why the answer that follows lands harder than a flat denial would. The frame has two halves and the second half is compulsory: the point you give away, then the reason it does not decide the question.

form.pattern: While it is true that + CLAUSE , + your answer    |    Admittedly / Granted , + CLAUSE . However , + your answer
notes: the point you give away comes first and the answer comes second, never the other way round
while it is true that needs a whole clause after it; granted and admittedly stand alone with a comma
one frame in a paragraph reads as an argument, two in the same paragraph read as agreement
the relation is marked once: no but after although, no however after while
form.negative: Nobody would deny that + CLAUSE , but + your answer
form.question: Ask yourself: what is the strongest thing they have, and can I survive saying it out loud?

left.text: the resorts really did bring work to the coast

right.text: almost none of that work lasts past September

spec.caption: The first box is a gift. It is only worth giving if the second box is heavier.

worked_example.sentence: While it is true that the resorts have brought year-round work to the coast, most of those posts are filled from outside the district.
worked_example.why_this_form: The reader has probably arrived already believing the jobs argument, so the sentence has to say it back to them before it can answer it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Although the resorts have brought work would set two facts side by side and never admit that anybody had argued for the first one.

notice_set.sentence: Granted, the ferry is cheaper. It also takes four hours longer than the bridge.
notice_set.question: Which one does the speaker want you to choose?
notice_set.why: The price is handed over first so that the four hours can be the thing that decides it.

notice_set.sentence: While it is true that the museum draws visitors, the town sees that money for six weeks a year.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker think the museum has solved the town's problem?
notice_set.why: The visitors are admitted and then answered, which is what somebody does when they are arguing against you.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody would deny that the scheme was expensive.
notice_set.question: Has the speaker finished making their point?
notice_set.why: A point handed to the other side on its own is just a point for the other side. The answer has not arrived yet.

notice_set.sentence: Admittedly the first winter was hard, but the second one paid for it.
notice_set.question: How does the speaker feel about the project now?
notice_set.why: The hard winter is given away and the second winter is kept, and what a speaker keeps is what they mean.

notice_set.sentence: The resorts brought work, whereas the fishing fleet lost half its crew.
notice_set.question: Is the speaker answering somebody here?
notice_set.why: Two facts stand side by side and neither one is presented as anybody's argument, so there is nobody to answer.

discovery.prompt: On the left and on the right the two facts are identical. What has changed about the situation the writer is standing in?
pairs: While it is true that the resorts brought work, most of the posts went to outsiders.
While the resorts brought work, most of the posts went to outsiders.
Granted, the ferry is cheaper. It also takes four hours longer.
The ferry is cheaper. It also takes four hours longer.
Nobody would deny that the scheme was expensive, but the road has paid for itself twice over.
The scheme was expensive, but the road has paid for itself twice over.

candidate_rules.text: On the left, somebody has already argued the first fact and the writer is answering them.
On the left, the writer is being polite about the other side.
On the left, the sentence has an extra word or two in front of the first fact.

teach.rule_line: Hand over the strongest thing they have, then take the argument back in the same breath.
teach.false_rule: That a concession makes you sound balanced. It only does that if the answer arrives. Left alone, it is the other side's sentence with your name on it.

contrast.question: Am I answering an argument, or just putting two facts side by side?

fork.answer: Two facts, side by side, and nobody is arguing about either of them
fork.selects: a plain contrast marker: whereas, while, on the other hand

fork.answer: One short fact that goes against me, and I want it out of the way inside the same sentence
fork.selects: despite or although in front of the fact

fork.answer: A whole argument on the other side that I intend to answer
fork.selects: a concession frame: while it is true that ... , ...

a.text: While it is true that the industry creates jobs, most of those jobs last one season.
a.means: Somebody has offered the jobs as an argument. The writer has taken it seriously, said it back, and is now answering it.

b.text: While the industry creates jobs, most of those jobs last one season.
b.means: Two facts placed side by side. The reader is told the jobs exist and that they are seasonal, and is left to weigh them.

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You chose the plain marker. That tells your reader nobody has argued the first half, so your paragraph reads as a description of a situation rather than as an answer to somebody. The argument you were having disappears.

edge_case.text: In Speaking Part 3 the same move is made with I mean, yes, but and fair enough, though. The frame is different and the move is identical. Know that, then leave those versions in speech.

contrast.stronger_test: Cover the second half of your sentence. If what is left is something you would be unhappy for a reader to think you believe, you have conceded. If it is just a fact, you have only contrasted.

worked_pairs.a: While it is true that visitors spend heavily in the old town, the money leaves on the six o'clock coach.
worked_pairs.b: While visitors spend heavily in the old town, the shops in the outer streets see none of it.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: the shops in the outer streets
worked_pairs.gloss: The first answers somebody who has offered the spending as proof. The second reports two facts about two different parts of a town.

worked_pairs.a: Granted, the festival fills the hotels, but the town pays for the clean-up all year.
worked_pairs.b: The festival fills the hotels, whereas the campsite stands empty until August.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first gives away a point in an argument. The second compares two places and takes nobody's side.

worked_pairs.a: Nobody would deny that the port created work; the question is who it created work for.
worked_pairs.b: The port created work, and the fishing fleet lost half its crew in the same decade.
worked_pairs.gloss: The first hands over the jobs so that the next clause can reopen the argument. The second simply reports two things that happened together.

errors.wrong: Although the resorts brought work to the coast, but the posts went to outsiders.
errors.right: Although the resorts brought work to the coast, the posts went to outsiders.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages mark a contrast at both ends of the sentence, so a bare second half feels unfinished and the hand reaches for but before the writer has noticed the marker already sitting at the front.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: but.
errors.l1_note: Very frequent where the first language marks contrast twice.

errors.wrong: Despite it is true that the fee is high, the road it pays for carries every lorry in the district.
errors.right: Although it is true that the fee is high, the road it pays for carries every lorry in the district.
errors.why_it_happens: Despite and although land on the same single word in many languages, and the concession frame that follows is a whole clause, which despite has no way of holding.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: Despite becomes Although.

errors.wrong: Admittedly, the cost was high. Admittedly, the delays were long.
errors.right: Admittedly, the cost was high. The delays were long too.
errors.why_it_happens: It has been stored as a way to start a sentence rather than as a move you make exactly once, so it fires everywhere and the writer finishes by arguing for the other side.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: the second Admittedly.

errors.wrong: Yeah, ok, the money does come in, but still.
errors.right: It is true that the money comes in, but very little of it stays.
errors.why_it_happens: The spoken version of this move is a shrug and a filler, and under time pressure the spoken version is the one that arrives first because it is the one the writer actually says.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one frame: Yeah, ok becomes It is true that.

title: Telling your reader how far you are willing to back what you just said

point_json.grammar_name: Stance and evaluation adverbials: arguably, crucially, to a large extent, on balance

teach.can_do: I can say how far I am backing a claim without writing I think.
teach.why_it_matters: One word, well placed, does the work of a whole hedging clause. The risk is real: four of them in a paragraph and nothing you write carries any weight.
teach.meaning: These words do not add facts. They tell your reader what to do with the fact you have just given them: how likely you think it is, how much of it holds, or how much weight it should carry in the argument. That is why one of them can change a paragraph without changing a single claim in it, and why the wrong one quietly reports a position you do not hold.

title: Choosing the grammar that fits the room you are in

point_json.grammar_name: Register: spoken grammar and written grammar

teach.can_do: I can tell which grammar belongs in the speaking room and which belongs on the page.
teach.why_it_matters: Learners lose marks twice over here: spoken grammar in Task 2, and essay grammar in Part 1, where a friendly question gets answered by a press release.
teach.meaning: Speaking and writing are not the same language at different volumes. Real-time speech joins short clauses with and and so, contracts whatever it can, reaches for get where writing reaches for be, and leaves out anything both people can already see. Writing has a reader who cannot ask you to say it again, so it packs more into each sentence, spells the small words out and marks the joins. Neither is better English. Each is wrong in the other room.

form.pattern: spoken: contractions + get-passive + two-word verbs + and / so    |    written: full forms + be-passive + single-word verbs + subordinators
notes: the ferry got cancelled belongs in an ear; the ferry was cancelled belongs on a page
don't, can't and it's are right in Part 1 and cost you something in Task 2
put off, sort out and go up out loud; postpone, resolve and rise on the page
a letter to a friend in GT Task 1 is spoken grammar written down, on purpose
form.negative: isn't and hasn't out loud; is not and has not on the page. Same meaning, different room.
form.question: Ask yourself which room the sentence is walking into before you build it.

feedback.feed_forward: Use the plain passive on the page.

payload.given: So the parade got called off twice and then they just moved it to the spring.

expected: was cancelled twice and was then moved to the spring
was cancelled twice before being moved to the spring
was called off twice and then moved to the spring

expected: it got moved to the spring, so we're going up then instead
it got moved to the spring, so we are going up then instead
it got moved to the spring, so were going up then instead

payload.context: Part 1. The examiner has asked whether the candidate enjoys music.

the sentences are built wrongly

was cancelled

payload.prompt_text: The examiner has asked what people in your town do at the weekend. Answer in two sentences, out loud, the way you would answer somebody who is about to reply to you.

feedback.why_key: The examiner is in the room and can hear you. The grammar that fits that room is the grammar that comes out without effort.
