payload.prompt_text: Open your last answer on news and social media. In one body paragraph, find every got, every shortened form and every two-word verb, and switch each one to its page version. Read it back and check that nothing has become unreadable. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: Register is not one decision. It is thirty small ones spread across a paragraph, and every one of them is visible in a single pass.
feedback.feed_forward: Sweep one paragraph for spoken forms and switch each one.

title: Spending your last three minutes on the mistakes that cost most

point_json.grammar_name: Self-editing: the four end checks, in priority order

teach.can_do: I can spend my last three minutes on the four mistakes that cost most, in order.
teach.why_it_matters: Accuracy at the end of a timed task is a procedure, not a feeling. Reading it through again finds almost nothing; running four named checks finds most of it.
teach.meaning: At the end of a timed task you have no attention left for everything at once, and reading the whole answer through again is the least useful thing you can do with three minutes, because your eye quietly repairs whatever you meant to write. What works instead is four separate passes, each hunting one thing only, run in the order in which the mistakes cost you most. Four narrow sweeps beat one wide one, every time, and they can be practised.

form.pattern: 1 where each sentence ends  →  2 each verb against its own subject  →  3 one time per paragraph  →  4 the small words in front of singular nouns
notes: check one: every sentence ends on a full stop, and no comma is doing a full stop's job
check two: put a finger on each verb and trace it back to its own subject, ignoring everything sitting in between
check three: read only the verbs of one paragraph, in order, and see whether they stay in one time
check four: for every singular countable noun, ask what is standing in front of it
form.negative: Do not read for meaning during these three minutes. Reading for meaning is exactly what hides the mistakes from you.
form.question: Ask yourself which of the four you are running right now. If the answer is all of them, you are running none of them.

spec.label: what does it cost if you leave it?

steps.gloss: your reader loses the sentence itself, so fix this one first

steps.text: each verb against its own subject
steps.gloss: visible in almost every line and quick to repair
your reader has to re-date every claim you make
costs least and takes longest, so it goes last

worked_example.sentence: The number of families sharing a home has risen. This is partly because rents in the city have doubled.
worked_example.why_this_form: Two of the four checks caught two separate things here: a comma holding two whole pieces of news together, and two verbs that had each copied the nearest noun.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Left alone, a reader meets one long run of words with no clear claim in it and decides the writer cannot see their own sentences, which is a much larger judgement than one comma deserves.

notice_set.sentence: The number of families sharing a home have risen sharply.
notice_set.question: How many things is the writer counting here?
notice_set.why: What rose is a count, and a count stays single no matter how many families it is counting.

notice_set.sentence: Rents in the city has doubled since the mill closed.
notice_set.question: What doubled?
notice_set.why: The rents are what doubled. The city is only where they are, and it has ended up standing next to the wrong word.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme was popular, it closed after two years.
notice_set.question: How many separate pieces of news is the writer giving you?
notice_set.why: Two whole pieces of news are leaning on one comma, and a comma cannot take that weight.

notice_set.sentence: Grandparents used to live nearby. Now families move away for work and the children only saw them twice a year.
notice_set.question: Is the writer talking about the past or about now?
notice_set.why: The writer moves from an old arrangement to the present one, and one word at the end is still standing in the wrong half.

notice_set.sentence: She works as nurse in a hospital near the coast.
notice_set.question: Is anything missing from what you can picture here?
notice_set.why: One job, one person: with nothing standing in front of it, an English reader pictures the idea instead of anybody at all.

discovery.prompt: Here are three drafts, each in its last minute. What did the writer on the right do that the writer on the left did not?
pairs: The market was busy, it moved to the retail park.
The market was busy, but it moved to the retail park.
The list of names taken at the door were long.
The list of names taken at the door was long.
He trained as electrician before the yard shut.
He trained as an electrician before the yard shut.

candidate_rules.text: On the right, the writer hunted one named thing at a time instead of reading it all through.
On the right, the writer had more time left at the end.
On the right, the sentences are longer, so more care went into them.

teach.rule_line: Four narrow passes, in cost order, beat one read-through every single time.
teach.false_rule: That reading your answer through again is checking it. Your eye repairs what you meant to write, so a general read-through finds only the mistakes you were never going to make.

errors.wrong: The scheme was popular, it closed after two years.
errors.right: The scheme was popular, but it closed after two years.
errors.why_it_happens: The two halves feel like one thought, so a comma feels like enough, and under time pressure nobody stops to ask whether each half could stand up on its own.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: but, after the comma.
errors.l1_note: Standard punctuation in several European languages, so it survives long after the grammar is secure.

errors.wrong: The number of families sharing a home have risen sharply.
errors.right: The number of families sharing a home has risen sharply.
errors.why_it_happens: Families is the last noun before the verb and it is plural, so the ending copies that rather than tracing back to the number, which is the thing that actually rose.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: have becomes has.

errors.wrong: Grandparents used to live nearby. Now families move away for work and the children only saw them twice a year.
errors.right: Grandparents used to live nearby. Now families move away for work and the children only see them twice a year.
errors.why_it_happens: Each verb gets chosen on its own and nothing ever reads the paragraph as one unit, so this arrives late in a timed answer, when no attention is left to spend.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: saw becomes see.

errors.wrong: She works as nurse in a hospital near the coast.
errors.right: She works as a nurse in a hospital near the coast.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages leave nothing in front of a job title, and the missing word changes no meaning at all, so nothing in the writer's own ear objects to it.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: a, before nurse.
errors.l1_note: Persistent for speakers of languages with no articles, long after the rule is known.

pays_in.note: The last three minutes are worth more than any structure you could add instead.
pays_in.model: The number of households sharing a home has risen, and rents have doubled since the mill closed.

pays_in.note: Task 1 is dense with numbers and single nouns, which is where two of the four checks pay.
pays_in.model: The proportion of adults living alone rose steadily, whereas the figure for shared housing fell.

pays_in.note: Finding where a writer's sentence really ends is half of reading a long paragraph accurately.
pays_in.model: The trial was popular; it ended after two years for reasons nobody has explained.

used_in.quote: A two-part answer runs long, and the drift between past and present arrives in the last paragraph of it every time.
Every sentence here has a long subject with a plural noun in the middle of it, which is check two's whole hunting ground.

payload.sentence: The number of households on the waiting list has grown in every one of the last five years.
payload.question: What is the writer counting?

feedback.why_key: What went up is a count, and a count stays single however many families it happens to cover.
feedback.feed_forward: Find what the sentence is really counting before you read on.

payload.sentence: The playground was well used, it was sold for housing.
payload.question: How many separate pieces of news are you being given?

feedback.why_key: Two whole pieces of news are leaning on a single comma, which was never built to hold either of them up.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the pieces of news before you count the punctuation.

items.decision_cue: afternoon, it shut in the spring

payload.context: From the last paragraph of a timed answer, written with four minutes left.
payload.sentence: The library was busy every afternoon, it shut in the spring.
reasons: two whole pieces of news are being joined by a comma
the second half has no main verb
the two halves are in different times
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Each half could stand up on its own, which is exactly the test. Two that can stand alone need something stronger than a comma between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether each half could stand alone before accepting a comma.

payload.context: Check two, run over one sentence of a draft.
payload.stem: The number of children living with a grandparent ___ (rise) sharply over the last decade.

expected: has risen

feedback.why_key: Grandparent is the nearest noun and the number is the real one. Trace it back past everything in between and the ending chooses itself.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to its own subject, past whatever sits between.

payload.context: Check four, run over one line of a Task 1 answer.
payload.stem: Her father trained as ___ electrician at the yard before it closed.

expected: an

feedback.why_key: One job and one person, so your reader needs something standing in front of that noun before they can picture anybody.
feedback.feed_forward: Check what is standing in front of each singular noun.

payload.given: The market was busy, it moved to the retail park.
payload.instruction: Repair it with the smallest edit you can make.

expected: , but it moved to the retail park
but it moved to the retail park
. It moved to the retail park
; it moved to the retail park

feedback.why_key: One word, one full stop or one semicolon. All three repairs cost the same and all three tell the reader where the first piece of news ended.
feedback.feed_forward: Repair a run-on with one mark or one word, not a rewrite.

payload.audio_text: The number of pupils walking to school has fallen again.

expected: the number of pupils walking to school has fallen again
the number of pupils walking to school has fallen again.

feedback.why_key: Has is unstressed and arrives straight after a plural noun, so a listener writing at speed puts the ending that the last word suggested.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold the subject in your head until the verb arrives.

payload.context: Build a sentence whose ending matches the proportion rather than the adults.

expected: the proportion of adults living alone has risen steadily

feedback.why_key: Four words sit between the proportion and the ending that belongs to it, and every one of them is a chance to lose track.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a long subject back to its first word before choosing.

items.decision_cue: wages in the district has fallen

payload.sentence: One reason is that wages in the district has fallen since the yard shut.
payload.error_span: wages in the district has fallen

expected: wages in the district have fallen

feedback.why_key: The district is only where the wages are paid. What fell is the wages, and the ending has copied whichever word stood nearest to it.
feedback.feed_forward: Ignore whatever sits between the subject and its verb.

items.decision_cue: affordable, most of them were sold

payload.sentence: The first flats were affordable, most of them were sold to landlords within a year.

expected: affordable, but most of them
affordable. Most of them
affordable; most of them

feedback.why_key: Each half could stand on its own, so the mark between them cannot do the job, and your reader loses track of where the first claim finished.
feedback.feed_forward: Split or join with one mark, then move to the next check.

items.decision_cue: the children only visited twice a year

payload.context: Check three, run over the closing paragraph of a timed answer.
payload.sentence: Grandparents used to be a bus ride away. Now most people settle where the work is and the children only visited twice a year.
reasons: one word at the end is still standing in the earlier half
two pieces of news are joined by a comma
something is missing in front of one of the nouns
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The paragraph moves to now in its second sentence and one word never made the move, so the reader has to re-date the whole claim.
feedback.feed_forward: Read only the verbs of a paragraph, in order, and nothing else.

payload.prompt_text: Write three sentences about why fewer families now live near their grandparents. Then run check one and check two over what you wrote, in that order, and correct anything they catch before you submit.

feedback.why_key: Running the checks on your own fresh sentences is the only version of this that transfers. Somebody else's mistakes are always easier to see.
feedback.feed_forward: Run one check at a time, in order, over your own writing.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on changing careers. Run all four checks over the last body paragraph, in cost order, three minutes on the clock: where each sentence ends, each verb against its own subject, one time per paragraph, then the small words. Report what each pass caught.

feedback.why_key: The last paragraph is where the mistakes gather, because it is written with the least attention left and read with none at all.
feedback.feed_forward: Start the clock, run the four passes in order, and stop.

title: Reporting what people generally think without saying who thinks it

point_json.grammar_name: The impersonal reporting passive

pays_in.note: It opens the paragraph where you set out a view before disagreeing with it.
pays_in.model: It is often argued that longer school days improve results, though the evidence is thin.

pays_in.note: It is how you report a general view in a discussion without claiming it as yours.
pays_in.model: It's generally thought that people read less than they used to.

pays_in.note: Passages mark their own hedged claims this way, and questions test whether you saw the hedge.
pays_in.model: The settlement is believed to have been abandoned within a generation.

teach.can_do: I can put a claim into an essay without owning it and without inventing somebody to blame for it.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between an essay that asserts and an essay that positions. It buys credit for the argument as well as for the grammar.
teach.meaning: Sometimes you need a claim in your paragraph that you are not prepared to sign your name to. This structure puts the claim on the page and leaves the believing to people in general. Nobody is named, no source is invented, and the sentence is honest about where it stands. It also lets you introduce a view in order to disagree with it in the next line, which is what most argument paragraphs are made of.

form.pattern: It is thought that + a full clause  —  or  —  X is thought to + verb
notes: the two carry the same meaning: It is thought that the scheme works, and The scheme is thought to work
an adverb in the middle sharpens it: widely accepted, generally assumed, commonly held
for something already over, the second pattern takes to have: the wall is thought to have failed in the storm
the verbs that fit are the reporting ones: think, believe, say, argue, assume, accept, suggest, know
form.negative: it is not generally accepted that the scheme has worked
form.question: Is it generally accepted that the scheme has worked?

spec.label: how far am I standing behind this claim?

steps.gloss: I am saying it, and you can hold me to it

steps.text: It is widely accepted that small classes raise attainment.
steps.gloss: other people say it and I am not arguing with them

steps.text: It has been suggested that small classes raise attainment.
steps.gloss: somebody has said it once, and I am about to look at whether it holds

worked_example.sentence: It is generally accepted that class size matters less than the quality of teaching.
worked_example.why_this_form: The claim needs to be in the paragraph so the next sentence can qualify it, and the writer has no study to point at and should not pretend to.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Stated flat, it would put the writer's own name on a finding they have not defended, which is a bigger promise than the paragraph can keep.

notice_set.sentence: It is widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
notice_set.question: Is the writer saying this is their own view?
options: No, they are reporting what people hold
notice_set.why: The claim is in the paragraph and the writer is standing beside it rather than behind it.

notice_set.sentence: Early reading habits shape later attainment.
notice_set.question: Who is answerable for this claim?
notice_set.why: With nothing in front of it, a claim belongs to whoever wrote it down.

notice_set.sentence: The sea wall is thought to have failed during the November storm.
notice_set.question: Is the failure certain?
options: No, it is what people believe
notice_set.why: The structure reports a belief about the past, which is exactly what you need when the cause is still being argued over.

notice_set.sentence: It has been suggested that the charge simply moved the traffic elsewhere.
notice_set.question: How many people hold this view, on the evidence of the sentence?
options: At least one, and possibly few
notice_set.why: Suggested is the weakest verb in the set, and it is the one to use before you take a claim apart.

notice_set.sentence: It is generally assumed that new roads reduce congestion, but the evidence is mixed.
notice_set.question: What is the second half of the sentence doing?
options: Pushing back against the first half
notice_set.why: Introducing a view in order to argue with it is the commonest reason to reach for this structure at all.

teach.rule_line: Report the claim, name nobody, then say what you think of it.
teach.false_rule: That this is a way of sounding academic. It shows where you stand, and a paragraph that uses it and never comes off the fence has used it wrongly.

errors.wrong: The scheme is thought that it reduces congestion.
errors.right: The scheme is thought to reduce congestion.
errors.why_it_happens: The two patterns are learned as one and then blended. Once the subject is at the front, the clause has nowhere to attach and the sentence carries the claim twice.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one join: that it reduces becomes to reduce.

errors.wrong: It widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
errors.right: It is widely accepted that early reading habits shape later attainment.
errors.why_it_happens: The adverb sits where the small word belongs and fills the gap to the eye, so the sentence looks complete while it is being written.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: is.

errors.wrong: Everyone knows that new roads simply fill up with new traffic.
errors.right: It is widely argued that new roads simply fill up with new traffic.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer wants weight behind the claim and reaches for the biggest available number of believers, which a reader immediately doubts.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one opening: Everyone knows that becomes It is widely argued that.

used_in.quote: A discussion answer needs both views on the page before either can be judged, and this is how the first one arrives.
Answers about what people generally do need a way to report a view without pretending to have counted.

payload.sentence: It is widely assumed that reading at home lifts later results.
payload.question: Whose view is this?

feedback.why_key: The writer has put the claim on the page without signing it, which leaves them free to qualify it next.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the opening words to see who is answerable.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph about road building.
payload.sentence: It is obvious to everyone that widening a motorway never eases congestion for long.
reasons: it claims more agreement than anybody can show
the verb form is wrong
the time is wrong
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: A reader who has not met this claim immediately becomes the exception, and the sentence has lost them in seven words.
feedback.feed_forward: Report a claim as widely held rather than as beyond argument.

payload.context: From the opening of a report on a coastal collapse.
payload.stem: It ___ (think) that the wall failed during the November storm.

expected: is thought

feedback.why_key: The small word before the participle is the whole structure, and it is the one most often left out.
feedback.feed_forward: Write is before the reporting word, always.

payload.context: From a summary of research into sleep.
payload.stem: Short sleep is believed ___ (increase) the risk of several long-term conditions.

expected: to increase

feedback.why_key: This pattern hands the claim to the subject and then needs an infinitive to carry the rest. Nothing else fits after believed here.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the second pattern with to, not with that.

payload.given: It is thought that the market improves footfall in the surrounding streets.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the market is the subject, keeping the same meaning.

expected: is thought to improve footfall in the surrounding streets
the market is thought to improve footfall in the surrounding streets

feedback.why_key: The claim does not change. Only the way in changes, and the two ways are worth having because paragraphs need both.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the subject forward and turn that into to.

payload.context: One sentence from a report on an abandoned settlement.

expected: the site is believed to have been abandoned within a generation

feedback.why_key: Four small words run in a fixed order in the middle, and none of them can be dropped or swapped.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the middle from the left, one word at a time.

payload.audio_text: It's generally thought that people read less than they used to.

expected: it's generally thought that people read less than they used to
it is generally thought that people read less than they used to
its generally thought that people read less than they used to

feedback.why_key: In speech the opening shrinks to a single syllable, and that syllable is the entire hedge.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the short opening even when you barely hear it.

payload.sentence: The scheme is thought that it reduces congestion in the centre.

expected: to reduce

feedback.why_key: Two ways in have been used at once, so the sentence announces its claim twice and finishes neither.
feedback.feed_forward: Pick one of the two patterns and finish it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the opening sentence of a paragraph that sets out the popular view that online courses are as good as classroom teaching, so that the next sentence can disagree with it.

feedback.why_key: A view you are about to argue with has to be on the page first, and it has to be somebody else's when it gets there.
feedback.feed_forward: Set the claim up so you can still walk away from it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the first three sentences of your online courses paragraph: the popular view reported without a named source, one qualification, and your own position stated plainly. Four minutes.

feedback.why_key: The structure only earns its place if the paragraph eventually comes off the fence, so the third sentence is the test.
feedback.feed_forward: End the three sentences with your own view, unhedged.

title: Using this shape in places where a verb cannot carry a time

point_json.grammar_name: Passive infinitives and passive -ing forms

pays_in.note: It states what has to happen without naming who has to do it.
pays_in.model: Older housing stock needs to be insulated before any of this is worth doing.

pays_in.note: It joins two stages of a process into one sentence.
pays_in.model: The sheets are stacked without being trimmed at this stage.

pays_in.note: Dense academic sentences are dense largely because of these forms.
pays_in.model: Having been abandoned twice, the site was finally cleared in the 1970s.

teach.can_do: I can use this shape after another verb, or after a preposition, where a full sentence will not fit.
teach.why_it_matters: It is what lets one sentence carry two events. Without it, learners write two short sentences and lose the connection between them.
teach.meaning: Not every verb in a sentence carries a time. After another verb, and after a preposition, English uses a form that has no time of its own and takes it from the sentence around it. This shape has those forms too, and they let you say that something has to be done, is about to be done, or happened without anybody noticing, all inside a sentence that has already started.

form.pattern: to be + past participle  ·  being + past participle  ·  having been + past participle
notes: after another verb: the roof needs to be replaced, the gate has to be locked
after a preposition: the lorry left without being weighed
for something finished first: having been signed off in the spring, the scheme went to tender
the time is carried by the first verb in the sentence, never by this part
form.negative: the report does not need to be rewritten
form.question: Does the report need to be rewritten?

rungs.text: The roof needs to be replaced.
The lorry left without being weighed.
Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender.

worked_example.sentence: The old cabling has to be replaced before the building can be let again.
worked_example.why_this_form: Has to already carries the time, so the verb after it has none of its own, and the cabling is on the receiving end of the work.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The old cabling has to replace would say the cabling goes off and replaces something else, which is a sentence about very unusual wiring.

notice_set.sentence: The pumps need to be serviced before the wet season starts.
notice_set.question: Are the pumps doing the servicing or having it done?
notice_set.why: The small word before the last one is what puts the pumps on the receiving end.

notice_set.sentence: The lorry left the yard without being weighed.
notice_set.question: Did anybody weigh the lorry?
notice_set.why: After a preposition the -ing form is the only one allowed, and this shape has its own version of it.

notice_set.sentence: Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender in May.
notice_set.question: Which happened first?
notice_set.why: The opening phrase reports the earlier event, which is how one sentence can hold two dates without saying either of them twice.

notice_set.sentence: The old panels are due to be removed next month.
notice_set.question: Have the panels gone yet?
notice_set.why: Due carries the time and points forward, so the whole sentence sits ahead of now.

notice_set.sentence: Nobody likes being told what to do at short notice.
notice_set.question: Who is doing the telling in this sentence?
notice_set.why: The teller is left out, exactly as in a full sentence of this kind, and the shape survives inside another verb.

teach.rule_line: Keep be in the sentence even when it cannot carry a time.
teach.false_rule: That the small word can go because the sentence is long already. It is the only thing putting the subject on the receiving end, and without it the sentence reverses.

errors.wrong: The roof needs to replaced before the winter.
errors.right: The roof needs to be replaced before the winter.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has to hold three verbs at once and the smallest of the three drops out. It carries no meaning of its own, so nothing warns them.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: be.

errors.wrong: The lorry left the yard without be weighed.
errors.right: The lorry left the yard without being weighed.
errors.why_it_happens: The rule that a preposition takes the -ing form is known, but it is applied to the last verb rather than to the first one, which is where it belongs.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: be becomes being.

errors.wrong: Having been approve in March, the plan went out to tender.
errors.right: Having been approved in March, the plan went out to tender.
errors.why_it_happens: Three words have already been produced correctly and attention has run out by the fourth, which is where the meaning actually lives.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one ending: approve becomes approved.

used_in.quote: A solutions paragraph is a list of things that need to be done, which is this structure repeated.

payload.sentence: The filters need to be changed before the dry season starts.
payload.question: Are the filters cleaning something else?
options: No, something is being done to them

feedback.why_key: Two small words in the middle turn the filters from the worker into the thing worked on.
feedback.feed_forward: Check for be before the last word of the pair.

payload.context: From a note about weighbridge procedure at a depot.
payload.sentence: No lorry may leave the yard without be weighed.
reasons: the word after without is in the wrong shape
may cannot be used here
the yard cannot be left
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: After a preposition English allows one shape only, and it is the first of the two verbs that has to take it.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the -ing on the first verb after a preposition.

payload.context: From a surveyor's report on an empty flat.
payload.stem: The wiring needs ___ (replace) before the flat can be let again.

expected: to be replaced

feedback.why_key: Need carries the time, so all three of the words after it are fixed and none of them can be spared.
feedback.feed_forward: Write all three words after need, every time.

payload.context: From a note on a fault in a sorting line.
payload.stem: Several boxes went through without ___ (scan) at all.

expected: being scanned

feedback.why_key: Without takes the -ing shape, and the boxes are what somebody failed to scan, so both parts are needed.
feedback.feed_forward: Combine the -ing with the participle after a preposition.

payload.given: The plan was approved in March. It went out to tender in May.
payload.instruction: Join the two into one sentence that opens with the earlier event.

expected: been approved in march the plan went out to tender in may
having been approved in march the plan went out to tender in may

feedback.why_key: One sentence now carries both events and their order, which is what a reader was working out for themselves before.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with the earlier event, then give the main clause.

payload.context: One line from a maintenance schedule.

expected: the old panels are due to be removed next month
next month the old panels are due to be removed

feedback.why_key: Five words run in one fixed order in the middle, and the only thing that can move is the time phrase.
feedback.feed_forward: Lock the middle, then place the time phrase.

payload.audio_text: Nobody likes being told what to do at short notice.

expected: nobody likes being told what to do at short notice

feedback.why_key: Being runs into the word after it and the pair sounds like one word, which is how it disappears from writing.
feedback.feed_forward: Split what you heard into two words before you write it.

payload.sentence: The roof needs to replaced before the winter, and the gutters need clearing.

expected: needs to be replaced

feedback.why_key: The second half of the sentence is fine, which is what makes the first half easy to read past.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the short words in the middle before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: Offices with long sitting hours are unhealthy. Write one sentence saying what has to change, without naming who should change it.

feedback.why_key: A solution stated this way commits to what must happen and leaves the argument about who out of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Say what must happen; leave out who must do it.

payload.prompt_text: Write the solutions paragraph of your sedentary working day answer. At least two sentences must say what needs to happen without naming an actor. Five minutes.

feedback.why_key: A whole paragraph of solutions is where the shape either becomes automatic or keeps losing its small words.
feedback.feed_forward: Count the small words in each sentence before you stop.

title: Saying how much of a group you mean without starting a new sentence

point_json.grammar_name: Relative clauses after a quantifier: most of which, several of whom

teach.can_do: I can give a total and then say what happened to part of it, inside one sentence.
teach.why_it_matters: This is the structure that turns the commonest punctuation error in academic writing into a complex sentence. One word is the whole difference.
teach.meaning: You often need to say two things about the same group: how many there were, and what happened to some of them. Written English lets you do both in one sentence by hanging the second fact on the first with a quantifier and a relative word. The clause is always news rather than a way of picking the group out, so it is always fenced off by a comma, and the relative word can never be dropped.

form.pattern: noun phrase , + quantifier + of + which / whom + verb ...
notes: which for things, whom for people, and after of there is no third option: that and who are both refused
any quantifier fits in the slot: most, some, several, three, half, none, all, the last of
the same shape works with a noun instead of a quantifier: the cost of which, the results of which
form.negative: None of which and neither of whom carry the negative on their own: the panel heard six witnesses, none of whom were named.
form.question: Ask how many out of how many. The answer is the phrase that goes in front of of.

left.role: two sentences taped together with a comma
left.text: ..., most of them came from one street.

right.text: ..., most of which came from one street.

spec.caption: One word turns a punctuation error into a complex sentence.

worked_example.sentence: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of which had to be discarded.
worked_example.why_this_form: The total and the exception arrive together, so the reader never has to hold two separate facts side by side and work out how they connect.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Three of them had to be discarded is a second sentence wearing a comma. It says the same thing while telling the reader you cannot hear a sentence boundary.

notice_set.sentence: The department interviewed forty applicants, most of whom had never worked in a laboratory.
notice_set.question: How many of the applicants had laboratory experience?
notice_set.why: Most is counting the ones without experience, which leaves the smaller share on the other side.

notice_set.sentence: The survey used six instruments, two of which failed in the first week.
notice_set.question: How many instruments were still working after that week?
notice_set.why: Six minus the two that failed. The second half of the sentence is arithmetic on the first half.

notice_set.sentence: The scheme, the cost of which has never been published, is now in its fifth year.
notice_set.question: Do we know what the scheme cost?
notice_set.why: The whole point of the fenced-off clause is that the figure has been withheld.

notice_set.sentence: The team submitted three reports, none of which reached the minister.
notice_set.question: Did the minister see any of the reports?
notice_set.why: None covers all three, so nothing at all arrived on that desk.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic wrote to nine families, all of whom replied within a week.
notice_set.question: How many families did not reply?
notice_set.why: All of them replied, so the number left over is zero.

teach.rule_line: After of, use which for things and whom for people. Nothing else fits there.
teach.false_rule: That whom is old-fashioned and who will always do instead. After of, who is not available at all.

errors.wrong: The council received two hundred objections, most of them came from one street.
errors.right: The council received two hundred objections, most of which came from one street.
errors.why_it_happens: The second fact clearly belongs with the first, so a full stop feels too heavy and a comma goes in instead. A comma cannot hold two sentences together, and the writer has no other tool to hand.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: them becomes which.

errors.wrong: The panel heard six witnesses, two of who were never named.
errors.right: The panel heard six witnesses, two of whom were never named.
errors.why_it_happens: Who is the familiar word and whom feels like decoration, so it gets quietly dropped. After of, English offers no choice at all, whatever the writer thinks of the word.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one letter: the m on the end of who.

errors.wrong: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of that had to be discarded.
errors.right: The trial produced fourteen readings, three of which had to be discarded.
errors.why_it_happens: That is the default relative word everywhere else, so it survives into a slot where it has never been allowed. Nothing in the sentence sounds wrong to the writer's own ear.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: that becomes which.

errors.wrong: The clinic wrote to nine families, much of whom replied at once.
errors.right: The clinic wrote to nine families, most of whom replied at once.
errors.why_it_happens: Much is stored as the general word for a large amount, and nobody checks whether the group it points back at can be counted. Families can be counted, so much has nothing to measure.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: much becomes most.

pays_in.note: A total and a striking part of it belong in one sentence, not two.
pays_in.model: Eleven countries were included, four of which accounted for almost the whole rise.

pays_in.note: It concedes a point and keeps the sentence moving at the same time.
pays_in.model: Several remedies have been proposed, none of which addresses why the shortage began.

pays_in.note: Passages hide their exceptions in this clause, and the questions live there.
pays_in.model: The programme trained sixty inspectors, half of whom left within two years.

used_in.quote: Describing four lines on one chart invites exactly this sentence: four sources, two of which rose steadily throughout.

payload.sentence: The laboratory ran twelve tests, five of which produced no reading at all.
payload.question: How many tests produced a reading?

feedback.why_key: The clause counts the failures, so what is left over is the number that worked.
feedback.feed_forward: Subtract the number in the clause from the total in front of it.

payload.sentence: We had about thirty on the course, half of whom dropped out by Christmas.
payload.question: Roughly how many finished the autumn term?

feedback.why_key: Half the group left, so half of the original thirty is what remained by the end of term.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the quantifier as a share of the group in front of it.

items.decision_cue: most of them closed within a year

payload.context: From a paragraph about new businesses in a small town.
payload.sentence: Nineteen shops opened on that street, most of them closed within a year.
reasons: a comma has been asked to hold two complete sentences together
the wrong quantifier has been chosen
the share has been hung on the wrong noun
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Most of them closed within a year could stand on its own, which is precisely why a comma cannot be the thing joining it on.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn them into which and the join becomes legal.

payload.context: From the methods section of a field report.
payload.stem: The team deployed eight sensors, three of ___ stopped transmitting within a fortnight.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: Sensors are things, and after of only which is available, however natural that may feel.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose which for things and whom for people after of.

payload.context: From a paragraph about community sentences.
payload.stem: The scheme supervised ninety offenders, none of ___ reoffended in the first year.

expected: whom

feedback.why_key: Offenders are people, and after of the only form English will take is the one ending in m.
feedback.feed_forward: Write whom whenever of points back at people.

payload.given: The council planted four hundred trees along the Verdon. About sixty of them did not survive the summer.
payload.instruction: Join these into one sentence.
payload.starter: The council planted four hundred trees along the Verdon, ___

expected: about sixty of which did not survive the summer
sixty of which did not survive the summer

feedback.why_key: The second fact is arithmetic on the first, so the two belong inside one sentence rather than side by side.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace them with which to join the two facts.

payload.context: Build one sentence about a small grants fund.

expected: the fund backed twelve projects, half of which ran over budget

feedback.why_key: The quantifier, of and which travel as a block, and the verb of the clause comes after all three of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep half of which together as one unit when you build.

payload.audio_text: We visited nine clinics, two of which had already shut.

expected: we visited nine clinics, two of which had already shut
we visited nine clinics two of which had already shut

feedback.why_key: Of and which are both unstressed and run together in speech, which is why they get heard as one blurred syllable and written as of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for two small words between the number and the verb.

items.decision_cue: several of them were never occupied

payload.sentence: The district built two thousand flats in a decade, several of them were never occupied.
payload.error_span: several of them were never occupied

expected: several of which were never occupied
several of which have never been occupied

feedback.why_key: The words after the comma make a whole sentence, and a comma is not strong enough to hold two of those together.
feedback.feed_forward: Change them to which and the comma becomes legal.

payload.context: Two sentences from different summaries of the same programme.
sentences: The programme funded thirty studies, few of which were ever completed.
The programme funded thirty studies, a few of which were ever completed.
meanings: Almost none of them finished, and the writer thinks that is the story.
A small number did finish, and the writer is pointing at those ones.

feedback.why_key: Few counts what is missing; a few counts what is there. One small word swaps disappointment for a modest success.
feedback.feed_forward: Decide whether you are counting the gap or the survivors.

payload.prompt_text: A research group applied for eleven grants and was turned down for eight of them. Write one sentence carrying both facts.

feedback.why_key: Two numbers about one group belong in one sentence, and this is the join that makes it possible without a semicolon.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the total first and hang the share on it with of which.

payload.prompt_text: Go back to your chart description of renewable electricity. Find a place where you gave a total and then a share, and rewrite the two sentences as one. Ninety seconds.

feedback.why_key: Chart answers are full of totals followed by shares, which is why this one structure lifts the whole paragraph rather than one sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Scan your draft for a comma followed by a number and them.

title: Commenting on the whole thing you just said, without starting again

point_json.grammar_name: Sentential which: a relative clause commenting on a whole clause

teach.can_do: I can add a comment about what I have just said, and make sure my reader knows what the comment is about.
teach.why_it_matters: It is the difference between a sentence that comments on your own point and a sentence that says something about a bridge you never meant to mention.
teach.meaning: Which does not always point at the noun in front of it. It can reach back and take the whole event you have just described, so that the clause comments on what happened rather than on any single thing inside it. Your reader decides which by asking what could plausibly have done what the clause says. When both answers are plausible, the sentence has two meanings, and you will never find out which one your reader took away.

form.pattern: a complete clause , + which + verb ...
notes: the comment clause always comes last; it cannot be lifted into the middle of the sentence
the comma is compulsory, because without it which fastens straight onto the nearest noun
that is refused here, and so is what, however natural what may feel
form.negative: The comment goes negative like any clause: ..., which did not surprise anybody who works there.
form.question: Ask which noun could plausibly have done it. If two candidates could, name the one you mean.

ends: which lands on the nearest noun
which lands on the whole event

marks.label: the deadline, which had been extended twice
the memo, which the lawyers had advised against

worked_example.sentence: The depot closed six weeks early, which left the drivers without a rota for October.
worked_example.why_this_form: A depot cannot leave anybody without a rota. Only the early closing can, so the reader carries which back over the whole event without noticing they did it.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Had the clause said which had been rebuilt in 2019, nothing but the depot could fit, and the comment would have stopped dead at the noun.

notice_set.sentence: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
notice_set.question: What had been advertised?
notice_set.why: Only a job can be advertised, so the words after the comma can belong to nothing else in the sentence.

notice_set.sentence: Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
notice_set.question: What did the office fail to understand?
notice_set.why: People fail to understand actions rather than job titles, so the comment reaches back over the whole thing he did.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
notice_set.question: What was cheaper to heat?
notice_set.why: Buildings are heated and moves are not, so there is only one candidate here.

notice_set.sentence: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved four jobs.
notice_set.question: What saved the four jobs?
notice_set.why: A building does not save jobs. The decision to move into it does, so the comment travels back over the whole event.

notice_set.sentence: The board approved the merger, which the unions had opposed for months.
notice_set.question: What had the unions been opposing?
notice_set.why: Both readings work here and nothing in the sentence chooses between them. That is the trap this whole point is about.

discovery.prompt: Each pair below ends differently. Work out what decides where the comment lands.
pairs: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved four jobs.
The depot closed six weeks early, which had been rebuilt in 2019.
The depot closed six weeks early, which left the drivers without a rota.

candidate_rules.text: What comes after the comma decides it: the comment lands on whatever could plausibly have done that.
The comment lands on the whole event whenever the clause is about how people reacted.
A comma in front of which always sends the comment back to the whole sentence.

teach.rule_line: Ask what could have done it. If two things could, name the one you mean.
teach.false_rule: That a comma in front of which always throws it back to the whole sentence. The comma only frees it; the verb decides where it lands.

contrast.question: Does the comment fit the nearest noun, or only the whole event?

fork.answer: It fits the nearest noun, and only that noun: leave it where it lands
fork.selects: a clause commenting on the noun

fork.answer: It only makes sense about the whole event: put it at the very end after a comma
fork.selects: a clause commenting on everything before it

fork.answer: Both work, so your reader cannot tell: replace which with a noun that names it
fork.selects: a summary noun such as a decision, a move, a refusal

a.text: Ivo missed the deadline for the grant, which had already been extended twice.
a.means: The deadline had been extended twice. The comment stops at the noun in front of it.

b.text: Ivo missed the deadline for the grant, which surprised everybody in the office.
b.means: Missing it is what surprised people. The comment reaches back over the whole event.

minimal_pair.only_difference: had already been extended twice / surprised everybody in the office

contrast.wrong_choice_note: You left which where it lands on the nearest noun. A reader takes it there first and only comes back if that reading collapses. If it does not collapse, they never come back, and they have read something you did not write.

edge_case.text: You will find a sentence-final which frowned on in a few style guides and used constantly by good writers. It is standard English. What is not standard is a which whose target the reader has to guess at.

contrast.stronger_test: Read only the words after the comma and ask what could have done that. If exactly one thing in your sentence could, you are safe. If two could, name it with a noun instead.

worked_pairs.a: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which was cheaper to heat.
worked_pairs.b: The clinic moved to a smaller building, which saved the trust four jobs.
worked_pairs.gloss: A building can be cheaper to heat; only a move can save jobs. The words after the comma say what was grabbed.

worked_pairs.a: Marek turned down the promotion, which had been advertised internally.
worked_pairs.b: Marek turned down the promotion, which nobody in the office understood.
worked_pairs.gloss: The post was advertised. The refusal was the thing nobody could follow. Same eight opening words, two different targets.

worked_pairs.a: The paper printed the leaked memo, which ran to forty pages.
worked_pairs.b: The paper printed the leaked memo, a decision that cost the editor her job.
worked_pairs.deciding_span_b: a decision that cost the editor her job
worked_pairs.gloss: In the second sentence both readings were live, so the writer named the thing outright and the ambiguity vanished.

errors.wrong: The board approved the merger, which the staff had been warning about for months.
errors.right: The board approved the merger, a decision the staff had been warning about for months.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows perfectly well which idea they meant, so the sentence reads cleanly to them. The reader has two candidates, takes the nearer one, and nothing later in the sentence corrects them.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word for a naming noun: which becomes a decision.

errors.wrong: Half the staff resigned in one week, what nobody had expected.
errors.right: Half the staff resigned in one week, which nobody had expected.
errors.why_it_happens: A great many languages use their question word for exactly this job, and what is the closest English match to it. English keeps what for a different job and will not lend it out.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: what becomes which.
errors.l1_note: Very common for speakers of Romance, Slavic and Germanic languages.

errors.wrong: They closed the ticket office which meant nobody could buy a ticket after six.
errors.right: They closed the ticket office, which meant nobody could buy a ticket after six.
errors.why_it_happens: Without the comma there is nothing to free which from the noun beside it, so the clause fastens onto the office and the reader is briefly told that an office meant something. The writer hears their own intended meaning and never sees the other one.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one comma in front of which.

pays_in.note: It comments on your own example without spending a whole new sentence.
pays_in.model: Fares rose twice in a single year, which pushed a good many regular passengers back into their cars.

pays_in.note: Part 3 answers comment on what you have just said, and this is the join.
pays_in.model: A lot of people work from home now, which has emptied the town centre at lunchtime.

pays_in.note: Writers bury their own view in this clause, and questions go looking for it.
pays_in.model: The scheme was extended for a further decade, which few of its early critics had predicted.

used_in.quote: Both sides of this prompt need a sentence that reports what happened and then says what the writer makes of it.

payload.sentence: The channel dropped the late bulletin, which had run since the 1970s.
payload.question: What had run since the 1970s?

feedback.why_key: A programme can run for fifty years. A single decision cannot, so the comment can only belong to the bulletin.

payload.sentence: The channel dropped the late bulletin, which upset a lot of older viewers.
payload.question: What upset the viewers?

feedback.why_key: The programme was the thing they liked, so it cannot be what upset them. Losing it is the only candidate left.
feedback.feed_forward: Test each candidate against the verb before you settle on one.

payload.sentence: Ticket sales fell sharply after the rise, what surprised nobody.
reasons: the wrong word is being used to point back at the whole event
the comma should not be there
the comment has been put in the wrong position
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: English gives this job to which and never lends it to what, however close the two feel in other languages.
feedback.feed_forward: Change what to which whenever it follows a comma.

expected: which

feedback.why_key: A bridge does not cost a town money in diversions; staying shut for a season does, so the comment takes the whole event.
feedback.feed_forward: Write which after the comma, never what and never that.

which added an hour to everybodys journey
which added an hour to everyone's journey
which added an hour to everyones journey

a move which added an hour to everybodys journey

payload.audio_text: They've scrapped the evening service, which nobody was told about.

expected: they've scrapped the evening service, which nobody was told about
they have scrapped the evening service, which nobody was told about
theyve scrapped the evening service which nobody was told about

expected: a decision which
