payload.context: The last train out of Marlow was busy every Friday and passengers are furious about losing it.
payload.stem: They scrapped the late train ___ was completely unnecessary.

options.why_this_means: That the train itself was unnecessary, so scrapping it was a sensible piece of housekeeping.
That scrapping it was the unnecessary act, whatever anybody thought of the train.

expected: , which

feedback.why_key: A busy train is not the thing nobody needed. The comma frees the comment so it can land on the scrapping instead.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the comma when your complaint is about the action.

items.decision_cue: dropped its evening course after two years

payload.context: A note about a college that dropped its evening course after two years.
payload.stem: The college dropped the evening course, which ___

options.why_this_means: That the course was the thing that never filled, so the comment is about the course.

options.text: left forty students without a class
options.why_this_means: That dropping it is what stranded the students, so the comment is about the decision.

follow_up.question: Which ending comments on the college's decision rather than on the course?

feedback.why_key: Both endings are correct English and both are useful. They send the comment to different places, and the verb is what does the sending.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose your ending by deciding what you want to comment on.

items.decision_cue: which had broken down twice a month

payload.context: Two sentences from different reports on the same hospital.
sentences: The trust replaced the old scanner, which had broken down twice a month.
The trust replaced the old scanner, which took eleven months to arrange.
meanings: The reason it went is that it kept failing.
Arranging the replacement is what dragged on for the best part of a year.

feedback.why_key: A scanner can break down and a scanner cannot take eleven months to arrange, so each ending sends the comment to the only place it fits.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the ending first and work backwards to its owner.

items.decision_cue: which the lawyers had advised against

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a newspaper and a set of private letters.
payload.sentence: The editor published the letters, which the lawyers had advised against.
reasons: a reader cannot tell whether the lawyers were against the letters or against publishing them
the comma should not be there
the comment sits too far from what it describes
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Lawyers can advise against a document and against an act, so both readings survive and the sentence quietly holds two meanings.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace which with a naming noun whenever two readings survive.

payload.sentence: Half the shops on the high street have closed, what has left the council with no easy answer.

expected: which has left the council
a collapse which has left the council

feedback.why_key: Shops closing is the thing that has left the council stuck, and English hands that job to which alone.
feedback.feed_forward: Change what to which and check the comma is there.

payload.prompt_text: A local paper has started charging for its website. Write one sentence that reports this and then comments on what doing it has caused.

feedback.why_key: The comment has to be something a paper could not do and a decision could, or the reader will attach it to the wrong thing.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that no noun in your sentence could have done the commenting verb.

payload.prompt_text: In your paragraph on the privacy of public figures, find your strongest example and add one comment clause to it. Then check whether any noun in the sentence could have done what your comment says. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: An example followed by your own comment on it is one of the few moves that answers a prompt and shows range in the same sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the comment, then reread it against every noun before it.

title: Splitting a sentence in two so one part cannot be missed

point_json.grammar_name: Cleft sentences: it is X that ... and what ... is

teach.can_do: I can split a sentence so that the part I care about cannot be read past.
teach.why_it_matters: English has almost no way of underlining a word in speech or in an essay. This structure is the way, and it does the job of a raised voice.
teach.meaning: A cleft takes one ordinary sentence and breaks it into two pieces so that one piece stands alone in the light and the rest is pushed into a clause behind it. Nothing new is being said. What changes is which part your reader treats as the news and which part they treat as already agreed. That makes it the tool for correcting an assumption, for setting two things against each other, and for holding the important word back until the end.

form.pattern: It + is / was + the part you want heard + that / who + the rest    |    What + clause + is / was + the part you want heard
notes: the it shape puts the spotlight early: it is the running costs that worry people
the what shape holds it back to the end: what worries people is the running costs
that works for people and things in the it shape; who is available for people
the verb after that agrees with the spotlit part, not with the it at the front
form.negative: The negative usually sits in the spotlight itself: it is not the rent that people object to.
form.question: Ask which single part of your sentence your reader might otherwise skim past. That part goes in the light.

left.text: The timing worries people.

right.role: one part moved into the light
right.text: It is the timing that worries people.

spec.caption: Nothing new has been said. One piece has been moved into the light and everything else into the shade.

worked_example.sentence: It is the running costs, not the building work, that will decide whether the scheme survives.
worked_example.why_this_form: The reader arrives expecting an argument about construction, so the sentence has to put the running costs where they cannot be skimmed and shove everything else back.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The running costs will decide whether the scheme survives reports the same fact and quietly lets the reader go on assuming the building work matters too.

notice_set.sentence: It was the noise that made them move, not the rent.
notice_set.question: Why did they move?
notice_set.why: The noise has been put in the light and the rent has been ruled out by name.

notice_set.sentence: What the council has not explained is where the money went.
notice_set.question: Has the council explained where the money went?
notice_set.why: The gap is held back to the very end, which is what makes it land.

notice_set.sentence: It was in March that the depot closed.
notice_set.question: What is the speaker putting right?
notice_set.why: March is standing in the light, so the date is the part the speaker thinks somebody has wrong.

notice_set.sentence: What surprised everybody was how quickly the shops emptied.
notice_set.question: Were people expecting the shops to empty that fast?
notice_set.why: Surprise means the speed was not expected, and the speed is the part held back until last.

notice_set.sentence: It is small firms that carry most of the cost.
notice_set.question: Who carries most of the cost?
notice_set.why: Small firms have been lifted out and put in front, which is where a reader looks first.

teach.rule_line: Use it when one part has to be corrected, set against something, or held back.
teach.false_rule: That this structure makes writing sound advanced. It sounds argumentative, and where nothing is in dispute it simply reads as odd.

errors.wrong: It is the timing what worries people, not the cost.
errors.right: It is the timing that worries people, not the cost.
errors.why_it_happens: Many languages use their question word to open this second half, and what is the closest English match, so the writer's ear raises no objection at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: what becomes that.
errors.l1_note: Frequent where the learner's first language uses its question word here.

errors.wrong: It is the delays that worries commuters most.
errors.right: It is the delays that worry commuters most.
errors.why_it_happens: The verb has to agree with the spotlit part, but the writer's ear is still holding the singular it is from three words earlier, and that is what the ending copies.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one letter: the s on worries.

errors.wrong: What most people object to. The way the charge was brought in.
errors.right: What most people object to is the way the charge was brought in.
errors.why_it_happens: The opening feels heavy enough to stand alone and the second part feels like the answer to it, so a full stop goes between them and the sentence never gets a main verb at all.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one full stop into the word is.

errors.wrong: It is my brother who taught me to cook.
errors.right: My brother taught me to cook.
errors.why_it_happens: The frame has been learned as a way of sounding impressive rather than as a way of singling one thing out against a rival. With nothing in dispute it adds four words and makes an ordinary sentence sound like a correction of somebody.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one frame: It is ... who.

pays_in.note: It corrects an assumption the prompt has planted in the reader's head.
pays_in.model: It is the shortage of small flats, not the price of large ones, that keeps young people at home.

pays_in.note: It marks which half of a long answer you actually want heard.
pays_in.model: What really changed things was the new bus route, not the car park.

pays_in.note: A writer's real claim often sits in the clause after that.
pays_in.model: It was the delay in publishing the figures that provoked most of the complaints.

used_in.quote: Both sides of this prompt rest on saying which factor really does the work, which is what this structure is for.

payload.sentence: It is the smallest firms that lose most when a payment is late.
payload.question: Who is worst affected?

feedback.why_key: The smallest firms have been lifted to the front and stood in the light, which is where the reader's eye goes first.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the part before that as the writer's real claim.

payload.sentence: What puts people off is the deposit, not the monthly rent.
payload.question: Which of the two is the bigger obstacle?

feedback.why_key: The deposit is held back to the end and the rent is ruled out by name, so the sentence is choosing between them.
feedback.feed_forward: Wait for the end of a what sentence before deciding.

payload.context: From a paragraph about town centre shops.
payload.sentence: It is the empty units what people notice first when they walk down the street.
reasons: the second half has been opened with the wrong word
the verb does not agree with the units
a comma belongs in front of the second half
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The second half of this structure opens with that or who. What has its own job elsewhere and English will not lend it out here.
feedback.feed_forward: Open the second half with that after it is.

payload.context: From a paragraph about household budgets.
payload.stem: It is the fixed bills that ___ (make) a small income impossible to plan around.

expected: make

feedback.why_key: The verb agrees with the fixed bills, which is the part in the light, and not with the it at the front of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the spotlit part, not to it is.

payload.given: Late payment closes small firms. Your reader assumes it is low demand.
payload.instruction: Put late payment where it cannot be missed.

expected: late payment that closes small firms
late payment, not low demand, that closes small firms

feedback.why_key: The reader has arrived with the wrong culprit in mind, and the only way to shift it is to stand the right one in front of them.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the corrected part straight after it is.

payload.given: Councils cannot find enough builders. That is the real obstacle to new housing.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that holds the obstacle back until the end.

expected: holds up new housing is the shortage of builders
stops councils building is the shortage of builders
councils cannot find is enough builders

feedback.why_key: Holding the answer back keeps the reader with you to the last word, which is the whole advantage of the what shape.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the two halves with is, never with a full stop.

payload.context: Build a sentence that keeps the answer until the end.

expected: what worries shoppers is the price of basics

feedback.why_key: Is is the hinge between the two halves, and without it the sentence is two pieces lying side by side.
feedback.feed_forward: Place is between the two halves before anything else.

payload.audio_text: It's the deposit that stops most people, not the rent.

expected: it's the deposit that stops most people, not the rent
it is the deposit that stops most people, not the rent
its the deposit that stops most people not the rent

feedback.why_key: Both hinges are unstressed in speech, so the whole frame can vanish and leave the listener with a list of two nouns.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small unstressed that in the middle.

payload.sentence: It is the entry costs that keeps them out of the market altogether.

expected: that keep them out

feedback.why_key: Costs is the part in the light and the verb belongs to it, however far away the singular it is now looks.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the verb back to the spotlit noun, not to it.

items.decision_cue: It was my sister who suggested

payload.context: The examiner has simply asked how the candidate chose their job. Nobody has disagreed with anything.
payload.sentence: It was my sister who suggested it, and it was the hours that appealed to me.
reasons: the second half opens with the wrong word
the verb does not agree
it is correct, but nothing is in dispute, so the sentence sounds like an argument
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is broken. The structure exists to correct somebody, and there is nobody to correct, so the answer sounds defensive.
feedback.feed_forward: Save this structure for a point somebody might dispute.

payload.prompt_text: Most people blame online shopping for empty high streets. You think business rates matter more. Write one sentence that puts the reader right.

feedback.why_key: A correction is exactly the situation this structure was built for, and a plain sentence would let the reader keep their original culprit.
feedback.feed_forward: Name the thing you are ruling out as well as the one you are choosing.

payload.prompt_text: Open your paragraph on very high salaries. Find the one sentence where you disagree with the other side and rewrite it as a split sentence. Use it once in the paragraph and no more. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: One of these in a paragraph marks your real claim. Two of them cancel each other out, because everything cannot be the important part.
feedback.feed_forward: Use it once, at the point of disagreement, then stop.

title: Attributing a view in an essay without saying 'some people say'

point_json.grammar_name: Attribution in academic writing

teach.can_do: I can attribute a view in an essay to a holder or a source instead of to nobody.
teach.why_it_matters: Some people say is the phrase that marks an essay as unattributed opinion. Three frames replace it, and each one buys you room to disagree.
teach.meaning: Academic attribution does two things at once. It puts a view on the page, and it puts a measured distance between that view and you. There are three frames and no more. Name the holder: Critics of the scheme argue that. Name nobody and let the passive carry it: It has been argued that. Name the source rather than the person: the 2019 review found that. Which frame you take decides how much of the claim lands on you, and it also decides whether your next sentence is able to push back against it.

form.pattern: HOLDER + reporting verb + that-clause  |  It + be + past participle + that-clause  |  SOURCE + verb + that-clause
notes: the holder frame: Critics argue that … / Supporters of the policy maintain that …
the passive frame: It has been argued that … / It is widely accepted that … — nobody is named, so there is nothing for an opponent to attack
the source frame: The review found that … / The data suggest that … — a source a reader could go and check
acknowledge and concede let you name the opposing view before you answer it: While it is widely acknowledged that …, …
that is not optional in these frames; it is the only thing holding the clause to the frame
form.negative: It has not been established that the charge reduces total traffic.
form.question: It might be asked whether the savings would ever materialise.

rungs.text: Loads of people reckon that…
Some people say that…
It is widely accepted that…
Critics of the scheme argue that…
The 2019 review found that…

spec.top_label: attributed to a source a reader could check

worked_example.sentence: It is widely accepted that congestion charging shifts journeys rather than removing them; what remains disputed is where they go.
worked_example.why_this_form: The passive frame puts an agreed point on the page without pretending the writer has counted anybody, and the second half moves straight to what is still open.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Some people say congestion charging shifts journeys hands the reader a vague crowd and an argument that can be waved away, because nothing has been agreed by anyone.

notice_set.sentence: It has been suggested that flexible hours reduce peak-time crowding.
notice_set.question: Does the sentence tell you who suggested it?
notice_set.why: The passive frame deliberately leaves the holder out, which is both its use and its limit.

notice_set.sentence: Critics of the policy argue that the savings have been overstated.
notice_set.question: Does the writer agree with the critics?
notice_set.why: Argue reports a case being made and takes no position on it, which leaves the next sentence free to go either way.

notice_set.sentence: The 2019 review found that the two schemes had similar running costs.
notice_set.question: Where could a reader go to check this?
notice_set.why: Naming a source is what makes a claim checkable, and checkable is what academic writing means by supported.

notice_set.sentence: While it is widely acknowledged that fees deter some applicants, the measured effect is small.
notice_set.question: What is the writer about to do?
options: accept the point and then limit it
notice_set.why: Acknowledge concedes ground on purpose so that the limit arriving after the comma has something to push against.

notice_set.sentence: It is often assumed that longer opening hours increase visitor numbers.
notice_set.question: Is the writer likely to agree in the next sentence?
options: No — assumed usually sets up a challenge
notice_set.why: Assume marks a belief held without evidence, which is a place to attack rather than a place to agree.

notice_set.sentence: The data suggest that the drop began before the charge was introduced.
notice_set.question: How strong is the claim being made?
notice_set.why: Suggest reports a lean in the evidence, which is honest when the evidence leans rather than settles.

discovery.prompt: The same idea is put on the page twice. Work out what the right-hand version gives the reader that the left-hand one does not.
pairs: Some people say that fees put students off.
It is often argued that fees deter applicants from lower-income households.
Everyone knows that the buses are unreliable.
Passenger surveys consistently report low satisfaction with reliability.
I think the charge has worked.
The evidence collected since 2019 suggests that the charge has worked.

candidate_rules.text: The right-hand versions attach the claim to a holder or a source, which is what lets a reader agree or disagree with something specific.
The right-hand versions are longer and use more formal words.
A sentence is academic if it starts with It is.

teach.rule_line: Name a holder, name a source, or use the passive frame — but name something.
teach.false_rule: That an essay becomes academic by adding some people say and according to many experts. Both attribute the claim to nobody, which is where it already was.

errors.wrong: Loads of people reckon that a four-day week would never work in hospitals.
errors.right: It is often argued that a four-day week would be unworkable in hospitals.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner has the idea and reaches for the words they would use to say it out loud. The content is fine; the frame belongs to a conversation and arrives on the page unchanged.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one span: Loads of people reckon that becomes It is often argued that.

errors.wrong: It has often argued that public transport should be free at the point of use.
errors.right: It has often been argued that public transport should be free at the point of use.
errors.why_it_happens: The frame is stored as one lump and under time pressure the middle of the lump falls out. Has argued is perfectly grammatical, which is why nothing in the writer's ear objects to it.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: been.

errors.wrong: Research proves that homework has no effect on examination results.
errors.right: Research suggests that homework has little effect on examination results.
errors.why_it_happens: Proves and no effect both feel more forceful, and force feels like persuasion. A reader who knows the area hears an overclaim and discounts the rest of the paragraph on the strength of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Swap one word: proves becomes suggests.

errors.wrong: It is widely accepted the charge has reduced traffic in the centre.
errors.right: It is widely accepted that the charge has reduced traffic in the centre.
errors.why_it_happens: That is droppable after said in speech and the habit crosses over. In this frame it is the only thing holding the clause on, and without it the sentence reads as two half sentences pushed together.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one word: that.

pays_in.note: It is the difference between an argued essay and a page of opinions.
pays_in.model: It is widely accepted that remote study widens access; what remains disputed is whether it improves outcomes.

pays_in.note: Which-view-matches-the-writer questions run entirely on attribution frames.
pays_in.model: It has been argued that the two measures were never comparable.

pays_in.note: Describing what a figure shows is attribution to a source.
pays_in.model: The chart shows that domestic demand fell in every year after 2014.

used_in.quote: A discussion prompt needs two attributed positions before the writer's own view can mean anything, and this is how they get attributed.
The passage separates what has been argued from what the author holds, and one question depends entirely on that separation.

payload.sentence: It has been argued that shorter degrees would suit older students better.
payload.question: Whose view is this?
options: somebody's, but the sentence does not say whose

feedback.why_key: The passive frame puts a real view on the page and deliberately declines to name who holds it.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the passive frame as a view without an owner.

payload.sentence: While it is widely acknowledged that the scheme reduced traffic, the effect on air quality was smaller than expected.
payload.question: What is the writer doing with the first half?
options: giving ground so the second half can push back

feedback.why_key: Acknowledging a point on purpose is what gives the limitation after the comma something solid to be measured against.
feedback.feed_forward: Read While it is acknowledged as a set-up for a limit.

payload.context: The opening sentence of a Task 2 body paragraph.
payload.sentence: According to many experts, printed newspapers will disappear within a decade.
reasons: no expert is named, so the claim is attributed to nobody
printed newspapers will not disappear
will disappear is the wrong verb form
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The phrase looks like a citation and functions as none. There is nobody a reader could go and check, so the claim is still just an opinion.
feedback.feed_forward: Name a source, or drop the crowd and use the passive frame.

payload.context: Opening an essay paragraph on funding for basic research.
payload.stem: It has long ___ (argue) that basic research pays for itself over decades rather than years.

expected: been argued

feedback.why_key: The frame is a passive, so been is doing the work of leaving the arguer out. Without it the sentence claims it did the arguing.
feedback.feed_forward: Check for been every time you write It has.

payload.context: The study is one survey of four hundred households, and the writer wants to be honest about that.
payload.stem: The survey ___ (suggest / prove) that households overestimate how much they recycle.

expected: suggests

feedback.why_key: One survey supports a lean. Proves would promise a settlement, and the reader would be entitled to ask where it came from.
feedback.feed_forward: Size the verb to the evidence you actually have.

payload.given: Some people say that class size does not matter much.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the claim is attributed to somebody, using the holder frame.

expected: critics of smaller classes argue that class size matters less than teaching quality
critics of the policy argue that class size does not matter much
critics of the reform argue that class size has little effect

feedback.why_key: Naming a holder gives your reader something to picture and gives your next sentence something to answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Replace the crowd with a named group.

payload.given: Everyone knows that sitting all day is bad for you.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it as an attributed claim using the passive frame, and hedge it to match ordinary evidence.

expected: it is widely accepted that prolonged sitting carries health risks
it is generally accepted that prolonged sitting carries health risks
it is widely accepted that sitting for long periods carries health risks

feedback.why_key: Widely accepted claims agreement without claiming a headcount, which is exactly as much as the evidence will carry.
feedback.feed_forward: Swap everyone knows for widely accepted.

payload.context: Build the passive attribution frame around this claim.

expected: it has been suggested that shorter shifts reduce clinical errors

feedback.why_key: Four fixed words open the frame and that closes it. Everything you actually want to say sits after that.
feedback.feed_forward: Build the frame first, then hang the claim on that.

payload.audio_text: It's been argued that trust in reporting has never recovered.

expected: it's been argued that trust in reporting has never recovered
it has been argued that trust in reporting has never recovered
its been argued that trust in reporting has never recovered

feedback.why_key: In speech the whole frame reduces to about two syllables, which is why been is the first thing to go missing when it reaches the page.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for been between the auxiliary and the participle.

payload.sentence: It has frequently claimed that recycling targets are set without reference to what councils can collect.

expected: it has frequently been claimed

feedback.why_key: Without been, the sentence says that it did the claiming, and there is no it in the paragraph for that to point at.
feedback.feed_forward: Insert been after the auxiliary in every passive frame.

payload.context: From an essay paragraph resting on a single national dataset.
payload.sentence: The dataset proves beyond doubt that automation has cut entry-level hiring in every region.
reasons: the verb and the phrase after it claim far more than one dataset can carry
automation has not cut entry-level hiring
proves is the wrong tense
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Beyond doubt is a promise no single dataset can keep, and in every region rules out the exceptions a reader will immediately think of.
feedback.feed_forward: Cut the intensifier before you cut anything else.

payload.context: Two opening sentences from different paragraphs of the same article.
sentences: It is often assumed that longer opening hours raise visitor numbers.
It is widely accepted that longer opening hours raise staffing costs.
meanings: The writer is about to challenge this, because assume marks a belief held without evidence.
The writer is taking this as settled and will build on it rather than argue about it.

feedback.why_key: Both frames are passive and both name nobody. The participle inside them tells the reader which claim is about to be taken apart.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the participle to see where the paragraph is going.

payload.prompt_text: Write the opening sentence of a body paragraph arguing that online courses widen access to study. Attribute the claim to somebody or to something, and do not use said, some people or according to.

feedback.why_key: An opening sentence that attributes gives the paragraph somebody to answer, and a paragraph with nobody to answer has nowhere to go.
feedback.feed_forward: Name a holder or a source in the first eight words.

payload.prompt_text: Write the concession paragraph for this prompt. It must acknowledge the opposing view using a passive attribution frame, then limit it using a named source. Do not use some people say. Eight minutes.

feedback.why_key: The concession paragraph is where an essay proves it has read the other side, and attribution is the only thing that proves it.
feedback.feed_forward: Check that every claim in the paragraph has an owner.

title: Turning something that happened into a thing you can then talk about

point_json.grammar_name: Nominalisation

teach.can_do: I can turn something that happened into a thing, so that my next sentence can measure it, explain it or argue about it.
teach.why_it_matters: It lets a paragraph refer back to a whole event in three words, and it is the commonest source of wrong word endings.
teach.meaning: Prices rose is an event: it happens, and then it is over. The rise in prices is a thing: it can be sharp or gradual, it can have a cause, it can be the subject of the next sentence, and it can be counted. English lets you convert one into the other, and the conversion is what makes it possible to talk about an event rather than merely report it. The price is weight. Every conversion makes a sentence heavier.

form.pattern: verb or adjective + an ending + a preposition + the rest
notes: common endings: -tion, -ment, -al, -ure, -ance, -ness, -th, and sometimes no change at all
each of these nouns keeps a preposition, and it is not always the one the verb used: a rise in, a solution to, an increase in, a fall in
the conversion nearly always needs the or a in front of it once it becomes a thing
when you convert, the person who did it disappears unless you put them back with by or a possessive
form.negative: The negative usually converts too: they did not comply becomes their failure to comply.
form.question: Ask whether the next sentence needs to say something about the event itself. If so, make it a thing.

left.role: an event, which happens and is over
left.text: Fuel prices rose sharply last winter.

right.role: a thing, which can be measured and argued about
right.text: the sharp rise in fuel prices

spec.caption: Once it is a thing, it can be the subject of your next sentence, or be counted, or be blamed.

worked_example.sentence: Fuel prices rose sharply last winter. That rise pushed a fifth of rural households into arrears.
worked_example.why_this_form: Making the event into a thing lets the second sentence open from something the reader already holds and puts the new figure at the end, where the weight lands.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: Because fuel prices rose sharply, a fifth of rural households fell behind says the same thing but opens on a marker rather than on the reader's own ground.

notice_set.sentence: The closure of the two branches was announced in March.
notice_set.question: Did the branches shut?
notice_set.why: What happened in March was the announcement. Whether the shutting itself has happened yet is left completely open.

notice_set.sentence: The two branches closed in March.
notice_set.question: Did the branches shut?
notice_set.why: As an event it is simply reported, and there is no announcement standing in front of it.

notice_set.sentence: There has been a sharp fall in the number of small savers.
notice_set.question: Are there more or fewer small savers than before?
notice_set.why: Fall carries the direction, and sharp measures it, which is something you cannot do to a verb without an adverb.

notice_set.sentence: Repayment of the loan begins in April.
notice_set.question: Who pays?
notice_set.why: Packing the action into a thing lets the writer leave the person out altogether, which is sometimes useful and sometimes evasive.

notice_set.sentence: The council's refusal to publish the figures surprised nobody.
notice_set.question: Were the figures published?
notice_set.why: The refusal is a thing that happened, and the possessive in front of it puts the council back in as the one who did it.

teach.rule_line: Make the event a thing when your next sentence needs to say something about it.
teach.false_rule: That these nouns make writing academic. They make a sentence heavier, and three in a row make it unreadable.

errors.wrong: There has been a steady improve in air quality since the depot shut.
errors.right: There has been a steady improvement in air quality since the depot shut.
errors.why_it_happens: The learner knows exactly which word they want and reaches for the shape they have met most often, which is the verb. Nothing in the sentence sounds wrong to them because the meaning arrived intact.
errors.smallest_fix: Add one ending: improve becomes improvement.

errors.wrong: The analyse of the figures took three weeks longer than expected.
errors.right: The analysis of the figures took three weeks longer than expected.
errors.why_it_happens: This pair changes more than an ending, so the usual pattern of adding something to the verb does not produce the right word and the learner has nothing else to fall back on.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one ending: analyse becomes analysis.

errors.wrong: The increase of rents has slowed since the spring.
errors.right: The increase in rents has slowed since the spring.
errors.why_it_happens: Of is the default for anything belonging to anything, so it arrives first. These nouns each keep their own preposition and it is rarely predictable from the verb they came from.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: of becomes in.

errors.wrong: Rise in fuel prices has hit rural households hardest.
errors.right: The rise in fuel prices has hit rural households hardest.
errors.why_it_happens: The event felt like a general fact when it was a verb, and turning it into a thing does not change how it feels. English marks a particular, identified thing with the, and this one is particular.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: the.
errors.l1_note: Very common where the first language has no articles at all.

pays_in.note: It names a trend so that the next sentence can compare it with another.
pays_in.model: The fall in coal use was steeper than the rise in wind generation over the same period.

pays_in.note: It lets a sentence open from the event described in the one before.
pays_in.model: The removal of the subsidy has been blamed for most of the increase.

pays_in.note: Passages compress whole clauses into these, which is what makes them dense.
pays_in.model: Widespread adoption of the technique followed its approval in 2016.

used_in.quote: Describing shares of a budget means naming rises and falls as things, then setting them against each other.

payload.sentence: The withdrawal of the free bus pass affected about nine thousand people.
payload.question: Was the pass taken away?

feedback.why_key: The event has been packed into a thing, but the thing still describes something that took place and the sentence treats it as done.
feedback.feed_forward: Unpack the heavy noun back into a verb to check what happened.

payload.sentence: There's been a big drop in the number of people paying cash.
payload.question: Are more or fewer people paying cash?

feedback.why_key: Drop carries the direction on its own, and big measures it, which is why the thing can be sized in a way the event could not.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the heavy noun for direction before anything else.

payload.context: From a draft about household borrowing.
payload.sentence: The reduction of interest rates in 2021 encouraged people to borrow more.
reasons: this noun keeps a different small word after it
the ending on the noun is wrong
the word the should not be there
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Reduction takes in when it is measuring a change in something. Of would be right if the rates themselves were being reduced in number.
feedback.feed_forward: Learn the small word as part of the noun, not separately.

payload.context: From a description of a chart on household spending.
payload.stem: The steady ___ (decline) in cash payments continued throughout the period.

expected: decline

feedback.why_key: This one converts without changing at all, which is exactly why learners add an ending it does not want.
feedback.feed_forward: Check whether the noun and the verb are already the same word.

payload.context: From a paragraph about regional employment.
payload.stem: There has been a sharp increase ___ part-time work across the whole district.

expected: in

feedback.why_key: Increase takes in when it names the thing that has grown, and this pairing has to be learned as one unit rather than worked out.
feedback.feed_forward: Store the noun and its small word together as one item.

payload.given: The council removed the subsidy in 2022. Fares went up by a quarter within six months.
payload.instruction: Start the second sentence with what the council did.

expected: of the subsidy pushed fares up by a quarter within six months
of the subsidy raised fares by a quarter within six months

feedback.why_key: Once the removal has become a thing, a sentence can make it the culprit, which no verb is able to do.
feedback.feed_forward: Convert the event, then make it the subject.

payload.context: Build one sentence comparing two lines on a chart.

expected: the fall in manufacturing was steeper than the rise in services

feedback.why_key: Two events have become two things, and only things can be set side by side and compared in one clause.
feedback.feed_forward: Convert both sides before you try to compare them.

payload.audio_text: There's been a sharp rise in the cost of borrowing.

expected: there's been a sharp rise in the cost of borrowing
there has been a sharp rise in the cost of borrowing
theres been a sharp rise in the cost of borrowing

feedback.why_key: The small words around the heavy noun are all unstressed, and they are the ones that go missing when a listener writes down only the content words.
feedback.feed_forward: Write the small words around the heavy noun first.

payload.sentence: Local firms objected to the develop of the waterfront on cost grounds.

expected: the development of the waterfront
the redevelopment of the waterfront

feedback.why_key: The slot after the wants a thing, and the verb has been dropped into it unchanged because it carried the right meaning already.
feedback.feed_forward: Add the noun ending whenever the word follows the or a.

items.decision_cue: The implementation of the modification of the procedure

payload.context: From a draft methods paragraph.
payload.sentence: The implementation of the modification of the procedure led to a reduction in the duration of the trial.
reasons: one of the endings is wrong
one of the small words is wrong
it is correct, but four heavy nouns in one sentence make it unreadable
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Every word here is right and the sentence still fails, because nothing in it does anything. Four things in a row and no events left.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn at least one of them back into a verb.

payload.prompt_text: Card payments overtook cash in your country around 2018 and the gap has widened since. Write one sentence that names both changes as things and compares them.

feedback.why_key: Two events cannot be compared inside one clause. Two things can, and that is the only reason to make the conversion here.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the small word after each noun before you submit.

payload.prompt_text: Open your description of the council budget chart. Find one place where you reported a change twice and rewrite it so the second mention is a thing you then measure. Then count the heavy nouns in the sentence and cut it back to two. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: The conversion earns its place once per sentence. Beyond that it stops compressing anything and simply removes the verbs.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep at most two heavy nouns in any one sentence.

title: Putting the one part that matters where nobody can read past it

point_json.grammar_name: Emphasis in production: clefts and fronting

teach.can_do: I can lift one part of a sentence into the light, and I know when not to.
teach.why_it_matters: Used once, at the point of disagreement, it marks your real claim. Used three times it cancels itself out. If nothing is in dispute, write the plain sentence.
teach.meaning: You already know how to build these shapes. This point is about deciding, inside a real paragraph, which part of a sentence needs lifting out, which shape to lift it with, and — far more often — deciding not to. English has three ways of putting one part under a light: it is X that, what the clause is is X, and simply moving X to the front. They cost different amounts of the reader's patience and they belong in different rooms.

form.pattern: It + is / was + X + that / who + REST    |    What + CLAUSE + is / was + X    |    X , + SUBJECT + VERB
notes: the it shape puts the part in the light first; the what shape holds it back until the end
moving the part to the front is the cheap version and the rest of the sentence stays as it was
the fronted version is at home out loud; the two longer shapes are at home on a page
no extra pronoun after a fronted part, and no comma before that in the it shape
form.negative: It is not the fee that people object to. The negative goes into the lit part, never into the second half.
form.question: Ask which single part of the sentence a tired reader would skim straight past.

left.text: the repayment schedule puts borrowers in trouble

right.role: what a tired reader cannot skim
right.text: it is the repayment schedule that puts borrowers in trouble

spec.caption: Nothing has been added. One part has been lifted under a light, and the sentence is now four words longer for it.

worked_example.sentence: It is the repayment schedule, not the interest rate, that puts borrowers in trouble.
worked_example.why_this_form: Every reader arrives blaming the rate, so the schedule has to be stood in front of them and the rate has to be named and ruled out.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: The repayment schedule puts borrowers in trouble reports the same thing and quietly lets the reader carry on blaming the rate as well.

notice_set.sentence: It is the fees that catch people out, not the rate.
notice_set.question: What does the speaker think catches people out?
notice_set.why: The fees have been put in front and the rate has been ruled out by name, so there is nothing left to guess.

notice_set.sentence: What the leaflet never mentions is the charge for paying early.
notice_set.question: Does the leaflet mention the charge?
notice_set.why: The missing thing is held back to the last three words, which is where a reader is still paying attention.

notice_set.sentence: That kind of debt most families never clear.
notice_set.question: Do most families clear this kind of debt?
notice_set.why: The kind of debt has been moved to the front so the sentence can be about it, and the answer lands at the end.

notice_set.sentence: What surprised the council was how few households applied.
notice_set.question: Did many households apply?
notice_set.why: Surprise plus how few tells you the number was small, and the number is held back to where it lands hardest.

notice_set.sentence: The complaints were not about the refund. It was the six-week wait that caused them.
notice_set.question: What were people angry about?
notice_set.why: The first sentence clears the refund out of the way so the second can put the wait where it cannot be missed.

teach.rule_line: Lift one part into the light only when a reader would otherwise blame the wrong thing.
teach.false_rule: That these shapes make a paragraph sound advanced. They sound argumentative, and where nothing is disputed they read as somebody correcting a person who is not in the room.

errors.wrong: That kind of delay we cannot afford it.
errors.right: That kind of delay we cannot afford.
errors.why_it_happens: Moving the part to the front leaves a hole where it used to sit, and the hand fills the hole with a pronoun so that the sentence feels finished again.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: it.
errors.l1_note: Very common where the first language keeps a pronoun in the original position.

errors.wrong: What the leaflet never mentions. The charge for paying early.
errors.right: What the leaflet never mentions is the charge for paying early.
errors.why_it_happens: The first part feels weighty enough to be a sentence, and what follows feels like its answer, so a full stop drops in between and neither part ever gets a verb.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: is, where the full stop is.

errors.wrong: What the tenants want are a written promise about the charges.
errors.right: What the tenants want is a written promise about the charges.
errors.why_it_happens: The plural noun three words back is still ringing when the verb is chosen, so the ending copies that instead of matching the single thing being asked for.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: are becomes is.

errors.wrong: It was the bus fare that I was complaining about.
errors.right: I was complaining about the bus fare.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape has been stored as a way of sounding advanced rather than as a way of ruling one thing out against another, so it fires with nobody to correct and adds four words to an ordinary answer.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one frame: It was ... that.

pays_in.note: One of these where you disagree marks your real claim in a paragraph.
pays_in.model: What the figures never show is how many households simply stopped applying.

pays_in.note: Moving the part to the front is the cheap version, and it belongs out loud.
pays_in.model: That sort of charge most people never even notice.

pays_in.note: A writer's real target usually sits in the lit part, not in the clause behind it.
pays_in.model: It was the six-week wait, rather than the refund itself, that drew the complaints.

used_in.quote: The prompt invites the obvious culprit, so the paragraph that names a different one has to say so where the reader cannot skim it.

payload.sentence: What the tenants were never told is the size of the service charge.
payload.question: Were the tenants told the size of the charge?

feedback.why_key: The missing thing is held back to the last words of the sentence, which is where a reader is still paying attention.
feedback.feed_forward: Hold on until the final words arrive before deciding.

payload.sentence: That kind of debt most families never clear.
payload.question: Do most families clear this kind of debt?

feedback.why_key: The kind of debt has been moved to the front so the sentence can be about it, and the answer arrives at the very end.
feedback.feed_forward: Read a fronted part as the topic, not as the subject.

payload.context: A candidate is explaining why nobody complains when prices creep up.
payload.sentence: That kind of increase the shops simply absorb it.
reasons: the moved part has been left behind as well
the sentence has no main verb
the verb does not match its subject
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The increase is named twice, once at the front and once as a small word at the end. English keeps one of them and drops the other.
feedback.feed_forward: Delete the leftover pronoun after a fronted part.

payload.context: From a paragraph about tenants and service charges.
payload.stem: What the tenants want ___ (be) a written promise about the charges.

expected: is

feedback.why_key: One promise is being asked for, so the verb matches the promise and not the tenants standing three words earlier.
feedback.feed_forward: Match the verb to the thing held back, not to the noun before it.

payload.given: The service charge empties a household budget. Your reader has arrived blaming the rent.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that stands the schedule in front of the reader.

expected: the service charge that empties a household budget
the service charge, not the rent, that empties a household budget

feedback.why_key: Your reader arrives holding the wrong culprit, and nothing dislodges it except standing the right one where they cannot get by.
feedback.feed_forward: Place the part you are correcting immediately after it is.

payload.given: Almost nobody used the new payment app. The bank had not expected that.
payload.instruction: Write one sentence that keeps the number back until the end.

expected: surprised the bank was how few people used the app
the bank had not expected was how few people used the app

feedback.why_key: Keeping the number until the end holds your reader through to the final word, and that is the only thing this shape buys you.
feedback.feed_forward: Join the two halves with was, never with a full stop.

payload.context: Build a spoken sentence that puts the charge first and leaves nothing behind it.

expected: that sort of charge most people never notice

feedback.why_key: The moved part sits at the front on its own, and no small word is left standing where it used to be.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the part to the front and leave no pronoun behind.

payload.audio_text: It's the delivery charge that catches people out, not the price.

expected: it's the delivery charge that catches people out, not the price
it is the delivery charge that catches people out, not the price
its the delivery charge that catches people out, not the price

feedback.why_key: Both hinges are unstressed, so the whole frame can disappear and leave a listener holding two nouns and no argument.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for the small unstressed that in the middle.

items.decision_cue: It was the parking charge that I was objecting to

payload.context: Part 1. The examiner has asked how the candidate gets to work. Nobody has disagreed with anything.
payload.sentence: It was the parking charge that I was objecting to, and it is the barrier that I would take out.
reasons: the frame is built wrongly
the verbs do not match their subjects
it is correct English, but nothing is in dispute, so it sounds like an argument with somebody
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing here is broken. The shape exists to correct somebody, there is nobody to correct, and the answer comes out sounding defensive.
feedback.feed_forward: Save this shape for something a listener might dispute.

payload.sentence: It is the monthly repayments that keeps borrowers awake, not the size of the loan.

expected: that keep borrowers awake

feedback.why_key: The repayments are standing in the light and the ending belongs to them, however distant that little word at the front now looks.
feedback.feed_forward: Trace the ending back to the lit part, not to the front.

payload.context: Two sentences from two reviews of the same refund scheme.
sentences: It was the six-week wait that drew the complaints.
What drew the complaints was the six-week wait.
meanings: The writer is putting the reader right at once, before they can settle on the refund itself.
The writer takes the reader through the complaints first and leaves the cause to land at the end.

feedback.why_key: Both light up the same words. One does it immediately, to correct; the other holds it back, to land. The choice is about your reader's patience.
feedback.feed_forward: Correct early with it is; land late with what.

payload.prompt_text: Most readers blame online shopping for empty town centres. You think the rents charged on small units matter more. Write one sentence that stands your reason in front of them and names the one you are ruling out.

feedback.why_key: Correcting somebody is what this shape was built for. A flat sentence lets your reader keep whichever culprit they walked in holding.
feedback.feed_forward: Say which one you are ruling out, not only which one you pick.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on town centre shops. Count these shapes in the whole essay. Keep the one that sits where you disagree with the prompt and turn every other one back into a plain sentence. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: One of these in an essay marks your real claim. Three of them flatten each other, since everything in a paragraph cannot be the deciding part.
feedback.feed_forward: Keep one, at the point of disagreement, and flatten the rest.

title: Opening on a negative word and swapping the next two round

point_json.grammar_name: Inversion after negative and restrictive adverbials

teach.can_do: I can turn a sentence round after an opening negative, and I know when not to.
teach.why_it_matters: Four things must be right at once and the reward is one sentence. If your ordinary sentences are not yet clean, leave this one alone and spend the nerve elsewhere.
teach.meaning: When a sentence opens on a word meaning never, rarely, only or not, English turns the next two words round: the small helping word jumps in front of the subject, exactly as it does in a question. The sentence is not a question and nothing about what it claims has changed. What has changed is where your reader's attention starts — on the never rather than on the person — which is why it reads as a claim being pressed rather than reported.

form.pattern: NEGATIVE OPENER + AUXILIARY + SUBJECT + MAIN VERB
notes: if there is no auxiliary in the sentence already, do, does or did comes in to be moved, exactly as in a question
rarely does a lender admit it; never had the charge been waived; only after the inquiry did the figures change
the turn happens once, in the clause the negative word opens, and nowhere else
not only X but also Y turns the first half only: not only did costs rise, but the service also got slower
form.negative: The negative is already in the opening word, so the verb itself stays positive: never has the fee been waived.
form.question: Ask yourself: is my first word never, rarely, seldom, only, not once, or under no circumstances?

left.text: the fund has rarely paid out in full

right.text: rarely has the fund paid out in full

spec.caption: The words are the same and the claim is the same. Only the first thing your reader meets has changed.

worked_example.sentence: Rarely has a scheme of this size come in under its own forecast.
worked_example.why_this_form: The paragraph is arguing that overspending is normal, so the sentence has to open on how unusual it is rather than on the scheme.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: A scheme of this size has rarely come in under its own forecast makes the identical claim and starts the reader on the scheme, which is not where the argument is.

notice_set.sentence: Not once has the fund paid out in full.
notice_set.question: Has the fund ever paid out in full?
notice_set.why: Not once covers every occasion there has ever been, so no case is left over.

notice_set.sentence: Only after the audit did the figures change.
notice_set.question: When did the figures change?
notice_set.why: The audit is put first because the timing is the part somebody is arguing about.

notice_set.sentence: Rarely does a small firm recover from a year like that.
notice_set.question: Do small firms usually recover?
notice_set.why: Rarely says it does happen, but almost never, which is a different claim from never at all.

notice_set.sentence: Not only did the costs rise, but the service got slower too.
notice_set.question: How many things went wrong?
notice_set.why: The frame exists to add a second thing to a first, and both halves are sitting here.

notice_set.sentence: Under no circumstances will the deposit be returned.
notice_set.question: Could the deposit ever be returned?
notice_set.why: Every case has been ruled out in advance, which is why this belongs on a notice rather than in a conversation.

teach.rule_line: After an opening negative, put the helping word in front of the subject.
teach.false_rule: That this makes a sentence sound advanced. It makes a claim sound pressed, and in an answer where nothing is being pressed it reads as somebody shouting in a library.

errors.wrong: Under no circumstances the fee can be waived.
errors.right: Under no circumstances can the fee be waived.
errors.why_it_happens: The opener has been learned as a piece of vocabulary rather than as a switch that changes the order after it, so the rest of the sentence comes out in its ordinary shape.
errors.smallest_fix: Move one word: can goes in front of the fee.

errors.wrong: Rarely do the fund pay out in full.
errors.right: Rarely does the fund pay out in full.
errors.why_it_happens: The helping word is chosen before the writer has looked past the opener to see what the subject actually is, and the commoner form arrives first.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: do becomes does.

errors.wrong: Not only must the firm to pay a fine, but it also loses the contract.
errors.right: Not only must the firm pay a fine, but it also loses the contract.
errors.why_it_happens: Once the order has been turned round, the writer loses track of which word the main verb is hanging from, and the default to arrives in front of it.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: to.

errors.wrong: Never have I seen a garden as fine as that one.
errors.right: I've never seen a garden that nice.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape has been drilled for essays and arrives in Part 1, where an ordinary friendly question has been asked and the answer comes back sounding like a speech.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one frame: Never have I.

pays_in.note: Once, in the paragraph where you are pressing hardest, and not again.
pays_in.model: Rarely has a policy been introduced with so little warning to the people it affects.

pays_in.note: A fronted negative tells you where a writer is putting their weight.
pays_in.model: Not once in the report is the cost of maintenance mentioned.

pays_in.note: Announcements use it, and the turned-round order throws listeners who expect a question.
pays_in.model: Under no circumstances should passengers cross the line here.

used_in.quote: The argument on this prompt turns on how unusual the spending is, which is exactly what a fronted negative is for.

payload.sentence: Not once has the scheme returned a surplus.
payload.question: Has the scheme ever returned a surplus?

feedback.why_key: Not once covers every occasion there has ever been, so there is no case left for the reader to wonder about.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the opening word first; it carries the claim.

payload.sentence: Under no circumstances should passengers cross the line here.
payload.question: Is this a question or an instruction?

feedback.why_key: The order looks like a question because the helping word has moved, but nothing is being asked. Every case has been ruled out in advance.
feedback.feed_forward: Check the opening word before you decide it is a question.

items.decision_cue: Under no circumstances the charge can be refunded

payload.context: From the terms attached to a savings account.
payload.sentence: Under no circumstances the charge can be refunded.
reasons: the two words after the opener have not been turned round
the charge can never be refunded at all
the opener needs a comma after it
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The opener has done its job and then been ignored. English expects the small word to jump the subject once that opener is in place.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn the next two words round after a negative opener.

payload.context: From a paragraph about small business lending.
payload.stem: Rarely ___ a small firm recover from a year of that kind.

expected: does

feedback.why_key: There was no helping word in the sentence, so one has to be brought in, and it has to match the single firm that follows it.
feedback.feed_forward: Bring in does or did, then match it to the subject.

payload.context: From a report on a delayed audit.
payload.stem: Only after the audit ___ the figures change.

expected: did

feedback.why_key: The change is over and done with, so the helping word brought in to be moved is the past one.
feedback.feed_forward: Put the time into the helping word, not the main verb.

payload.given: A fund of this kind has rarely paid out in its first year.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it so the sentence opens on how unusual it is.

expected: has a fund of this kind paid out in its first year
has a fund of this kind paid out in its first year.

feedback.why_key: The helping word was already in the sentence, so nothing had to be brought in. It only had to jump the subject.
feedback.feed_forward: Move the helping word you already have, and add nothing.

payload.context: Build one sentence that adds a second problem to a first.

expected: not only did costs rise but the service also got slower

feedback.why_key: Only the first half turns round. The second half keeps its ordinary order, with also sitting inside it rather than at the front.
feedback.feed_forward: Turn the first half only, and leave the second alone.

payload.audio_text: Rarely does the ferry run in weather like this.

expected: rarely does the ferry run in weather like this
rarely does the ferry run in weather like this.

feedback.why_key: Does is unstressed and sits between two content words, so a listener expecting ordinary order will hear the ferry first and lose it.
feedback.feed_forward: Listen for a small unstressed word straight after the opener.

items.decision_cue: Never have I encountered a town so completely reshaped

payload.context: Part 1. The examiner has asked whether the candidate's home town has changed. Nothing is in dispute.
payload.sentence: Never have I encountered a town so completely reshaped by a single road.
reasons: the two words after the opener have not been turned round
the helping word does not match the subject
it is correct, but nothing is being pressed here, so it sounds like a rehearsed line
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: Nothing is broken. The shape presses a claim hard, and a friendly question about a garden gives it nothing to press against.
feedback.feed_forward: Save the turned-round order for a point somebody might resist.

items.decision_cue: Rarely do a scheme of this kind

payload.sentence: Rarely do a scheme of this kind come in on budget, and never in its first year.

expected: does a scheme

feedback.why_key: One scheme, so one form of the helping word. The opener pulls the eye away from the subject and the ending gets picked without it.
feedback.feed_forward: Look past the opener to the subject before choosing do or does.

payload.context: Two sentences from the same report on a delayed audit.
sentences: Only after the audit did the figures change.
The figures changed only after the audit.
meanings: The timing is what the writer is pressing, and the reader meets it before anything else.
The same fact, reported evenly, with the figures as the thing the sentence is about.

feedback.why_key: Both sentences are true and both are correct. One presses the timing at the reader; the other simply reports it in passing.
feedback.feed_forward: Front the opener only when the timing is the argument.

payload.prompt_text: You are arguing that governments almost never fund research that will not pay back within ten years. Write one sentence that opens on how unusual it is, not on the governments.

feedback.why_key: Opening on the rarity puts the argument in the reader's first three words instead of burying it in the middle of the sentence.
feedback.feed_forward: Open on the negative word, then jump the subject.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on funding for space research. Find the single sentence where you press hardest and turn that one round after a negative opener. Check the helping word matches the subject, then leave every other sentence exactly as it is. Three minutes.

feedback.why_key: One of these in an essay is a raised voice at the right moment. Three of them is a candidate who shouts through the whole answer.
feedback.feed_forward: Use it once, where you press hardest, then stop.

title: Dropping if and starting the sentence with had

point_json.grammar_name: Conditional inversion: had, were and should at the front

teach.can_do: I can write an unreal past sentence without using if, and I know what it buys me.
teach.why_it_matters: It buys one thing: a formal sentence with no if in it. If the third conditional is not yet automatic, spend the nerve on something that pays more.
teach.meaning: This is the same unreal sentence you already build with if, with the if taken out and the had moved to the front. Nothing about the meaning moves: the thing did not happen, and the sentence says what would have followed if it had. What changes is only how it sounds — heavier, more written, a little more formal than the same idea with if in it. That is the whole return, which is why the rest of the sentence has to be perfect.

form.pattern: Had + SUBJECT + past participle , + would have + past participle    |    Were + SUBJECT + to + VERB , ...    |    Should + SUBJECT + VERB , ...
notes: the if disappears; it never sits in front of had
had the licence been renewed, the office would not have lost a week of work
the negative is not shortened at the front: had it not been for the backup, never hadn't it been for the backup
should at the front is the polite one about a thing that might still happen: should you need help, call the desk
form.negative: Had the team not tested it — the not goes after the subject, and had never shortens at the front of the sentence.
form.question: Ask yourself whether you could write the same sentence with if. If you could not, this shape will not rescue it.

marks.label: the outage would have lasted an hour

worked_example.sentence: Had the update been tested on one machine first, the outage would have lasted an hour rather than a week.
worked_example.why_this_form: The paragraph already has two sentences beginning with if, and this version makes the same unreal claim without adding a third.
worked_example.what_the_other_would_mean: If the update had been tested on one machine first carries an identical claim in a slightly lighter voice, and loses the writer nothing at all.

notice_set.sentence: Had the backup run that night, the records would still exist.
notice_set.question: Do the records still exist?
notice_set.why: The whole sentence is about a night that went differently, so the records went with it.

notice_set.sentence: Had the update been tested, the outage would have lasted an hour.
notice_set.question: How long did the outage actually last?
notice_set.why: The one-hour outage is the version that never occurred, so the real one must have run longer than that.

notice_set.sentence: Should you need a replacement, the desk will order one.
notice_set.question: Does the speaker know that you need a replacement?
notice_set.why: This one is about something that might still happen, not about something that did not.

notice_set.sentence: Were the system rebuilt today, it would still run the same software.
notice_set.question: Is anyone rebuilding the system?
notice_set.why: The rebuild is imagined in order to make a point about the software, which means nobody is actually doing it.

notice_set.sentence: Had it not been for the paper records, the whole month would have been lost.
notice_set.question: Was the month lost?
notice_set.why: The paper records are the reason it was not, and saying so is the only reason this sentence exists.

teach.rule_line: Take out if, move had to the front, and change nothing else in the sentence.
teach.false_rule: That this is a more advanced conditional. It is the same conditional wearing a coat, and the version with if scores exactly the same when it is clean.

errors.wrong: Have the alarm been fitted, the loss would have been far smaller.
errors.right: Had the alarm been fitted, the loss would have been far smaller.
errors.why_it_happens: The writer knows the shape opens on a form of have and reaches for the one they use most often, and the sentence loses the very word that made it unreal.
errors.smallest_fix: Change one word: Have becomes Had.

errors.wrong: If had the council acted sooner, the cost would have been lower.
errors.right: Had the council acted sooner, the cost would have been lower.
errors.why_it_happens: The shape is learned as an extra thing you add to a conditional rather than as a replacement for the if, so both markers end up in the same sentence.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete one word: If.

errors.wrong: Had the team would have tested it, the outage would have been shorter.
errors.right: Had the team tested it, the outage would have been shorter.
errors.why_it_happens: Would have belongs in the other half of the sentence, and once the order is turned round the writer loses track of which half they are standing in.
errors.smallest_fix: Delete two words: would have, from the first half.

errors.wrong: Had the licence been renewed, the office would lose no time at all.
errors.right: Had the licence been renewed, the office would have lost no time at all.
errors.why_it_happens: The first half is safely in the unreal past and the second half slides into the present unreal, because would arrives before the writer has settled which time they are in.
errors.smallest_fix: Insert one word: have, after would.

pays_in.note: It breaks up a paragraph in which every sentence has started with if.
pays_in.model: Had the scheme been funded for a second year, the results would have been worth reading.

pays_in.note: Should you need is the standard polite offer at the end of a formal letter.
pays_in.model: Should you require any further information, please contact me at the address above.

pays_in.note: A fronted had signals an unreal past, and a reader who misses it takes away the opposite fact.
pays_in.model: Had the second alarm been fitted, the fire would have been caught in minutes.

used_in.quote: The second half of this prompt asks what would have kept students in science, which is an unreal past claim in every paragraph.

payload.sentence: Had the backup run that night, the records would still exist.
payload.question: Do the records still exist?

feedback.why_key: The sentence is built around a night that went the other way, and everything in it follows from that night not having happened.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the first half as something that did not happen.

payload.sentence: Should you need a replacement, the desk will order one.
payload.question: Does the writer know that you need a replacement?

feedback.why_key: This opener is about something that might still happen, so nothing has been decided and nothing has been ruled out yet.

items.decision_cue: If had the office renewed the licence

payload.context: From a draft paragraph about a failed software rollout.
payload.sentence: If had the office renewed the licence, no time would have been lost.
reasons: the sentence marks the condition twice
the second half is in the wrong time
the first half needs a comma
nothing wrong, it's fine

feedback.why_key: The moved had is doing the job that if used to do. Keeping both leaves the reader with two openers and one condition.
feedback.feed_forward: Choose one marker: either if or the moved had.

payload.context: From a report on an outage that lasted a week. Nobody tested the update.
payload.stem: ___ the update been tested on one machine first, the outage would have lasted an hour.

expected: had

feedback.why_key: The past form is the word that makes the sentence unreal. Any other form of it puts the testing back into the real world.

payload.given: If the warning had been passed on, the crew would have turned back.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it without the word if.

expected: the warning been passed on, the crew would have turned back
the warning been passed on the crew would have turned back

feedback.why_key: Only two things moved: if left and had came forward. Every other word in the sentence stayed exactly where it was.

payload.given: Had the second year been funded, the results would have been worth reading.
payload.instruction: Rewrite it with if, keeping the meaning identical.

expected: the second year had been funded, the results would have been worth reading
the second year had been funded the results would have been worth reading

feedback.why_key: Going back the other way proves what the shape is doing, and it is the version to fall back on when the fronted one will not come out clean.

payload.context: Build the closing line of a formal letter.

expected: should you need any further information please contact the desk

feedback.why_key: The opener takes the subject straight after it and a plain verb after that. Nothing is added and no if appears anywhere.

payload.audio_text: Had we tested it first, we'd have caught it in an hour.

expected: had we tested it first, we'd have caught it in an hour
had we tested it first, we would have caught it in an hour
had we tested it first, wed have caught it in an hour

feedback.why_key: The shortened we'd could be had or would, and only the have that follows it settles which. Miss that and the sentence changes time.

payload.context: Two sentences from a review of an ageing computer system.
sentences: Had the system been rebuilt in 2019, it would be running current software today.
Were the system rebuilt today, it would still run the same software.
meanings: Nobody rebuilt it, and the software the office is using now is the price of that.
Nobody is rebuilding it, and doing so would not fix what the writer is complaining about.

feedback.why_key: One sentence looks back at a decision nobody took. The other imagines one nobody is taking. The openers are what separate them.
feedback.feed_forward: Read the opener to place the sentence in past or present.

payload.prompt_text: A council rolled out new software with no trial and lost a week's records. Your paragraph already has two sentences beginning with if. Write one more about what a trial would have saved, without using if.

feedback.why_key: The claim is identical to the if version. What you have bought is a paragraph whose sentences no longer all begin the same way.
feedback.feed_forward: Open with had, then say what would have followed.

payload.prompt_text: Open your answer on fewer science students. Find one sentence beginning with if that is already clean and rewrite it without the if. If the new version is not clean on the first try, put the if back and move on. Two minutes.

feedback.why_key: Putting the if back is a real result, not a failure. A clean ordinary conditional beats a broken formal one every time it is marked.
feedback.feed_forward: Try it once, and restore if if it does not come out clean.
